tip: After Chromium is killed with pkill, the next launch shows a 'Restore pages' bubble; set exit_type to Normal and exited_cleanly to true in the profile Preferences file before launching.
pkill -f name also matches the shell that runs the command and kills it with exit code -15; use pkill -x name or a bracket pattern like [c]hromium instead.
For filling web forms, controlling the page through its DOM (a numbered list of inputs with names and labels) is far more reliable than clicking screen pixels.
xdotool only works on X11; on Raspberry Pi OS with Wayland switch the session to X11 with raspi-config before using mouse and keyboard automation.
In a systemd unit, a trailing # comment on an EnvironmentFile line becomes part of the value and can crash the service; keep comments on their own lines.
Quote shell variables as "$var"; an unquoted value that contains spaces or glob characters is split into several arguments.
Start bash scripts with set -euo pipefail so a failing command, an unset variable or a failure inside a pipe stops the script instead of being ignored.
Without pipefail the exit status of a pipeline is the status of its last command, so false piped into true counts as success.
Inside double brackets [[ ]] bash does not word-split unquoted variables, which makes string tests safer than single brackets.
Use mktemp to create temporary files or directories; fixed names in the temp folder are predictable and can collide between runs.
Use command -v tool to test whether a program is installed; it prints nothing and returns a non-zero status when the program is missing.
To keep a command running after the terminal closes, start it with nohup and redirect its output, for example nohup cmd > out.log 2>&1 &.
pkill -f matches the whole command line, including the shell that runs pkill itself, which can kill your own command; use pkill -x for an exact process name or a bracket pattern such as [c]hromium.
kill sends SIGTERM by default so a program can clean up; reserve kill -9 for processes that ignore it because it prevents cleanup and can leave lock files behind.
Use timeout 30 cmd to stop a command that may hang; it exits with status 124 when the time limit is reached.
Redirect both output streams with cmd > file 2>&1; the order matters, because 2>&1 > file sends error output to the terminal instead of the file.
tee -a file appends command output to a log while still showing it on screen; plain tee overwrites the file.
Preview a bulk delete with find first: find . -name '*.log' -mtime +7 -print lists what would be removed before you add -delete.
Combine find -print0 with xargs -0 so file names containing spaces or newlines are handled correctly.
grep -r --include='*.py' pattern . restricts a recursive search to one file type, which is much faster on large trees.
ss -tlnp lists listening TCP ports with the owning process; it replaces netstat, which is often not installed on current systems.
When a write fails with No space left on device, check both df -h for free space and df -i for free inodes; either can be exhausted.
Write cd dir || exit 1 in scripts; if cd fails and the script carries on, later commands run in the wrong directory.
A trailing & only backgrounds a command inside the current shell session; it is usually stopped when the session ends unless nohup or setsid is used.
Variables exported in your shell are not visible to a systemd service; set them in the unit with Environment= or in an EnvironmentFile.
sudo resets most environment variables for the command it runs; pass values explicitly, for example sudo VAR=value cmd, though sudoers policy may restrict this.
A heredoc whose delimiter is quoted stops the shell from expanding variables and command substitutions inside the text.
Use printf instead of echo when text may begin with a dash or contain backslashes, because echo behaves differently between shells.
Files created with sudo belong to root and may not be editable later by your normal user; ls -l shows the owner.
A script needs the executable bit (chmod +x) and a first line like #!/usr/bin/env bash, otherwise it is run by whatever shell started it.
Before a destructive command with a wildcard, run ls with the same pattern to see exactly which files match.
diff -u old new shows exactly what changed between two files, which is a good check before overwriting one with the other.
Use $(command) for command substitution instead of backticks; it nests cleanly and is easier to read.
In bash, ${var:-default} gives a default when var is unset or empty, and ${var:?message} aborts with a message when it is.
Use ${var%suffix} and ${var#prefix} to strip text from a variable without calling sed or cut.
Arrays in bash are written arr=(a b c) and expanded with "${arr[@]}" in quotes, which keeps each element as a separate word.
read -r avoids treating backslashes as escapes when reading lines, and while IFS= read -r line preserves leading spaces.
A while read loop fed by a pipe runs in a subshell, so variables set inside it are lost afterwards; feed it with redirection (done < file) instead.
The exit status of the last command is in $?, but it is overwritten by every later command, including a test; save it in a variable if you need it twice.
Use trap 'cleanup' EXIT in a script to remove temporary files whether the script ends normally or with an error.
wait with no arguments waits for all background jobs of the current shell, which is the simple way to run several tasks in parallel and then continue.
Use sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to count how often each line occurs and list the most frequent first; uniq only merges adjacent duplicates.
Use cut -d, -f2 to take a column from simple comma separated text, and awk -F, when fields may need arithmetic or conditions.
sed -i edits a file in place; on macOS it needs an argument after -i, but on Linux sed -i 's/a/b/' file works directly.
Use sed -n '10,20p' file to print only a range of lines, and head -n 20 file | tail -n 11 as an equivalent.
Use basename and dirname to split a path into file name and folder without regular expressions.
Use realpath to turn a relative path into an absolute one and to resolve symbolic links.
Use ln -s target linkname to create a symbolic link; the target is stored as written, so a relative target is relative to the link's folder.
Use stat -c '%U %a %s' file to print owner, octal permissions and size in one line.
Use du -sh * | sort -h to see which folders take the most space; sort -h understands units like K, M and G.
Use free -h to see memory use; the available column is more meaningful than free because the kernel uses spare memory for caching.
Use top or htop to find processes using CPU; in top press 1 to see each core separately and M to sort by memory.
Use ps aux | grep [n]ame to find a process without matching the grep command itself.
Use pgrep -a name to list matching processes with their full command lines, and pgrep -c name to count them.
Use lsof -i :8080 to see which process holds a port; ss -tlnp is a lighter alternative that needs no extra package.
Use watch -n 2 command to repeat a command every two seconds and show the changing output.
Use date +%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S to build timestamps for file names that sort correctly in directory listings.
Use cat -A file to reveal hidden characters such as tabs, carriage returns and trailing spaces that break scripts and config files.
Windows line endings (carriage return plus newline) break shell scripts with errors like bad interpreter; convert them with sed -i 's/\r$//' file.
Use xargs -n1 to run a command once per input item and xargs -P4 to run up to four at a time.
Use env -i cmd to run a command with an empty environment, which is useful for reproducing problems caused by missing variables.
The alias command only affects interactive shells; scripts do not expand aliases, so use a function or the full command there.
Use type name to see whether a word is an alias, a function, a builtin or a program on disk.
A command prefixed by a variable assignment, as in LANG=C sort file, sets that variable only for that one command.
Use exit codes deliberately: 0 means success, and values 1 to 255 mean failure; 126 means found but not executable and 127 means command not found.
Exit code 130 means the command was stopped with Ctrl+C, and 137 means it was killed by SIGKILL (128 plus 9), often by the out-of-memory killer.
Exit code -15 reported by a tool means the process received SIGTERM; with pkill -f this is often the command killing its own shell.
Brace expansion such as file_{a,b,c}.txt is done by bash before the command runs, so it works even for names that do not exist yet.
Use seq 1 10 or {1..10} to generate number sequences for loops; the brace form cannot contain variables.
Use a for loop over a glob (for f in *.txt) instead of parsing ls output, which breaks on names with spaces.
If a glob matches nothing, bash passes the pattern itself to the command; use shopt -s nullglob to get an empty list instead.
Use shopt -s globstar to let ** match files in nested folders in bash.
Use rsync -a --dry-run src/ dst/ to preview a copy; a trailing slash on the source means copy the contents, without it the folder itself is copied.
Use cp -a to copy folders while preserving permissions, timestamps and links; plain cp does not keep them all.
Use mv file file.bak before editing an important file so you can restore it; mv within one filesystem is atomic.
Use tar -czf archive.tar.gz folder to create a compressed archive and tar -tzf archive.tar.gz to list it without extracting.
Use tar -xzf archive.tar.gz -C target to extract into a specific folder; the folder must already exist.
Use zip -r and unzip -l for zip archives; unzip -o overwrites existing files without asking.
Use gzip -k file to compress while keeping the original, and zcat or zless to read compressed files without unpacking.
Use md5sum or sha256sum to compare files or verify a download; sha256sum -c checks a list of stored sums.
Use curl -fsSL to fail on HTTP errors and stay quiet; without -f curl prints the server's error page and still exits with success.
Use curl -I to look at response headers only and curl -o file to save a download; wget -c resumes an interrupted download.
Use jq to read JSON on the command line, for example jq -r '.name' file prints the field without quotes.
Use column -t to align text into readable columns and nl to number lines.
Use history | grep word to find an old command, and press Ctrl+R in an interactive shell to search the history as you type.
Press Ctrl+C to interrupt a running command, Ctrl+Z to suspend it, and then bg to continue it in the background or fg to bring it back.
Use screen or tmux to keep a terminal session alive when the SSH connection drops; reattach later with screen -r or tmux attach.
Use script -c cmd file to record the output of a command, including terminal control characters, for later review.
Use yes | cmd only when a command truly asks yes or no repeatedly; for installers prefer their own non-interactive flag such as -y.
Use read -t 5 to give a prompt a timeout, and test the exit status because it is greater than 128 when the timeout expires.
Use [ -f file ], [ -d dir ] and [ -s file ] to test for a regular file, a directory and a non-empty file.
Use getopts or a case statement over $1 to parse options in a script instead of counting positional arguments by hand.
Use "$@" in quotes to pass all arguments on unchanged; unquoted $@ or $* splits arguments containing spaces.
Arithmetic in bash uses $(( )), for example $((a + b)); the expr command is slower and needs spaces and escapes.
Floating point numbers are not supported in bash arithmetic; use bc or awk for decimals.
Compare numbers with -eq, -lt and -gt inside [ ]; using = or < compares them as text, so 10 sorts before 9.
Use set -x to print every command as it runs, which is the quickest way to see why a script behaves unexpectedly; set +x turns it off.
Use bash -n script to check syntax without running it, and shellcheck for common mistakes when it is installed.
Use a lock to stop two copies of a script running at once, for example flock -n lockfile cmd, which exits at once if the lock is taken.
Use disown or setsid when a background job should not receive the hangup signal from the closing terminal.
Use ulimit -n to see the maximum number of open files; too many open files errors in servers often need a higher limit in the service or session.
Use uname -a, cat /etc/os-release and hostnamectl to identify the operating system, kernel and architecture before searching for instructions.
Use uptime to see the load average; a load above the number of CPU cores means processes are waiting for CPU or disk.
Use dmesg to read kernel messages about hardware, drivers and out-of-memory kills; on many systems reading it needs sudo.
Use which -a name to list every copy of a command on the path, which explains why an older version runs than the one just installed.
The PATH variable is searched from left to right, so a copy in an earlier folder shadows later ones; print it with echo $PATH.
After editing a file read by the shell at login, such as .bashrc, run source ~/.bashrc or open a new terminal for the change to apply.
Use alias only for interactive convenience; put reusable logic in scripts so cron-like tools and services can run it without your shell setup.
File permissions are three octal digits for owner, group and others; 644 means owner read and write, everyone else read only, and 755 adds execute.
A directory needs the execute bit to be entered or searched; a folder with read but no execute permission lists names but cannot be opened.
chmod u+x file adds execute for the owner only, while chmod a+r file makes it readable by everyone.
Use chown user:group file to change the owner; changing the owner of a file to another user normally requires root.
Permission denied on a script usually means the executable bit is missing; ls -l shows it and chmod +x adds it.
A file created by a program running as root, such as a service started by systemd, can be unreadable for your normal user until its mode or owner is changed.
The sticky bit on a shared folder such as the temp directory stops users from deleting each other's files; ls -ld shows it as a t at the end.
umask controls the default permissions of new files; with umask 022 new files are 644 and new folders are 755.
Use ls -ld folder to see the permissions of the folder itself instead of its contents.
Hidden files start with a dot and are not shown by plain ls or matched by the * wildcard; use ls -a or the pattern .[!.]* to include them.
Use mkdir -p a/b/c to create nested folders in one step; it does not complain if they already exist.
Use touch file to create an empty file or update a modification time, and touch -d to set a specific date.
Use rm file to delete a file and rmdir folder to delete an empty folder; both are permanent because there is no trash on the command line.
Use ls -lh to show sizes in human readable form and ls -lt to sort by newest first.
Use find / -name pattern 2>/dev/null to search the whole disk while hiding permission errors.
Use find -type f -size +100M to locate large files, and find -newer file to list files changed after a reference file.
Use locate name for a fast filename search; it reads a database that is refreshed by updatedb, so new files may not appear yet.
Use head -n 20 file for the start and tail -n 20 file for the end of a file; tail -f follows lines as they are appended.
Use less file to scroll through a large file; press slash to search, n for the next match and q to quit.
Use wc -l file to count lines, wc -w for words and wc -c for bytes.
Use file name to identify a file's real type; the extension can be wrong or missing.
Use strings binary to read printable text inside a binary file, and xxd or hexdump -C to see its raw bytes.
Use grep -n to show line numbers, grep -i for case insensitive search and grep -v to invert the match.
Use grep -E for extended regular expressions and grep -F to search for a literal string that contains special characters.
Use grep -c to count matching lines and grep -l to list only the names of files that match.
Use grep -A 3 -B 3 to print three lines of context after and before each match.
Use awk '{print $1}' to print the first whitespace separated column, and awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}' to sum a column.
Use sed 's/old/new/g' to replace every occurrence on each line; without g only the first match on a line changes.
When a sed pattern contains slashes, use another delimiter such as sed 's|/old/path|/new/path|' to avoid escaping.
Use tr -d '\r' to remove carriage returns and tr a-z A-Z to change letter case in a stream.
Use sort -u to sort and remove duplicates in one step, and sort -n for numeric order.
Use comm -12 on two sorted files to list the lines they have in common, and diff to see all differences.
Use paste to join files side by side and join to merge lines that share a key field.
Use split -l 1000 file prefix to cut a large file into pieces of 1000 lines.
Use cat file1 file2 > both to join files, and cat > file followed by Ctrl+D to type text into a new file.
Use echo text >> file to append a line and echo text > file to overwrite the file; the single arrow destroys the old content.
Redirecting a file onto itself, as in sort file > file, empties it before sort reads it; write to a temporary file or use sort -o file file.
Use sort -o file file to sort a file in place safely, because sort finishes reading before it writes.
Use truncate -s 0 file to empty a file without deleting it, which keeps its owner, mode and any open handles valid.
A deleted file that a process still holds open keeps using disk space until that process exits; lsof | grep deleted finds such files.
Use readlink -f to print where a symbolic link finally points, and ls -l to see the immediate target.
A hard link is another name for the same file data and cannot cross filesystems; a symbolic link is a pointer that can break if the target moves.
Use mount or findmnt to see which filesystems are mounted where, and lsblk to list disks and partitions.
A USB drive that mounts read only often has filesystem errors; the kernel remounts read only after errors, and dmesg shows the cause.
Use fsck only on an unmounted filesystem; running it on a mounted one can corrupt data.
Use df -h /path to see free space on the filesystem that contains a given folder.
The folder /tmp is often cleared on reboot and may live in memory, so do not keep files there that must survive a restart.
Use ~ or $HOME for the home folder in scripts; a path starting with ~ is expanded by the shell only when the tilde is unquoted.
Config files that have an extension like .conf are plain text, but a stray space, tab or missing newline at the end can still break parsing; check with cat -A.
JSON files do not allow comments or trailing commas; python3 -m json.tool file validates and pretty prints a file.
YAML uses spaces for indentation and forbids tabs; a tab character in a YAML file causes a parse error.
CSV fields that contain commas or line breaks must be wrapped in double quotes; use a CSV library instead of splitting on commas.
Text files should be read and written as UTF-8 explicitly; relying on the system default encoding can break accented letters on other systems.
A byte order mark at the start of a UTF-8 file can make the first line or key look wrong; open it with the utf-8-sig encoding in Python to strip it.
Use iconv -f latin1 -t utf-8 to convert a file from an old encoding to UTF-8.
Use ls | wc -l to count entries in a folder and find . -type f | wc -l to count all files below it.
Use du -sh --apparent-size to see the logical size of files, which differs from disk usage for sparse files and small files.
Keep a backup copy before changing a configuration file, for example cp file file.bak, and restore it with cp file.bak file if something breaks.
Use diff file.bak file to review a configuration change, and patch to apply a saved diff to another copy.
Use inotifywait -m folder from the inotify-tools package to watch a folder for changes.
Use logrotate or a size check to stop log files from filling the disk; a service that logs every second can fill a small SD card within days.
SD cards wear out with constant writes; keep logs in memory or reduce writes with a tool such as log2ram if the card holds important data.
Use sync before removing a USB drive or powering off, and unmount first with umount; pulling a drive mid-write can corrupt it.
Use cat /proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo and /proc/loadavg to read system information directly from the kernel.
Use ls /dev/tty* and dmesg to find the name of a newly attached serial device; USB serial adapters usually appear as ttyUSB0 or ttyACM0.
A user must be in the dialout group to open serial ports without sudo; add it with usermod -aG dialout user and log in again.
Group changes made with usermod -aG take effect only in new login sessions; run id to see the groups of the current session.
Use getent passwd user to look up a user account and id user to see its numeric id and groups.
Use stat file to see access, modify and change times; the change time updates when permissions or the owner change, not only when content does.
Use ls -i to show inode numbers; two names with the same inode are hard links to the same file.
Spaces in file names must be quoted or escaped in the shell; consider avoiding spaces in names that scripts will handle.
The tilde backup suffix and the .swp suffix are left behind by editors; a .swp file next to a config means an editor crashed or is still open.
Use nano file for a simple terminal editor; Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits and Ctrl+W searches.
In vim press i to insert text, Escape to leave insert mode, :wq to save and quit, and :q! to quit without saving.
Use sudoedit file instead of sudo nano file when editing system files, so the editor runs as your user and only the save is done as root.
Use install -m 644 src dst to copy a file and set its mode in one step, which is handy in setup scripts.
Write files atomically by saving to a temporary name in the same folder and then renaming it; readers never see a half written file.
Use ls -la --time-style=full-iso to see exact modification times when you compare which of two files is newer.
Use cmp file1 file2 to check whether two files are identical byte for byte; it prints nothing when they match.
Use ls -d */ to list only directories in the current folder.
Use tree -L 2 to see a folder structure two levels deep; if tree is missing, find . -maxdepth 2 gives a similar view.
git status shows what is changed and staged, and git diff shows unstaged changes while git diff --staged shows what the next commit will contain.
Check git status before every commit and git diff --staged before committing to make sure only the intended changes are included.
Set your identity once with git config --global user.name and user.email; otherwise commits fail with an error asking who you are.
Use git add -p to review and stage changes piece by piece, which avoids committing debugging leftovers.
Use git restore file to discard unstaged changes in a file and git restore --staged file to unstage it; both keep other files untouched.
Use git log --oneline --graph --decorate for a compact history, and git log -p file to see every change of one file.
Use git show commit to see what a commit changed and git blame file to see who last changed each line.
Create a branch with git switch -c name and return with git switch main; switching with uncommitted changes can fail if they conflict.
Use git stash to put uncommitted work aside, git stash list to see it and git stash pop to bring it back.
Undo the last commit but keep its changes with git reset --soft HEAD~1; git reset --hard HEAD~1 also throws the changes away.
git reflog lists where HEAD has been, so a commit that seems lost after a reset or a bad rebase can often be recovered from it.
Use git commit --amend to fix the last commit message or add a forgotten file, but avoid it after the commit has been pushed and shared.
Use git revert commit to undo a commit by creating a new commit; it is safe for history that others already have.
A .gitignore file only affects untracked files; a file that was already committed stays tracked until removed with git rm --cached file.
Put secrets such as keys and .env files in .gitignore before the first commit; removing a secret later does not remove it from history.
If a secret was committed, treat it as leaked and replace it at the provider, because deleting the file in a new commit leaves it in the history.
Use git clone --depth 1 url for a shallow clone that downloads only the latest snapshot, which is much faster for large repositories.
Use git pull --rebase to keep a linear history when you have local commits and the remote moved on; resolve conflicts, then git rebase --continue.
A merge conflict shows markers made of less-than, equals and greater-than characters in the file; edit the file to the final text, remove the markers, then git add and commit.
Use git merge --abort or git rebase --abort to return to the state before a merge or rebase that went wrong.
git push is rejected as non fast forward when the remote has commits you lack; fetch and integrate them first instead of forcing the push.
If a force push is really needed, use git push --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen.
Use git remote -v to see where a repository pushes and fetches, and git remote set-url origin url to change it.
Use git fetch to download new commits without changing your files, then compare with git log HEAD..origin/main.
Use git branch -d name to delete a merged branch and git branch -D name to delete an unmerged one; the capital letter forces it.
Use git tag v1.0 to mark a release and git push origin v1.0 to publish it; tags are not pushed by a normal push.
Use git diff --stat to get a short summary of changed files and git diff --name-only to list only their names.
Use git clean -n to preview which untracked files git clean would delete before running git clean -f.
Use git config --list --show-origin to see which config file sets a value when git behaves unexpectedly.
Use git log --since='2 days ago' --author=name to filter history by time and author.
Use git bisect to find the commit that introduced a bug by marking commits good or bad; git bisect run script can automate it.
Use git cherry-pick commit to copy a single commit onto the current branch.
Authentication over HTTPS no longer accepts account passwords on GitHub; use a personal access token, or SSH keys, when asked for credentials.
Use a fine grained token limited to one repository and the minimum permissions; a leaked broad token exposes everything the account can access.
Use git config --global credential.helper store only on trusted machines, because it saves the token in plain text; a cache helper keeps it in memory for a limited time.
Use git rev-parse --short HEAD to get a short commit id for logs or version strings.
Use git describe --tags --always to build a readable version name from the nearest tag or the commit id.
Large binary files make repositories slow; keep them out of git or use Git LFS, and note that files over 100 megabytes are rejected by GitHub.
Commit line endings consistently; a .gitattributes file with text=auto reduces noisy diffs between Windows and Linux.
A detached HEAD means you checked out a commit instead of a branch; create a branch with git switch -c name before committing, or the commits are easy to lose.
Use git commit -m with a short clear subject line; a history of messages like fix or update makes later debugging much harder.
Use git worktree add path branch to have a second working folder for another branch without cloning again.
Use git submodule update --init --recursive after cloning a repository that contains submodules, or those folders stay empty.
Use git grep pattern to search tracked files quickly; it ignores untracked and ignored files.
Use git shortlog -sn to count commits per author.
Set git config pull.rebase true or merge once, otherwise recent git versions warn about divergent branches when you pull.
Use git config core.fileMode false when file permission changes after copying a repository between systems show up as modified files.
A repository folder owned by a different user triggers a dubious ownership error; fix the owner, or mark it safe with git config --global --add safe.directory path.
Running git as root in a folder owned by another user, for example through sudo, can create root owned files inside .git that later break normal use.
Use git archive --format=zip HEAD -o out.zip to export a clean snapshot without the .git folder.
Use git update-index --assume-unchanged only as a temporary hack; for local settings, keep a separate untracked file and ignore it.
Before a risky history rewrite create a backup branch with git branch backup, so you can return to the old state at any time.
Use git checkout -- path or git restore path only when you are sure; discarding uncommitted edits cannot be undone.
Use git ls-files to list tracked files and git ls-files --others --exclude-standard to list untracked files that are not ignored.
Use git commit --allow-empty -m message to create a commit with no changes, for example to trigger a build.
Use git push -u origin branch the first time to link a local branch to the remote, so later git push and git pull need no arguments.
An empty remote repository has no branch yet; the first push with git push -u origin main creates it.
Hooks in .git/hooks are not part of the repository; share checks through a tracked folder and git config core.hooksPath.
Use python3 -m venv .venv and source .venv/bin/activate to keep project packages separate; installing into the system Python can conflict with packages managed by the operating system.

On recent Debian and Raspberry Pi OS releases pip refuses system wide installs with an externally-managed-environment error; use a virtual environment, apt packages, or pip --break-system-packages when you accept the risk.
Run pip as python3 -m pip so that it installs for the same interpreter that will run your script.
ModuleNotFoundError usually means the package is not installed for the interpreter that runs the script; check with python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'.
A script named after a library, such as random.py or flask.py, shadows that library and causes confusing import errors; rename the file and delete its __pycache__ folder.
Use if __name__ == "__main__": to run code only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported.
A mutable default argument such as def f(x=[]) is created once and shared by every call; use None as the default and create the list inside the function.
Python indentation must be consistent; mixing tabs and spaces causes TabError, so configure the editor to use four spaces.
Use f-strings such as f"{name}: {value:.2f}" for formatting; the part after the colon controls the format of a number.
Use with open(path, encoding='utf-8') as f: so the file is closed even when an error occurs, and set the encoding explicitly.
Use pathlib.Path for file paths: Path('a') / 'b' joins parts, Path.exists() tests, and read_text() and write_text() read and write files.
Catch specific exceptions such as FileNotFoundError or ValueError; a bare except hides real bugs and also catches KeyboardInterrupt.
Output of a Python program started by systemd or a pipe may be buffered and appear late; use python3 -u or print(..., flush=True).
Use json.dumps(obj, ensure_ascii=False) to keep non ASCII characters readable in the output, and json.loads to parse text.
Dictionary iteration order follows insertion order in modern Python, but never modify a dictionary while looping over it; loop over list(d) instead.
Use enumerate(items) when you need an index and zip(a, b) to walk two lists together; zip stops at the shorter list.
Use a list comprehension [x*2 for x in items if x > 0] for simple transformations, and a generator expression inside sum() to avoid building a list.
Use collections.Counter to count items and collections.defaultdict(list) to group items without checking if a key exists.
Compare floating point numbers with math.isclose; 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 because of binary representation.
Division with / always returns a float in Python 3 and // returns the floor; use // when you need an integer result.
Strings are immutable; building a long string with += in a loop is slow, so collect the parts in a list and use ''.join(parts).
Use str.strip(), split() and partition() for text processing; split() without arguments splits on any whitespace and drops empty parts.
Use the re module with raw strings, r'\d+', so backslashes reach the regular expression engine unchanged.
Use datetime.now(timezone.utc) for timezone aware times; datetime.utcnow() returns a naive object and is deprecated.
Use time.monotonic() to measure elapsed time; time.time() can jump when the system clock is corrected, which happens often on a Raspberry Pi without a battery clock.
Use argparse for command line options; it generates help text and reports errors, and it is part of the standard library.
Read environment variables with os.environ.get('NAME', 'default'); os.environ['NAME'] raises KeyError when the variable is missing.
Environment values are always strings, so convert them with int() or compare with 'true'; the string '0' is truthy in an if test.
Use threading.Thread(target=fn, daemon=True) for background work that should not keep the program alive, and join() to wait for a normal thread.
Because of the global interpreter lock threads do not speed up CPU heavy Python code; use multiprocessing for that and threads for waiting on network or disk.
Use concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor to run many network requests in parallel and collect results with map or as_completed.
Protect shared data between threads with threading.Lock and use queue.Queue to pass work between them; Queue is already thread safe.
A signal handler registered with signal.signal can only be set in the main thread; use it to shut a service down cleanly on SIGTERM.
Use requests with a timeout, such as requests.get(url, timeout=10); without a timeout a call can wait forever.
Call response.raise_for_status() after a requests call so HTTP errors such as 404 or 500 raise an exception instead of being treated as data.
The standard library urllib.request needs no installation; set a User-Agent header, because some servers reject the default one.
Use sqlite3 from the standard library for small local databases; use ? placeholders instead of string formatting to avoid SQL injection.
SQLite connections should be closed or used with a context manager that commits; changes are lost if you forget conn.commit().
Use dataclasses with @dataclass for simple record types; they generate __init__ and __repr__ for you.
Use typing hints and run a checker such as mypy only if it helps; hints are not enforced when the program runs.
Use pytest for tests: name files test_*.py and functions test_*, then run pytest in the project folder.
Use python3 -m py_compile file.py to find syntax errors without running the program, and python3 -m pyflakes for unused names.
Use python3 -X dev or python3 -W error to turn warnings into visible problems while testing.
Use breakpoint() to start the debugger at a line, and python3 -m pdb script.py to debug from the start.
Use traceback.print_exc() inside an except block to log the full stack trace of a handled error.
A function without a return statement returns None, so using the result of list.sort() or list.append() gives None; those methods change the list in place.
Use sorted(items, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) to sort without changing the original list.
Copy a list with list(items) or items.copy(); plain assignment copies only the reference, and nested lists need copy.deepcopy.
Use is None rather than == None for the None check, and use == to compare values, not is.
Use try / finally or a context manager to release resources such as sockets, files and GPIO pins even when an error occurs.
Use contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError) to ignore one expected error in a clean way.
Use itertools for common loops: chain joins sequences, islice takes a slice from an iterator and product builds combinations.
Generators with yield produce items lazily, so they can process files larger than memory one line at a time.
Use functools.lru_cache on a pure function to cache results of repeated calls.
Keep configuration out of code: read it from a .env file or environment variables, and never commit keys or tokens.
Use secrets.token_hex(16) to create random tokens; the random module is not suitable for passwords or keys.
Use hmac.compare_digest to compare tokens or signatures; a normal comparison can leak information through timing.
Use hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() for checksums; md5 and sha1 are fine for checking file changes but not for security.
Use struct.pack and struct.unpack to read and write binary data such as sensor frames with a fixed layout.
Use bytes.hex() and bytes.fromhex() to convert between binary data and readable hexadecimal text.
Use io.BytesIO or io.StringIO to treat text or bytes in memory like a file, which is useful in tests and for images.
Use shutil.copy, shutil.move and shutil.rmtree for file operations in Python; shutil.which finds a program on the path.
Use tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() for scratch folders that are cleaned up automatically.
Use glob.glob('*.txt') or Path.glob('**/*.txt') to find files by pattern; the result order is not guaranteed, so sort it.
Use os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True) to create folders without raising an error when they already exist.
os.getcwd() depends on where the program was started, for example by systemd; use Path(__file__).resolve().parent for files that live next to the script.
Use socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=3) to check if a TCP port is reachable from Python.
Use http.server for a quick local file server: python3 -m http.server 8000 serves the current folder, but it is not meant for production.
Use serial.Serial('/dev/ttyUSB0', 115200, timeout=1) from pyserial for serial devices, and always set a timeout so reads cannot block forever.
Use gpiozero for simple GPIO work on a Raspberry Pi, for example LED(17).on(); it hides pin setup details and cleans up on exit.
Use time.sleep in loops that poll hardware or a network service; a loop without a pause can use a full CPU core.
Use Pillow to work with images: Image.open(path), img.resize((w, h)) and img.save(path); install it with apt python3-pil or pip install pillow.
Use numpy for fast array math; a Python loop over millions of numbers is much slower than a vectorized numpy expression.
A UnicodeDecodeError means the bytes are not valid in the chosen encoding; try encoding='latin-1' or errors='replace' to see the data.
A KeyError names the missing key; use dict.get(key, default) when a missing key is normal.
A RecursionError means a function calls itself too deeply; replace the recursion with a loop or check the stop condition.
Use isinstance(x, (int, float)) to test types; type(x) == int fails for subclasses.
Use set for fast membership tests: x in a_set is much faster than x in a_list for large collections.
Use str.format or f-strings for messages, and avoid building SQL or shell commands from user input with them.
Use python3 -c 'import module; print(module.__file__)' to see where an imported module comes from when the wrong version loads.
Use pip list --outdated and pip show package to check versions, and pip freeze > requirements.txt to record the exact versions that work.
Pin versions in requirements.txt, for example flask==3.0.0, so a later release cannot break a working setup.
Run long lived Python programs under systemd or a supervisor and let them restart on failure; an unhandled exception ends the process.
Use atexit.register(function) to run cleanup code when the interpreter exits normally; it does not run if the process is killed with SIGKILL.
Use logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) while debugging and a higher level in normal use; messages below the chosen level are not shown.
Use python3 -m http.server --bind localhost to limit a quick test server to the local machine instead of every network interface.
A minimal Flask app needs app = Flask(__name__), a function with @app.route('/'), and app.run with the host option set to all interfaces to be reachable from other devices.
By default Flask listens only on the loopback address; pass the all interfaces host value to app.run to reach it from other computers on the network.
Never run the Flask debug mode on a network facing server; the interactive debugger allows running code from the browser.
The built in Flask server is for development; for real use put the app behind gunicorn or another production server.
Flask finds templates in a folder named templates and static files in a folder named static next to the application module.
TemplateNotFound usually means the templates folder is misplaced or misspelled, or the working directory differs from the app's location.
Use render_template('page.html', value=x) to fill a Jinja template; Jinja escapes HTML by default, so do not mark user input as safe.
Use request.form for submitted form fields, request.args for query parameters and request.get_json() for a JSON body.
A route accepts only GET unless you pass methods=['GET', 'POST']; a 405 Method Not Allowed error means the method is not listed.
Return jsonify(data) or a plain dict from a view to send JSON with the right content type.
Use redirect(url_for('endpoint')) after handling a POST so a page reload does not submit the form again.
Set app.secret_key to a long random value from the environment before using session; sessions are signed with it and users could forge them if it leaks.
Use abort(404) to return an error page and @app.errorhandler(404) to customize it.
Use app.test_client() to test routes without starting a server.
Use @app.before_request to check authentication for every route; returning a response from it stops the request.
Set cookies with response.set_cookie(..., httponly=True, samesite='Strict'), and add secure=True when the site is served over HTTPS.
A cookie marked Secure is not stored when the page was loaded over plain HTTP; login pages that set one on HTTP will seem to log in and then bounce back.
Limit login attempts and compare passwords with hmac.compare_digest; a simple shared token needs rate limiting too.
Use app.config['MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH'] to limit upload size; larger requests get a 413 error.
Use werkzeug.utils.secure_filename on uploaded file names before saving them, and never use the client's name as a path.
Use send_from_directory to serve downloads from one folder; it blocks paths that leave that folder.
Flask apps that run in several threads need locks around shared global data; module level variables are shared by all requests.
Use app.run(threaded=True), which is the default, if long requests such as streaming should not block others.
Stream long responses with a generator and Response(generate(), mimetype='text/event-stream') for server sent events; disable buffering in any proxy in front.
Browsers cache static files; add a version query string such as ?v=2 or set a cache control header when a changed file does not show up.
A page that loads over HTTPS must not request scripts or APIs over plain HTTP; browsers block this as mixed content.
Use flask --app file run --debug during development; it reloads on code changes, while production should run without debug.
Use CORS headers only for the origins that need them; allowing every origin with credentials is a common security mistake.
Use url_for('static', filename='x.css') instead of hard coded paths so links keep working when the app is mounted under a prefix.
Use gunicorn with -w 2 and a bind option plus module:app to serve a Flask app; on a small Raspberry Pi two workers are usually plenty.
HTTP status 200 means success, 301 and 302 mean redirects, 400 a bad request, 401 not authenticated, 403 not allowed, 404 not found and 500 a server error.
A 502 or 504 from a proxy means the program behind it did not answer in time or is not running; check that service first.
The HTTP header Content-Type tells the browser how to read the body; a wrong type such as text/plain for HTML shows the source instead of the page.
Use curl -v to see request and response headers and the TLS handshake when a request fails in an unclear way.
A browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request before cross origin calls that use custom headers or methods other than simple ones.
A certificate is only valid for the exact names it lists; opening a server by its numeric address shows a warning unless the certificate lists that address.
Browsers trust certificates only from authorities in their store; a self signed certificate always causes a warning until you add it as trusted.
Let a reverse proxy such as nginx or caddy handle HTTPS in front of a small app; the app itself can stay on plain HTTP on the local machine.
Port numbers below 1024 normally need root; run an app on 8080 or higher, or give it the capability to bind low ports.
The Host header selects the site on servers that host several; sending a request to the wrong name returns another site or an error.
Cookies are sent only to the host and path they were set for; a cookie set on one port of a host is also sent to other ports of the same host, because cookies ignore ports.
Large JSON responses compress well; enable gzip in the proxy for text content to save bandwidth on slow links.
A timeout and a refused connection are different problems: refused means nothing listens on that port, timeout usually means a firewall or a wrong address.
Use ETag or Last-Modified headers and conditional requests to avoid downloading unchanged data repeatedly.
URL encode query values with urllib.parse.quote or urlencode; characters like &, spaces and non ASCII letters break unencoded URLs.
A webhook endpoint must answer quickly with a 2xx status; do slow work in the background and answer first, or the sender retries.
Rate limits return status 429, often with a Retry-After header; wait that long and then retry with growing delays instead of retrying instantly.
Retry only requests that are safe to repeat, such as GET; repeating a POST can create duplicate orders or records.
Use ping -c 4 on a host name to test reachability; if a numeric address works but the name fails, the problem is DNS and not the link.
Use ip addr to list interfaces and addresses; the older ifconfig command may not be installed on recent systems.
Use ip route to see the default gateway; no default route means no traffic leaves the local network.
Use ss -tlnp to list listening TCP ports and the program that owns each; a service bound to the loopback address cannot be reached from other machines.
Use curl -I to fetch only the response headers of a page, which is a quick way to see redirects and status codes.
Use curl -L to follow redirects and curl -o file to save the result instead of printing it.
Use curl -sS -f in scripts so errors are shown and a failing HTTP status gives a non zero exit code.
Use curl --max-time 10 in scripts so a hung server cannot block the script forever.
Use curl --retry 3 to retry transient failures automatically.
Use wget -c to resume an interrupted download of a large file.
Use nslookup or dig to check DNS answers; compare with a public resolver to tell if your local resolver is wrong.
If a name resolves slowly, check whether IPv6 lookups time out; many small devices wait several seconds before falling back to IPv4.
Use hostname -I to print the machine's addresses on one line.
Static addresses on current Raspberry Pi OS are set through NetworkManager with nmcli, not by editing dhcpcd.conf as on older releases.
Use nmcli device status to see which connections are up and nmcli connection show to list saved profiles.
Use nmcli device wifi list to scan for wireless networks and nmcli device wifi connect with the name and a password option to join one.
Wi-Fi power saving can cause lag and dropped connections on a Raspberry Pi; check it with iw dev wlan0 get power_save and turn it off if the link is unstable.
Use rfkill list to see whether Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is blocked by software; rfkill unblock all lifts the block.
Set the Wi-Fi country with raspi-config; without it the wireless radio can stay disabled on first boot.
A 5 GHz network will not show up on a device that only supports 2.4 GHz; check the band when a network is missing from the scan.
Hidden network names must be entered manually and still work; the name is not a security feature.
Use ssh -v to debug a failing connection; it shows which keys are offered and where authentication stops.
Use ssh-keygen -t ed25519 to create a modern key pair and ssh-copy-id to install the public key on a server.
Keep the private key file readable only by you, mode 600; ssh refuses to use a key that other users can read.
Disable password login in the ssh server settings once key login works, and restart the ssh service afterwards.
Use scp or rsync over ssh to copy files between machines; rsync only sends the changed parts.
Use ssh -L to forward a local port to a service on the remote side, for example to view a remote web page through a tunnel.
Use ssh -N -f with a forward option to keep a tunnel in the background without opening a shell.
The ssh option ServerAliveInterval keeps idle connections from being dropped by routers and firewalls.
A Host entry in the ssh client config file lets you connect with a short name instead of typing user, port and key every time.
If ssh says the remote host identification has changed, the machine was reinstalled or something is intercepting; verify before removing the old entry with ssh-keygen -R.
mDNS names such as raspberrypi followed by the local suffix work only when avahi is running on the device and the client supports multicast DNS.
Use arp -a or ip neigh to list devices recently seen on the local network.
Use nmap -sn on your own subnet to find live devices; scan only networks you own or have permission to scan.
Use traceroute or mtr to find where along the path packets are delayed or lost.
Use iperf3 between two machines to measure real network throughput without disk effects.
Use speedtest style checks only as a rough guide; a wired connection to the router is the baseline when comparing Wi-Fi.
A weak Wi-Fi signal shows in iwconfig or iw dev wlan0 link as a low signal level; move the device or use a wired connection for servers.
Use tcpdump -i any port 80 -n to watch traffic for one port; capture only what you need and delete the files afterwards.
Use ufw status to see the firewall; allow only the ports you need, for example ufw allow 22/tcp.
Enable the firewall only after allowing ssh, or you can lock yourself out of a remote machine.
Use fail2ban or ssh rate limits on machines reachable from the internet; automated login attempts start within minutes of exposure.
Do not forward ports on the router to services without authentication; use a VPN such as WireGuard to reach home devices instead.
Use wg show to check a WireGuard tunnel; a handshake time of more than a few minutes ago means the peers are not exchanging traffic.
WireGuard keys are a private and a public pair; share only the public key and keep the private key out of backups that others can read.
If a VPN breaks local network access, check whether it routes all traffic through the tunnel and add a rule for the local subnet.
A dynamic home address changes; use a dynamic DNS service or a tunnel when you need to reach the device from outside.
Carrier grade NAT blocks incoming connections even with port forwarding; check whether the router's external address matches what a what is my address site shows.
Set the system time with timedatectl; wrong time makes HTTPS fail with certificate not yet valid errors.
Use timedatectl status to check that the clock is synchronized; a Raspberry Pi has no battery clock and depends on network time after boot.
Use resolvectl status to see which DNS servers are in use on systems with systemd-resolved.
Edit /etc/resolv.conf only when you know what manages it; NetworkManager or resolved will overwrite manual changes.
Use getent hosts name to test name resolution the same way programs do, including the hosts file.
The hosts file maps names to addresses before DNS is asked; a stale entry there can override correct DNS.
Use nc -zv host port to check whether a TCP port is open, and nc -l to listen for a quick test.
Use python3 -m http.server 8000 in a folder to share files on the local network temporarily; stop it when you are done.
A connection that works with curl but not in a browser is often a proxy, certificate or cache problem rather than a network problem.
Environment variables HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY affect many command line tools; unset them when a tool cannot reach a local service.
Use no_proxy to exclude local names and addresses from proxy settings.
Ethernet link problems often come from a bad cable; check the link light and use ethtool to read the negotiated speed.
A negotiated speed of 100 Mbit on a gigabit port suggests a damaged cable or connector.
Use ip link set wlan0 down and up to restart an interface without rebooting.
Use journalctl -u NetworkManager to see why a connection failed or dropped.
Use systemctl restart NetworkManager when the network state is stuck, but remember it briefly disconnects remote sessions.
A device with two active interfaces may answer on one and send replies out the other, which breaks connections; give the wanted interface the lower route metric.
Use bluetoothctl to scan, pair, trust and connect Bluetooth devices from the command line.
Pairing works only when the device is in pairing mode; trust the device afterwards so it reconnects automatically.
Use sockets bound to the loopback address for internal services such as a local database; this keeps them off the network by default.
Port 80 and 443 are the web defaults, 22 is ssh, 53 is DNS, 123 is time and 5353 is multicast DNS.
Use lsof -i :8000 to see which process holds a port when a program says the address is already in use.
The error address already in use usually means an old copy of the program is still running or the port is in TIME_WAIT; stop the old process and retry.
Use SO_REUSEADDR when you write a server so it can restart quickly on the same port.
Use socket timeouts in Python with settimeout; a blocking socket call without a timeout can hang a program forever.
Use requests with a timeout argument; by default requests waits forever for a response.
Use requests.Session to reuse connections when making many calls to the same server.
Check response.status_code or call raise_for_status before using a response body in Python.
Use urllib.request in scripts that must run without installing extra packages.
Use the ipaddress module in Python to validate and compare addresses and subnets instead of regular expressions.
Private address ranges are 10.x.x.x, 172.16 to 172.31 and 192.168.x.x; they are not reachable from the internet.
A /24 subnet means the first three numbers identify the network and the last identifies the device, which allows 254 usable devices.
Reserve a fixed address for a device in the router's DHCP settings instead of setting it on the device; this avoids conflicts.
Two devices with the same address cause random disconnects; check for duplicates with arping -D when a connection works only intermittently.
Use systemctl status name to see whether a service is running, its recent log lines and the last exit code.
Use systemctl enable --now name to start a service immediately and at every boot.
After editing a unit file run systemctl daemon-reload, otherwise systemd keeps using the old version.
Use journalctl -u name -f to follow a service's log live, and -n 100 to see only the last hundred lines.
Use journalctl -b to show only messages since the current boot and -b -1 for the previous boot.
Use journalctl -p err to show only errors and worse, which quickly cuts through noisy logs.
Use journalctl --since "1 hour ago" to limit logs by time.
Limit journal size with SystemMaxUse in the journald settings so logs do not fill a small SD card.
Use journalctl --disk-usage to see how much space the logs take and journalctl --vacuum-size=200M to trim them.
Set Restart=on-failure and RestartSec=5 in a service so it comes back after a crash without restarting in a tight loop.
Set StartLimitIntervalSec and StartLimitBurst to stop a broken service from restarting forever; a service that exceeds the limit shows failed.
Use After=network-online.target and Wants=network-online.target for services that need a working network at start.
The network.target only means the network software started; network-online.target waits until a connection is up.
Use WorkingDirectory in the unit file so relative paths in your program resolve the same way as when you test by hand.
Use User= to run a service as a normal user instead of root; this limits the damage if the program is compromised.
Use Environment= or EnvironmentFile= to pass settings; quotes and inline comments in an environment file are not handled like in a shell.
Use full paths in ExecStart; systemd does not use your shell's PATH or aliases.
Shell features such as pipes, redirects and variable expansion do not work in ExecStart unless you run through a shell explicitly.
Use ExecStartPre for setup steps and prefix the command with a minus sign if a failure there should be ignored.
Python output is buffered when not on a terminal; set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 or use python3 -u so logs show up in the journal immediately.
Use Type=simple for programs that stay in the foreground, which is correct for most Python and Node services.
Use systemctl list-units --failed to see every failed service on the machine.
Use systemctl reset-failed to clear the failed state after you fixed a service.
Use systemctl edit name to create an override file instead of changing the packaged unit; overrides survive package updates.
Use systemctl cat name to see the full effective unit including overrides.
Use systemd-analyze blame to see which services slow down boot and systemd-analyze critical-chain for the chain of waits.
Use systemctl list-timers to see scheduled timer units and when they run next.
A systemd timer needs both a .timer file and a .service file; enable the timer, not the service.
Use OnCalendar in a timer for clock based schedules and OnBootSec for delays after boot; Persistent=true runs missed jobs after downtime.
Use systemd-analyze calendar with an expression to check when it would fire before you rely on it.
Use systemctl --user for services that belong to your own login session; they need loginctl enable-linger to run without being logged in.
Use loginctl enable-linger username so user services keep running after you log out and start at boot.
User services need the XDG_RUNTIME_DIR variable set when started over ssh; otherwise systemctl --user may say it cannot connect to the bus.
Services run without a screen; graphical programs started by a service need DISPLAY and XAUTHORITY set to the logged in desktop session.
Use MemoryMax and CPUQuota in a unit file to keep a runaway program from freezing a small machine.
Use TimeoutStopSec to control how long systemd waits for a service to stop before killing it.
A service stuck in activating usually means the program exits or never reports ready; check the type and the log.
Exit status 203 EXEC means systemd could not run the program; check the path and the execute permission.
Exit status 217 USER means the user named in the unit does not exist.
Exit status 200 CHDIR means the working directory does not exist.
Exit status 226 NAMESPACE or permission errors often come from protection settings like ProtectSystem or PrivateTmp that block paths the program needs.
Use ReadWritePaths with ProtectSystem=strict to allow writes to only the folders a service really needs.
Use NoNewPrivileges=true in services that do not need to gain rights; it is a cheap hardening option.
Use systemd-run --user --scope to start a one off command inside a managed group, which makes it easy to limit or stop later.
Use systemctl mask name to stop a service from starting at all, even as a dependency; unmask reverses it.
Use systemctl is-active name in scripts; it prints the state and returns a non zero code when the service is not running.
Use systemctl is-enabled name to see whether a service starts at boot.
Use logger -t mytag message to send a line to the system log from a shell script.
Use SyslogIdentifier in the unit file to give the log lines a readable tag.
Use StandardOutput=append:/var/log/name.log if you want a plain log file in addition to the journal.
Use logrotate for plain log files; without rotation they grow until the disk is full.
Use dmesg -T to see kernel messages with readable time; look there for disk, USB and power problems.
Messages about under-voltage in dmesg on a Raspberry Pi mean the power supply or cable is too weak.
Use udevadm monitor to watch device events while plugging in USB hardware.
Use a udev rule with a SYMLINK to give a USB device a stable name that does not change with plug order.
Use lsusb to list USB devices and lsblk to list disks and partitions.
Use fstab with the nofail option for external drives so a missing drive does not stop the boot.
Use UUIDs in fstab instead of device names like sda1, which can change between boots.
Use blkid to find a partition's UUID and findmnt --verify to check fstab before rebooting.
Test fstab changes with mount -a before rebooting; a bad line can drop the system into emergency mode.
Use systemctl get-default and systemctl set-default multi-user.target to boot without a graphical desktop.
Use systemctl poweroff or reboot instead of pulling power; abrupt power loss can corrupt an SD card.
Use hostnamectl set-hostname to change the machine name and update the hosts file as well.
Use timedatectl set-timezone Europe/Istanbul style names to set the zone; list names with timedatectl list-timezones.
Use cron with @reboot for a simple start at boot job; systemd services are better when you need restarts, logs and ordering.
A cron job runs with a minimal environment; use full paths and set PATH at the top of the schedule file.
Redirect output of cron jobs to a log file, because mail delivery is usually not set up and errors disappear silently.
The percent sign has a special meaning in cron lines and must be escaped with a backslash.
Use flock to stop two copies of a scheduled script from running at once.
Use flock -n lockfile command so a second run exits immediately when the first is still running.
Use nice and ionice to run heavy background jobs without slowing down interactive use.
Use timeout 30 command to stop a command that hangs, and check exit code 124 to detect the timeout.
Use nohup or systemd to keep a job running after the terminal closes; plain background jobs end when the session ends.
Use tmux or screen to keep an interactive session alive over an unstable ssh connection.
Use watch -n 2 command to repeat a command and see changes in place, for example watch -n 2 vcgencmd measure_temp.
Use uptime to see load averages; on a four core machine a load much above four means processes are waiting for the CPU.
Use top or htop sorted by memory to find programs that use the most RAM; press M in top to sort by memory.
Use free -h to see memory; the available column matters more than the free column because Linux uses spare memory for caching.
Use swapon --show to see swap; heavy swapping on an SD card is slow and wears the card.
Use df -h to see free disk space and du -sh * in a folder to find what takes the space.
Use ncdu when installed for an interactive view of disk usage per folder.
A disk that is full of small files can run out of inodes; df -i shows inode usage.
Use kill -TERM before kill -KILL so a program has a chance to clean up; use pkill -f with care because it matches whole command lines.
Use pgrep -af pattern to list matching processes with their full command lines before killing anything.
A process in state D is waiting for input or output and cannot be killed; look for disk or network mount problems.
A zombie process is already dead and only waits for its parent to collect it; fix or restart the parent.
Use ulimit -n to see the open file limit; programs that open many sockets may need it raised in the unit file with LimitNOFILE.
Use strace -p pid -f to see what a stuck program is doing at the system call level.
Run apt update before apt install so the package list is current; installing from an old list often fails with 404 errors.
Use apt upgrade for normal updates and apt full-upgrade when packages need to be added or removed to finish the upgrade.
Use apt search keyword and apt show name to find a package and read its description before installing.
Use apt list --installed with grep to check whether a package is already installed.
Use dpkg -L package to list the files a package installed and dpkg -S path to find which package owns a file.
Use apt remove to keep configuration files and apt purge to delete them as well; apt autoremove clears unused dependencies.
Use apt -s install package to simulate an install and see what would change before doing it.
Use apt-mark hold package to stop one package from being upgraded and unhold to allow it again.
Error could not get lock means another apt process is running; wait for it instead of deleting the lock file.
If apt reports broken packages, try apt --fix-broken install and dpkg --configure -a before anything more drastic.
Use apt clean to free disk space used by downloaded package files; it is safe on a small SD card.
Use apt-cache policy package to see the installed version, the candidate version and which repository provides it.
Add third party repositories only from sources you trust; they can replace system packages with their own.
Use sudo -n true to test whether sudo works without a password prompt in scripts.
Use DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive with apt -y in scripts so installs do not stop at configuration questions.
Use unattended-upgrades for security updates on machines that run unattended, and check its log occasionally.
pip on current Debian based systems refuses system wide installs with an externally managed environment error; use a virtual environment or the break system packages option on purpose.
Create a virtual environment with python3 -m venv .venv and activate it with source .venv/bin/activate to keep project packages separate.
Run the virtual environment's interpreter directly, such as .venv/bin/python script.py, in services and cron jobs instead of activating it.
Use python3 -m pip so pip belongs to the same interpreter you will run the script with.
Use pip freeze to list installed versions and requirements files to reproduce an environment on another machine.
Use pip install -r requirements.txt to install a list of packages and pin versions with double equals for repeatable installs.
Use pip show package to see the installed version and where it lives.
Use pip install --upgrade package to update one package and pip list --outdated to see what has newer versions.
Use pip install --no-cache-dir on devices with little disk space.
When pip fails building a package, check whether a ready made apt package exists, such as python3-numpy; it installs faster on a Raspberry Pi.
Wheels for ARM may be missing for new Python versions; compiling can take a long time on a Raspberry Pi and may need build-essential and development headers.
The error No module named x after installing usually means pip and python belong to different interpreters.
Use python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" to see which interpreter is running.
Use python3 -m site to see where packages are searched; useful when an installed module is not found.
Use pipx to install command line tools written in Python in their own environments.
Use npm install in a folder with a package file and npm ci for exact installs from the lock file.
Use npm ls --depth=0 to list top level packages and npm outdated to see updates.
Use npx package to run a tool without installing it globally.
Use node --version and npm --version to check versions; old Node versions from system repositories can be too old for current packages.
Do not run npm with sudo for project installs; it creates root owned files that later cause permission errors.
Use nvm or the vendor's repository to get a current Node version instead of the distribution's old one.
Delete the node_modules folder and install again when strange module errors appear after changing Node versions.
Use pip download or apt download to fetch packages on one machine and copy them to a machine without internet.
Use dpkg -i file followed by apt -f install to install a downloaded deb file and pull in its dependencies.
Use snap or flatpak only if you need them; they use more disk space and start slower on small devices.
Use apt-get changelog package or the package's own changelog to see what changed in an update.
Use needrestart or checkrestart after upgrades to see which services still run old libraries and should be restarted.
Use sudo apt install --reinstall package to repair a package whose files were damaged or deleted.
Use dpkg --get-selections or apt-mark showmanual to record manually installed packages and rebuild a machine later.
Use ldd program to see which shared libraries a program needs; missing ones show as not found.
Error while loading shared libraries means a library is missing; search for the package with apt-file or apt search.
Use which and type -a command to find which copy of a program runs when several versions are installed.
Use update-alternatives --config to choose between installed versions of a tool such as python or editor.
Use make -j2 on a Raspberry Pi 3 or smaller; using all cores while compiling can run out of memory.
Use cmake and ninja when a project supports them; builds are usually faster than with plain make.
Check the architecture with uname -m; aarch64 and arm64 are the same 64 bit ARM, armv7l is 32 bit ARM and x86_64 is a normal PC.
Download the build that matches the architecture; an exec format error means the binary is for another processor type.
Use getconf LONG_BIT to see whether the userland is 32 or 64 bit, which can differ from the kernel on Raspberry Pi.
Use lsb_release -a or cat /etc/os-release to see the distribution and release name before following a guide.
Guides written for older releases often use commands that were renamed; check the release name before copying settings.
Use cargo and rustup for Rust tools, but expect long compile times on small boards; look for prebuilt binaries first.
Use go install or downloaded binaries for Go tools; a Go program is usually one static file that is easy to copy.
Use docker only when you need isolation; on small boards it costs memory and disk, and containers still need updates.
Use docker ps -a to see all containers and docker logs name to read their output.
Use docker system df and docker system prune to see and clean disk usage from images and stopped containers.
Mount only needed folders into containers and avoid running them as root where possible.
Use docker compose up -d to start a defined set of services and docker compose logs -f to follow them.
Do not publish a container port to every interface unless it must be reachable; bind it to the loopback address for local only use.
Use sqlite3 file.db with .tables and .schema to inspect a database from the command line.
Use sqlite3 .backup or the backup API for a safe copy of a database that is in use; copying the file while it is written can give a broken copy.
Use PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL to let readers and a writer work at the same time in SQLite.
Use parameter placeholders in SQL queries instead of string formatting; this prevents injection and quoting errors.
Use with conn: in Python sqlite3 so a transaction commits on success and rolls back on an error.
Use CREATE INDEX on columns that you filter or join on; a slow query on a big table often just needs an index.
Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to see whether a query uses an index.
SQLite allows one writer at a time; a database is locked error means another connection holds a write; use a timeout and short transactions.
Use json with ensure_ascii=False to keep non ASCII letters readable when saving JSON files.
Write files with encoding utf-8 explicitly; the default encoding can differ between systems and break non ASCII text.
Write to a temporary file and then rename it over the target so a crash never leaves a half written file.
Use csv.DictReader to read spreadsheet exports by column name instead of by position.
Use openssl rand -hex 16 to create a random token for a password or secret instead of making one up.
Use the secrets module in Python for tokens and passwords, not the random module.
Store secrets in environment files with mode 600 outside the project folder, and never commit them to git.
Use gpg or age to encrypt backups before copying them to places you do not fully control.
Use sha256sum to verify a downloaded file against the published checksum before running or installing it.
Use rsync -a --delete with a dry run first (-n) when mirroring folders, because delete removes files in the target.
Use dd with great care; check the target device name twice with lsblk, because writing to the wrong disk destroys its data.
Use Raspberry Pi Imager and its advanced settings to set the hostname, user, Wi-Fi and ssh before the first boot.
Back up the whole SD card image before big changes; a copy of key folders is not enough to restore a working system quickly.
Use vcgencmd measure_temp to read the processor temperature; sustained values above 80 degrees cause throttling.
Use vcgencmd get_throttled to check for under-voltage or throttling; zero means no problem has happened since boot.
A lightning bolt or under-voltage warning means the power supply is too weak; use the official supply or one rated at least 3 A for a Pi 4.
Long thin USB cables drop voltage; use a short thick cable for the power supply.
Add a heat sink or a fan to a Raspberry Pi 4 that runs continuously; passive cooling alone often reaches throttling temperatures under load.
Use raspi-config for the Wi-Fi country, ssh, interfaces such as I2C and SPI, and boot options.
Enable ssh on first boot by placing an empty file named ssh in the boot partition, or use the imager settings.
Use a good quality SD card of class A1 or A2; cheap cards fail early and slow everything down.
Constant writes wear out an SD card; log to memory or reduce writes on devices that must run for years.
Boot from an SSD over USB for better speed and reliability; Raspberry Pi 4 supports USB boot after a firmware update.
Use sudo rpi-eeprom-update to check the boot firmware of a Pi 4 or Pi 5.
Use sudo raspi-config nonint commands in scripts to change settings without the menu.
Use cat /proc/cpuinfo or cat /proc/device-tree/model to find out which Raspberry Pi model you have.
Use pinout in the terminal to see a drawing of the GPIO header for your board.
GPIO pins work at 3.3 V; connecting 5 V signals directly to an input can destroy the pin.
Never draw more than a few milliamps from a GPIO pin; drive LEDs through a resistor and motors through a transistor or driver board.
Use a resistor of about 330 ohm in series with an LED on a 3.3 V pin.
Use gpiozero for simple GPIO work in Python; LED, Button and Servo classes hide the low level details.
On Raspberry Pi 5 older GPIO libraries such as RPi.GPIO may not work; use gpiozero with lgpio or libgpiod instead.
Use pull up or pull down resistors on button inputs; a floating input reads random values.
Debounce buttons in software with a short delay or the bounce_time option, or one press can count several times.
Use PWM to dim LEDs or drive servos; hardware PWM pins give steadier signals than software PWM.
Servos can draw large current when moving; power them from a separate supply and connect the grounds together.
Always connect the ground of separately powered parts to the ground of the Raspberry Pi.
Enable I2C in raspi-config and use i2cdetect -y 1 to list the addresses of connected devices.
If i2cdetect shows no device, check wiring of SDA and SCL, the power of the module and whether I2C is enabled.
Many I2C modules already have pull up resistors; adding more in parallel can make the bus unreliable.
Two I2C devices with the same address conflict; many modules have jumpers to change the address.
Enable SPI in raspi-config and check that the spidev device files exist under /dev.
Use a level shifter between 3.3 V logic and 5 V modules for I2C and serial connections.
The serial console and a serial device compete for the same UART; disable the login shell on serial in raspi-config when attaching hardware.
Use the device file /dev/serial0 in code; it always points to the right UART on different models.
Add your user to the dialout group to open serial ports without root, and log in again for the change to apply.
Add your user to the gpio, i2c and spi groups when a program gets permission denied on hardware.
Use the camera with rpicam-still and rpicam-vid on current Raspberry Pi OS; the older raspistill tools were replaced.
Use rpicam-hello to test that the camera is detected before debugging software.
Camera ribbon cables must be pushed in fully with the contacts facing the right way; a loose cable is the most common reason for no camera detected.
Switch the camera ribbon cable only when the Raspberry Pi is powered off.
Use libcamera based tools for CSI cameras and Video4Linux tools for USB webcams.
Use v4l2-ctl --list-devices to see which video devices exist and v4l2-ctl --list-formats-ext for supported resolutions.
Use ffmpeg with the v4l2 input to record from a USB webcam, and lower the frame size if the device is slow.
Use aplay -l and arecord -l to list sound cards, and alsamixer to set volumes.
Select the audio output with raspi-config or the desktop volume menu; HDMI audio may take over from the headphone jack.
Use speaker-test -t wav -c 2 to check that sound output works.
USB microphones show up as a new capture card; set it as the default in the ALSA settings if programs use the wrong input.
Use espeak or a similar offline engine for simple speech output without internet.
If HDMI shows nothing, check the boot partition config file for hdmi_force_hotplug and hdmi_group settings, and try a different cable.
Use the config file in the boot partition for hardware options such as overlays; edit it only with a backup and from a working card reader if the system does not boot.
Use dtoverlay entries in the boot config file to enable extra hardware, and check the overlay documentation for parameters.
Use vcgencmd get_mem arm and gpu to see the memory split; a headless Pi can give less memory to the GPU.
Raspberry Pi 4 has no real shutdown button; use a GPIO pin with the gpio-shutdown overlay to add a safe power button.
A Raspberry Pi 4 powers off to a low power state only; it draws power until the cable is unplugged.
Use a real time clock module such as one based on the DS3231 if the device runs without network and needs correct time at boot.
A fake hardware clock restores the last saved time at boot; time can still be wrong until network time arrives.
Use a USB hub with its own power supply for many USB devices; the Pi cannot power power hungry drives on its own.
USB 3 devices can disturb 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth; use a short extension cable to move them away from the Pi.
