ssh -D 1080 user@host opens a SOCKS proxy on your computer that sends browser traffic through the remote machine.
ssh -J jumphost user@target connects through a jump host in one command; add ProxyJump to a Host entry in the SSH config to make it permanent.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates a modern key pair, and ssh-copy-id user@host installs the public key so password login is no longer needed.
ssh -o ServerAliveInterval=30 keeps an idle connection alive through routers that drop quiet sessions; set it in the SSH config for all hosts.
If SSH shows REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED after reinstalling a Pi, remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R hostname.
scp -r folder user@host:/path copies a folder to another machine; rsync -avz --progress is better for large or repeated copies because it sends only changes.
sshfs user@host:/path /mountpoint mounts a remote folder like a local one; unmount it with fusermount -u /mountpoint.
Disable SSH password login only after you tested key login: set PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and restart ssh.
sshd -t checks the SSH server configuration for errors; run it before restarting ssh after any change so you do not lock yourself out.
Raspberry Pi OS needs the ssh service enabled: raspi-config interface options, or an empty file named ssh in the boot partition before the first start.
tcpdump -i wlan0 -nn port 80 shows packets on a port without name lookups; add -w file.pcap to save them for later analysis.
arp -a or ip neigh shows devices your computer recently talked to, with their MAC addresses.
iperf3 -s on one computer and iperf3 -c address on another measure the real network speed between them.
vnstat shows traffic per day and month from a small database, a light way to watch data use on a Pi.
iftop -i wlan0 shows live traffic per connection and nethogs shows it per program; both need root.
ufw allow 22/tcp opens SSH and ufw enable turns the firewall on; always allow SSH before enabling it on a remote machine.
ufw status verbose shows the rules and the default policy, and ufw limit 22/tcp slows down repeated login attempts.
fail2ban bans addresses with many failed logins; fail2ban-client status sshd shows who is banned right now.
Port numbers below 1024 need root unless the program has the capability: setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep program lets it listen on port 80 without root.
If a service works with localhost but not from another computer, check the listen address, the firewall and that both computers are in the same subnet.
Use a reverse proxy such as nginx or caddy in front of Flask or other apps to handle HTTPS, compression and slow clients.
Let's Encrypt certificates need a public domain name and an open port 80 or 443; for home networks without that use a tunnel or a private certificate.
Wake-on-LAN needs the target to support it and a magic packet to its MAC address; it does not work over most Wi-Fi connections.
A router restart can change the public address; use a dynamic DNS name or an outbound tunnel if you need to reach a Pi from outside.
Port forwarding exposes a service to the whole internet; prefer a VPN or an outbound relay connection, and never expose an admin interface without strong authentication.
WireGuard is a fast, simple VPN that runs well on a Raspberry Pi; wg-quick up wg0 starts an interface from a config file.
Tailscale joins your devices into a private network without opening router ports; tailscale status lists them and tailscale up connects.
MTU problems show as connections that start and then hang; try ping -M do -s 1400 host to find the largest packet that passes.
A DNS name that works in a browser but not in a script may be cached in the browser; test with dig or getent hosts name.
getent hosts name resolves a name the same way programs do, including /etc/hosts, while dig asks DNS servers directly.
Check which program uses a port with ss -ltnp 'sport = :5000' or lsof -i :5000, then decide whether to stop it or choose another port.
time curl -o /dev/null -s url measures total response time, and curl -w with time_connect and time_starttransfer splits it into steps.
Use timeouts on every network call in programs; a missing timeout is the most common reason why a script hangs forever when Wi-Fi drops.
A script that depends on the network should retry with growing waits: 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds, and give up after a limit, instead of failing at the first error.
Check Wi-Fi signal with iw dev wlan0 link; values below minus 75 dBm are weak and cause drops and slow speeds.
The 2.4 GHz band reaches farther through walls but is crowded; 5 GHz is faster at short range. A Raspberry Pi 3 and later supports both, the Pi Zero W only 2.4 GHz.
Use a USB Wi-Fi adapter or a short Ethernet cable when the built-in Wi-Fi of a Pi in a metal case has a poor signal.
vcgencmd measure_temp prints the CPU temperature of a Raspberry Pi, and vcgencmd get_throttled shows undervoltage or overheating flags; 0x0 means everything is fine.
vcgencmd get_throttled bit 0 means undervoltage now and bit 16 means undervoltage has happened since boot; use a better power supply and cable when either is set.
A Raspberry Pi 4 needs a 5 V 3 A USB-C power supply; weak supplies and thin cables cause random freezes, SD card corruption and a lightning bolt icon.
A Raspberry Pi 5 wants a 5 V 5 A power supply for full USB power; with a weaker supply it limits USB current to 600 mA.
The CPU of a Pi 4 starts to slow down at 80 degrees Celsius; add a heat sink or a fan if vcgencmd measure_temp stays above 70 under load.
vcgencmd measure_clock arm shows the current CPU frequency, and vcgencmd get_mem arm and vcgencmd get_mem gpu show the memory split.
cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep Model shows the exact board model, and cat /proc/device-tree/model prints it as one string.
cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp prints the CPU temperature in thousandths of a degree, which works without the vcgencmd tool.
raspi-config opens the configuration menu for SSH, Wi-Fi country, interface options and boot behavior; sudo raspi-config nonint do_ssh 0 enables SSH in scripts.
raspi-config nonint do_wifi_country TR sets the Wi-Fi country in scripts; the country code must match where the device is used.
The Raspberry Pi Imager lets you set the hostname, user, Wi-Fi and SSH before the first start through the advanced options, so no monitor is needed.
Use a good SD card from a known brand, class A1 or A2, with at least 16 GB; cheap cards cause corruption and slow systems.
An SD card wears out with constant writes; reduce logging, move heavy writes to a USB SSD, and consider log2ram for a long lifetime.
A USB SSD is much faster and more reliable than an SD card; a Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 can boot from USB, and raspi-config sets the boot order.
Shut the Pi down with sudo shutdown -h now or sudo poweroff before unplugging power; pulling the plug while it writes can corrupt the card.
A read-only root file system with an overlay protects the SD card from corruption on devices that lose power often; raspi-config offers it under Performance Options.
The boot partition is /boot/firmware on Bookworm and /boot on older releases; config.txt and cmdline.txt live there.
Settings in config.txt after a section header such as [pi4] or [cm5] apply only to that board; put shared settings under [all] at the end.
dtoverlay=dwc2,dr_mode=peripheral in config.txt makes the USB-C port act as a device, for example to appear as a serial port on a computer; it must be under [all] for a Pi 4.
The USB-C port of a Pi 4 can be a USB device only when it is connected to a computer and powered from it; with a separate power supply on that port there is no data connection.
enable_uart=1 in config.txt turns on the serial console on the GPIO pins 14 and 15, and the Pi 5 also has a dedicated debug connector.
gpu_mem=16 gives most memory to the system on a Pi without a display; the default is already low on Bookworm for the Pi 4 and later.
hdmi_force_hotplug=1 makes the Pi start its HDMI output even when no screen was detected at boot, useful for VNC on a headless Pi.
A headless Pi with VNC needs a virtual screen: set a resolution in raspi-config Display Options or add a dummy HDMI plug.
arm_boost=1 in config.txt enables the higher CPU clock of the Pi 4; over_voltage and arm_freq overclock further and need good cooling.
dtparam=audio=on enables the sound output and dtparam=i2c_arm=on, dtparam=spi=on enable the I2C and SPI buses.
i2cdetect -y 1 lists I2C devices on bus 1 and shows their addresses; install the i2c-tools package and enable I2C in raspi-config first.
GPIO pins work at 3.3 V and are not 5 V tolerant; a 5 V signal on a pin can damage a Raspberry Pi.
Each GPIO pin should supply only a few milliamps (about 16 mA at most); drive LEDs with a resistor of at least 330 ohm and motors through a driver.
Use the gpiozero library for GPIO in Python on Raspberry Pi OS: LED(17).on() and Button(2).wait_for_press() need no extra setup.
On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm the old RPi.GPIO library may not work on a Pi 5; use gpiozero with lgpio or rpi-lgpio instead.
gpioinfo and gpioget from the gpiod package read pin states from the command line without Python.
pinctrl get 17 shows the function and level of a GPIO pin on Bookworm, and pinctrl set 17 op dh drives it high; raspi-gpio is the older tool.
Hardware PWM on GPIO 18 gives stable servo and motor signals; software PWM jitters when the CPU is busy, so servos twitch.
A hobby servo needs its own 5 V supply for the motor and a common ground with the Pi; powering it from the 5 V pin can reset the Pi.
libcamera-hello and libcamera-still replaced raspistill; on Bookworm the commands are rpicam-hello and rpicam-still.
rpicam-still -o photo.jpg takes a picture and rpicam-vid -t 10000 -o video.h264 records ten seconds of video with a Raspberry Pi camera.
rpicam-hello --list-cameras shows which cameras are detected and their modes; an empty list means a bad cable, a wrong connector or a disabled camera.
The camera ribbon cable must be fully seated and the contacts face the right direction; a loose cable is the most common reason a camera is not found.
Picamera2 is the Python library for Raspberry Pi cameras on Bookworm; install it with apt (python3-picamera2) and not with pip.
A USB webcam works with ffmpeg -f v4l2 -i /dev/video0 or with OpenCV; v4l2-ctl --list-devices shows which video device belongs to which camera.
v4l2-ctl --list-formats-ext shows resolutions and frame rates a camera supports, so you can pick modes that fit the USB bandwidth.
arecord -l lists sound capture devices and aplay -l lists playback devices; use plughw:1,0 style names to pick a USB sound card.
alsamixer adjusts volume and capture level in the terminal, and the F6 key selects a different sound card.
Bluetooth on the Pi is controlled with bluetoothctl: power on, scan on, pair ADDRESS, connect ADDRESS; use trust ADDRESS so it reconnects at boot.
dmesg | tail shows the latest kernel messages such as USB plug events and power warnings; run dmesg -w to watch new ones live.
lsusb lists USB devices and lsblk shows disks and partitions; after plugging in a device, dmesg tells which name it got.
If a USB device disconnects at random on a Pi, suspect the power supply first, then a hub without its own power, then the cable.
A USB 3 device and cable close to a 2.4 GHz antenna can disturb Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on a Raspberry Pi 4; use an extension cable to move it away.
rpi-eeprom-update shows the bootloader version of a Pi 4 and 5 and sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a installs an available update.
Use sudo apt full-upgrade to update the firmware and kernel of Raspberry Pi OS together, then reboot; do not use rpi-update on a system you rely on.
free -h shows memory use and swap; a Pi that runs out of memory kills programs, so add zram or a swap file when you run large tasks.
Default swap on Raspberry Pi OS is a small file managed by dphys-swapfile; change CONF_SWAPSIZE in /etc/dphys-swapfile and restart the service.
zram swap compresses memory instead of writing to the SD card and is a good choice on a Pi with 2 GB or less; the package is called zram-tools.
top and htop show CPU and memory per process; in htop press F6 to sort and F9 to stop a process.
iostat -x 1 from the sysstat package shows disk load; a high await value on an SD card means it is the bottleneck.
Use df -h and du -sh /var/log/* to find what filled the disk; a full SD card makes many programs fail in strange ways.
Run sudo fsck -f /dev/mmcblk0p2 only on an unmounted card; to check the root partition use touch /forcefsck or fsck.mode=force in cmdline.txt and reboot.
Make a backup of the whole SD card with dd on another computer or Win32 Disk Imager on Windows; shrink the image with PiShrink to save space.
Raspberry Pi OS Lite has no desktop and uses much less memory; use it for servers and agents, and install a desktop only when you need one.
On Bookworm the default desktop uses Wayland (labwc on Pi 4 and 5); programs such as xdotool need X11, so switch with raspi-config Advanced Options, Wayland.
Auto login to the desktop is set in raspi-config System Options, Boot / Auto Login; kiosk and automation setups need it.
A Pi that starts but shows only a rainbow screen has a missing or corrupt boot file; reflash the SD card and check the power supply.
The green activity LED blinking in patterns shows boot errors: for example 4 flashes mean start.elf was not found.
The Pi 4 and 5 have a hardware watchdog; RuntimeWatchdogSec=15 in /etc/systemd/system.conf lets systemd reboot a frozen Pi automatically.
The Pi has no power button on older models; add a button between GPIO 3 and ground with dtoverlay=gpio-shutdown to start and shut down.
vcgencmd display_power 0 turns an HDMI display off and vcgencmd display_power 1 turns it on, saving power on a headless setup.
vcgencmd measure_volts core and vcgencmd get_config int show voltages and settings applied from config.txt.
Pi OS keeps its logs under /var/log; look at /var/log/syslog if it exists, and always check journalctl first on Bookworm because it uses the journal only.
The default user pi was removed from Raspberry Pi OS images; create your user in the Imager or with userconf in the boot partition before the first start.
Use passwd to change a password and sudo raspi-config nonint do_hostname name to rename the Pi; log in again afterwards.
A USB drive with exFAT or NTFS needs the packages exfatprogs or ntfs-3g; ext4 is the best choice for a drive that only the Pi uses.
Mount a USB drive at boot with an /etc/fstab line that uses UUID=... and the nofail option, so a missing drive does not block the boot.
blkid prints the UUID and type of every disk and partition, the right values for an fstab line.
mount -a tests all fstab lines; run it after editing fstab, because a wrong line can stop the next boot.
Use lsblk -f for an overview of partitions, file systems and mount points in one table.
A Pi can run Docker, but memory is tight; use docker stats to see usage and limit containers with --memory.
Use timedatectl and a working network for the clock; a Pi that boots with a wrong date shows certificate errors in browsers and fails apt update.
For a DS3231 real time clock module add dtoverlay=i2c-rtc,ds3231 to config.txt so the Pi keeps time without network.
Check Pi model and memory in scripts with cat /proc/device-tree/model and grep MemTotal /proc/meminfo before you decide what to install.
Keep the Pi cool and supplied: most mysterious crashes of a Raspberry Pi are power problems, so check get_throttled before debugging software.
A case with an aluminum body can act as a heat sink, but also blocks Wi-Fi; use an external antenna or an Ethernet cable.
Use screen or tmux over SSH so a long job survives when the connection drops; tmux attach reconnects to it.
Read the error message completely and from the first line; the first error often causes all the later ones.
Change one thing at a time while debugging and test after each change; otherwise you cannot tell what fixed or broke it.
Make a copy of any config file before editing it, for example cp file file.bak, so you can return to a working state.
When a command fails with permission denied, check the owner and mode with ls -l and the user with id before you use sudo.
Search for the exact error text in quotes; adding the program name and version narrows results to relevant answers.
Use --help or man command before searching the web; the manual pages on the system match the installed version.
man -k word or apropos word searches manual page titles when you do not know the command name.
Use tldr or cheat style summaries for common commands, and keep your own notes of commands that took you time to find.
Keep a log of what you changed on a system: date, file and reason; it saves hours when something breaks weeks later.
Test destructive commands first with an option that only prints what would happen, such as rsync -n, find without -delete, or git clean -n.
Quote file names with spaces in every command and script, and avoid spaces in names you create yourself.
UTF-8 is the right choice for all text files; set LANG=en_US.UTF-8 or tr_TR.UTF-8 and use locale -a to see what is installed.
A secret such as an API key should live in an environment file with mode 600 that is not in version control; add the file name to .gitignore.
Never paste secrets into chat tools, issues or screenshots; if one leaked, revoke it and create a new one at once.
Rotate API keys and passwords when a device is lost or sold; a key in an old SD card image is still valid.
Back up before upgrading: configuration in /etc, your home folder and databases; test that the backup can be restored.
The 3-2-1 rule for backups: three copies, on two kinds of storage, one of them in another place.
Document the setup steps in a README as you do them; the person who needs it later is usually you.
Use version control even for single scripts and config folders; git init takes a second and gives you undo.
Prefer boring, well-known tools for important jobs; a plain cron or systemd timer is easier to debug than a custom scheduler.
Idempotent scripts can run twice without harm: check whether something exists before creating it, and use mkdir -p and ln -sfn.
Log with timestamps and levels in long running programs; a message without a time cannot be matched with other events.
A health check that tests the real function, such as an actual request, finds more problems than one that only checks that the process exists.
Set limits on everything that grows: log size, cache size, queue length and retry counts; unbounded growth fills a small disk sooner or later.
Handle the case that the network, disk or another service is not there; embedded and home systems lose power and Wi-Fi regularly.
Use time zones on purpose: store times in UTC and convert only for display; mixing local and UTC times causes errors twice a year.
Check available disk space and memory before large tasks; df -h and free -h take two seconds.
A tool that asks for confirmation interactively blocks automation; look for a flag such as -y or --yes, or set an environment variable for non-interactive mode.
Read a command's exit code, not only its output; many failures print nothing but return a non-zero code.
Use absolute paths in cron jobs, services and scripts that other programs start; the working directory and PATH are different there.
Large language models can be confidently wrong; verify commands from AI answers on a test system, and read them before running them as root.
Use a dedicated low-privilege user for programs that face the network, so a bug in them cannot take over the whole system.
Keep software small and update it regularly; most break-ins use known bugs in outdated programs.
Choose long passphrases over short complex passwords, and use a password manager so each service has its own.
Enable two-factor authentication on accounts that control your servers, your code and your email.
Use ping, then curl, then the real program when testing connectivity; each step removes one layer of possible problems.
A reboot fixes many symptoms but hides causes; look at the logs from before the reboot with journalctl -b -1 before you restart a failing system.
Measure before you optimize: use time, top or a profiler to find the real bottleneck instead of guessing.
Write small scripts that do one thing and combine them; they are easier to test and replace than one large script.
Keep a rescue plan for remote systems: a second access path, a tested backup and a known good image, before changing network or SSH settings.
Use a staging copy for risky changes: test on a second SD card or a virtual machine, then repeat the steps on the real device.
Name things clearly: files, services, branches and variables with meaningful names save more time than comments.
Check the date of tutorials: commands and package names for Raspberry Pi OS changed with Bullseye and Bookworm, so old guides may not work.
enumerate(items, start=1) numbers items from one instead of zero, so you need no manual counter.
dict.get(key, default) returns the default when the key is missing and never raises KeyError.
collections.defaultdict(list) creates a missing list on first access, so you can append without checking whether the key exists.
collections.deque(maxlen=100) keeps only the last 100 items and drops the oldest automatically, a good fixed size log buffer.
str.partition('=') splits only at the first separator and always returns three parts, safe for key=value lines where the value contains an equals sign.
f-strings can format numbers: f"{x:.2f}" gives two decimals, f"{x:,}" adds thousands separators and f"{x:>8}" right-aligns.
pathlib.Path('a') / 'b' joins paths on every system, and Path.read_text() and write_text() replace open with read.
Path.glob('*.txt') lists matching files and rglob searches subfolders too.
json.dumps(obj, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) keeps non-English letters readable and formats the output for humans.
json.dumps(obj, separators=(',', ':')) gives the smallest JSON without spaces.
Read a JSON file with json.load(open(path, encoding='utf-8')) and always give the encoding; the default depends on the system.
datetime.now(timezone.utc) gives an aware time; a plain datetime.now() has no zone and causes mistakes when you compare times.
zoneinfo.ZoneInfo('Europe/Istanbul') gives a real time zone from the standard library, no extra package needed on Python 3.9 and later.
datetime.fromisoformat('2026-01-02T03:04:05') parses ISO dates without extra packages, and .isoformat() writes them.
timedelta(days=1) added to a date gives the next day; subtracting two datetimes gives a timedelta with total_seconds().
time.monotonic() is the right clock to measure durations because it never jumps back when the system time changes; time.time() can.
time.perf_counter() gives the most exact timer for short code sections.
Use with open(path) as f: so the file is closed even if an error occurs; iterate over f line by line for large files instead of f.read().
Read configuration from environment variables with os.environ.get('NAME', 'default'); use int() on the value because it is always text.
Use logging.getLogger(__name__) in each module and configure logging once in the main program; avoid print for anything that should reach a log.
logging.exception('message') inside an except block logs the message with the full traceback.
RotatingFileHandler('app.log', maxBytes=1000000, backupCount=3) limits log files to about 4 MB in total, important on an SD card.
itertools.islice(iterable, 5) takes the first five items of any iterator without loading everything.
itertools.chain.from_iterable(list_of_lists) flattens one level of nesting without a nested loop.
itertools.batched(items, 3) splits into chunks of three in Python 3.12 and later; before that use a small loop with slicing.
any() and all() stop at the first decisive item, so any(x > 5 for x in big) is fast with a generator expression.
Use a set for membership tests on many items: x in my_set is constant time while x in my_list scans the whole list.
Set operations: a & b is the intersection, a | b the union, a - b the difference and a ^ b items in only one of them.
dict merge with the | operator works in Python 3.9 and later: {**a, **b} does the same in older versions, and the right side wins.
Dictionary comprehension builds a mapping in one line: {k: v for k, v in pairs if v}.
Type hints such as def f(x: int) -> str are not enforced at run time, but editors and tools such as mypy use them to find bugs.
Catch specific exceptions; a bare except: also catches KeyboardInterrupt and hides bugs. Use except Exception at most.
shutil.disk_usage('/') returns total, used and free bytes, handy to check space before writing large files.
shutil.which('ffmpeg') returns the full path of a program or None, the right way to test whether a tool is installed.
secrets.token_urlsafe(32) creates a strong random token; never use the random module for passwords or keys.
hmac.compare_digest(a, b) compares secrets in constant time and prevents timing attacks; do not use == for tokens.
hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() gives a file or text fingerprint; read big files in chunks and call update for each chunk.
hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', password, salt, 600000) derives a key from a password; use a random salt and a high iteration count.
uuid.uuid4().hex gives a random 32 character identifier that is safe to use as a file name or key.
struct.pack('>I', 5) writes a number as four bytes in network order and struct.unpack reads it back, the tool for binary protocols.
int.to_bytes(4, 'big') and int.from_bytes(b, 'big') convert numbers and bytes without the struct module.
str.encode('utf-8') makes bytes and bytes.decode('utf-8', errors='replace') never fails on bad input, which is useful for logs from devices.
unicodedata.normalize('NFC', text) makes equal looking Turkish and accented text compare equal; use casefold() instead of lower() for case insensitive compares.
Turkish letters need care: 'I'.lower() gives i, not ı, in Python. Replace explicitly when you handle Turkish text: text.replace('I','ı').lower().
re.sub(pattern, lambda m: ..., text) lets a function compute each replacement.
Use raw strings r'\d+' for regular expressions so backslashes are not treated as escapes.
textwrap.dedent and textwrap.shorten clean multi line strings and shorten text to a width with an ellipsis.
Keep references to tasks created with asyncio.create_task; a task without a reference can be garbage collected before it finishes.
sys.exit('message') prints the message to standard error and exits with code 1, a short way to end a script after an error.
Python's venv isolates packages per project: python3 -m venv .venv, then .venv/bin/pip install name. Use the full path to the venv python in systemd services.
pip install --break-system-packages is needed on newer Debian based systems outside a venv; a venv or pipx avoids the flag completely.
pip freeze > requirements.txt records installed versions and pip install -r requirements.txt restores them; pin versions of programs that run unattended.
pip list --outdated shows packages with newer versions; update one at a time and test, rather than upgrading everything at once.
python3 -m py_compile file.py checks syntax without running the program, a quick test before restarting a service.
python3 -m timeit 'sum(range(100))' measures small snippets and chooses the number of loops for you.
python3 -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py lists where a program spends time; start there before you change code for speed.
python3 -m pdb script.py starts the debugger; breakpoint() inside code stops there, n goes to the next line and c continues.
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv makes a venv that can still use apt packages such as picamera2 and gpiozero on Raspberry Pi OS.
unittest ships with Python: python3 -m unittest discover runs files named test_*.py, and self.assertEqual(a, b) shows both values on failure.
Use assert only in tests; Python removes assert statements with the -O option, so never use them to validate user input.
Never use pickle.load on data you did not create; it can run code. Use JSON for data exchange.
Use yaml.safe_load, never yaml.load without a loader, when you read YAML files.
Open files with encoding='utf-8' on Windows too; its default code page can break Turkish characters.
print(..., flush=True) or python3 -u makes output appear at once in logs; otherwise output is buffered when not connected to a terminal, so systemd logs seem empty.
Set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 in a service file to get log lines in the journal immediately.
A script named like a standard module, such as random.py or json.py, breaks imports of the real module; rename it.
if __name__ == '__main__': keeps code from running when the file is imported; put the program start there.
sys.path and python3 -c 'import x; print(x.__file__)' show where a module is loaded from, the fastest way to find which copy is used.
List comprehension with a condition is faster and clearer than append in a loop: [x*2 for x in items if x > 0].
Generator expressions such as sum(x*x for x in data) do not build a list and use almost no memory.
Use ''.join(parts) to build long strings; adding strings in a loop with += is slow for large counts.
str.startswith accepts a tuple: name.endswith(('.jpg', '.png')) checks several endings at once.
Use round(x, 2) for display only; floats are inexact, so compare with math.isclose and use decimal.Decimal for money.
divmod(a, b) returns quotient and remainder together, for example minutes and seconds from a number of seconds.
min(items, key=...) and max(items, key=...) return the whole item with the smallest or largest key; add default=None for empty lists.
Slicing: items[::-1] reverses a list, items[-3:] gives the last three and items[::2] every second item.
sys.getsizeof shows only the shallow size of an object; for real memory use tracemalloc or the memory column in top.
urllib.parse.urlparse splits a URL and parse_qs reads the query; urlencode builds one with correct escaping.
urllib.parse.quote escapes text for use in a path, and unquote reverses it.
With the requests library always pass timeout=10; without it a call can hang forever. Use raise_for_status() to turn HTTP errors into exceptions.
requests.Session reuses connections and shared headers, which is much faster for many requests to the same server.
Retry network calls with a loop and growing sleep, and only retry errors that can pass, such as timeouts and 503, never 400 or 401.
Check Content-Length or stream with iter_content when you download large files; do not hold them in memory.
http.server is for tests only; for real use pick aiohttp, Flask with a production server or another proper server.
platform.machine() returns aarch64 or armv7l on a Raspberry Pi, and platform.system() the operating system name.
os.cpu_count() gives the number of cores, and os.getloadavg() the load of the last one, five and fifteen minutes on Linux.
os.stat(path).st_mtime gives the modification time; compare it with time.time() to find old files.
Use zipfile and tarfile from the standard library; extract only trusted archives or check member names, because ../ in names can write outside the target folder.
gzip.open(path, 'rt') reads compressed text files like normal files, and gzip.compress(bytes) works in memory.
zlib.compress and zlib.decompress shrink data in memory; level 1 is fast, level 9 is small.
Use super().__init__() in subclasses so the base class is initialized; forgetting it is a common source of missing attributes.
Use typing.Optional or the X | None syntax for values that may be missing, and check for None before you use them.
Prefer is None and is not None for None tests, and == for values; is on numbers and strings is unreliable.
Keep functions short and give them one job; if you need and in the name, split it into two functions.
grep -rn "text" --include="*.py" . searches only Python files and shows line numbers; -l lists just file names and -c counts matches per file.
grep -v "text" file removes matching lines, grep -i ignores case and grep -w matches whole words only.
grep -E 'a|b' uses extended regular expressions so alternation and + work without backslashes.
grep -F 'a.b' searches a fixed string without treating the dot as a pattern, safer for text with special characters.
grep -o 'pattern' prints only the matching part of each line, handy for extracting numbers or words.
grep -A2 -B2 pattern shows two lines after and before each match; -C2 does both.
grep -q returns only an exit code and prints nothing, ideal in if statements: if grep -q word file; then ...
sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file edits a file in place and keeps a backup with the .bak ending.
sed -n '5,10p' file prints only lines five to ten, and sed -n '/start/,/end/p' prints a block between two patterns.
sed '/^#/d;/^$/d' removes comment lines and empty lines, leaving the active configuration.
sed with a different delimiter avoids escaping slashes in paths: sed 's|/old/path|/new/path|'.
awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}' adds up a column of numbers, and NR gives the line number.
awk 'length > 80' file prints lines longer than 80 characters, and awk 'NR>1' skips a header line.
awk '!seen[$0]++' removes duplicate lines and keeps the original order, which sort -u does not.
cut -d, -f2 file.csv takes the second comma separated field; cut -c1-10 takes the first ten characters.
sort -n sorts numbers, -r reverses, -k2 sorts by the second column and -u removes duplicates; use sort -h for sizes like 10K and 2M.
sort | uniq -c | sort -rn counts how often each line appears and shows the most frequent first.
tr -d '\r' removes Windows carriage returns; a script with CRLF line endings fails with bad interpreter errors.
tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' changes case, tr -s ' ' squeezes repeated spaces and tr -cd '0-9' keeps only digits.
wc -l counts lines, wc -w words and wc -c bytes; wc -l < file prints the number without the file name.
head -n 5 and tail -n 5 show the start and end; tail -n +2 skips the first line and tail -f follows a growing file.
tee file writes output to the screen and a file at once; tee -a appends; use sudo tee to write a root owned file from a pipeline.
xargs runs a command for each input item: find . -name '*.tmp' -print0 | xargs -0 ls, with -0 to handle odd file names.
find . -name '*.log' -mtime +7 lists files older than seven days; -mmin -10 means changed in the last ten minutes.
find . -type f -size +100M lists files above 100 MB, the quick way to find what fills a disk.
find ... -exec cmd {} + passes many files to one command call and is faster than -exec cmd {} ;.
find . -type d -empty lists empty folders; add -delete only after you checked the list.
find . -newer file lists files changed after another file, useful to see what a build or an install touched.
ls -lhS sorts by size with human readable units, ls -lt by time, ls -ltr oldest first and ls -d */ lists only folders.
du -sh * | sort -h shows folder sizes in order; du -h --max-depth=1 limits the depth.
df -h shows free space per mount and df -i shows free inodes; a disk can be full of tiny files even when space is free.
stat file shows size, owner, mode and times; stat -c '%a %U %s' file prints chosen fields in one line.
file name tells the real type of a file whatever its ending is, a quick check for downloads and unknown data.
ln -s target linkname creates a symbolic link and ln -sfn target linkname replaces an existing link; readlink -f shows where it finally points.
cp -a keeps permissions, times and links when copying folders, and cp -u copies only newer files.
mv -n and cp -n never overwrite an existing file, and mv -v shows what happens.
mkdir -p a/b/c creates all levels and does not fail when the folder exists; mkdir -m 700 sets the mode at once.
touch -d '2026-01-01 10:00' file sets a file time, and touch -r other file copies the time of another file.
basename path gives the file name and dirname gives the folder; ${var##*/} and ${var%/*} do the same without starting a program.
${var%.*} removes the extension and ${var##*.} gives only the extension of a file name.
${var:-default} uses a default when the variable is empty, ${var:=default} also assigns it and ${var:?message} stops with an error.
${#var} gives the length of a string and ${var^^} makes it uppercase, ${var,,} lowercase in bash.
${var/old/new} replaces the first match in a variable and ${var//old/new} replaces all matches, without sed.
Arrays in bash: arr=(a b c), ${arr[@]} lists all, ${#arr[@]} counts and arr+=(d) appends; always quote "${arr[@]}".
Associative arrays need declare -A map; then map[key]=value and ${!map[@]} lists the keys.
Use [[ ]] in bash tests: it handles empty variables and patterns safely, for example [[ $name == a* ]].
Numeric tests: use (( a > b )) or -gt, -lt and -eq; the operators > and < inside [ ] compare text and redirect files.
$(( a + b )) does integer math in the shell and $(( x % 2 )) gives the remainder; for decimals use awk or bc.
bc -l does decimal math: echo 'scale=2; 10/3' | bc gives 3.33.
for f in *.txt; do ...; done loops over files with spaces safely when you quote "$f"; never parse the output of ls.
seq 1 5 and brace expansion {1..5} generate number lists; {a,b}.txt expands to a.txt b.txt and {01..10} keeps leading zeros.
case "$x" in a) ... ;; b|c) ... ;; *) ... ;; esac is clearer than many if statements for several values.
Use local inside shell functions so variables do not leak, and return a status with return n; output goes to stdout.
trap 'cleanup' EXIT runs a function whenever the script ends, also after errors, the right place to delete temporary files.
mktemp creates a unique temporary file and mktemp -d a unique folder; never use fixed names like /tmp/out.
Always quote variables: "$var". Without quotes spaces split the value and a star can expand to file names.
"$@" passes all arguments unchanged including spaces, while $* joins them; use "$@" when you forward arguments.
$? holds the exit code of the last command and $$ the process number; save $? at once if you need it later.
Exit codes: 0 means success, 1 general error, 2 wrong usage, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, 130 stopped with Ctrl+C.
command1 && command2 runs the second only on success and command1 || command2 only on failure; a && b || c is not a real if-else.
2>&1 sends error output to the same place as normal output; &> file or > file 2>&1 saves both; 2>/dev/null hides errors.
Order matters: command > file 2>&1 works, while command 2>&1 > file sends errors to the terminal only.
Here documents write multi line text: cat <<'EOF' > file keeps $ signs unchanged because of the quotes around EOF.
Process substitution diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2) compares the output of two commands without temporary files.
paste -sd, file joins all lines with a comma, and paste a b puts files side by side.
comm -12 sorted1 sorted2 prints lines that are in both sorted files, comm -23 only in the first.
join combines two sorted files on a common field like a database join.
column -t aligns text into a table; if it is missing, printf with widths such as %-10s gives the same.
printf is safer than echo for escapes and formats: printf '%s\n' "$var" never misreads a value that starts with a dash.
printf '%05d' 42 pads numbers with zeros and printf '%x' 255 prints hexadecimal.
date +%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S makes a file name friendly time stamp; date -d '1 day ago' and date -d @1700000000 convert times.
date +%s gives seconds since 1970; subtracting two values measures how long something took.
sleep 0.5 accepts decimals on Linux, and timeout 10 command stops a command after ten seconds with exit code 124.
timeout -s KILL 5 command sends a hard kill if the program ignores the normal stop signal.
watch -n 2 command repeats a command every two seconds and shows the output in place; watch -d highlights changes.
nohup command & keeps a program running after the terminal closes, but systemd services or tmux are better for anything important.
jobs, fg, bg and Ctrl+Z let you pause a program and continue it in the background; disown removes a job from the shell.
ps aux | grep name also lists the grep itself; use pgrep -af name or the trick grep [n]ame to avoid it.
pgrep -f pattern lists process numbers and pkill -f pattern ends them; check with pgrep -af first.
lsof -p PID lists the files a program has open and lsof +D folder shows who uses a folder; useful when a disk will not unmount.
strace -f -e trace=file program shows which files a program tries to open, a quick way to find a missing config or a permission problem.
ulimit -n shows the open file limit of the shell; servers with many connections need a higher value, set LimitNOFILE in a service file.
nice -n 10 command starts a program with lower priority and renice changes a running one; ionice -c3 limits disk priority.
export VAR=value makes a variable visible to child programs; VAR=value command sets it for one command only.
env shows all variables, env -i starts a program with an empty environment and printenv NAME prints one value.
alias ll='ls -lah' in ~/.bashrc creates shortcuts; aliases do not work in scripts, use functions there.
Ctrl+R searches the command history, !! repeats the last command, sudo !! repeats it with sudo and Ctrl+L clears the screen.
history -c clears the history of the session; commands that start with a space are not saved when HISTCONTROL=ignorespace is set.
cd - goes back to the previous folder, pushd and popd keep a stack of folders, and cd without arguments goes home.
~/.bashrc runs for interactive shells and ~/.profile or ~/.bash_profile for login shells; put environment variables in ~/.profile.
source file or . file runs a script in the current shell, so its variables and functions remain after it ends.
bash -x script prints every command as it runs, and set -x and set +x switch the trace on and off for part of a script.
Use shellcheck on every script; it finds quoting mistakes and unsafe patterns, and most editors can run it for you.
Shebang lines: #!/usr/bin/env bash finds bash in the path, #!/bin/bash is fixed; make the file executable with chmod +x.
chmod 600 for private files, 644 for normal files, 755 for programs and folders; chmod -R changes whole trees, so use it with care.
umask 077 makes new files private to the owner; check the current value by typing umask.
id shows your user and groups, groups name shows another user's groups and usermod -aG group user adds a user to a group; log in again to apply.
sudo -u user command runs a command as another user and sudo -i opens a root shell; visudo checks the syntax of the sudoers file before saving.
Redirection with sudo: sudo echo x > /root/file fails because the redirect runs as you; use echo x | sudo tee /root/file instead.
A cron job has a minimal environment: use full paths, redirect output with >> /path/log 2>&1 and test the command in env -i first.
flock -n /tmp/job.lock command stops a cron job from starting again while the last run is still going.
rsync -a --delete source/ dest/ makes dest an exact copy; the trailing slash on the source matters, and rsync -n shows what would change first.
tar czf archive.tar.gz folder creates a compressed archive, tar xzf extracts it and tar tf lists contents; -C dir chooses the folder.
tar --exclude='*.log' leaves out files, and tar xf archive path extracts only one member.
gzip -k keeps the original file, gunzip -c file.gz prints without extracting, and zcat reads compressed files directly; xz compresses smaller but slower.
zip -r archive.zip folder and unzip -l archive.zip list files; unzip -d dir extracts into a folder.
md5sum and sha256sum create checksums and sha256sum -c file.sha256 verifies downloads; always compare with the published value.
split -b 10M file part_ cuts a big file into pieces and cat part_* > file joins them again.
diff -u old new shows changes in the format that patch understands; diff -r compares folders and diff -q only says whether files differ.
cmp file1 file2 compares files byte by byte and exits with 0 only when they are equal, quicker than diff for binaries.
od -c file and xxd file show the real bytes, useful to see hidden characters like carriage returns or byte order marks.
strings file prints readable text inside binary files, useful to find version numbers and messages in programs.
iconv -f ISO-8859-9 -t UTF-8 file converts old Turkish text files to UTF-8; file -i shows the guessed encoding.
rev reverses each line and tac prints a file from the last line to the first.
shuf -n 1 file picks a random line and shuf -i 1-10 gives numbers in random order.
yes | command answers y to every question and yes text | head -n 5 prints a line five times, handy for tests.
nl numbers lines of a file and cat -n does the same; cat -A shows tabs as ^I and line ends as $ to find hidden characters.
expand and unexpand convert tabs and spaces; fold -w 60 wraps long lines at a width.
jq '.name' file.json reads one field from JSON, jq -r removes quotes, jq -c prints compact lines and jq '.[] | select(.x > 1)' filters items.
jq -n --arg v "$value" '{key: $v}' builds JSON with correct escaping, never create JSON by joining strings in a script.
curl -s url | jq -r '.items[].name' lists a field of every item in an array response.
envsubst fills ${VAR} placeholders in a template from the environment, a simple way to create config files.
Use getopts in bash to read options such as -v and -f file in scripts; shift removes handled arguments.
read -p 'Question: ' -r answer asks the user, read -t 5 stops waiting after five seconds and read -s hides typed text for passwords.
Use printf '%s\n' "${array[@]}" | sort to sort the elements of an array, one per line.
mapfile -t lines < file reads a file into an array without a loop, one line per element.
Use readonly for constants and declare -r in scripts; trying to change them stops the script and finds typos.
[ -f file ], [ -d dir ], [ -s file ] and [ -x file ] test for a file, a folder, a non-empty file and an executable; [ -z "$v" ] tests for an empty value.
$RANDOM gives a random number from 0 to 32767 in bash; it is fine for jitter and tests, not for secrets.
Brace expansion creates files in bulk: touch file_{a,b,c}.txt, and mv file.{txt,bak} renames in one short command.
Globs: ** matches folders recursively after shopt -s globstar, and shopt -s nullglob makes an unmatched pattern expand to nothing instead of itself.
Run long jobs with ionice and nice so the system stays responsive: nice -n 19 ionice -c3 command.
screen -S name starts a named session, Ctrl+A then D detaches and screen -r name returns; tmux does the same with tmux new -s name and tmux attach -t name.
tmux new -d -s job 'command' starts a command in a detached session; tmux ls lists sessions and tmux kill-session -t job ends one.
In tmux, Ctrl+B then % splits vertically, Ctrl+B then " splits horizontally, Ctrl+B then arrow keys move between panes and Ctrl+B then [ scrolls back.
Terminal tip: Ctrl+C stops a program, Ctrl+D ends input, Ctrl+Z pauses, Ctrl+A and Ctrl+E jump to line start and end, Ctrl+W deletes a word.
return jsonify(data) sets the JSON content type; returning a dict directly also works in Flask 1.1 and later.
request.get_json(silent=True) returns None for bad JSON instead of raising an error, so you can answer with a clear 400 message.
request.args.get('page', 1, type=int) reads a query parameter with a default and converts it, without crashing on bad input.
Use abort(404) or abort(400, 'message') to stop a request with an HTTP error from anywhere in a view function.
Never run app.run(debug=True) on a network reachable machine; the debugger allows code execution. Use a production server instead.
gunicorn -w 2 --threads 4 suits small boards like a Raspberry Pi; each worker uses memory, so more workers are not always better.
SECRET_KEY must be long, random and kept out of the code: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = os.environ['SECRET_KEY']; changing it logs everyone out.
Session cookies in Flask are signed, not encrypted; do not store secrets in session, and set SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY and SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax'.
Set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True when the site runs on HTTPS so the cookie never travels over plain HTTP.
Use Blueprint to split a large app into files, and register them with app.register_blueprint(bp, url_prefix='/api').
@app.errorhandler(404) and @app.errorhandler(500) return your own pages or JSON for errors, so users never see a raw traceback.
@app.before_request runs before each request and @app.after_request after it; use them for logging, authentication checks and security headers.
Add security headers in after_request: X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, X-Frame-Options or a Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors rule, and Referrer-Policy.
send_from_directory('folder', filename) serves a file safely; never join user input into a path yourself, because ../ escapes the folder.
werkzeug.utils.secure_filename cleans an uploaded file name; also limit upload size with app.config['MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH'].
Check the file type of uploads by content and not by the name the browser sends; store uploads outside the static folder.
render_template escapes variables in Jinja2 automatically; avoid the safe filter and Markup on user text, which allows script injection.
url_for('view_name') builds links from function names so they stay correct when you change a route; url_for('static', filename='a.css') links static files.
jsonify and Response with mimetype='text/event-stream' can stream events to a browser; use a generator and set Cache-Control no-cache.
Flask's development server handles one request at a time by default for long streams; use threaded=True or a real server for streaming.
Store configuration in environment variables or a config file read at start; keep a separate config for testing and production.
Use Flask-Limiter or a reverse proxy limit to slow down login attempts and API abuse; a plain Flask app accepts unlimited requests.
CSRF protects forms that use cookies for login: use Flask-WTF or send a custom header such as X-Requested-With, which browsers cannot add cross-site without a permission check.
CORS: set Access-Control-Allow-Origin only for origins you trust; a star together with cookies is blocked by browsers and a star alone exposes your API to any site.
Put the app behind a proxy and use ProxyFix from werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix so request.remote_addr and url_for use the real address and scheme.
Do not keep global state in module variables when you run several gunicorn workers; each worker has its own copy. Use a database or file.
Use SQLite with WAL mode for small Flask apps; open a connection per request and close it in teardown_appcontext.
Return proper status codes: 201 after creating something, 204 with no content, 400 for bad input, 401 for not logged in, 403 for forbidden and 404 for missing.
Validate input at the edge: check types, lengths and allowed values before you use data from requests.
Hash passwords with werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash, or better scrypt or argon2, and check with check_password_hash; never store plain passwords.
Write a small /health route that returns ok after it touched the database; monitors and load balancers can use it.
Use flask shell to open a Python shell with the app context, which is the quickest way to test database code.
Enable template auto reload and the reloader only in development; in production they cost time and can restart workers unexpectedly.
Chrome and Edge open developer tools with F12; the Network tab shows each request, its timing and headers, and Preserve log keeps entries across page loads.
In the Network tab, Copy as cURL repeats a request in the terminal, a fast way to reproduce a problem outside the browser.
The Console tab shows JavaScript errors with the file and line; click the link to jump to the code and set a breakpoint there.
Application tab in developer tools shows cookies, local storage and service workers; Clear site data resets a page to a clean state for tests.
A hard reload with Ctrl+Shift+R ignores the cache; developer tools also has a Disable cache option that works while it is open.
Service workers cache pages aggressively; if an old version keeps showing, unregister it in the Application tab or use Update on reload.
Mixed content: an HTTPS page cannot load HTTP scripts or frames; browsers block them, except for localhost addresses which count as secure.
The microphone and camera APIs need a secure context and a user permission; the permission is stored per origin, so a changed address asks again.
A page inside an iframe needs allow="microphone; camera" on the iframe tag to use these devices, and the parent page must also be allowed.
Content-Security-Policy limits where scripts, frames and connections may come from; read the console message to see which directive blocked something.
SameSite cookies are not sent in cross-site frames by default; a login inside an iframe on another site needs SameSite=None and Secure, or a different design.
localStorage keeps data per origin with about 5 MB of space and no expiry; sessionStorage lasts until the tab closes; neither is safe for secrets.
IndexedDB stores large structured data in the browser and works with files; use it instead of localStorage when you need more than a few megabytes.
fetch does not reject on HTTP errors like 404 or 500; check response.ok yourself and handle network errors in catch.
Use AbortController with fetch to cancel a request or set a timeout: controller.abort() after setTimeout.
WebSocket connections are not covered by CORS; check the Origin header on the server so other sites cannot use your socket with the visitor's cookies.
navigator.clipboard.writeText needs a secure context and a click or key press; older fallbacks use a hidden textarea and document.execCommand('copy').
Web Speech API speech recognition works in Chrome and Edge but sends audio to a vendor server and fails without network; it does not exist in Firefox.
navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({audio:true}) asks for the microphone; on error read err.name: NotAllowedError means denied, NotFoundError means no device.
Autoplay of sound is blocked until the user clicks or taps the page once; start audio from a button handler.
Set meta viewport width=device-width, initial-scale=1 so pages are not shown as tiny desktop pages on phones.
Use 100dvh instead of 100vh for full screen layouts on phones; 100vh ignores the moving address bar and cuts off content.
prefers-color-scheme: dark in CSS follows the system theme, and a data-theme attribute on the html element lets users override it.
CSS custom properties such as --bg and --fg defined on :root make light and dark themes a matter of changing a few values.
Use rem units and clamp() for font sizes so text scales with user settings and screen width without media queries.
Buttons must be real button elements; they work with the keyboard and screen readers, while a clickable div does not.
Every image needs an alt text, and every form field a label; these two fixes solve most accessibility problems.
Color contrast of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text keeps it readable; developer tools shows the ratio in the color picker.
A web page can be installed as an app with a manifest and a service worker; on Android Chrome shows Install, and standalone mode hides the address bar.
For Windows apps with a web interface, WebView2 gives an embedded Chromium browser that is already part of Windows 11 and most Windows 10 systems.
In an Android WebView set JavaScript on, DOM storage on and allow mixed content only if needed; service workers need a secure origin and may not work for custom schemes.
chromium-browser --kiosk url starts full screen without any bars, the usual way to show a dashboard on a Raspberry Pi display.
Add --noerrdialogs --disable-infobars --check-for-update-interval=31536000 to a kiosk command to hide error bubbles and update notices.
--user-data-dir=/path starts Chromium with its own profile folder, so settings and logins of a kiosk do not mix with other uses.
--autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required lets kiosk pages play sound without a click.
--use-fake-ui-for-media-stream accepts the microphone permission automatically; use it only on a device you control, and with a fixed address.
--remote-debugging-port=9222 opens a debugging interface on localhost for automation; never expose that port to the network.
--headless=new with --screenshot=file.png url takes a screenshot without a window, handy to test a page on a server.
Chromium on a Raspberry Pi 4 needs hardware acceleration enabled and enough memory; close other programs and use a light page for smooth results.
Use --disable-features=Translate to hide the translate bubble and --password-store=basic to avoid the keyring prompt on a kiosk.
A crash message "Chromium didn't shut down correctly" after a power loss can be removed by setting exit_type to Normal in the Preferences file of the profile before the next start.
Playwright can control Chromium from Python or Node.js: page.goto, page.click, page.screenshot; run it headless on a server.
With Playwright use page.wait_for_selector or expect-style waits instead of fixed sleeps; tests become faster and less flaky.
Playwright can emulate a phone: browser.new_context(**playwright.devices['Pixel 5']) sets size, user agent and touch.
Playwright grants permissions with context.grant_permissions(['microphone']) and can fake devices with the fake media stream flags.
Use context.storage_state(path='state.json') in Playwright to save a login and reuse it later without signing in again.
xdotool needs X11; it does not work on Wayland. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm switch to X11 in raspi-config before you use it.
xdotool type --delay 50 'text' types text with a short delay between keys, which helps programs that drop fast input.
xdotool key ctrl+c sends a key combination and xdotool key Return presses the Enter key; names follow the X key symbols.
xdotool mousemove 100 200 click 1 moves the pointer and left clicks; xdotool getmouselocation prints the current position.
xdotool search --name 'title' finds window numbers and xdotool windowactivate ID brings a window to the front before typing into it.
xdotool getactivewindow getwindowname prints the title of the focused window, a good check before sending keys to the right program.
xdotool does not type some non-English letters reliably; for such text put it on the clipboard with xclip and send ctrl+v instead.
xclip -selection clipboard sets the clipboard from standard input and xclip -o reads it, a robust way to paste text of any language.
wmctrl -l lists windows and wmctrl -a title raises one by name; xprop shows window properties after you click on a window.
xrandr lists screens and resolutions, and xrandr --output HDMI-1 --mode 1920x1080 changes the mode of an output.
xset s off -dpms disables screen blanking and power saving, needed for dashboards and kiosks that must stay on.
unclutter -idle 1 hides the mouse pointer after a second without movement, a standard tool for kiosks.
Wayland has no universal tool like xdotool; ydotool works through the kernel input device and needs its daemon and root rights.
scrot file.png takes a screenshot on X11 and grim file.png on Wayland compositors such as labwc; check which session type with echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE.
Every input needs a label tied by for and id; placeholders disappear while typing and are not labels.
Use the right input type: email, tel, number, url, date and password give phones a better keyboard and free validation.
autocomplete values such as username, current-password, new-password and one-time-code let password managers and phones fill fields correctly.
inputmode="numeric" with pattern="[0-9]*" shows the number keypad on phones for codes without the quirks of type number.
For a six digit sign-in code use autocomplete="one-time-code" so phones can offer the code from a message.
Disable the submit button only while the request runs and show an error message near the field when the server refuses, in plain words that say what to change.
Never trust browser side validation alone; repeat every check on the server, because requests can be sent without the page.
Show password requirements before the user types, and allow paste into password fields so password managers work.
Keep forms short; every extra field loses people. Ask for an email address instead of a username when you send codes anyway.
After a failed login give one general message such as wrong email or password; messages that say which part is wrong help attackers.
Limit attempts for sign-in codes and make them expire quickly, for example after ten minutes, with a few tries per code.
Keep focus order natural and set autofocus only on the first field of a short form; screen reader users depend on a logical order.
Pressing Enter in a form should submit it; use a real form element and a submit button instead of key handlers on inputs.
Use button type="button" for buttons that must not submit a form; the default type inside a form is submit.
Save a draft of long forms in localStorage so a refresh or lost connection does not delete the user's work.
Design for touch: buttons should be at least 44 by 44 pixels with space between them so fingers hit the right one.
Show clear states for loading, empty, error and success; a screen without feedback feels broken even when it works.
Use the language of the user in labels and messages and put texts into one file, so adding another language needs no code changes.
Keep one primary action per screen, make it visible and name it with a verb that tells what happens, such as Save changes or Send code.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion by turning off non-essential animations; it matters for users with motion sensitivity.
Keep dark mode text slightly softer than pure white on pure black and test both themes for contrast; shadows work poorly on dark backgrounds, use borders.
Do not rely on color alone to show a state; add an icon or text so color-blind users see the difference.
Confirm destructive actions with a clear message that names what will be deleted, and offer undo when possible.
Use native desktop windows through WebView2, Qt or Tauri for apps that should not depend on a browser; they start faster than Electron and use less memory.
Test on the smallest screen first; if a layout works at 360 pixels wide it usually scales up well.
git init -b main creates a repository whose first branch is already called main, without changing global settings.
git status -sb prints a short status with the branch line first, easy to read and to use in scripts.
git status --porcelain prints a stable machine readable format; an empty output means a clean working tree.
git add -p stages a file piece by piece, so one commit contains only the related changes; y stages, n skips, s splits a piece.
git add -A stages new, changed and deleted files in the whole repository; git add . in older versions did not stage deletions outside the folder.
git commit -m "message" -m "second paragraph" gives a commit a subject and a body; the subject should fit in about 50 characters.
git commit --amend --no-edit adds staged changes to the last commit without changing its message; never amend commits that others already pulled.
git commit --amend -m "new message" fixes the message of the last commit.
git commit --allow-empty -m "text" makes a commit without changes, which is a simple way to trigger a build.
git log --oneline --graph --all shows the history of all branches as a small tree in the terminal.
git log -n 5 --format='%h %an %ar %s' prints the last five commits in a custom one line format.
git log -S"text" finds commits that added or removed a piece of text; git log -G"regex" matches changes by a regular expression.
git log --since="2 weeks ago" --until="yesterday" limits the history by date, and --author="name" by author.
git shortlog -sn counts commits per author and sorts them, a quick view of who did how much.
git diff --name-only lists only the names of changed files, and --name-status adds a letter for added, modified or deleted.
git diff --word-diff shows changes inside a line by word, handy for prose and long configuration lines.
git diff --check finds whitespace errors such as trailing spaces before you commit.
git show --stat HEAD summarizes which files the last commit changed and how many lines.
git blame -L 10,20 file shows who changed lines ten to twenty last; add -w to ignore whitespace changes.
git restore file discards unstaged changes of a file and git restore --staged file removes it from the staging area, both without moving the branch.
git restore --source=HEAD~1 file brings back the version of a file from an older commit into the working directory.
git switch -c name creates and moves to a new branch, git switch - returns to the previous branch.
git branch --show-current prints only the name of the current branch, which suits prompts and scripts.
git branch -m old new renames a branch; git branch -d name deletes a merged branch and -D forces deletion of an unmerged one.
git branch --merged lists branches whose work is already in the current branch, the safe candidates to delete.
git merge --no-ff branch always creates a merge commit, which keeps the fact that there was a branch visible in the history.
git merge --ff-only branch refuses to create a merge commit and fails when a fast forward is not possible; it is a safe way to update a branch.
git merge --abort returns to the state before a merge that ended in conflicts, if you do not want to solve them now.
Conflict markers are the lines <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>; remove them after you choose the final text, then git add the file and commit.
git checkout --ours file or git checkout --theirs file picks one side of a conflict for a whole file; in a rebase the meaning of the two sides is swapped.
git rebase main puts your branch commits on top of the latest main; do it only on branches that nobody else uses.
git rebase --abort stops a rebase and returns the branch to the state before it, the exit if it goes wrong.
git cherry-pick commit copies one commit onto the current branch, and git cherry-pick -x adds a line that names the original commit.
git revert commit makes a new commit that undoes an older one; it is the safe undo for commits that were already shared.
git reset --mixed HEAD~1 undoes the last commit and unstages its changes but leaves the files as they are; it is the default mode of git reset.
git reset --hard discards all local changes for good; check git status and git stash first because untracked files are not touched but changed files are lost.
git reflog lists where HEAD has been, so even after a bad reset or a deleted branch you can find the lost commit and return with git reset --hard HEAD@{1}.
git stash push -m "name" saves changes with a label and git stash list shows them; git stash pop applies the newest and removes it.
git stash push -u also stores untracked files, and git stash show -p shows what a stash contains.
git stash apply keeps the stash after applying, git stash pop removes it; git stash drop deletes one you do not need.
git clean -n shows which untracked files would be deleted, git clean -fd deletes them with folders; always run the -n version first.
git tag -a v1.0 -m "text" creates an annotated tag with author and date; git tag -l 'v1.*' lists tags by pattern.
git push origin --tags sends all tags and git push origin :refs/tags/name deletes a tag on the remote.
git remote prune origin or git fetch --prune removes local references to branches that no longer exist on the remote.
git push --force-with-lease is a safer force push: it fails if somebody else pushed in the meantime; never use plain --force on shared branches.
git push -u origin branch sets the upstream once, and later git push and git pull work without arguments.
git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true sets the upstream automatically at the first push of a new branch (Git 2.37 and later).
git clone --depth 1 url downloads only the latest commit, which saves time and space on a Raspberry Pi; git fetch --unshallow gets the full history later.
git clone --branch name --single-branch url downloads only one branch.
git worktree add ../folder branch checks out a second branch in another folder, so you can work on two branches without stashing.
git bisect finds the commit that introduced a bug by binary search: git bisect start, git bisect bad, git bisect good commit, then mark each step; git bisect run script automates it.
git grep "text" searches only tracked files and is faster than grep -r; git grep -n shows line numbers and git grep -c counts matches per file.
git ls-files lists tracked files; git ls-files --others --exclude-standard lists new files that are not ignored yet.
git check-ignore -v file tells which ignore rule hides a file, the answer when a file mysteriously is not added.
A .gitignore pattern with a slash at the start such as /build matches only in the top folder; a trailing slash such as logs/ matches folders only; ! brings back an ignored name.
Files that are already tracked are not ignored by .gitignore; remove them from tracking with git rm --cached file and commit.
git rm --cached -r folder stops tracking a folder but keeps the files on disk.
git mv old new renames a file and stages the rename in one step; git also detects renames afterwards from similar content.
git config --global user.name and user.email set the author of your commits; git config user.email without --global sets it for one repository only.
git config --global alias.st "status -sb" creates a shortcut; after that git st runs git status -sb.
git config --global core.editor nano sets the editor for commit messages, and git config --global core.autocrlf input avoids Windows line ending problems on Linux.
A .gitattributes line such as * text=auto eol=lf keeps line endings the same for everybody on all systems.
git config --global credential.helper store keeps a token in a plain text file; on a shared computer use a cache helper such as git config --global credential.helper 'cache --timeout=3600'.
Use a fine-grained personal access token limited to one repository instead of your password; it can be revoked without changing the account.
Never commit secrets. If one was committed, revoke and replace it at once; deleting it in a later commit does not remove it from the history.
git commit -S signs a commit with a key and git log --show-signature shows whether signatures are valid; a signed tag proves a release came from you.
git rev-parse --short HEAD gives the short hash that is handy for version strings and file names.
git rev-list --count HEAD counts the commits of the current branch.
git cat-file -p HEAD prints the content of a commit object, and git cat-file -t shows the type of an object.
git hash-object file prints the hash git would give a file, equal for the same content on any computer.
A pre-commit hook is an executable file named pre-commit in .git/hooks; if it exits with a non-zero code the commit is stopped, a good place for syntax checks.
git commit --no-verify skips the hooks once; use it only when you know why the hook fails.
git config core.hooksPath .githooks lets a repository share its hooks, because the folder .githooks can be committed while .git/hooks cannot.
git sparse-checkout set folder checks out only chosen folders of a large repository.
git lfs track "*.psd" stores large binary files outside the normal history; install git-lfs first and commit the .gitattributes file it changes.
Large binaries and generated files bloat a repository forever; keep models, images and builds out of git or use release assets and git lfs.
git filter-repo is the modern tool to remove a file from the whole history; it rewrites all commit hashes, so everybody must clone again.
git revert -m 1 merge_commit undoes a merge commit and keeps the first parent, usually the main branch.
git rebase -i HEAD~3 lets you reorder, squash or reword the last three commits; use fixup to join a commit without keeping its message.
git commit --fixup=commit and git rebase -i --autosquash move fix commits next to the ones they repair automatically.
git config rerere.enabled true makes git remember how you solved a conflict and apply the same solution when it repeats.
git log --first-parent --oneline shows the history of the main line only, with each merge as one entry.
git diff --stat main shows a compact summary of how much differs from main, good before opening a pull request.

git update-index --assume-unchanged file hides local changes of a tracked file such as a personal setting, and --no-assume-unchanged undoes it; a better way is a template file plus a local ignored copy.
A commit message should say why, not only what: a short subject in the imperative mood, an empty line, then a body for the reason.
Make small commits that each do one thing and build; they are easier to review, to revert and to bisect.
Pull before you push and run your tests before each commit; a broken main branch costs the whole team time.
On a Raspberry Pi keep repositories small with git clone --depth 1 and prefer git pull --ff-only in update scripts so a failed update never leaves a half merged state.
ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of default=nw=1:nk=1 file prints only the length of a media file in seconds.
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vn -c:a copy audio.m4a copies the audio track without re-encoding, which is instant and lossless.
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=-2:720 out.mp4 resizes to 720 pixels high and keeps the ratio; -2 makes the width an even number as most encoders need.
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 23 -preset veryfast out.mp4 balances size and speed; a lower crf means better quality and a bigger file, and veryfast keeps encoding short on weak computers.
ffmpeg -framerate 30 -i frame_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p out.mp4 turns numbered pictures into a video that plays in every player.
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fps=1 frame_%03d.png saves one picture per second, and -frames:v 1 saves only a single frame.
ffmpeg -i in.wav -ar 16000 -ac 1 out.wav converts audio to 16 kHz mono, the format most speech recognition tools expect.
ffmpeg -i in.mp3 -b:a 128k out.mp3 sets the audio bitrate, and -q:a 2 selects a good variable bitrate for mp3.
ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy out.mp4 joins files with the same codec; list.txt has one line file 'name.mp4' per file.
ffmpeg -hide_banner -i file prints only the stream information of a file; the line with Stream shows codec, size and bitrate.
ffmpeg -encoders and ffmpeg -decoders list what your build supports; grep for the name, for example ffmpeg -encoders | grep libx264.
ffmpeg -loglevel error -i in out keeps the output quiet except for real errors, and -y overwrites without asking, which scripts need.
ffmpeg -f v4l2 -i /dev/video0 -frames:v 1 shot.jpg takes a picture from a USB camera on Linux; -video_size 1280x720 selects the size.
ffmpeg -f alsa -i hw:1,0 -t 5 out.wav records five seconds from a sound card on Linux; arecord -l shows the card numbers.
ImageMagick convert in.png -resize 50% out.png halves a picture; mogrify -resize 800x *.jpg changes many files in place, so work on copies.
sqlite3 db.sqlite '.tables' lists tables, '.schema table' shows how a table is built and '.mode column' with '.headers on' makes output readable.
JSON in a text editor: a trailing comma, single quotes or a comment makes JSON invalid; python3 -m json.tool file shows the line of the first error.
YAML uses spaces for indentation and never tabs; a colon followed by a space separates key and value, and values like yes, no and on may be read as booleans, so quote them.
Config files that hold secrets, such as .env, should have mode 600 and must not be in the web server's folder; check with ls -l.

A .env file holds KEY=value lines without spaces around the equals sign; values with spaces or special characters need quotes, and the file is read by the program or by systemd, not by the shell, unless you source it.
ls -ld folder shows the permissions of a folder itself; a program needs the execute bit x on every folder in the path to reach a file inside.
setfacl and getfacl give finer permissions per user when the three classes owner, group and others are not enough; install the acl package first.
The sticky bit on a shared folder, chmod +t, lets users delete only their own files; /tmp has it and shows a t in the permissions.
lsattr and chattr +i file make a file immutable, so even root cannot change it until chattr -i; useful to protect a configuration that a tool keeps rewriting.
du -h --max-depth=1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -h shows which top level folders use the most space; add -x to stay on one file system.
ncdu folder is an interactive disk usage browser in the terminal where you can walk into folders and see sizes at once; install it with apt.
find / -xdev -type f -size +50M 2>/dev/null lists big files on the root file system only, without crossing into other mounts.
Deleted files that a program still has open keep using space until the program ends; lsof +L1 lists them, and restarting the program frees the space.
Hard links share the same data under two names and cannot cross file systems; ls -i shows the inode number, equal for hard links.
A symbolic link to a missing target is a dangling link; find -xtype l lists them.
mkfifo name creates a named pipe that lets two programs exchange data through a file name without writing it to disk.
mount | grep tmpfs and df -h /tmp show whether /tmp lives in RAM; on a Raspberry Pi RAM based folders protect the SD card from writes.
/dev/shm is a RAM disk on Linux that is always there; files in it are fast and disappear at reboot.
Use mktemp -d inside scripts for temporary folders and remove them with trap, never fixed names that other users could guess.
md5sum folder/* | sort > sums.txt and md5sum -c sums.txt later check that files did not change, a cheap integrity test for copies.
sha256sum -c file.sha256 --ignore-missing checks only the files that exist, useful when a checksum list covers more files than you downloaded.
rsync -a --exclude='*.tmp' source/ dest/ skips patterns, and --exclude-from=file reads patterns from a file.
rsync --link-dest=previous new/ makes snapshot style backups where unchanged files are hard links to the last backup and use no extra space.
tar -tvf archive lists contents with sizes and dates before you extract; extracting into an empty folder with -C avoids a mess.
zstd is faster than gzip at the same size: tar -I zstd -cf out.tar.zst folder; xz -9 gives the smallest files but needs time and memory.
pigz or xz -T0 use all CPU cores for compression, which helps on multi core boards; a single core Pi Zero gains nothing.
7z a -p -mhe=on secret.7z folder creates an archive that hides even the file names; zip's classic password is weak, so prefer 7z or age for secrets.
age -p -o file.age file encrypts a file with a passphrase, and age -d -o file file.age decrypts it; gpg -c does the same with a more complex tool.
openssl enc and gpg are fine for files at rest but never invent your own encryption; use a tested tool with authenticated encryption such as age or AES-GCM from a library.
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -dates -subject shows when a certificate expires; openssl s_client -connect host:443 reads the certificate from a live server.
file --mime-type -b name prints the MIME type such as text/plain or image/png, useful to check uploads and downloads.
exiftool file shows picture metadata such as camera, time and GPS position; exiftool -all= file removes it before you share a photo.
