Names of files should avoid spaces, accents and the characters : * ? " < > | because Windows cannot store them, which breaks copies between systems.
Windows paths use backslashes and drive letters, Linux paths use slashes; in code use path libraries (pathlib in Python, filepath in Go) instead of joining text.
File names on Windows and macOS are not case sensitive, on Linux they are; two files named A.txt and a.txt can exist together on Linux and break a copy to Windows.
A CSV file from Excel in Turkish settings often uses semicolons and a comma as decimal sign, and the encoding may be Windows-1254; set both explicitly when you read it.
dos2unix file converts Windows line endings; without it use sed -i 's/\r$//' file. A script with CRLF fails with the message bad interpreter.
A file with a byte order mark at the start (EF BB BF) can break scripts and JSON; remove it with sed -i '1s/^\xEF\xBB\xBF//' file.
iconv -f UTF-8 -t ASCII//TRANSLIT converts accented letters to plain ones when a system cannot handle them; Turkish ş becomes s.
Large log files are best read with less +F (follow) or less -S (no line wrap); press / to search and n for the next match.
logrotate rotates logs by size or time: a file in /etc/logrotate.d with rotate 4, weekly, compress and missingok keeps a month of logs; logrotate -d file tests it without changing anything.
A script that writes a log should write to a fixed place such as /var/log/name or the journal and have a size limit; a log without a limit fills the SD card some day.
inotifywait -m -e modify,create folder watches a folder and prints events as they happen; install inotify-tools; a cron job is simpler when a delay of a minute is fine.
fswatch on macOS and inotifywait on Linux react to file changes; polling with find -newer is slower but works everywhere.
A text file should end with a newline; many tools such as wc, diff and git warn about no newline at end of file because lines are counted by newline characters.
Sort file names naturally with sort -V, so file2 comes before file10; ls -v does the same.
rename 's/old/new/' *.txt renames many files at once with a Perl pattern (the perl rename package); rename -n shows the result first.
A for loop with mv and parameter expansion renames safely without extra tools: for f in *.jpeg; do mv -- "$f" "${f%.jpeg}.jpg"; done.
Use -- before file names that may start with a dash, as in rm -- "$f" or mv -- "$a" "$b", so they are not read as options.
Before you delete with a wildcard, run ls with the same pattern and read the list; rm -i asks for each file and is worth the seconds in a folder you do not know.
Move deleted files to a trash instead of removing them: install trash-cli and use trash-put file, trash-list and trash-restore.
Put scripts you run often into ~/bin or /usr/local/bin and make them executable; check that the folder is in PATH with echo $PATH.
cron fields are minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week; */5 * * * * means every five minutes and 0 3 * * 1 means Mondays at 03:00.
Cron uses the system time zone; check with timedatectl, and remember that a job at 02:30 can be skipped or repeated on the day the clock changes.
A cron job that prints something sends it by mail on many systems; add >/dev/null 2>&1 or a log file to a job that runs often.
systemd timers are the modern replacement for cron: they log to the journal, can catch up after downtime with Persistent=true and show their next run with systemctl list-timers.
at now + 10 minutes runs a command once after a delay, and atq lists waiting jobs; it needs the atd service and suits one time tasks.
id -un prints your user name and whoami does the same; id -u prints the number, and 0 means root.
getent passwd name shows the account entry including home folder and shell; getent group name lists the members of a group.
useradd -m -s /bin/bash name creates a user with a home folder, and passwd name sets the password; adduser asks the questions for you on Debian.
usermod -aG sudo name gives a user administrator rights on Debian and Ubuntu; the user must log in again, check with id name.
A service account without login: useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin name; it can own files and run services but nobody can log in as it.
sudo -l shows what you may run with sudo, and visudo edits the sudoers file with a syntax check so you cannot lock yourself out.
last shows recent logins and reboots, lastb shows failed logins (as root) and w shows who is logged in now and what they run.
who -b prints the time of the last boot, and uptime -p prints the running time in words.
dmesg -T shows kernel messages with readable times, and dmesg --level=err,warn shows only problems.
journalctl -k -b lists kernel messages of this boot, a good place to see USB, disk and power problems.
lsmod lists loaded kernel modules, modprobe name loads one and modprobe -r name removes it; modinfo name shows its parameters.
sysctl -a | grep name searches kernel settings, sysctl -w name=value changes one until the next boot and a file in /etc/sysctl.d makes it permanent.
sysctl vm.swappiness shows how eagerly Linux swaps; a low value such as 10 keeps programs in RAM longer and is kinder to an SD card.
/proc/meminfo has all memory numbers; MemAvailable is the best answer to how much memory programs can still use, better than the free column.
/proc/loadavg shows the load of the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes; a load above the number of cores means processes are waiting.
nproc prints the number of processor cores that programs may use, which is the number to compare a load average with.
/proc/PID/status and /proc/PID/cmdline show the state and the full command line of a running process; tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/PID/cmdline makes the arguments readable.
ls -l /proc/PID/exe shows which program file a process really runs, and ls -l /proc/PID/cwd its working folder.
ps -eo pid,ppid,%cpu,%mem,etime,cmd --sort=-%mem | head shows the top memory users with how long they run.
ps -o pid,ni,cmd -p PID shows the nice value of one process, and ps -ejH or pstree -p shows the process tree.
kill PID sends SIGTERM, which lets a program clean up; kill -9 PID cannot be caught and should be the last choice.
kill -0 PID sends no signal and only tells through its exit code whether the process exists and may be signalled.
kill -HUP PID makes many daemons reload their configuration, and kill -USR1 is used by some programs to rotate logs or print status.
A zombie process is a finished child that its parent did not collect; it uses no memory and goes away when the parent ends or is restarted.
wait in a shell script waits for all background jobs, and wait PID for one; $! holds the number of the last background job.
Run commands in parallel from a script with & and wait, or with xargs -P; limit the number so a small board is not overloaded.
command & disown keeps a job alive after the terminal closes; setsid command starts it in its own session so no hangup signal reaches it.
exec replaces the shell with a program in a script, so no extra process stays; it is good at the end of a start script.
Use a here string to feed text to a command: grep -c a <<< "banana" avoids a pipe and an extra echo.
In bash, set -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail when any part fails, otherwise only the exit code of the last command counts.
PIPESTATUS is an array with the exit codes of every part of the last pipeline in bash: false | true; echo ${PIPESTATUS[@]} prints 1 0.
Use [[ -n "$var" ]] to test for a non empty value and ${var:-} inside set -u scripts so an unset variable does not stop the script.
Arithmetic in bash: ((i++)) returns status 1 when the old value was 0, which stops scripts under set -e; use i=$((i+1)) instead.
Do not parse ls; use globs, find -print0 with read -d '' or find -exec. File names can contain spaces and newlines.
find -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do ...; done handles every possible file name inside a loop.
A subshell in parentheses runs in its own environment: (cd /tmp && command) does not change the folder of the script.
Functions can return text only through output; capture it with result=$(function) and use return only for a status code from 0 to 255.
Use readarray or mapfile -t to read lines into an array, and "${arr[@]}" with quotes to pass them on without splitting.
printf -v var '%s-%s' a b stores formatted text in a variable without a subshell, faster than var=$(printf ...) in loops.
declare -p name prints how a variable is defined, including arrays, which helps debugging scripts.
type name tells whether a word is an alias, function, builtin or file; type -a name shows all matches in order.
bash -n script checks only the syntax without running anything, and shellcheck script finds common mistakes.
bash -u script and set -u stop at the first use of an unset variable, which finds typos in variable names.
In a script, cd "$(dirname "$0")" moves to the script's own folder, so relative paths work whatever the current folder was.
readlink -f "$0" gives the real path of a script even when it was called through a link, the base for finding files next to it.
Check for root at the start of scripts that need it: if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then echo "run with sudo"; exit 1; fi.
echo "text" >&2 sends a message to standard error, so it does not mix with the output a script returns to other programs.
Use exit codes consistently in scripts: 0 for success and different small numbers for different failures, so callers and systemd can react.
A lock file with mkdir is atomic: if mkdir /tmp/job.lock 2>/dev/null; then ...; rmdir /tmp/job.lock; fi stops two runs at once without extra tools.
sleep infinity keeps a process alive without using CPU, which is useful as the main command of a container or a test.
seq -f '%03g' 1 3 prints numbers with leading zeros, and seq 10 -2 0 counts down in steps.
printf '%s\n' {a..e} prints letters from a to e, one per line, a quick way to make test data.
Use the shell's built in test of a number: [[ $x =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] is true only when the value is made of digits.
BASH_REMATCH holds the groups of the last =~ match, so you can pull parts out of a string without sed.
Compare versions with sort -V: printf '%s\n' 1.10 1.9 | sort -V | tail -1 prints 1.10, because the comparison is numeric per part.
du -sb file prints the size in bytes exactly, and stat -c %s file does the same; use them in scripts instead of parsing ls.
numfmt --to=iec 123456789 converts a number of bytes to a readable size, and numfmt --from=iec 2K converts the other way.
date -d "2026-12-25" +%A prints the weekday of a date, and date -d "+3 days" +%F computes a future date in a script.
date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ prints the time in the ISO 8601 UTC format used by logs and APIs.
TZ=Europe/Istanbul date shows the time in another time zone for one command, without changing the system setting.
expr and bc can calculate but the shell does integer math by itself with $(( )); for floating point use awk 'BEGIN{print 10/4}'.
awk -v name=value passes a shell value into awk safely; never build the awk program by pasting a variable into it.
awk 'NR==FNR{a[$1]=$2; next} $1 in a {print $0, a[$1]}' file1 file2 joins two files on the first column without sorting.
awk '{ $1=""; print substr($0,2) }' removes the first column and keeps the rest of the line as it is.
awk 'END{print NR}' counts lines, and awk 'length($0)>m{m=length($0)} END{print m}' finds the longest line.
sed -n '$p' prints the last line, sed '1d' deletes the first and sed '$!N;s/\n/ /' joins every two lines.
sed -E 's/([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)/\2-\1/' swaps two numbers using groups; -E enables extended regular expressions without backslashes.
sed '/start/,/end/d' deletes a block between two marker lines, and sed '/pattern/a new line' adds a line after each match.
sed 's/[[:space:]]*$//' removes trailing spaces from every line, and sed 's/^[[:space:]]*//' removes leading spaces.
sed -i '/^$/N;/^\n$/D' file squeezes several empty lines into one, a cleanup for log and text files.
grep -c '' file counts lines even when the last line has no newline, which wc -l misses.
grep -rl text folder lists the files that contain the text, and grep -rL text folder lists the files that do not.
grep --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=node_modules -r text . skips folders that only waste time.
grep -P uses Perl regular expressions with lookahead and \d, available in GNU grep: grep -oP '(?<=id=)\d+' prints only the number after id=.
grep -m1 pattern stops after the first match, a speed gain on big files; grep -x matches whole lines only.
zgrep and zcat read compressed log files directly, so you can search old rotated logs without unpacking them.
tr -s '\n' removes empty lines and tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' lowercases text for plain ASCII; Turkish dotted letters need other tools.
uniq only removes neighbouring duplicates, so sort first; sort -u does both at once and uniq -d shows only the repeated lines.
sort -t, -k2,2nr sorts a CSV by the second column as a number in reverse; -k2,2 limits the key to one column.
head -c 100 file prints the first 100 bytes, and tail -c 100 the last; useful for peeking into big or binary files.
head -n -1 prints everything except the last line, and tail -n +2 everything except the first.
split -l 1000 file part_ cuts a text file into pieces of 1000 lines, and csplit splits at patterns.
wc -L file prints the length of the longest line, and wc -m counts characters instead of bytes.
fmt -w 60 text wraps paragraphs at a width, and fold -s -w 60 breaks lines at spaces.
od -An -tx1 file prints bytes as hexadecimal without addresses, and od -An -c shows control characters, a quick look into a file.
printf and echo -n differ between shells; in scripts use printf '%s' for text without a newline.
Use $'...' for special characters in bash: $'\t' is a tab and $'\n' a newline, handy in tr and cut.
Brace expansion happens before variables, so {1..$n} does not work; use seq or a for ((i=1;i<=n;i++)) loop.
trap 'echo error on line $LINENO' ERR shows where a script failed when set -e stops it.
trap '' INT ignores Ctrl+C in a script section, and trap - INT restores the default.
getopts is built in and handles short options; for long options such as --name use a while loop with case on $1 and shift.
Use ${1:?usage: script file} at the top of a script to stop with a message when a required argument is missing.
Use basename "$0" for the program name in usage messages and "$#" for the number of arguments.
In bash, $SECONDS counts the seconds since the shell started, a simple timer without date.
Run a command with a changed locale for stable output: LC_ALL=C sort gives byte order and the same result on every computer.
Use LC_ALL=C grep for faster searches in big ASCII files; UTF-8 locales make grep slower.
env -i bash --noprofile --norc starts a clean shell, the quick way to test a script without your own settings.
Shell options: shopt -s extglob enables patterns such as !(*.log) and +(a|b); shopt -s dotglob makes * match hidden files too.
globstar with shopt -s globstar lets ** match folders recursively: ls **/*.py lists every Python file below.
cp --reflink=auto and cp --sparse=always save space on file systems that support them; on ext4 they do nothing special but do no harm.
install -m 755 file /usr/local/bin/ copies a file and sets the mode in one step; install -d makes folders with a mode.
truncate -s 0 file empties a file without deleting it, so programs that hold it open keep writing to the same file; truncate -s 1G makes a sparse file.
tee -a log appends, and command 2>&1 | tee log shows output on the screen while saving it, handy for long installs.
script -q -c "command" log runs a command in a pseudo terminal and records everything, useful for programs that behave differently without a terminal.
stdbuf -oL command makes a program flush output line by line, so a pipe or log shows lines at once instead of in big chunks.
unbuffer from the expect package or python3 -u fixes delayed output in pipes; without it a program that writes to a pipe buffers its output.
yes '' | head -n 3 | wc -l prints three empty lines; yes y | command answers every question of an installer with y.
A program that asks for input can be fed with printf 'a\nb\n' | program, and with expect when it needs a real terminal.
watch -n1 'command' repeats every second; watch -g stops when the output changes, which suits waiting for a state.
timeout --foreground 5 command works for commands that read from the terminal, and timeout -k 2 5 command sends a kill two seconds after the first stop signal fails.
nohup writes to nohup.out when output is not redirected; always redirect with nohup command >log 2>&1 & to control the file.
pidof name prints the process numbers of a program by exact name, and pgrep -x name does the same with matching on the exact name.
killall name ends all processes with that exact name, pkill -f pattern matches the whole command line; check with pgrep -af first.
lsof -i :8000 shows which process listens on a port, and fuser -n tcp 8000 does the same; ss -ltnp is usually already installed.
A process that listens on a port should be started by a service manager; if you started it by hand in a terminal it ends when the terminal closes.
ulimit -a lists the limits of the shell; ulimit -u shows the process limit, and a fork bomb protection sets it low for normal users.
ionice -c3 command runs with idle disk priority and nice -n 19 with the lowest CPU priority, ideal for backups on a Raspberry Pi.
taskset -c 0 command pins a process to the first CPU core, and taskset -p PID shows the current mask; this helps measure or limit a program.
free -m shows megabytes and free -h shows human sizes; the available column counts memory that can be freed, so a low free value alone is no problem.
vmstat 1 5 prints memory, swap, disk and CPU activity every second five times; a high si and so means the system is swapping.
uptime shows the load averages; on a four core computer a load of 4 means all cores are fully used.
lscpu shows the processor model, number of cores and architecture, and lsblk shows disks; lspci and lsusb list the devices on those buses.
hostname -I prints all IP addresses of the computer in one line, the quickest way to find the address of a Pi.
uname -a prints kernel version and architecture; uname -m alone gives aarch64, armv7l or x86_64, the first thing to check before downloading a program.
cat /etc/os-release shows the distribution and version, and lsb_release -a does the same where installed; look here before you follow a guide.
systemd-analyze verify checks every unit it is given, also for dependencies that do not exist; an error such as Unit not found names the missing unit.
Unit file section and key names are case sensitive: ExecStart is right and execstart is ignored with a warning in the journal.
systemd-analyze calendar "Sat,Sun 22:00" shows the next weekend evenings; use it before you trust an OnCalendar line.
OnBootSec=2min starts a timer two minutes after boot and OnUnitActiveSec=1h repeats it one hour after the last run, a plain interval without calendar times.
systemd-analyze timestamp "2026-12-31 23:59" shows how systemd reads a time, including the UTC form and how long until then.
systemd-escape "a b" gives a name safe for units with spaces turned into \x20; systemd-escape -p /var/log gives var-log.
systemd-path lists the standard folders systemd knows, for example systemd-path user-configuration for user units.
systemd-tmpfiles can create and clean folders at boot from files in /etc/tmpfiles.d; a line d /run/name 0755 user group - creates a folder in RAM each start.
RuntimeDirectory=name in a service creates /run/name owned by the service user at start and removes it at stop, better than mkdir in a script.
StateDirectory=name creates /var/lib/name for persistent data and CacheDirectory=name creates /var/cache/name; LogsDirectory=name creates /var/log/name, all with the right owner.
ConditionPathExists=/path in the Unit section skips a service silently when a file is missing; AssertPathExists makes the start fail instead.
ConditionACPower=true starts a service only on mains power and ConditionHost=name only on one computer; the Condition lines never make a unit fail, they skip it.
ExecCondition=/path/test runs before ExecStart and a non-zero exit below 255 skips the service without marking it as failed.
ExecStopPost=/path runs after the service ended whatever the reason, a place for cleanup that must always happen.
SuccessExitStatus=143 treats exit code 143 (stopped by SIGTERM) as success so systemctl stop does not leave a failed state for programs that return it.
RestartPreventExitStatus=2 stops restart loops for an exit code that means a configuration error, so a broken service does not retry forever.
StartLimitIntervalSec=0 in the Unit section turns off the start rate limit, but fix the cause of the crash loop instead.
OnFailure=name.service starts another unit when this one fails, for example to send a message or restart a dependency.
Type=notify lets a program tell systemd when it is ready through sd_notify; Type=exec waits until the program is really started.
WatchdogSec=30 expects the program to send a keep-alive within 30 seconds, otherwise systemd restarts it; the program must call sd_notify WATCHDOG=1.
Environment variables of a running service are shown by systemctl show -p Environment name and in /proc/PID/environ.
systemctl show -p MainPID --value name prints only the process number of a service, ready for scripts.
systemctl show -p ActiveEnterTimestamp --value name prints when a service last became active.
systemctl show --property=NRestarts name tells how often systemd restarted a service since it started, a quick measure of flapping.
systemctl is-failed name returns 0 when the unit is in the failed state; combined with journalctl -u name it is the first step in every service problem.
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running lists running services, and --state=failed only the broken ones.
systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled lists services that start at boot, an overview of what a system really runs.
systemctl get-default shows the boot target, and systemctl isolate multi-user.target switches to the text mode right now without reboot.
systemctl rescue and systemctl emergency start recovery modes with a root shell; they need the root password and stop most services.
Add systemd.unit=rescue.target to the kernel command line in cmdline.txt on a Raspberry Pi to boot into a repair shell when the normal start fails.
Add init=/bin/sh to the Pi's cmdline.txt only as a last resort to reset a password; remount the root file system read-write first with mount -o remount,rw /.
systemd-analyze plot > boot.svg draws the boot as a time chart that you can open in a browser.
Mask services you never need, such as bluetooth.service or ModemManager.service on a headless Pi, with systemctl mask; it saves memory and boot time.
ModemManager and wpa_supplicant services are not needed on a wired headless Pi; stopping unused services is the cheapest speed up.
systemd-networkd and NetworkManager both manage the network; do not run two managers on the same interface or the settings fight each other.
systemd-timesyncd is a simple client for network time; timedatectl timesync-status shows the server and the offset.
journalctl --since today --until "1 hour ago" -u name limits a log search in time, and journalctl -r shows the newest lines first.
journalctl --list-boots lists the boots with numbers, so journalctl -b -2 can show the log before the last two boots.
journalctl -u name --output=short-iso prints sortable ISO times, and -o json-pretty shows every field of an entry for debugging.
journalctl _PID=1234 or _COMM=python3 filter by fields of the entries; journalctl -F _SYSTEMD_UNIT lists all values of a field.
journalctl --vacuum-time=7d removes entries older than a week, and --vacuum-files=5 keeps five journal files.
journalctl --verify checks the journal files for corruption, useful after a power loss on an SD card.
In journald.conf Storage=volatile keeps the log only in RAM, which saves SD card writes but loses the log at reboot; Storage=persistent keeps it.
RateLimitIntervalSec and RateLimitBurst in journald.conf decide when a noisy service gets its messages dropped; the log then says Suppressed messages.
systemd-cat -t name command sends the output of a command to the journal with a tag, good for scripts run by hand.
loginctl list-sessions shows logins and loginctl terminate-session id ends one; loginctl show-session id shows the type, x11 or wayland.
loginctl lock-sessions locks all desktop sessions and loginctl poweroff shuts down the computer through logind.
systemd-inhibit --what=sleep command command keeps the computer from sleeping while the command runs; systemd-inhibit --list shows who blocks sleep.
systemctl suspend, hibernate and hybrid-sleep exist on PCs; a Raspberry Pi has no suspend, so power it off or leave it running.
systemctl mask sleep.target suspend.target hibernate.target stops a PC from ever sleeping, useful for a home server on a laptop.
hostnamectl shows hostname, machine id, kernel, architecture and virtualisation in one view, a good first command on a new system.
localectl set-locale LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8 sets the system language and localectl set-keymap tr sets the console keyboard layout.
timedatectl show -p Timezone --value prints only the time zone name, handy in scripts.
systemd-analyze security --no-pager name shows an exposure score from 0 to 10; lower is better, and each line explains one possible hardening setting.
ProtectHome=true hides /home from a service, ProtectKernelTunables=true makes /proc/sys read-only and PrivateDevices=true hides most device files.
DynamicUser=yes lets systemd create a temporary user for a service, so no account needs to be made by hand.
CapabilityBoundingSet= with an empty value removes all Linux capabilities from a service; add AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE to allow low ports only.
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 lets a service use only IP sockets, and IPAddressDeny=any with IPAddressAllow=localhost blocks all other network traffic of a service.
LimitNOFILE=65536 raises the open file limit of a service, because ulimit settings from the shell do not apply to services.
TasksMax=100 limits the number of processes and threads of a service, a protection against runaway forks.
MemoryHigh=200M slows a service down before MemoryMax kills it, a softer limit for small computers.
Slice=name.slice groups services under a common resource limit; systemd-cgtop shows CPU, memory and IO per group live.
systemctl set-property name MemoryMax=500M changes a limit of a running service at once and keeps it in a drop-in; add --runtime to make it temporary.
A user service lives in ~/.config/systemd/user and starts with systemctl --user enable --now name; it needs loginctl enable-linger to run without a login.
journalctl --user -u name shows the log of a user service, and systemctl --user daemon-reload applies unit changes.
graphical-session.target is the right dependency for a user service that needs the desktop: PartOf=graphical-session.target and After=graphical-session.target.
A socket unit can start a service on the first connection: ListenStream=8080 in name.socket starts name.service when somebody connects.
Accept=yes in a socket unit starts one service instance per connection, and Accept=no hands the socket to one long running service.
systemctl list-sockets shows the ports that systemd listens on for services, and what unit they start.
A path unit PathExists=/file starts a service when a file appears, and PathModified watches content changes; remember to enable the .path unit.
Mount units are named after the path: /mnt/data becomes mnt-data.mount; an entry in /etc/fstab is turned into a unit automatically at boot.
x-systemd.automount in an fstab option mounts a drive on first access, and x-systemd.device-timeout=10 stops a missing drive from delaying the boot for a minute and a half.
nofail in fstab lets the boot continue when a drive is missing; without it a missing USB disk can drop the Pi into emergency mode.
systemd-fsck runs a file system check at boot, and fsck.mode=force in the kernel command line forces a check once.
A swap file can be a unit too: swapon --show lists swap, and dphys-swapfile manages the file on Raspberry Pi OS.
systemctl daemon-reexec restarts systemd itself without a reboot, which is rarely needed but can free a stuck manager.
coredumpctl gdb opens the last crash in gdb, and coredumpctl list shows the programs that crashed with the signal and time.
systemd-run --pty command starts a command in a transient service with a terminal, and --property=MemoryMax=100M limits it like a service.
systemd-run --on-calendar="*-*-* 03:00" command creates a transient timer without writing files; systemctl list-timers shows it.
systemctl --state=failed --no-legend prints only the failed unit names, easy to count in a monitoring script.
systemctl status shows the last log lines of a service; add -n 50 for more, or use journalctl -u name -n 50 --no-pager.
After= and Requires= are different: After= only orders, Requires= creates the dependency; use both when a service needs another one running first.
Wants= is a weak dependency that does not stop your service when the other one fails; BindsTo= stops it when the other ends.
Before= and After= in a drop-in change the start order without editing the original file; remember to run daemon-reload.
A unit in /etc/systemd/system overrides one with the same name in /lib/systemd/system, and systemctl cat shows which file is used.
systemctl revert name removes all your overrides of a unit and returns to the packaged version.
Reload does not exist for many services; ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID defines it and is the standard way to make a service reread its configuration.
$MAINPID in ExecReload and ExecStop is replaced by the main process number, so a unit can signal its own program.
Use ExecStart=/bin/bash -c 'exec python3 /path/app.py' when you need shell features but still want the program to be the main process.
Restart=on-abnormal restarts after signals, timeouts and watchdog failures but not after a normal error exit, a middle way between on-failure and always.
TimeoutStartSec=infinity lets a slow service such as a big database start without being killed by the default 90 second limit.
Raspberry Pi OS is based on Debian; the Bookworm release uses Debian 12, NetworkManager, Wayland on the desktop and a journal only log, which differs from Bullseye guides.
Check the version of Raspberry Pi OS with cat /etc/os-release and the kernel with uname -r before you follow an install guide.
On a 64 bit Raspberry Pi OS dpkg --print-architecture gives arm64; many programs ship separate downloads for arm64 and armhf, so pick the right one.
A Raspberry Pi 4 with 4 GB or more of RAM runs well with a 64 bit system; 32 bit images are better for the Pi Zero, Pi 1 and for tiny memory.
The Pi Zero 2 W has four cores but only 512 MB of RAM; add swap or zram for compilers, and avoid running a full browser and a model server together.
Compiling big programs on a Raspberry Pi is slow and can run out of memory; use make -j2 instead of -j4 on boards with 1 GB, or cross compile on a PC.
pip install on a Raspberry Pi may take a long time because packages such as numpy are compiled; piwheels, the default extra index on Raspberry Pi OS, offers ready made wheels.
Raspberry Pi OS configures piwheels in /etc/pip.conf, so pip downloads prebuilt packages for the Pi when they exist; check that file if installs compile unexpectedly.
A Raspberry Pi should be powered through the official supply or a good 5 V 3 A one; the throttled flags in vcgencmd get_throttled tell whether voltage dropped.
The Pi 4 USB-C power port also works as the data port for the USB gadget mode only when powered through the GPIO header or a splitter; with a normal setup use the host cable for both.
USB gadget mode of the Pi lets it appear as a serial port, network card or storage on a computer; it needs dtoverlay=dwc2 and the right modules in cmdline.txt or a gadget script.
modules-load=dwc2,g_serial in cmdline.txt turns the Pi into a USB serial device at boot; it is one line, so add it to the existing line with a space and never create a second line.
cmdline.txt must stay a single line; a stray newline in the middle makes the Pi ignore everything after it and may stop the boot.
Edit cmdline.txt and config.txt only after making a copy; a typo can stop the Pi from booting, but the SD card can be fixed on another computer because the boot partition is plain FAT.
The boot partition of a Pi SD card shows up on Windows and macOS as a small drive; the ssh and userconf files placed there enable SSH and create a user at the first boot.
An empty file named ssh in the boot partition turns on the SSH server at the first boot, and userconf.txt holds the user name and a password hash created with openssl passwd -6.
wpa_supplicant.conf in the boot partition no longer sets Wi-Fi on Bookworm; use the Raspberry Pi Imager or nmcli instead.
nmcli device wifi connect name password pass --ifname wlan0 joins a Wi-Fi network on Bookworm, and nmcli connection show lists what is saved.
nmcli connection modify name connection.autoconnect-priority 10 makes one saved Wi-Fi network preferred over others when several are in range.
Wi-Fi power saving can make SSH sessions feel slow on a Pi; iw dev wlan0 set power_save off turns it off until the next boot, and a NetworkManager setting makes it permanent.
The Pi has no hardware clock; timedatectl shows System clock synchronized: yes when it has network time, and a wrong clock breaks HTTPS and apt.
Use sudo raspi-config nonint get_ssh to read whether SSH is on (0 means enabled), and do_ssh 0 to turn it on; the nonint mode suits setup scripts.
raspi-config nonint do_boot_behaviour B4 sets boot to the desktop with auto login, and B2 sets console with auto login; B1 is console with password.
raspi-config nonint do_i2c 0 enables the I2C bus and do_spi 0 the SPI bus; 0 means on and 1 means off in the nonint interface.
raspi-config nonint do_expand_rootfs grows the root partition to fill the SD card, needed after writing a small image to a big card on some images.
df -h / shows how much of the SD card is used; if the root file system looks small after flashing, expand it with raspi-config.
Raspberry Pi OS Lite boots into a text console and uses about 100 MB of RAM idle, a good base for an agent that only needs a browser on demand.
With a desktop the Pi 4 uses 300 to 500 MB of RAM; Chromium alone can need 500 MB or more per heavy tab, so close tabs in automation.
A kiosk or automation Pi should hide the mouse cursor, turn off screen blanking and disable the lock screen, otherwise a sleeping screen blocks screenshots.
xset s off, xset -dpms and xset s noblank turn off screen saver and power saving under X11; on Wayland the compositor settings do it.
raspi-config Display Options, Screen Blanking turns off blanking on X11 images; on Wayland labwc it is handled by the idle settings of the desktop.
HDMI audio, the headphone jack and USB sound cards are different devices; aplay -l lists them and a setting in the desktop or alsamixer picks the default.
A Pi can use a USB microphone with arecord -D plughw:1,0 -f cd test.wav; check the level in alsamixer so recordings are not silent.
The Pi has no built in microphone input; a USB sound card or USB microphone is the simplest way to record sound.
A Raspberry Pi Camera Module works with the rpicam tools on Bookworm; the old raspistill and the legacy camera stack are gone, so old scripts need updating.
libcamera and rpicam-apps need a recent kernel; if rpicam-hello shows no cameras after an update, check the ribbon cable and run sudo apt full-upgrade.
GPIO numbering has two schemes: BCM numbers like GPIO17 and physical pin numbers like pin 11; gpiozero uses BCM numbers by default, so mixing them up is a common wiring bug.
pinout shows a picture of the GPIO header in the terminal when gpiozero is installed, so you do not need a printed chart.
Use a level shifter between a 5 V device and a Pi GPIO pin, or a voltage divider with two resistors on an input; never connect 5 V directly.
Pull-up and pull-down resistors keep an input pin at a defined level; gpiozero Button uses an internal pull-up by default, so the button connects the pin to ground.
A relay board often needs 5 V power and an active-low signal; test with a multimeter or an LED first, and use a board with optocouplers to protect the Pi.
A DHT22 temperature sensor needs a pull-up resistor on the data line and a delay of two seconds between readings; the adafruit-circuitpython-dht library is the maintained choice.
A DS18B20 temperature sensor uses the 1-Wire bus: add dtoverlay=w1-gpio to config.txt and read the files under /sys/bus/w1/devices/.
I2C devices share two wires and each has an address; i2cdetect -y 1 shows them, and two devices with the same address need a multiplexer or a different address setting.
SPI devices need the SPI bus enabled in raspi-config and a chip select pin each; spidev gives access from Python with spidev.SpiDev().
PWM on the Pi: pins 12, 13, 18 and 19 have hardware PWM; software PWM from gpiozero jitters under load, so servos shake.
A servo should get its own 5 V supply with a common ground; powering it from the Pi's 5 V pin can brown out the Pi when the motor starts.
Debounce buttons in software or with a small capacitor; gpiozero Button already debounces with bounce_time when you set it.
GPIO access from a service needs the right group; the user must be in the gpio group on older systems, and on Bookworm the /dev/gpiochip devices are used.
A Pi can run without a monitor but needs an HDMI dummy plug for some remote desktop and screenshot tools, because without a display the graphics session has no screen.
VNC on the Pi: sudo raspi-config nonint do_vnc 0 turns on the server, and a fixed resolution in raspi-config Display Options is needed for a headless Pi.
RealVNC on Bookworm works with Wayland through wayvnc; on X11 images the older RealVNC server is used, so pick the viewer that matches.
Remote desktop through xrdp works on X11 sessions; it needs the xrdp package and an X session, and does not share the desktop that is on the HDMI screen.
Use ssh -X user@pi to show a single graphical program on your own computer, and ssh -Y if -X gives errors; the program runs on the Pi but draws on your screen.
Use sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y about once a month on a Pi that is online; reboot afterwards when the kernel or firmware changed.
sudo apt install unattended-upgrades enables automatic security updates; for a device that must never reboot unexpectedly, configure Automatic-Reboot to false.
dpkg -l | grep raspberrypi shows the packages that carry firmware and kernel; holding them with apt-mark hold avoids surprises on a working system.
A Pi that was working and stopped after an update can often be repaired by booting an old kernel: copy the previous kernel image back or restore an SD card backup.
Back up a running Pi with rsync of /etc, /home and /opt, and keep a list of installed packages with dpkg --get-selections > packages.txt for a quick rebuild.
The best backup of a Pi is a full SD card image after the setup works; store it on another computer and label it with the date.
Use two SD cards, one for tests and one for the working system; swapping cards is quicker than undoing a bad experiment.
Label SD cards and keep the card in the Pi's slot with the contacts facing the board; a loose card gives read errors and a filesystem that turns read-only.
If the root file system turns read-only, dmesg shows I/O errors; the card or power is failing, so back up what you can and replace the card.
A Pi that boots with a read-only file system after a crash may need fsck from another computer; ext4 partitions of the card can be checked with e2fsck on Linux.
Use f3 or badblocks on Linux to test a new SD card for fake capacity before you trust it; fake cards lose data when they are full.
Write the OS image with Raspberry Pi Imager or balenaEtcher and use the verify option; a failed write is a common cause of random errors.
Enable the hardware watchdog with dtparam=watchdog=on and RuntimeWatchdogSec=15 in /etc/systemd/system.conf so the Pi reboots itself when it freezes.
A UPS HAT or a small battery keeps a Pi running through short power cuts and allows a clean shutdown; a sudden power loss is the main cause of corrupted SD cards.
Put a heat sink on the CPU, the RAM and the USB controller of a Pi 4; the USB controller also gets hot and can cause USB errors when it throttles.
A fan controlled by the Pi 5 firmware starts at 50 degrees by default; the temperature steps can be changed with dtparam=fan_temp0 and the related lines in config.txt.
Use vcgencmd measure_temp in a cron or timer and log the value; a graph over a day shows whether your cooling is enough under load.
The Pi 5 has a power button and an RTC battery connector; with a small battery connected the clock keeps the time without network.
The Pi 5 does not provide a 3.5 mm audio jack or an analog video output, and its USB gadget mode works on the USB-C port only.
A Pi 5 boots faster from an NVMe SSD through a HAT; set the boot order with raspi-config and enable PCIe with dtparam=pciex1 in config.txt.
Use a USB 3 SSD on a Pi 4 with a good case or adapter; some adapters need the quirks option usb-storage.quirks=VID:PID:u in cmdline.txt to work with UAS.
The Pi 4 can boot from USB when the bootloader is up to date; sudo rpi-eeprom-update shows the version and raspi-config lets you pick USB boot.
A Pi that boots only with a keyboard attached usually has a power or boot order problem; try another power supply and a minimal config.txt.
Use a fixed address through a DHCP reservation in the router so the Pi keeps the same address after a restart; the Pi itself needs no static setting then.
If wlan0 does not appear on the Pi, run rfkill list and set the Wi-Fi country; a blocked radio is the usual reason on a fresh install.
Raspberry Pi OS needs the Wi-Fi country set before the radio turns on; raspi-config Localisation Options, WLAN Country does it, or nmcli radio wifi on after setting the country.
A Bluetooth keyboard or speaker is paired with bluetoothctl: power on, agent on, scan on, pair, trust and connect; trust makes it reconnect after a reboot.
Bluetooth audio on a Pi needs pipewire-audio or pulseaudio-module-bluetooth installed; without it a connected speaker shows no sound output.
A Pi that shares its internet through a USB cable needs a network gadget; with g_ether the host computer sees a new network card and the Pi uses the address 169.254 or a static one.
A Pi can be an access point with NetworkManager: nmcli device wifi hotspot ifname wlan0 ssid name password pass creates one without extra packages on Bookworm.
For a fast first setup use Raspberry Pi Imager's OS customisation: it sets hostname, user, Wi-Fi, locale and SSH keys, so the Pi is reachable at the first boot.
Keep a note of the Pi's hostname, user, and how you reach it; a Pi without a screen is easy to lose track of when the address changes.
str.strip('abc') removes any of the characters a, b and c from both ends, not the text abc; this surprises many people.
str.split(None, 1) splits on any whitespace only once, str.rsplit(',', 1) splits once from the right, good for a file name and its extension.
str.splitlines() splits at all kinds of line breaks and does not leave an empty last item, unlike split('\n').
str.zfill(5) pads a number text with zeros on the left and keeps the sign: '42'.zfill(5) gives 00042.
str.center, ljust and rjust align text in a fixed width; f"{text:^20}" and f"{text:<20}" do the same in an f-string.
str.isdigit() is True for characters such as superscript two; use str.isdecimal() or a regular expression when you need real digits.
str.translate with str.maketrans replaces many single characters at once and is faster than many replace calls.
str.format_map(dict) fills placeholders from a dictionary and works with defaultdict for missing keys, handy for templates.
'%s' % tuple needs a tuple, so '%s' % (value,) is safe when the value itself may be a tuple; f-strings avoid the problem.
int('0x1f', 16) and int('1f', 16) both give 31, int('0b101', 0) detects the base from the prefix, and hex(), bin() and oct() go the other way.
Integers in Python have no size limit, so 2**1000 works; but float conversion of huge ints raises OverflowError.
Floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3; use round for display, math.isclose for comparison and decimal.Decimal for money.
decimal.Decimal('1.10') + Decimal('2.20') is exactly 3.30; always create Decimal from a string, not from a float.
fractions.Fraction(1, 3) keeps exact fractions, and Fraction('0.25') gives 1/4, useful for exact ratios.
round(2.5) gives 2 and round(3.5) gives 4, because Python rounds half to even; use Decimal with ROUND_HALF_UP for school rounding.
math.floor, math.ceil and int differ for negative numbers: int(-1.5) is -1, math.floor(-1.5) is -2.
a // b rounds down toward minus infinity and a % b has the sign of b, so -7 // 2 is -4 and -7 % 2 is 1.
statistics.mean, median and stdev give simple statistics without numpy; statistics.median_low and median_high pick real data points.
random.sample(items, 3) picks three different items, random.choice picks one and random.shuffle shuffles a list in place; use random.seed(1) to repeat a test.
random.choices(items, weights=[5,1], k=3) picks with replacement and weights, for example for a loot table in a game.
math.hypot(x, y) gives the distance from the origin and math.dist(p, q) the distance between two points, with fewer rounding errors than a hand made formula.
math.atan2(y, x) gives the angle of a direction in all four quadrants; math.degrees converts it, a basic tool for aiming in games and robots.
Clamp a value with max(low, min(high, x)); a small function clamp(x, lo, hi) keeps sensor values and slider positions inside limits.
Linear interpolation is a + (b - a) * t with t from 0 to 1; map a value from one range to another with (x - a1) / (a2 - a1) * (b2 - b1) + b1.
bisect.bisect_left(sorted_list, x) finds a place in a sorted list in logarithmic time, and bisect.insort inserts and keeps the order.
heapq.nsmallest(3, items) and nlargest return the extremes without sorting everything, and heapq.heappush with heappop makes a priority queue.
sorted(items, key=str.lower) sorts ignoring case, and sorted with a tuple key such as (-score, name) sorts by score descending and name ascending.
list.sort() returns None and changes the list; sorted() returns a new list; assigning x = x.sort() loses the list.
list.index(x) raises ValueError if x is missing; check with x in list first or catch the error, and use enumerate when you need positions of all matches.
dict.pop(key, None) removes a key and never raises; del d[key] raises KeyError for a missing key.
Dictionaries keep insertion order since Python 3.7; sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]) gives a sorted view, and dict(sorted(...)) a sorted copy.
dict.fromkeys(items) removes duplicates and keeps the order: list(dict.fromkeys([3,1,3,2])) gives [3, 1, 2], while set() loses the order.
collections.ChainMap(a, b) looks up a key in several dictionaries in order without copying them, a clean way to layer settings.
collections.namedtuple('P', 'x y') makes light read-only records with names; typing.NamedTuple adds type hints, and dataclasses add mutability.
A tuple with one item needs a comma: (1,) is a tuple and (1) is only the number one in parentheses.
Unpacking with a star takes the rest: first, *rest = [1, 2, 3] gives rest as [2, 3], and a, b = b, a swaps two variables.
The underscore is the usual name for a value you ignore: a, _ = pair, and in a loop for _ in range(3) repeats three times.
set.add, set.discard and set.remove: remove raises KeyError for a missing item, discard does not.
frozenset can be a dictionary key or a set item, because it is hashable; a normal set cannot.
Compare floats and sequences carefully: [1,2] == [1,2] is True, [1,2] is [1,2] is False because is compares identity.
Small integers and some strings are cached, so a is b can be True by accident; never use is to compare values.
Chained comparisons work: 0 < x < 10 is the same as 0 < x and x < 10, and x is evaluated once.
and and or return one of their operands, not only True or False: name = user_input or 'default' picks the default for empty text.
Values that count as false are None, 0, 0.0, empty text, empty lists, dicts and sets; if items: tests for non empty, but 0 is false too, so use is None for missing.
The conditional expression a if cond else b is an expression; nest it only once, because chains become hard to read.
Use range(len(x)) only when you really need the index; otherwise iterate over the items directly or with enumerate.
reversed(items) and sorted(items, reverse=True) are iterators and lists; reversed works on sequences and does not copy them.
itertools.product('ab', repeat=2) makes all combinations with repetition, permutations orders items and combinations picks subsets.
itertools.accumulate([1,2,3]) gives running totals 1, 3, 6, and itertools.pairwise(items) (Python 3.10) gives neighbouring pairs.
itertools.cycle repeats an iterable forever, itertools.repeat(x, n) repeats a value n times and itertools.count(10, 5) counts 10, 15, 20 and so on.
itertools.zip_longest(a, b, fillvalue=0) pairs lists of different length and fills the missing places instead of cutting.
itertools.takewhile and dropwhile cut a stream at a condition, itertools.filterfalse keeps the items that fail the test.
functools.partial(func, 2) fixes the first argument and returns a new function, a clean replacement for small lambdas in callbacks.
functools.reduce(lambda a, b: a*b, items, 1) folds a list into one value; for sums and products prefer sum and math.prod.
Late binding trap: lambdas created in a loop all see the last value of the loop variable; bind it with a default argument: lambda i=i: i.
typing.TypedDict describes the keys of a dict for type checkers, typing.Protocol describes behaviour without inheritance and typing.Literal limits a value to given constants.
from __future__ import annotations delays the evaluation of type hints, so a class can mention itself in its own methods.
sys.stdin.read() reads all input and for line in sys.stdin reads line by line, which lets a script work in a pipe.
print(*items, sep=', ', end='') prints without a newline and with a separator; file=sys.stderr sends the text to standard error.
input() always returns text; convert with int() or float() and catch ValueError, and strip() removes the newline and spaces.
Path.suffix, stem, name and parent split a path: Path('/a/b.tar.gz').suffix is .gz and suffixes gives ['.tar', '.gz'].
Path.with_suffix('.bak') and with_name('x.txt') build a new path from an old one without string operations.
Path.resolve() gives the absolute path with links resolved and Path.home() the home folder; Path.cwd() is the current folder.
os.environ['NAME'] raises KeyError when the variable is missing and os.environ.get returns None; os.getenv does the same as get.
os.path.expanduser('~/x') turns the tilde into the home folder and os.path.expandvars('$HOME/x') fills environment variables.
os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True) is the old way and Path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) the new way of making all missing folders.
os.getpid() gives the process number and os.kill(pid, 0) tests if a process exists; psutil gives much more on any system.
os.urandom(16) gives random bytes from the system, secrets.token_bytes(16) is the same with a clearer name for secrets.
time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') formats the local time and time.gmtime() gives UTC; datetime.strptime parses text back to a datetime.
datetime.timestamp() gives seconds since 1970 and datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, tz=timezone.utc) builds an aware datetime from it.
calendar.monthrange(2026, 2) returns the weekday of the first day and the number of days, so the last day of February 2026 is 28.
datetime.date.today().isocalendar() gives the ISO year, week number and weekday, and date.weekday() counts Monday as 0.
dateutil.relativedelta adds months correctly, which timedelta cannot do; Jan 31 plus one month gives Feb 28; install python-dateutil.
The GIL lets only one thread run Python code at a time; threads help with waiting on network and disk, while multiprocessing helps with CPU heavy loops.
if __name__ == '__main__': is required around multiprocessing code on Windows and macOS, because child processes import the file again.
shlex.quote(text) makes a value safe for a shell command line and shlex.split(line) splits a command line like the shell does; avoid shell=True with user input.
signal.alarm(5) raises SIGALRM after five seconds on Linux, a simple timeout for a block of code; it does not exist on Windows.
socket.gethostname() and socket.gethostbyname(name) give the host name and an IPv4 address; socket.getaddrinfo returns all addresses, IPv6 too.
A TCP stream has no message boundaries: recv(1024) may return half a message or two; send a length prefix such as struct.pack('>I', n) or a newline and read until it arrives.
selectors or select.select wait for many sockets at once without threads; asyncio builds on the same system calls and is easier for new code.
http.client and urllib.request need no extra packages: urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10).read() fetches a page, but requests is easier for headers, sessions and JSON.
JSON has no tuples, sets or bytes and its keys are always text: json.dumps({1: 'a'}) gives {"1": "a"}, so integer keys come back as text.
tomllib.loads(text) parses TOML into a dict in the standard library of Python 3.11 and later, and it reads only; writing needs a package such as tomli-w.
pickle is not safe for data from others and breaks between Python versions; shelve and sqlite3 are better for simple local storage and json for exchange.
binascii.hexlify and bytes.hex give hexadecimal text; int.from_bytes(b, 'little') reads little endian numbers as used by most microcontrollers.
A checksum such as zlib.crc32(data) finds accidental damage in data and is not a security check; use hashlib.sha256 or an HMAC for security.
hmac.new(key, msg, 'sha256').hexdigest() signs a message with a shared secret, and hmac.compare_digest checks it without timing leaks.
secrets.choice(alphabet) and secrets.token_hex(16) are the right tools for passwords and tokens, because random is predictable.
Passwords must be stored as salted slow hashes: hashlib.scrypt or pbkdf2_hmac with a random salt and a high cost, never plain sha256 of the password alone.
ssl.create_default_context() gives a client context that checks certificates and host names; never turn verification off with CERT_NONE except in a throw-away test.
importlib.import_module('name') loads a module by a text name, and importlib.util.find_spec('name') tells whether a module is installed without importing it.
sys.version_info >= (3, 9) tests the Python version in code, and sys.platform starts with linux, win32 or darwin.
python3 -m site shows the folders where packages are installed, and python3 -m pip --version shows which Python a pip belongs to, the fix for packages installed for the wrong Python.
python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' shows which interpreter runs, useful inside virtual environments and services.
python3 -m venv .venv then .venv/bin/python script.py runs a script with its packages without activating; services should use this full path.
pip install --no-cache-dir saves space on an SD card, and pip cache purge empties the cache; pip download -d folder fetches wheels for an offline install.
pip show name prints version, location and dependencies of an installed package, and pip show -f lists its files.
A requirements.txt line such as name==1.2.3 pins an exact version; add hashes with pip-compile --generate-hashes for installs that must never change.
pyproject.toml is the modern project file: [project] holds name, version and dependencies, and [build-system] names the build tool such as setuptools or hatchling.
python3 -m build creates a wheel and a source archive from pyproject.toml, and twine upload sends them to a package index; test on TestPyPI first.
python3 -m compileall folder compiles all files to bytecode and reports syntax errors in every file of a project at once.
python3 -W ignore script.py hides warnings and python3 -W error turns them into exceptions; the warnings module can filter one category in code.
python3 -O removes assert statements and python3 -OO also docstrings; never rely on assert for checks that must always happen.
python3 -i script.py runs a script and then leaves you in the interactive prompt with all its variables, a quick way to debug a state.
python3 -m pydoc name shows the documentation of a module in the terminal and python3 -m pydoc -k word searches module summaries.
help(object) and dir(object) are the fastest way to explore a library in the prompt; vars(obj) shows attributes as a dict.
inspect.signature(func) shows the parameters of a function, and inspect.getsource(func) prints its source; both help when documentation is missing.
sys.excepthook can catch every uncaught error of the main thread to log it; threading.excepthook does the same for threads, so background errors are not lost.
faulthandler.enable() prints a traceback when the interpreter crashes or hangs on a signal; faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(30) shows where a program is stuck.
gc.collect() forces a cleanup of reference cycles and gc.get_count() shows the generation counters; manual calls rarely help, but are useful in tests for leaks.
Prefer composition to deep inheritance: keep an object as an attribute and call its methods; it is easier to test and to change later.
Use __all__ = ['name'] in a module to list the public names that from module import * exports, and start private helper names with an underscore.
Avoid circular imports by moving shared code to a third module or importing inside a function; the error says cannot import name because the module was only half loaded.
Module level code runs once at the first import; keep it free of side effects such as network calls so that importing the module in tests is safe.
Name constants in capital letters, classes in CapWords and functions and variables in snake_case; PEP 8 is the common style, and ruff or black format code automatically.
zip(a, b, strict=True) raises an error when the lists have different lengths instead of silently cutting the longer one; it needs Python 3.10 or later.
Write files safely by writing to a temporary name and then calling os.replace; the replace is atomic, so a power loss never leaves a half written file.
argparse with action='store_true' makes a flag that is False by default and True when given.
dataclasses.dataclass creates __init__, __repr__ and comparison for simple data classes; field(default_factory=list) is the correct way to have a list default.
Never use a mutable default such as def f(x=[]); the same list is shared by all calls. Use None and create the list inside.
functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None) caches results of a pure function; cache_clear() empties it.
itertools.groupby groups only neighbouring equal items, so sort the data by the same key first.
Use the walrus operator when you need a value and a test together: if (n := len(items)) > 10: print(n).
match statements in Python 3.10 and later compare structure: match command.split(): case ['go', direction]: ...
int(x) raises ValueError on bad text; wrap user input in try/except ValueError instead of testing with isdigit(), which fails on negative numbers.
raise NewError('text') from err keeps the original error as the cause in the traceback.
try/except/else/finally: else runs only when no error happened and finally always runs, a good place to release resources.
contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError) ignores one expected error in a with block, shorter than try/except/pass.
Write your own context manager with @contextlib.contextmanager and yield; code after yield runs on exit, also after errors if you use try/finally.
tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() creates a folder that is deleted when the with block ends, ideal for tests.
csv.writer(f).writerow(row) quotes fields correctly; never build CSV lines with join, because commas in the data break it.
sqlite3 is part of Python: connect, execute with ? placeholders and commit. Never format values into SQL text with f-strings.
sqlite3.Row as row_factory lets you read columns by name: row['name'] instead of row[0].
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL in SQLite allows readers during a write and is faster on most systems; it is a good default for small servers.
Use with conn: in sqlite3 to commit on success and roll back on an exception; it does not close the connection.
sqlite3 executemany inserts many rows in one call and is much faster than looping with execute and commit each time.
threading.Event is a clean stop signal for worker threads: loop with while not stop.is_set(): and use stop.wait(1) instead of time.sleep(1).
queue.Queue is thread safe; put items in one thread and get them in another, with task_done and join to wait for work to finish.
Mark background threads with daemon=True so they do not block program exit; use normal threads when they must finish their work.
concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor runs many I/O tasks in parallel with map; use ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU heavy work.
threading.Lock in a with block protects shared data; without it two threads can update the same counter at once and lose changes.
asyncio.run(main()) starts an event loop once at the top of the program; never call it from inside a running loop.
asyncio.gather(*tasks) runs coroutines at the same time and returns results in order; add return_exceptions=True so one failure does not hide the others.
asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=5) cancels a coroutine after five seconds with TimeoutError, the standard way to bound a network call.
Never call blocking functions such as time.sleep or requests.get inside async code; use asyncio.sleep and an async client, or run them with asyncio.to_thread.
asyncio.Semaphore(5) limits how many tasks run at once, for example five parallel downloads.
asyncio.Queue connects producers and consumers inside an event loop; put and get are awaitable and respect maxsize.
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handler) lets a program close files and connections cleanly when systemd stops it.
atexit.register(function) runs cleanup code when the interpreter exits normally; it does not run after a kill or a crash.
unittest.mock.patch replaces a function during a test, so tests do not need a real network or hardware.
Use yield in a function to produce values one by one; the function runs only as far as the consumer asks, ideal for reading huge files.
copy.deepcopy copies nested data completely; list.copy() and a slice copy only the outer list, inner lists stay shared.
socket.settimeout(5) makes blocking reads fail after five seconds instead of waiting forever; set it on every socket you create.
socket.setsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, 1) lets a server restart at once without the address already in use error.
Bind a test server to port 0 and the system picks a free port; read it back with getsockname()[1].
os.chmod(path, 0o600) restricts a file to its owner; create secret files with os.open(path, os.O_CREAT|os.O_WRONLY, 0o600) so they are never readable by others.
os.walk(path) goes through a folder tree; modify dirnames in place to skip folders such as .git.
fcntl.flock on a lock file stops two copies of a script from running at the same time on Linux.
memoryview and bytearray avoid copies when you handle large binary buffers and slice them.
enum.Enum gives named constants with safe comparison; use auto() so you do not number values by hand.
__slots__ in a class removes the per-object dictionary and saves memory when you create very many small objects.
@property turns a method into an attribute that can compute or validate values while callers still write obj.name.
@staticmethod and @classmethod: use a classmethod for alternative constructors such as Config.from_file(path).
sqlite3 db.sqlite '.backup copy.sqlite' makes a consistent copy of a database that is in use; copying the file with cp can give a broken copy.
sqlite3 db 'PRAGMA integrity_check;' prints ok when a database is healthy; run it after a power loss on a Raspberry Pi.
VACUUM in SQLite rebuilds the file and frees the space of deleted rows; it needs free disk space about the size of the database.
CREATE INDEX on the columns you filter or sort by speeds up queries a lot; EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether SQLite uses it.
A trailing backslash continues a command on the next line, and a pipe or && at the end of a line does the same without a backslash.
bytes and str are different types: b'a' + 'a' raises TypeError; encode text with .encode() before sending and decode bytes with .decode().
A moving average of the last n values with collections.deque(maxlen=n) and sum(d) / len(d) smooths noisy sensor data without storing the whole history.
Python sorts are stable, so sorting by one key and then by another keeps the first order among equal items; sort by the minor key first.
Removing items from a list while looping over it skips items; loop over a copy, or build a new list with a comprehension.
dict.setdefault(key, []).append(x) creates the list on first use, a one line grouping pattern; defaultdict(list) does the same.
dict.items() while changing the dictionary raises RuntimeError; loop over list(d.items()) when you delete keys.
Only hashable objects can be dictionary keys or set members; lists and dicts are not, use tuples or frozensets instead.
A class that defines __eq__ without __hash__ is unhashable; define both when objects should work in sets and as keys.
for ... else runs the else block only when the loop did not hit break, a neat pattern for search loops.
while True with break is fine for loops that need the first pass; the walrus operator removes duplicate reads: while (line := f.readline()):.
functools.cache is a shorter name for lru_cache(maxsize=None) in Python 3.9 and later, and functools.cached_property computes an attribute once per object.
functools.wraps(func) inside a decorator keeps the name and docstring of the wrapped function, so logs and help show the right name.
A decorator with arguments needs three levels of functions: the outer takes the arguments, the middle takes the function and the inner is the wrapper.
A closure keeps access to variables of the surrounding function; use nonlocal to change them, otherwise the assignment makes a new local variable.
*args collects extra positional arguments in a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments in a dict; a bare * in the signature makes later arguments keyword only.
A slash in a function signature, def f(a, /, b), makes the arguments before it positional only (Python 3.8 and later).
Call a function with a list or dict of arguments using f(*args, **kwargs); the star unpacks the list into positional arguments.
Docstrings in triple quotes are available at run time as func.__doc__ and through help(func); a one line summary first makes tools show it well.
abc.ABC with @abstractmethod makes a base class that cannot be created until subclasses implement the methods.
__repr__ should help debugging and __str__ should help users; define __repr__ first, because print falls back to it.
__eq__, __lt__ and functools.total_ordering give you all comparisons from two methods; dataclass(order=True) does the same from the fields.
dataclass(frozen=True) makes instances immutable and hashable, so they work as dictionary keys.
dataclasses.asdict(obj) turns a dataclass into a dict and dataclasses.replace(obj, x=5) makes a changed copy.
__enter__ and __exit__ make a class usable in a with block; __exit__ gets the error details and returns True only to hide the error.
Iterators need __iter__ and __next__; a generator function is shorter, and yield from passes items of another iterable through.
A generator can receive values with send(): x = yield value; this is the base of coroutines but rarely needed in new code, use asyncio.
open(path, 'a') appends, 'x' creates and fails if the file exists, 'rb' and 'wb' work with bytes and need no encoding.
Path('f').read_text(encoding='utf-8') and write_text(text, encoding='utf-8') are one line replacements for open and read; both close the file for you.
Path.iterdir() lists a folder, Path.rglob('*.py') searches below it and Path.stat().st_size gives the size in bytes.
Path.unlink(missing_ok=True) deletes a file without an error when it is not there, and shutil.rmtree deletes a whole folder tree; check the path first.
shutil.copy2 keeps times, shutil.copytree copies a folder with dirs_exist_ok=True in Python 3.8 and later, and shutil.move works across drives.
shutil.make_archive('name', 'zip', 'folder') creates a zip of a folder in one call, and shutil.unpack_archive extracts known formats.
os.scandir(path) is faster than os.listdir when you need file types or sizes, because it gets that information without an extra call.
os.replace(src, dst) overwrites the target atomically, os.rename may fail on Windows when the target exists.
os.fsync(f.fileno()) after f.flush() forces data to the disk, needed when a power loss must not lose a write; combine it with write to a temp file and os.replace.
time.sleep accepts floats; for waiting on a condition use threading.Event.wait(timeout) so the wait can end early.
Never compare naive and aware datetimes: it raises TypeError; use aware times everywhere or convert with astimezone.
threading.Timer(5, func).start() calls a function once after a delay and .cancel() stops it; for repeated jobs write a loop with Event.wait(interval).
Daemon threads are killed abruptly at exit and may leave files half written; join normal threads and use a stop Event for clean shutdown.
multiprocessing.Pool(2).map(func, items) runs a function in parallel processes; the function must be defined at module level so it can be pickled.
queue.Queue(maxsize=10) blocks producers when full, which gives natural backpressure; get(timeout=1) lets a worker check a stop flag regularly.
concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures) yields results as they finish and future.result(timeout=5) waits with a limit; exceptions are raised in result().
Use socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=5) to connect with a timeout; it tries all addresses of the name for you.
socket.sendall(data) sends everything and raises on failure, while send may send only a part; always use sendall for TCP.
socket.socketpair() makes two connected sockets inside one program, a convenient way to test protocol code without a network.
json.loads(text) raises json.JSONDecodeError with the line and column of the error, so catch it and show a clear message to the sender.
json.dump(obj, f, indent=2, sort_keys=True) writes stable files that diff well in git; default=str lets json write dates by converting unknown types to text.
NaN and Infinity are not valid JSON; json.dumps(float('nan'), allow_nan=False) raises an error, which protects other parsers from bad data.
configparser reads INI files: parser.read('a.ini'), parser['section']['key'] and parser.getint, getboolean convert types; tomllib reads TOML in Python 3.11 and later.
traceback.format_exc() returns the text of the current exception, and traceback.print_exc() prints it; log it with logging.exception inside the except block.
tracemalloc.start() then tracemalloc.take_snapshot().statistics('lineno') shows which lines allocate the most memory, the tool to find a leak.
weakref.ref(obj) keeps a reference that does not stop the object from being freed; WeakValueDictionary makes caches that clean themselves.
A mutable class attribute such as items = [] is shared by all instances; set lists in __init__ or use dataclass field(default_factory=list).
Properties with a setter validate values on assignment: @x.setter def x(self, v): ...; raise ValueError for bad input.
Inheritance order follows the MRO: ClassName.__mro__ shows it, and super() calls the next class in that order, which matters with several parents.
A subnet mask of /24 means 256 addresses with 254 usable hosts; /16 means 65536 addresses and /30 gives only 2 usable hosts.
Two computers can talk directly only when both addresses are in the same subnet; otherwise traffic goes to the gateway, so a wrong mask makes devices on the same cable unreachable.
IPv6 addresses are written in hexadecimal with colons, ::1 is localhost and fe80::/10 is link-local; scope the address with %wlan0 when you connect to a link-local one.
Port numbers go from 0 to 65535: 0 to 1023 are well known, 1024 to 49151 registered and 49152 to 65535 are used for temporary client ports.
Common ports: 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 123 NTP, 443 HTTPS, 1883 MQTT, 3306 MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL, 5900 VNC and 3389 remote desktop.
TCP guarantees order and delivery with retransmission, UDP does not; use UDP for live audio, games and discovery, TCP for files, web and commands.
UDP packets above about 1472 bytes are fragmented on Ethernet and often lost; keep datagrams under 1200 bytes for safe delivery over the internet.
The usual Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes, and a TCP segment then carries up to 1460 bytes of data; VPNs and PPPoE lower the MTU, which causes connections that hang on large transfers.
DNS names are case insensitive and each label may have 63 characters at most, the whole name 253; underscores are not allowed in host names.
A DNS answer has a TTL that says how long it may be cached; after changing a record the old address can still be used for that long.
Record types: A is an IPv4 address, AAAA an IPv6 address, CNAME an alias, MX mail servers, TXT text such as SPF, and NS the name servers of a zone.
dig +short TXT name shows text records and dig +trace name follows the delegation from the root, which finds where a wrong answer comes from.
nslookup name works on Windows and Linux for a quick lookup; nslookup name server asks a chosen DNS server, for example a public resolver, to compare answers.
If a site opens by address but not by name, DNS is the problem; if it opens by name on one computer but not on another, check the DNS server setting and the hosts file.
A hosts file entry overrides DNS on that computer: on Windows it is C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts and on Linux /etc/hosts, one address and name per line.
mDNS names ending in .local are resolved through multicast on the local network and need avahi on Linux, Bonjour on macOS; Windows 10 and 11 support them too.
Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap on 2.4 GHz; pick the least crowded of the three, and use 20 MHz width there because 40 MHz overlaps neighbours.
5 GHz Wi-Fi has more channels and less interference but shorter range; DFS channels may switch away when a radar is detected, which interrupts connections for a minute.
A mesh or a second access point should use the same SSID and password but a different channel, and be connected by cable when possible, because wireless backhaul halves the speed.
WPA2 or WPA3 with a long passphrase protects Wi-Fi; WEP and open networks are unsafe, and WPS with a PIN should be turned off in the router.
A guest network keeps visitors and cheap IoT devices away from your computers; enable client isolation on it so devices cannot reach each other.
Wi-Fi speed in the router's list is the link rate, not real throughput; expect about half of it in practice, and measure with iperf3 between two devices.
Ethernet gives lower delay and steady speed; Gigabit needs Cat5e or better cable and all four pairs, and a damaged cable often falls back to 100 Mbit.
ethtool eth0 shows the link speed and duplex of a cable connection; 100Mb/s on a Gigabit port points to a bad cable or a poor switch port.
Powerline adapters and USB Ethernet dongles work well for a Pi in a far room; avoid extension cords with surge protectors, which block the signal of powerline adapters.
A switch connects devices in one network and forwards by MAC address, a router connects networks by IP address; a home router combines both with a firewall and DHCP.
DHCP gives a device address, mask, gateway and DNS server for a lease time; renew with sudo dhclient -r && sudo dhclient on older systems or nmcli connection up name on NetworkManager.
Two DHCP servers in one network, for example a router and a forgotten access point, cause random address conflicts; turn DHCP off on the second device.
A duplicate IP address makes both computers lose connections at random; arping -D -I eth0 address tests whether an address is already in use.
NAT lets many private devices share one public address; incoming connections from outside need port forwarding, UPnP or a tunnel, because the router does not know where to send them.
Hairpin NAT problems: a service reachable from outside by the public name may fail from inside the same network; use the local address or split DNS at home.
A reverse tunnel such as ssh -R 9000:localhost:22 user@server makes a computer behind NAT reachable through a server; autossh restarts the tunnel when it drops.

Cloudflare Tunnel and similar services connect outward from your device, so no router port needs to be opened; the traffic passes through the provider, so end to end encryption in your app still matters.
WebSocket keeps one connection open for messages in both directions; proxies and mobile networks close idle ones, so send a ping every 20 to 30 seconds.

HTTP status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client made an error, 5xx the server failed; 401 means not logged in, 403 not allowed, 429 too many requests, 502 and 504 a bad or slow upstream server.
HTTP methods: GET reads and must not change data, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part of a resource and DELETE removes; OPTIONS is used by browsers for CORS checks.
A 301 redirect is permanent and cached by browsers, 302 and 307 are temporary; 307 and 308 keep the request method, 301 and 302 may turn POST into GET.
HTTP caching: Cache-Control: max-age=3600 lets a response be reused for an hour, no-store forbids caching and ETag with If-None-Match lets the server answer 304 Not Modified.
Compression with Content-Encoding gzip or br cuts text transfers by 70 percent or more; enable it in the reverse proxy and never compress already compressed images or video.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection and needs HTTPS in browsers; HTTP/3 uses UDP and helps on lossy mobile networks, and both are switched on in the reverse proxy.
Chunked transfer encoding sends a response without knowing its size in advance; each chunk starts with its length in hexadecimal and the end is a zero length chunk.
Server-sent events send text lines starting with data: over a normal HTTP response with Content-Type text/event-stream; browsers reconnect by themselves and EventSource needs no library.
A long polling request waits on the server until data arrives and then returns; it works through every proxy and is a fallback when WebSocket is blocked.
Keep-alive connections reuse one TCP connection for several requests; clients that open a new connection per request waste time on handshakes, so use a session object.
Certificates expire after at most 398 days for public sites, and Let's Encrypt gives 90 day certificates that renew automatically with certbot or caddy.
A self-signed certificate encrypts but proves nothing; browsers warn, and apps must pin or import it deliberately instead of switching verification off.
