HSTS tells browsers to use HTTPS only for a site for a given time (Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000); set it only when HTTPS works everywhere on that name.
The Host header lets one server answer for many names; a request to the address without the right Host header reaches the default site.
X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto are set by reverse proxies and can be forged by clients, so trust them only from your own proxy and configure it explicitly.
Rate limit by user or address at the proxy; 429 with a Retry-After header tells well behaved clients when to try again.
Open only the ports you need on the router, and prefer a VPN for admin access; services such as SSH exposed to the internet get attacked within minutes.
Change nothing about the SSH port as a security measure alone; keys, disabled password login and fail2ban matter, a changed port only reduces log noise.
PermitRootLogin no and AllowUsers name in sshd_config reduce the attack surface; test a second session before you close the first when you change SSH settings.
ssh -v user@host prints how the connection and authentication proceed; -vvv shows more and is the first tool when a key is not accepted.
ssh-agent keeps unlocked keys in memory so you type the passphrase once; ssh-add -l lists loaded keys and ssh -A forwards the agent, which you should use only to trusted hosts.
scp has an old protocol with weaknesses; sftp or rsync over SSH are better, and recent scp versions use sftp inside.
sftp user@host opens an interactive session with get, put, ls, cd and lcd; add -b file to run commands from a file in a script.
A reverse SSH tunnel plus a keep-alive can give you remote access to a Raspberry Pi behind NAT, but a managed tunnel or VPN is easier to keep secure.
ssh user@host command runs one command without a shell session; quote the command so your local shell does not expand wildcards or variables before sending it.
ssh -t user@host sudo command allocates a terminal, which sudo needs to ask for a password; without -t you see a message about no tty present.
When SSH hangs at login, UseDNS no in sshd_config and a working DNS on the server remove the delay of reverse lookups.
Wake a computer with etherwake or wakeonlan and its MAC address; the target needs Wake-on-LAN enabled in firmware and ethtool -s eth0 wol g on Linux.
A magic packet is six bytes of 0xFF followed by the target MAC address repeated sixteen times, sent as a UDP broadcast, usually to port 9.
MAC addresses have six bytes; the first three identify the manufacturer; many phones use random private addresses per Wi-Fi network, so a router's list may show a new device after a reset.
arp -n and ip neigh show the table of recently seen neighbours with their MAC addresses; ip neigh flush all clears it when a device changed its network card.
nmap -sT -p 22,80,443 host checks only three ports; scanning other people's networks without permission can be illegal, so scan your own devices.
nmap -sV host tries to find service versions and -O guesses the operating system; run it on your own Pi to see what it exposes to the network.
curl --interface wlan0 url sends the request through one network card, which tests each connection when a computer has both Ethernet and Wi-Fi.
Metrics in ip route decide which route wins when two match: the lower value is preferred, so Ethernet gets a lower metric than Wi-Fi by default on most systems.
If a computer has two networks and the wrong one carries internet traffic, check ip route and the default route metrics before you blame the router.
Bridge, bond and VLAN settings belong in NetworkManager or systemd-networkd; test them from a console, because a wrong setting cuts off the SSH session you use to change it.
A VLAN adds a tag to Ethernet frames so one cable carries several separate networks; the switch port must be configured as trunk or access to match.
Network time: NTP uses UDP port 123; chrony or systemd-timesyncd keep clocks within milliseconds, and timedatectl shows whether the clock is synchronized.
Syslog uses UDP port 514 by default; a remote log server such as rsyslog or a journal upload keeps logs of a device that fails.
MQTT is a light publish and subscribe protocol on port 1883 (8883 with TLS), well suited for sensors on a Pi; mosquitto is the usual broker and mosquitto_pub and mosquitto_sub test it.
MQTT topics use slashes like home/livingroom/temperature, + matches one level and # matches all levels below; retained messages give a new subscriber the last value at once.
Use an MQTT username and password and TLS when the broker is reachable beyond your own network; an open broker on the internet gets used by strangers.
Home Assistant, Node-RED and Grafana run well on a Raspberry Pi 4 and connect to sensors through MQTT; give each a fixed address and back up their configuration folders.
A captive portal intercepts the first web request on public Wi-Fi; open a plain http site such as the connectivity check address of your system to get the login page.
Test internet access in scripts by connecting to a small known endpoint with a short timeout, not by ping alone, because ICMP is blocked on some networks.
ping uses ICMP, which firewalls often drop; a missing ping answer does not prove that a host or its services are down.
traceroute shows stars when routers do not answer; the route can still work, so judge by the last hops that answer and by loss in mtr.
Packet loss above 1 percent hurts voice and video, and above 5 percent makes TCP slow; mtr shows at which hop the loss starts, but only loss that continues to the end counts.
Bufferbloat makes the connection slow under load; a router with smart queue management (SQM, fq_codel) keeps delay low while downloads run.
Speed tests measure only the connection to one server; test to several, and measure inside your home with iperf3 to separate Wi-Fi limits from the internet connection.
Latency numbers: under 20 ms is excellent, 50 to 100 ms is fine for most things, above 150 ms makes remote desktop and voice calls feel slow.
Bandwidth is measured in bits, files in bytes: a 100 Mbit/s line transfers at most 12.5 megabytes per second, divide by 8.
A 1 GB file over 50 Mbit/s takes about 160 seconds at full speed (1000 * 8 / 50), and in practice a little more because of protocol overhead.
Check which program uses the network with ss -tp or nethogs; on Windows resource monitor and netstat -b show the same.
On Windows netstat -ano lists connections with the process number, and tasklist | findstr PID shows the program; ipconfig /all shows the full adapter settings.
On Windows ipconfig /flushdns clears the DNS cache, ipconfig /release and /renew refresh the DHCP lease and netsh winsock reset repairs broken network stacks, followed by a reboot.
Windows Defender Firewall asks the first time a program listens on a port; allow it for private networks only, and remove old rules in wf.msc when you no longer use a program.
Test a port from Windows with Test-NetConnection host -Port 22 in PowerShell; it shows whether the TCP connection succeeds.
A phone hotspot is a quick network for a Pi: the Pi joins it as Wi-Fi, and the phone's connected devices list shows the address.
Android and iOS apps may block plain http traffic; local devices usually need http, so apps that talk to them need a cleartext exception or a secure tunnel.
A phone on mobile data cannot reach 192.168.x.x addresses of your home; use a VPN, a tunnel service or a relay server that your device connects to.
Websites on the same Wi-Fi may be reachable by IP but blocked by client isolation in the router; turn isolation off on the network that carries your own devices.
CSS box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border, which is the saner default; set it for all elements with *, *::before, *::after.
Flexbox centers things easily: display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; and gap sets the space between children without margins.
CSS grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) makes a responsive card layout without media queries.
min-width: 0 on a flex or grid child lets long text shrink instead of overflowing; without it a long word can push the layout wider than the screen.
overflow-wrap: anywhere breaks long words and addresses to fit, and text-overflow: ellipsis needs overflow: hidden and white-space: nowrap on the same element.
position: sticky; top: 0 keeps a header in view while scrolling, and it needs a parent without overflow set to hidden or auto, or it does not stick.
z-index only works on positioned elements or flex and grid children; a stacking context created by transform or opacity can trap a child under another layer.
Use CSS variables for colors: :root { --bg: #fff } and var(--bg); a dark theme only redefines the variables inside a media query for prefers-color-scheme.
color-scheme: light dark tells the browser to draw form controls and scrollbars in the matching theme, a one line fix for white inputs on a dark page.
accent-color changes the color of checkboxes, radios and range sliders with one line, and appearance: none lets you style them completely.
The :focus-visible selector shows a focus ring for keyboard users only; never remove outlines without giving a visible replacement.
Use rem for font sizes and em for spacing inside components, so everything scales with the user's text size setting.
A fluid font size with clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 1.5rem) grows with the window between a minimum and a maximum without any media query.
Media queries should be mobile first: write the small screen CSS first and add @media (min-width: 768px) for larger screens.
Use aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 to keep boxes in shape while loading images and videos, and object-fit: cover to fill a box without stretching a picture.
Images need width and height attributes so the browser reserves space and the page does not jump; loading="lazy" delays images below the fold.
Serve images in modern formats such as WebP or AVIF with a fallback in a picture element, and resize them to the display size; huge images are the biggest cause of slow pages.
SVG icons scale without loss and take their color from currentColor, so one icon works in light and dark themes.
Fonts: font-display: swap shows text at once in a fallback font; limit weights, and prefer system fonts such as system-ui for tools that must load fast.
User-select: none stops accidental text selection on buttons, but never on content people may want to copy, such as codes and addresses.
Use the dialog element with showModal() for popups; it handles focus, the Escape key and the backdrop without a library.
The details and summary elements make accordions without JavaScript, and the datalist element gives an input suggestions.
querySelector returns the first match or null; check for null before you use it, because a typo in a selector then breaks the script with a confusing error.
Event delegation: add one listener to a parent and check event.target.closest('.item'); it works for items added later and saves memory.
addEventListener('click', fn, { once: true }) removes the listener after the first call, and { passive: true } on scroll and touch events keeps scrolling smooth.
Use textContent to put text into the page and never innerHTML with data from users, because innerHTML runs scripts in event attributes and enables XSS.
createElement and append build safe DOM nodes from data; template literals with innerHTML are only safe for text you wrote yourself or escaped.
async functions return promises; await only works inside them, and a missing await gives a Promise object instead of the value, a frequent bug.
Wrap await in try/catch or add .catch to a promise; an unhandled rejection shows only in the console, and the page then seems to do nothing.
Promise.all runs promises in parallel and fails when one fails; Promise.allSettled waits for all and reports each result.
fetch with credentials: 'same-origin' sends cookies to your own site only; 'include' sends them to other origins too and needs matching CORS headers.
A JSON request needs the header Content-Type: application/json and JSON.stringify(body); forgetting the header makes many servers ignore the body.
Date in JavaScript counts months from 0, so new Date(2026, 0, 1) is January; new Date('2026-01-01') is parsed as UTC while a date with a time and no zone is local time.
Use Intl.DateTimeFormat and toLocaleString('tr-TR') to show dates and numbers in the user's language instead of formatting them by hand.
The == operator converts types; use === and !== to avoid surprises such as '0' == false being true.
Use const by default and let when a value changes; var is function scoped and hoisted, which causes bugs in loops.
Optional chaining a?.b?.c and the nullish operator a ?? b handle missing data without errors; || also replaces 0 and empty text, ?? only null and undefined.
Array methods map, filter, reduce, find and some replace most loops; sort changes the array in place and compares as text unless you give a function.
Numbers in JavaScript are 64 bit floats: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 and integers above 2^53 lose precision; BigInt is available for large integers.
localStorage stores only text, so use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse; wrap access in try/catch because it throws in private windows and when storage is full.
setInterval keeps running when a tab is hidden but at a slow rate; for animations use requestAnimationFrame and stop timers when the page is hidden with the visibilitychange event.
Debounce events that fire often, such as input and resize, by waiting 200 to 300 ms after the last event before you do the work.
Use the Page Visibility API (document.hidden) to pause polling while a tab is in the background, and resume with a fresh request when it returns.
navigator.onLine only says whether a network card is connected, not whether the internet works; test with a small request and a timeout.
Service workers cache files for offline use but also keep old versions alive; version the cache name and delete old caches in the activate event.
A web app manifest with name, icons, start_url and display: standalone makes a site installable; 192 and 512 pixel icons are needed for Android.
The viewport meta with viewport-fit=cover and env(safe-area-inset-bottom) keeps controls out of the notch and the home bar on phones.
touch-action: manipulation removes the double tap zoom delay on buttons, and inputs with a font size under 16 pixels make iOS zoom the page on focus.
Test pages with the browser's device mode and on a real phone; hover states, fixed positions and the on-screen keyboard behave differently on touch devices.
Content Security Policy: default-src 'self' blocks inline scripts and other origins; add a nonce or hash for the inline code you really need rather than unsafe-inline.
Set cookies with HttpOnly (no script access), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite=Lax; session cookies without these flags are easier to steal or misuse.
Never put secrets in front end code, local storage or URLs; anything the browser receives can be read by the user and by other scripts on the page.
Subresource Integrity: script and link tags with integrity="sha384-..." and crossorigin reject a changed file from a CDN, and pinning exact versions avoids surprises.
Open links with target="_blank" together with rel="noopener" so the new page cannot reach window.opener; modern browsers imply it but older ones do not.
postMessage with an exact targetOrigin and a check of event.origin is the safe way for a page and an iframe to talk; never use '*' with sensitive data.
An iframe can be restricted with the sandbox attribute and allow list; sandbox without allow-same-origin gives the page a unique origin that cannot read your cookies.
Do not put a login page into an iframe on another site; X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors block it on purpose to prevent clickjacking.
Browsers block third party cookies more and more, so embedded logins and tracking inside iframes fail; use a top level login or a token passed by postMessage.
The Clipboard API read needs a permission prompt and a secure context; writeText works after a user gesture on most browsers, and execCommand copy is the old fallback.
File input with accept="image/*" and capture opens the camera on phones; use FileReader or URL.createObjectURL to preview a file before upload.
Notification and geolocation APIs need a user gesture and a secure context; ask only when the user takes an action that needs them, or browsers may block the prompt for good.
WebRTC audio and video need HTTPS or localhost; calls between two devices often need a TURN server when both are behind strict NAT, and STUN alone fails there.
getUserMedia constraints such as echoCancellation, noiseSuppression and sampleRate improve speech capture; the actual values are in track.getSettings().
MediaRecorder records a stream into chunks; the supported formats differ, so test MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported('audio/webm') and keep the chunks until stop.
Speech synthesis with speechSynthesis.speak(new SpeechSynthesisUtterance(text)) works without a server; the available voices come from the device and load asynchronously.
The Web Audio API needs a user gesture before it starts on iOS and Chrome; create the AudioContext in a click handler or call resume() there.
Pointer events unify mouse, touch and pen: use pointerdown, pointermove and pointerup, and setPointerCapture to keep receiving moves outside the element.
Prevent default scrolling on touch drags only with touch-action: none on the element; calling preventDefault on a passive listener has no effect and logs a warning.
The canvas element needs a size in attributes, not only in CSS, or drawings look blurry; multiply by devicePixelRatio for sharp lines on high density screens.
requestAnimationFrame runs before the next screen repaint, usually 60 times a second; compute movement from elapsed time, not from the number of frames.
Web Workers run JavaScript in another thread, so heavy work does not freeze the page; they talk to the page with postMessage and cannot touch the DOM.
A WebView in an app is a normal web engine with its own storage and cookies; enable DOM storage and JavaScript explicitly and test on the oldest Android version you support.
In Chrome, chrome://inspect lets you debug a page of an Android WebView or a Chrome tab on a phone over USB; the app must enable WebView debugging.
Lighthouse in developer tools audits speed, accessibility and best practices and gives a list of concrete fixes; run it in a private window without extensions.
Flask's request.form holds form fields, request.files holds uploads and request.json holds a parsed JSON body; use request.get_data() when you need the raw bytes, for example to check a signature.
A route can limit methods with @app.get('/') and @app.post('/') in Flask 2 and later, which is shorter than methods=['GET', 'POST'].
A trailing slash decides redirects: a route defined as /about/ redirects /about to it, while a route defined as /about gives 404 for /about/; define the form you want to publish.
make_response(body, 201) builds a response you can change, for example resp.headers['X-Name'] = 'v' and resp.set_cookie(...) before returning it.
A view may return a tuple (body, status, headers): return 'x', 202, {'X-A': '1'} is the short form of make_response.
redirect(url_for('name')) after a successful POST avoids a second submit when the user reloads the page; this is the post/redirect/get pattern.
Flask's g object lives for one request and holds data such as a database connection; current_app and request are proxies to the active app and request.
session['key'] = value stores small values in a signed cookie; keep it under about 4 KB, and set session.permanent = True with PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME for a longer login.
flash('message') stores a one time message in the session and get_flashed_messages() reads it in the next page, a simple way to confirm a saved form.
abort(403) raises an HTTPException, so code after it does not run; a custom handler with @app.errorhandler(403) shapes the answer for browsers and for JSON clients.
@app.errorhandler(Exception) catches unexpected errors; log them with app.logger.exception and return a short JSON message, never the traceback, in production.
app.config.from_prefixed_env() reads environment variables that start with FLASK_ into the config, so settings need no code changes between machines.
app.config['MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH'] = 1024 * 1024 rejects bigger request bodies with a 413 answer, protecting a small server from huge uploads.
Jinja2 templates: {{ value }} prints with escaping, {% if %}, {% for %} and {% set %} are control tags, and {{ value|default('none') }} handles missing values.
In Jinja2 the filter |tojson makes a value safe to put into a script tag, which is the right way to hand data from Flask to JavaScript.
Jinja2 autoescape turns < into < in HTML templates; render_template_string also escapes, so user text cannot inject tags unless you mark it |safe.
A custom Jinja filter is added with @app.template_filter('name'), and context_processor makes variables available in every template without passing them in each view.
url_for with _external=True builds a full address including the scheme and host, needed for links in emails; SERVER_NAME or a ProxyFix setting decides the host.
Blueprints keep routes in separate files: bp = Blueprint('api', __name__, url_prefix='/api') and app.register_blueprint(bp); url_for('api.name') includes the blueprint name.
A Flask app factory, def create_app(): app = Flask(__name__); ...; return app, makes tests easier because each test can create a fresh app with its own settings.
app.test_client() keeps cookies between calls, so you can test a login flow: post the login, then get a protected page with the same client.
app.test_cli_runner() runs your own flask commands in tests, and @app.cli.command('name') adds a command you can call as flask name.
Streaming response: return Response(generator(), mimetype='text/plain') sends data as the generator yields it, so long jobs show progress without waiting for the end.
Server-sent events from Flask: yield f'data: {text}\n\n' with mimetype text/event-stream and the header Cache-Control: no-cache; gunicorn needs threaded workers or gevent for many open streams.
after_this_request(func) runs code after one specific response, for example to delete a temporary file after send_file finished; the function must return the response.
send_file(path, as_attachment=True, download_name='name.txt') forces a download with a chosen file name; conditional=True supports range and cache headers.
The jsonify function and the default provider in Flask sort keys alphabetically in old versions; app.json.sort_keys = False keeps the insertion order in Flask 2.2 and later.
Responses to JSON clients should have a stable shape, for example {"error": "text"} with the right status code, so front end code needs only one error path.
request.headers.get('X-Name') reads a request header case insensitively, request.cookies holds cookies and request.remote_addr the client address, which is the proxy's address unless ProxyFix is set.
request.is_json is True when the Content-Type is JSON, and request.get_json(force=True) parses the body even without that header, which is useful with sloppy clients.
Cookies: resp.set_cookie('n', 'v', max_age=3600, httponly=True, secure=True, samesite='Lax') and resp.delete_cookie('n') remove it; secure cookies are not sent over plain HTTP.
Use itsdangerous.URLSafeTimedSerializer(secret).dumps(data) to make signed, expiring tokens for e-mail links, and loads(token, max_age=3600) checks the signature and the age.
secrets.compare_digest or hmac.compare_digest should compare tokens in views; plain == leaks timing information and is a bad habit for secrets.
werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash(password) adds a random salt and a method prefix; check_password_hash(hash, password) verifies it, and the hash can be stored as text.
Flask-Login keeps the user in the session; protect views with @login_required, and always check ownership of the object in the view, not only that somebody is logged in.
Never trust an id from the URL: query by id and the logged in user together, for example WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?, or any user can open other people's data by changing a number.
Validate and limit every input: maximum length, allowed characters and numeric ranges; return 400 with the field name so the front end can show a clear message.
Escape user text in HTML with markupsafe.escape, and in SQL with parameters only; two different escapes protect two different places.
Add security headers in one after_request function: nosniff, a frame rule, a referrer policy and a Content-Security-Policy; test them with the browser's developer tools.
A middleware before Flask can be a plain WSGI wrapper: app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(app.wsgi_app, x_for=1, x_proto=1) trusts exactly one proxy in front of the app.
A health route should be cheap and open: @app.get('/healthz') returning 'ok' lets the host and your monitors check the service without logging in.
Use app.url_map to list all routes: for r in app.url_map.iter_rules(): print(r.rule, r.methods), a quick check that every blueprint is registered.
Static files are served from the static folder at /static; in production let the web server serve them and set long cache headers with a version in the file name.
SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT controls how long browsers cache static files; set it to a few hours in production, and change the file name when the content changes.
waitress-serve --port 8000 module:app is a production server that also works on Windows; it is pure Python and easy to install on any computer.
Long running work should not run inside a request: start a background thread, a queue worker or a separate process and return a job id that the client can poll.
A thread started in a view can use the app context only if you pass it: with app.app_context(): inside the thread function.
Global dictionaries as state work only with one process; with several gunicorn workers each has its own copy, so use a database, Redis or a file with locking.
SQLite with Flask: open a connection per request (g), set row_factory = sqlite3.Row, use WAL mode and a timeout, and close in @app.teardown_appcontext.
SQLAlchemy sessions must be closed or removed at the end of each request; Flask-SQLAlchemy does it for you, and db.session.rollback() after an error clears a broken transaction.
Migrations: use Flask-Migrate (Alembic) to change tables of a live database; flask db migrate creates a script, flask db upgrade applies it, and back up the database first.
Hosted databases on free plans may sleep or limit connections; keep the connection count low and reconnect with a retry on the first request after a pause.
PythonAnywhere free accounts allow outbound requests only to a list of sites and sleep the web app after inactivity; check the whitelist before you plan integrations.
On PythonAnywhere the app runs from a WSGI file; after changing code press Reload on the Web tab, and error logs are linked on the same page.
Free web hosts that sleep an idle app take a minute to wake up; a small request every few minutes from a device that is always on keeps them awake.
Keep uploaded files outside the code folder and out of version control, because redeploys on most hosts replace the file system; use object storage or a mounted disk for data you must keep.
Log with the logging module and include the request id or user; on hosts the standard output is the log, so printing to stdout and stderr is enough.
Flask debug mode reloads on file changes and shows an interactive debugger; the PIN in the console protects it, but never leave it on when the server is reachable.
pytest with Flask: a fixture that yields app.test_client() lets each test call routes; assert on status_code and response.get_json() and keep one assert per behavior.
When a Flask route returns None it raises a TypeError; make sure every code path returns a response, including the else branch of an if.
apt-cache show name prints the full control record of a package including Depends, Size and Description; apt-cache depends name lists its dependencies.
apt-cache search --names-only word looks only in package names, which gives a shorter and cleaner list than a search through all descriptions.
apt-cache rdepends name lists the packages that depend on name, which shows what would be affected if you remove it.
apt-cache madison name shows all available versions and the repositories they come from, useful before you pin or downgrade a package.
apt-get install --reinstall name restores the files of a package that you deleted or broke, without removing its configuration.
dpkg -c file.deb lists the files inside a package and dpkg -I file.deb prints its control information, before you install it.
dpkg -s name shows whether a package is installed and its status; dpkg -s name | grep Status prints install ok installed when it is fine.
dpkg -V name verifies the installed files of a package against the stored checksums, and prints nothing when all is as installed.
dpkg --get-selections lists installed packages in a format that dpkg --set-selections and apt-get dselect-upgrade can restore on another system.
dpkg-divert moves a packaged file aside permanently so a package upgrade does not overwrite your own version; list diversions with dpkg-divert --list.
dpkg --add-architecture armhf lets a 64 bit system install 32 bit packages after apt update; dpkg --print-foreign-architectures shows what is enabled.
apt list --upgradable shows packages with newer versions, and apt list --installed | grep name finds an installed package by name.
apt-mark showhold lists packages that are held back, and apt-mark showauto lists packages that were installed as dependencies and may be removed by autoremove.
apt autoremove --purge removes unused dependencies together with their configuration; check the list it shows because it can also remove tools you used without knowing.
apt-get --purge remove name removes a package with its configuration files; dpkg -l | grep '^rc' lists packages that were removed but left configuration files behind.
The file /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/ holds apt settings, for example APT::Install-Recommends "false"; to stop installing recommended packages on a small system.
apt-config dump shows all active apt settings, and apt-config dump | grep Install-Recommends tells whether recommended packages are installed.
Never mix Debian releases casually: installing one package from testing can pull a new libc and break the system; use backports or a container instead.
apt show name | grep -E 'Depends|Installed-Size' prints the dependencies and the disk space a package needs, useful on a small SD card.
apt-get clean empties the package cache and apt-get autoclean removes only versions that can no longer be downloaded; both are safe.
du -sh /var/cache/apt and /var/lib/apt/lists show how much space apt uses for downloaded packages and package lists; the lists can be deleted and fetched again by apt update.
When apt update says a repository changed its Release information, run apt update --allow-releaseinfo-change once; for repositories you trust.
Hash sum mismatch errors are usually caused by a bad mirror or a proxy; delete /var/lib/apt/lists/* with care, run apt update again, or switch to another mirror.
Repository lines in /etc/apt/sources.list.d need signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/name.gpg in the deb line; the key file is added with gpg --dearmor, not with the old apt-key.
Keep only repositories you trust: every added repository can replace system packages, because apt installs the highest version it finds unless you pin it.
add-apt-repository is only for Ubuntu PPAs; on Debian and Raspberry Pi OS write the source file by hand, and remember that PPAs are built for Ubuntu libraries.
Flatpak and snap bring their own libraries; on a Raspberry Pi with little memory prefer apt packages, and use a container only for software that needs a different base system.
On Debian 12 and Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm pip refuses to install into the system Python (externally managed environment); use a venv, pipx, or the apt package python3-name.
pipx install name puts a command line tool into its own virtual environment and a link in ~/.local/bin; install pipx with apt and run pipx ensurepath once.
Node.js from apt can be old; check apt-cache policy nodejs and use the official repository or nvm when a project needs a newer version.
Install a specific version with apt install name=1.2.3-1; apt-cache madison name shows the exact version strings that are available.
A package that asks for a service restart after upgrade uses needrestart or checkrestart; restart the listed services or reboot to run the new libraries.
Check the date of the last upgrade in /var/log/apt/history.log and the details of every command in /var/log/apt/term.log, useful to see what changed before a problem.
dpkg.log in /var/log lists each package install, upgrade and removal with times; grep ' install ' /var/log/dpkg.log shows what was installed recently.
Lock errors such as Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend mean another package program runs; wait for it with ps aux | grep -E 'apt|dpkg' instead of deleting lock files.
On a fresh Raspberry Pi OS the first boot may run an upgrade or key setup in the background; wait a few minutes if apt reports a lock right after the first start.
Offline installs: apt-get download the package and all its dependencies on a connected computer with the same architecture and release, copy the .deb files and run dpkg -i *.deb.
A local repository from a folder of .deb files is made with dpkg-scanpackages or apt-ftparchive; it lets several devices install the same set without internet.
Unattended upgrades are configured in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades; set Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot to false on a device that must not restart by itself.
apt-listchanges and apt-listbugs show news and known bugs before an upgrade; they are helpful on Debian testing, less needed on a stable Raspberry Pi OS.
Backports bring newer packages to a stable Debian release; enable the backports line and install with apt install -t bookworm-backports name.

The Raspberry Pi foundation repository adds the firmware, kernel and Pi specific tools, and the standard Debian repository adds everything else; both are in /etc/apt/sources.list.d on Raspberry Pi OS.
Use apt-get -y install name || echo failed in scripts to continue, or set -e to stop at the first failed install, so a half set up device is never left unnoticed.
When a program crashes on start, run it by hand in a terminal first; the error you see there is usually hidden when the same program runs as a service or from an icon.
Reproduce a bug with the smallest example you can make; half of all bugs reveal their cause while you cut the example down.
Write down what you expected, what happened instead and the exact error text before you ask for help; most questions answer themselves at that point.
When two things changed at once and something broke, undo one of them; guessing which one caused it costs more than a clean test.
A bug that appears only sometimes is usually about timing, memory, network or a shared resource; log times and states instead of staring at code.
Add logging first, then fix; a fix without a log line to prove it worked often turns out to be a lucky change.
Check the simple things first: power, cable, disk space, date and time, permissions and whether the service is really running.
Compare a working system with a broken one: diff their config files, package lists and versions; the difference is almost always the cause.
Use binary search on changes: if version 10 works and version 20 fails, test 15; git bisect does this for commits automatically.
Rubber duck debugging works: explaining the problem line by line to somebody or something makes you notice the wrong assumption.
Read the documentation of the exact version you run; behavior and option names change between versions, and old forum answers may be wrong now.
Release notes and changelogs explain why something stopped working after an update; read them before you update a system you depend on.
Keep a rollback path before you change a working system: a backup, a snapshot, a copy of the config or a second SD card.
Make changes during a time when a failure does no harm, and never right before you must leave or sleep; a half finished change is the worst state.
Test restore, not only backup: a backup that was never restored once is a hope, not a backup.
Store backups on a different device and in a different place than the original; one fire, theft or power surge should not take both.
Automate backups and let them tell you when they fail; a backup job that nobody checks silently stops working after a few months.
Document passwords and recovery steps in a safe place, such as a password manager and a printed copy of the recovery codes in a drawer.
A password manager with a long master passphrase and two factor authentication protects better than reusing one clever password everywhere.
Two factor authentication with an app or a hardware key is far safer than SMS; save the recovery codes when you enable it.
Phishing messages create urgency and ask for a login or a code; open the site by typing the address yourself and never give a verification code to anyone who contacts you.
Check the address bar before you type a password, and prefer bookmarks for banks and accounts; look-alike domains use small spelling changes.
Keep the operating system, browser and router firmware up to date; most real attacks use known holes that already have a fix.
Use separate accounts: a normal account for daily work and administrator rights only when needed; malware then has less power.
Do not run programs from untrusted sources and never pipe a download into a shell without reading it first; download, inspect, then run.
Verify downloads with the checksum or signature that the publisher lists on its own site, not on the page that hosts the file.
Free Wi-Fi in public places is open to snooping; use HTTPS sites, a VPN, and do not enter important passwords on an unknown network.
Cover or disable the camera and microphone permissions of apps that do not need them; review the permission list of your phone every few months.
Logging out and revoking sessions on lost devices stops access; most services have a page that lists active sessions and lets you end them.
Never share screenshots that show API keys, tokens, addresses or codes; crop or hide them, because bots search public images and posts for secrets.
A leaked secret must be replaced, not only hidden; creating a new key and deleting the old one is the only safe answer, even if the leak was brief.
Give each program its own API key with the least rights it needs, so one leak can be removed without breaking everything else.
Keep keys and tokens in environment files or a secret store with permission 600, outside the project folder that you commit or share.
Rate limits and quotas of APIs are part of the design: cache answers, back off on 429 errors and keep a counter so a loop cannot burn your quota in minutes.
Budget alerts on cloud and AI accounts prevent surprises; set a low limit first and raise it when you know the real use.
Read the pricing page for free tiers before you build on them: sleep after inactivity, monthly hours and storage limits decide whether a project works.
Free hosting plans change without notice; keep your data and configuration exportable so that moving to another host takes an hour, not a week.
Choose boring technology for the parts you cannot afford to lose: files, SQLite, cron and plain HTTP have worked for decades and are easy to repair.
Prefer one simple tool that you understand to three clever ones; every extra moving part is another thing that breaks at night.
Write the README before the code is finished: what it is, how to install, how to run and how to test; it forces simple design and helps your future self.
Put a short troubleshooting section in every README with the three problems that happened to you; the next person with the same problem will thank you.
Use meaningful names for files and functions; a name that says what something does needs no comment and survives refactoring.
Comment on why, not what: the code already says what it does, while the reason for a surprising choice is lost without a note.
Keep functions small and files focused; when you scroll for a minute to understand one function, split it.
Delete dead code and unused files; version control remembers them, and a smaller project is easier to understand.
Make errors visible: a message that says what failed, with which input, and what to try next, saves hours compared with a generic failed.
Fail early and loudly for programming errors, and handle expected problems such as a missing network quietly with retries and a clear status.
Validate input at the border of the program and trust the data inside it; checks everywhere make code noisy and still miss cases.
Use timeouts for every external call and decide in advance what happens when it times out; waiting forever is never a good answer.
Retries need a limit, growing waits and some randomness; a hundred devices retrying every second can bring down a server that just recovered.
Idempotent operations can be repeated safely; design requests and scripts so that running them twice gives the same result as running them once.
Keep state in one place; two copies of the same information drift apart, and the bug appears when they disagree.
Use UTC for stored times and convert to the local time zone only when you show them; store the original zone name when the local time matters.
Store money as integers of the smallest unit, such as cents, or as decimals; binary floats give results like 0.30000000000000004.
Use UTF-8 everywhere and declare it in files, databases, HTTP headers and HTML; mixed encodings show up as question marks and broken Turkish letters.
File names and user text can contain spaces, quotes, accents and emoji; test your program with such input before real users do.
Sort and compare text with the rules of the language when it matters: Turkish dotted and dotless i behave differently from English in uppercase and lowercase.
Never build SQL, shell commands or HTML by joining strings with user input; use parameters, argument lists and escaping functions.
Add a version number to files and protocols you share between programs, so a new program can still read old data and tell when it cannot.
Small, frequent releases are safer than big rare ones; each change is easy to understand and to undo.
Keep a changelog with dates and a short reason for each change, even for a personal project; memory fades quickly.
Use a task list with one next action per item; a vague item such as improve the system is never finished, while fix the retry delay in the sync script can be done today.
Estimate your own time with a factor of two or three; unknowns such as installs, drivers and network problems take most of the time.
Take breaks when stuck; a walk often solves what an hour at the screen did not, and tired changes at night cause the next problem.
Learn one editor and the shell well; speed in editing, searching and running commands makes every project faster than any new framework.
Keep a notes file with commands that took you a long time to find; searching your own notes is faster than searching the web again.
Screenshots of an error plus the full text of the log are the best way to ask for help; a photo of the screen cuts off the lines that matter.
When asking an AI assistant for commands, say your system, version and what you already tried, and ask it to explain each command before you run it.
Treat AI answers as drafts: test them in a safe place, read what a command deletes or changes, and compare with the official documentation for anything important.
Do not paste secrets, private data or other people's personal information into online tools or AI chats that you do not control.
For a long task with an AI assistant, ask for a plan and a list of checks first, then work in small steps and verify each result before the next.
Tell an AI assistant the limits of the task: which folder it may change, which commands are off limits and what must never be deleted.
Keep sensitive actions behind a human confirmation: deleting data, spending money, sending messages and changing network or security settings should ask first.
An automation that runs unattended needs a kill switch, a log, a limit on what it can change and an alert when it does something unusual.
Test automations on a copy of the data or a spare device first; a script that works on three files may remove three thousand when a path is wrong.
Use dry run modes whenever a tool offers them: rsync -n, git clean -n, apt-get -s and find without -delete show the effect before it happens.
A scheduled job needs a timeout, a lock against overlapping runs and a log with a date; without them one stuck run blocks all later runs.
Monitor with a simple heartbeat: the device calls a URL or writes a file every few minutes, and an alert fires when the signal stops.
Disk full, memory exhausted, certificate expired and clock wrong cause a large share of all outages; check these four first.
Certificates, domains, API keys and subscriptions expire; put the dates in a calendar with a reminder two weeks before.
A spare SD card with a ready image, a spare power supply and a spare cable turn a failed Raspberry Pi from a weekend project into a five minute swap.
Label cables and devices with their purpose and address; after a year nobody remembers which black cable goes where.
Keep a simple diagram of the network and devices: which address and name each one has, how they connect and which ports are forwarded.
Use a fixed address or a name for each device on the home network through DHCP reservations, so scripts and bookmarks keep working after restarts.
Power is the most underrated cause of problems in small computers: a good supply, short thick cables and a surge protector prevent corruption and odd behavior.
Heat shortens the life of electronics: keep devices ventilated, away from direct sun, and clean dust from fans and heat sinks once a year.
Back up phone photos and documents automatically to a second place; phones get lost and broken more often than computers.
Keep the installers and licences of important software in one folder with notes; reinstalling a computer takes hours when you must hunt for them.
Windows keyboard shortcuts that save time: Win+E opens files, Win+V shows the clipboard history, Win+Shift+S takes a screenshot area and Win+Ctrl+D adds a virtual desktop.
Windows key combination Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens the task manager directly, and Win+R opens the run box where you can type cmd, powershell or a folder path.
In PowerShell, Get-Help command -Examples shows examples for any command, and Get-Command *word* searches commands by name.
PowerShell can run Linux-like tasks: Get-ChildItem lists files, Select-String searches text and Get-Content -Wait follows a file like tail -f.
Windows Terminal with the Windows Subsystem for Linux gives a real Linux shell on Windows; wsl --install sets it up and files of both systems can be shared by path.
On Windows, long paths and reserved names such as CON, NUL and COM1 cannot be used as file names, and the folder length limit of 260 characters can break deep project trees.
Windows file names are not case sensitive and use backslashes; Git and Python code that run on both systems should use forward slashes or path libraries.
Task Scheduler runs programs at logon or on a schedule on Windows; choose Run whether user is logged on or not for background jobs and check the History tab for errors.
Windows Defender may flag small unknown executables made by hobby tools; sign your programs or submit them to Microsoft for analysis, and tell users how to verify the file.
Run a program as a normal user unless it truly needs administrator rights; asking for elevation without need makes people click through every prompt.
Android developer options turn on USB debugging; adb devices lists connected phones, adb install app.apk installs a package and adb logcat shows the log of apps.
adb logcat -s tag shows only one tag and adb logcat -c clears the log, a quick way to catch a crash message of your own app on a phone.
adb shell pm list packages | grep name finds an installed package, adb uninstall package removes it and adb shell am start -n package/activity starts it.
An APK must be signed with the same key to update an installed app; if the signature differs, Android refuses the update and the old app must be uninstalled first.
Android WebView apps need the INTERNET permission, and cleartext HTTP is blocked from Android 9 unless the manifest or network security config allows it for a host.
Android keeps background apps limited; battery optimisation can stop services, so ask users to exempt long running apps or use a foreground service with a notification.
On Android 13 and later notifications need a runtime permission, and microphone and camera need permission each time the policy says so; request them when the user starts the feature.
Test mobile apps on an old and a small phone, with a slow network and with the screen rotated; most real problems show up there.
A QR code can carry a link or short text for pairing a device with a phone; keep it under about 300 characters so it stays easy to scan.
Raspberry Pi projects need a way in: SSH keys, a known address and a fallback such as a serial or USB gadget connection, so a wrong network setting is not the end of access.
Document the steps to rebuild your main device from a blank card: image version, packages, config files and services; the day you need it you will not remember.
Version your configuration files in git, for example /etc changes with etckeeper or a private repository, so you can see what changed and restore an older state.
Keep secrets out of version control but track a template file such as .env.example with the names of the variables and harmless sample values.
A project folder with README, a start script, a requirements file and a sample config is ready for others and for you after a break.
Use a Makefile or a small run script for common commands such as start, test and deploy, so they are written down once and not retyped from memory.
Check exit codes and output of every step in deploy scripts and stop at the first failure; a script that continues after an error spreads damage.
Deploy by copying to a new folder and switching a symbolic link, so a failed release can be undone by pointing the link back to the old folder.
Keep the last working version available; before you replace a program or image, copy the old one aside with a date in the name.
Print versions in logs at start: program version, Python version, operating system and device model make bug reports from other machines much easier.
A watchdog that restarts a hung program is a bandage; find and fix the hang, and log each restart so you know how often it happens.
Memory leaks show as slowly growing memory in top over days; restart policies hide them, but a graph of memory use points to the code that grows.
When the system feels slow, look at CPU, memory, swap, disk and network in that order with top, free, iostat and ss before you guess.
An SD card that is nearly full or very old makes the whole system slow; check df -h and consider an SSD for anything that writes a lot.
Prefer reading logs with filters (grep, journalctl -p) over scrolling; start from the time of the problem and look a minute before it.
A good error report includes: what you did, what you expected, what happened, the exact text of the error, the version and the time; with those a problem is half solved.
Say thank you and share the fix when you solve a problem you asked about; the next person with the same error finds the answer, and communities stay helpful.
In JavaScript 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 because numbers are binary floating point; compare with a small tolerance or work in integers such as cents.
The loose operator == converts types, so '0' == false is true; use === and !== to compare without conversion.
Array.prototype.sort() without a function sorts as text, so [10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9]; pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numbers.
The nullish operator ?? replaces only null and undefined, while || also replaces 0 and empty text, so use ?? for numbers that may be zero.
Optional chaining a?.b?.c returns undefined instead of throwing when a part is missing, and a?.[0] and a?.() work the same way.
Numbers above 2 to the power 53 lose precision in JavaScript; use BigInt, written 123n, for large integers such as ids and byte counts.
typeof null is 'object' for historic reasons and NaN is not equal to itself; use value === null and Number.isNaN(value) for these checks.
parseInt('12px') gives 12 but Number('12px') gives NaN; Number is stricter, and parseInt needs the base as second argument for safe results.
toFixed returns text and rounds binary values, so (1.005).toFixed(2) gives '1.00'; use Intl.NumberFormat or integer cents for money.
In the Date constructor months start at 0, so new Date(2026, 0, 1) is January 1; a date-only text such as 2026-01-01 is read as UTC, a text with time and no zone as local time.
A date text with a time and no zone is parsed in the local time zone and one that ends in Z in UTC, so the same text can give different hours on different computers.
toLocaleString('tr-TR') formats numbers the Turkish way, with dots for thousands and a comma for decimals, and the Intl API does the same for dates and currencies.
Intl.DateTimeFormat('tr-TR', { timeZone: 'Europe/Istanbul' }) formats a date for a chosen time zone, so server and browser show the same day.
Sort text with localeCompare and a language: ['ç','c','d'].sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, 'tr')) puts ç after c, while the default sort uses code points.
toUpperCase and toLowerCase accept a locale: 'i'.toLocaleUpperCase('tr') gives the dotted capital İ, which matters for Turkish text.
A var inside a loop is shared by all callbacks, so closures see the last value; let creates a new variable for each round.
Promises run before timers: a then callback runs before a setTimeout of 0 milliseconds, because microtasks come first in the event loop.
An async function always returns a promise, so forgetting await gives you a Promise object instead of the value.
Promise.allSettled waits for every promise and reports status and value of each, while Promise.all rejects as soon as one fails.
Promise.race resolves with the first settled promise, which is the usual way to add a timeout to a request together with a timer promise.
JSON.stringify skips undefined and functions and turns NaN into null, so a round trip through JSON changes such values.
structuredClone(obj) makes a deep copy including dates, maps and sets, while a JSON round trip turns dates into text and drops maps.
[...new Set(array)] removes duplicates and keeps the first occurrence in order, a one line deduplication for primitive values.
Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj).map(...)) transforms the values or keys of an object, and Object.entries gives pairs you can sort.
Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i) creates the list [0, 1, 2], and new Array(3) alone makes empty slots that map and forEach skip.
Array.prototype.at(-1) returns the last item and String.prototype.at(-1) the last character, easier than length - 1.
includes finds NaN while indexOf does not, and indexOf returns -1 for a missing item, so test it with === -1 and never with a plain if.
Object keys that look like integers come first in ascending order, so the order of keys in an object is not always the insertion order; use a Map when order matters.
A Map keeps insertion order for any key type and has a size property, and a Set holds unique values; both are iterable with for...of.
URL and URLSearchParams parse and build addresses safely: new URL(text).searchParams.get('x') reads a parameter and set() encodes the value for you.
encodeURIComponent encodes a value for use inside a query or path, and encodeURI leaves characters such as / and ? alone; mixing them up breaks addresses.
crypto.randomUUID() gives a random identifier in browsers on secure pages and in Node, and crypto.getRandomValues fills typed arrays with secure random numbers; Math.random is not secure.
TextEncoder().encode('ş').length is 2, because UTF-8 uses more than one byte for many letters; string length counts UTF-16 units, not bytes or visible characters.
Template literals with backticks allow multi-line text and ${expression}; tagged templates and String.raw keep backslashes unchanged.
String.prototype.replaceAll replaces every match and padStart and padEnd make fixed width text, for example '5'.padStart(3, '0') is '005'.
Destructuring with defaults and renaming makes options easy: const { a = 1, b: other } = obj; and function arguments can be destructured the same way.
The spread operator copies arrays and objects one level deep: {...a, x: 1} gives a changed copy, but nested objects are still shared.
Closures remember the variables of the place where a function was made, so counters and private state need no class: function make() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }
this inside a normal function depends on how it is called and inside an arrow function it comes from the surrounding code, which is why callbacks use arrow functions.
Set a default parameter with = in the signature; a default is used only when the argument is undefined, not for null or 0.
try/catch with async functions needs await inside the try block; without await the promise rejects after the block ended and nothing catches it.
Number.isInteger and Number.isFinite check values without converting them; the global isNaN and isFinite convert first and give surprising answers.
Math.max(...array) fails with very large arrays because of the argument limit; use array.reduce((a, b) => Math.max(a, b)) for huge lists.
The comma sort trap: ['b', 'a', 'C'].sort() puts C first because capital letters come before small ones; sort with localeCompare for human order.
A for...in loop walks keys including inherited ones, a for...of loop walks values of iterables; use Object.keys or for...of with entries for plain objects.
The event loop never runs two pieces of JavaScript at once; a long loop freezes the page, so split work into chunks with setTimeout or move it to a Web Worker.
CSS custom properties are inherited and resolved at use: an element can set --c: red and a child can use var(--c), the base of light and dark themes.
The media feature prefers-color-scheme follows the system theme; in tests Playwright can switch it with color_scheme='dark' or page.emulate_media.
A grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(100px, 1fr)) puts as many columns as fit: in a container 320 pixels wide three columns of 100 pixels fit.
display: none removes an element from layout and from the accessibility tree, visibility: hidden keeps its space; elements that are hidden are not found as visible by tests.
Setting innerHTML with untrusted text runs event handlers such as onerror in an image tag, while textContent shows the text as it is; use textContent for user data.
Event delegation works because events bubble: one click listener on a parent can handle items that are added later, using event.target.closest('.item').
localStorage can throw a SecurityError on pages without a normal origin, so wrap every use in try/catch and keep a fallback in a variable.
Playwright can wait for what the user sees: page.get_by_text('Save').click() and expect-style waits such as page.wait_for_selector replace fixed sleeps in tests.
Playwright locators auto wait for an element to be attached and visible before they click or type, so most manual waiting code is not needed.
page.screenshot(path='x.png', full_page=True) saves the whole page, and locator.screenshot() only one element, a quick way to check a layout on a server without a screen.
Playwright can emulate a phone: new_page(viewport={'width': 390, 'height': 844}, is_mobile=True, has_touch=True) triggers the mobile layout and touch events.
Playwright can read the console of a page with page.on('console', handler), so JavaScript errors in your own page show up in the test output.
A page error such as an uncaught exception arrives through page.on('pageerror', handler); log both console and pageerror when you test a web app.
Chromium can run headless to render a page into a picture: the new headless mode behaves like a normal browser and is selected with --headless=new on recent versions.
Playwright can use a persistent profile with launch_persistent_context(user_data_dir), so cookies and logins stay between runs like in a real browser profile.
storage_state saves cookies and local storage after a login: context.storage_state(path='s.json'), and new_context(storage_state='s.json') starts logged in without typing the password again.
Playwright can grant permissions in a test context: new_context(permissions=['microphone']) answers the permission prompt automatically, and chromium flags can fake the device.
The command line flag --user-data-dir selects the profile folder, and two Chromium processes cannot use the same folder at the same time; the second one opens a window in the first process instead.

A stale SingletonLock file in a profile after a crash stops Chromium from starting with a message about the profile being in use; delete SingletonLock, SingletonCookie and SingletonSocket in the profile folder when no Chromium runs.
--disable-gpu and --disable-dev-shm-usage help in containers and small devices when Chromium crashes at start; the second flag makes it use /tmp instead of the small /dev/shm.
--no-sandbox is needed when Chromium runs as root in a container, but it removes an important protection; prefer a normal user and keep the sandbox on a desktop.
--window-size=1280,720 and --window-position=0,0 place a browser window at a fixed size, important for automation that clicks on pixel positions.
--force-device-scale-factor=1 stops the browser from scaling pages on a high density display, which keeps screenshot coordinates equal to screen coordinates.
--app=url opens a page in a window without tabs or an address bar, the quickest way to make a web interface look like an application, but it is still the browser.
Chromium --kiosk starts full screen; exit with Alt+F4 or by killing the process, and combine it with an autostart entry for display systems.
Chromium policies in /etc/chromium/policies/managed as JSON files can set the homepage, block extensions and turn off the password manager for kiosks and managed devices.
ctrl+shift+delete opens the clear browsing data page, ctrl+shift+n a private window and ctrl+shift+t restores the last closed tab.
chrome://version shows the exact version and the profile path, chrome://gpu shows hardware acceleration and chrome://flags lists experiments.
chrome://net-export records network events to a file, and the network tab in developer tools shows requests, timing and why a request failed, such as blocked by CSP or mixed content.
A page that works in a normal window but not in an automated one may check navigator.webdriver or need real user gestures; allow scripts only on pages you own or have permission for.
Chromium keeps one process per site and tab, so memory grows with open pages; on a Raspberry Pi use one window, close tabs and avoid pages with video or heavy scripts during automation.
Chromium on Wayland needs --ozone-platform=wayland or auto detection; on X11 images the default works, and tools such as xdotool only control X11 windows.
Hardware video decoding on a Raspberry Pi needs the right Chromium build; video that stutters in the browser may play smoothly in a dedicated player such as mpv.
Extensions with broad permissions can read every page you visit; install only those you trust, and keep a separate profile without extensions for automation.
xdotool needs a running X11 session; on Wayland it types into nothing, so check echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE and switch the Raspberry Pi desktop to X11 when you need it.
xdotool key --clearmodifiers ctrl+l releases keys that the user may still hold, which prevents a stuck shift key from changing what the script sends.
xdotool key accepts several keys in one call separated by spaces: xdotool key ctrl+a BackSpace types select all and delete in one command.
xdotool type --delay 30 --clearmodifiers 'text' types slowly enough for web forms; very fast typing drops characters in browsers on a busy Pi.
xdotool mousemove --sync x y click 1 waits until the pointer arrived before it clicks, and xdotool click --repeat 2 --delay 100 1 makes a double click.
xdotool getdisplaygeometry prints the screen size and xdotool getwindowgeometry ID the position and size of a window, needed to turn a picture position into a click position.
xdotool search --class chromium lists Chromium windows, and xdotool windowfocus ID gives one the keyboard focus before you type into it.
xdotool windowsize ID 1280 720 and windowmove ID 0 0 give a window a known size and place, so recorded click positions stay valid.
xdotool key super opens menus on some desktops and Escape closes them; know which window has focus before sending shortcuts, because keys go to the focused window.
Scroll with xdotool click 5 (down) and xdotool click 4 (up), repeated with --repeat; page scroll keys Page_Down and space work in browsers as well.
xdotool behaves like a person typing, so special letters may be mapped wrongly with other keyboard layouts; paste text through the clipboard with xclip when exact characters matter.
xclip -selection clipboard -i < file puts a file's text on the clipboard and xdotool key ctrl+v pastes it, which handles long text and non English letters reliably.
wmctrl -a name raises a window by title and wmctrl -r name -b add,maximized_vert,maximized_horz maximizes it, both work on X11 desktops without a mouse.
scrot -o file.png takes a screenshot on X11 and import -window root file.png does it with ImageMagick; grim does it on Wayland compositors such as labwc.
A screenshot of the screen and a mouse position check before clicking is more reliable than blind coordinates; verify that the pointer is inside the target before typing.
Label every control with text, not only an icon; an icon alone may be clear to its designer but not to a new user, and screen readers need a name.
Make the clickable area at least 44 by 44 pixels on touch screens and keep 8 pixels of space between neighbouring buttons.
Put the main action in a stable place, use a clear verb for its name and style secondary actions quietly; a screen with three equal looking buttons confuses.
Show progress for anything slower than a second: a spinner for short waits, a progress bar with text for longer ones, and a way to cancel.
Say what happened and what to do next in error messages: Wrong password, try again or reset it, not Error 401.
Empty states are chances to guide: instead of an empty list say what the list will contain and show the one button that adds the first item.
Use the same word for the same thing everywhere: if the button says Save the confirmation should say Saved, not Updated or Done.
Do not hide important information in tooltips; touch devices have no hover, so put it on the screen or behind a clearly visible help button.
Contrast of text to background should be at least 4.5 to 1; light grey on white looks elegant but cannot be read in sunlight or by many older users.
Offer light and dark themes that follow the system by default and let the user override it; remember the choice and apply it before the first paint to avoid a flash.
Design the language switch as a visible control that shows each language in its own name, and keep texts in one table so a new language needs no code change.
Plan for long words and different text length: German and Turkish translations are often 30 percent longer than English, so buttons and labels must grow or wrap.
Confirm destructive actions with the name of the thing and a button that says what it does, such as Delete device, and make undo available when possible.
Keep forms short, group related fields, put labels above fields on phones and mark only the optional fields when most fields are required.
Keyboard support is part of the design: Tab order follows reading order, Enter submits, Escape closes dialogs and focus returns to where it was.
A native window with a custom title bar must still support drag, double click to maximize, resize from the edges and the standard shortcuts, or it feels broken.
Use one accent color for actions and keep status colors for status: green for success, red for errors, and add an icon or text so color-blind users understand.
Animations should explain a change, last 150 to 250 milliseconds and respect the reduced motion setting; decoration that moves without a reason distracts.
On first start show only what is needed to begin and move advanced options into a settings page; every extra choice slows a new user down.
Show connection state clearly for devices and remote services: connecting, online and offline with different colors and words, updated while the screen is open.
type=email, tel, url and number show the right keyboard on phones, and inputmode=numeric with pattern gives a number pad without the problems of type=number.
The required, minlength, maxlength and pattern attributes give instant checks, but the server must repeat every check because requests can skip the page.
A form field needs a label element connected with for and id, and the label text should say what to enter; placeholder text disappears and is no label.
Disable the submit button while the request runs and show the result near the button; double submits create duplicate records on slow connections.
Keep the typed values when validation fails; clearing a long form because of one wrong field is the fastest way to lose users.
A hidden CSRF token or a custom header protects cookie based forms from being submitted by other sites; JSON APIs that require a custom header get this protection for free.
File uploads: check size and type on the server, store files outside the web folder under random names and never trust the file name or type sent by the browser.
Passwords: allow long passphrases and paste, show a visibility toggle and measure strength by length, not by rules that force symbols and capitals.
Sign-in codes by e-mail should be short lived, usable once and limited in attempts, and the message should say which site asked and how long the code works.
Do not tell which part of a login was wrong; one message such as wrong e-mail or password does not help an attacker find valid accounts.
Add a clear way back: a cancel or back button on every step of a multi step form, and show the number of steps so users know how much is left.
str.split() without an argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty parts, while split(' ') keeps empty strings between double spaces.
Late binding in lambdas: a lambda made in a loop sees the final loop value unless you bind it with a default argument, lambda i=i: i.
round() uses banker's rounding, so round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4; use the decimal module with ROUND_HALF_UP when you need school rounding.
Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2') equals Decimal('0.3') exactly, so use Decimal built from strings for money instead of float.
The walrus operator := assigns inside an expression, which removes a repeated call: if (n := len(items)) > 3: print(n).
f-strings accept format specs: f'{x:.2f}' for decimals, f'{x:,}' for thousands, f'{x:>8}' for alignment and f'{x=}' for quick debugging.
collections.Counter counts items and most_common(n) lists the top n, replacing a manual dictionary loop.
collections.defaultdict(list) creates the list on first access, so grouping needs no if key in dict check.
collections.deque with maxlen keeps only the last n items, a simple log buffer: deque(maxlen=3) drops the oldest on append.
itertools.islice takes a slice from any iterator, such as the first lines of a huge file: list(islice(f, 5)).
zip stops at the shortest input; itertools.zip_longest fills the gaps, and zip(strict=True) raises an error when lengths differ.
enumerate(items, start=1) gives numbers that begin at one, handy for lists shown to people.
sorted(items, key=lambda x: (x.a, -x.b)) sorts by several fields with mixed direction, and sorted is stable, so equal items keep their order.
dict union with | merges two dictionaries and the right side wins: {'a': 1} | {'a': 2} is {'a': 2}.
List comprehension with a condition filters and transforms at once; use a generator expression inside sum() or any() so no list is built in memory.
any() and all() stop at the first deciding item; all([]) is True and any([]) is False, a trap for empty lists.
A slice copy items[:] makes a shallow copy of a list, and items[::-1] reverses it without changing the original.
Negative indexes count from the end and slices never raise IndexError: 'abc'[5:] is an empty string, but 'abc'[5] raises.
str.removeprefix and str.removesuffix remove an exact start or end, unlike strip, which removes a set of characters.
str.partition splits at the first separator into three parts and never fails, which is simpler than split for key=value text.
casefold() is the stronger version of lower() for comparing text in different languages, and unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s) makes composed letters equal.
Python 3 reads text files as the locale encoding unless told otherwise, so pass encoding='utf-8' to open() to get the same result on every system.
pathlib makes paths readable: Path('a') / 'b.txt' joins, .suffix and .stem split names, .read_text() and .write_text() handle small files.
Path.glob('**/*.py') searches recursively and rglob('*.py') does the same; both return generators, so wrap them in sorted() for a stable order.
Write files atomically: write to a temporary file in the same folder and call os.replace(tmp, final), so readers never see half a file.
json.dump(data, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) keeps non English letters readable, and sort_keys=True gives stable output for diffs.
json.loads raises json.JSONDecodeError with line and column, so catch that exception for user supplied text instead of a bare except.
A JSON Lines file stores one object per line; append with a single write per record and read with a loop, which survives a crash better than one big array.
csv.DictReader reads rows as dictionaries and csv.writer quotes fields with commas; open the file with newline='' so line ends stay correct.
sqlite3 is built in: use ? placeholders for values, never string formatting, and wrap changes in with conn: to commit or roll back automatically.
sqlite3 row_factory = sqlite3.Row lets you read columns by name: row['a'], which is clearer than index numbers.
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL lets readers and one writer work at the same time in SQLite, a good default for small servers.
SQLite INSERT OR REPLACE and ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE make an upsert; the second form keeps the other columns of the row.
datetime.now(timezone.utc) gives an aware time; the zoneinfo module provides time zones such as ZoneInfo('Europe/Istanbul') without extra packages.
datetime.fromisoformat parses ISO text and isoformat() writes it; strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M') makes human readable text.
timedelta does date arithmetic: date + timedelta(days=30), and subtracting two dates gives a timedelta with .days and total_seconds().
time.monotonic() never goes backwards, so use it for timeouts and measurements, and time.time() only for wall clock timestamps.
shlex.quote makes a value safe inside a shell command and shlex.split splits a command line the way a shell does, respecting quotes.
argparse builds a command line interface with help text for free: add_argument('--port', type=int, default=8080) and parse_args().
logging with basicConfig(level=..., format=...) is better than print for programs that run for days; use logger.exception in an except block to include the traceback.
RotatingFileHandler(path, maxBytes, backupCount) keeps log files from filling a small SD card.
threading.Event is a clean stop signal: a worker loops with while not stop.wait(2): and the main thread calls stop.set() to end it quickly.
threading.Lock protects data that several threads change; use with lock: so the lock is released even when an error happens.
queue.Queue is thread safe and its get(timeout=...) raises queue.Empty, so a consumer thread can wait without a busy loop.
daemon threads stop when the main program ends without finishing their work; use them for background keep alive loops, not for saving data.
concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor runs many slow input and output calls in parallel; map() returns results in the original order.
asyncio.wait_for raises TimeoutError when a coroutine is too slow, and it cancels the coroutine for you.
Never call time.sleep inside async code because it blocks the whole loop; use await asyncio.sleep, and run blocking functions with asyncio.to_thread.
dataclasses reduce boilerplate: @dataclass gives __init__, __repr__ and ==, field(default_factory=list) is the safe way to default a list.
enum.Enum gives named constants with a fixed set of values, so a typo raises an error instead of passing silently as text.
functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None) remembers function results, and cache_info() shows hits and misses; arguments must be hashable.
functools.partial fixes some arguments of a function in advance, which is useful for callbacks that need extra data.
A context manager from contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator into a with block; code after yield runs even when an error happens inside the block.
contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError) ignores a named error in one line, cleaner than try/except/pass for removing a file that may not exist.
Catch specific exceptions; a bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, which stops Ctrl+C from working.
The else block of try runs only when no error happened, and finally always runs; keep the try block short so you do not hide errors from other lines.
assert statements are removed with python -O, so never use them to validate user input; raise ValueError instead.
__name__ == '__main__' lets a file be both a module and a script, so tests can import it without starting the program.
sys.exit(1) ends a script with an error code that shell scripts and systemd can read; exit code 0 means success.
python3 -m venv .venv creates an isolated environment; use .venv/bin/pip so packages do not mix with the system and do not need sudo.
python3 -m py_compile file.py checks syntax without running the file, a quick test after editing a script on a remote device.
python3 -m json.tool file.json validates and pretty prints JSON, and python3 -m http.server serves the current folder for a quick test.
python3 -m timeit measures small snippets: python3 -m timeit -n 1000 '"a".upper()' prints the average time per loop.
python3 -X dev or PYTHONDEVMODE=1 turns on extra warnings and checks that help find unclosed files and wrong resource use.
python3 -u or PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 writes output at once, so logs from a service appear in journalctl without delay.
os.environ.get('NAME', 'default') reads settings from the environment, and keeping secrets there instead of in code keeps them out of the repository.
secrets.token_urlsafe(32) makes a strong random token and secrets.compare_digest compares secrets in constant time; random and == are not suitable.
