hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() makes a fingerprint to check files; for passwords use a slow function such as hashlib.scrypt or pbkdf2_hmac with a random salt.
struct.pack and struct.unpack convert numbers to bytes for binary protocols: '<H' is a little endian unsigned 16 bit number.
int(text, 16) reads hexadecimal and format(n, '08b') writes a number as eight binary digits; bit operations & | ^ << >> work on integers.
re.compile once and reuse the pattern; use raw strings r'\d+' to avoid double backslashes, and re.fullmatch when the whole text must match.
A greedy pattern .* matches as much as possible and .*? as little as possible, which matters when extracting text between two markers.
re.sub accepts a function as replacement, so each match can be changed with code: re.sub(r'\d+', lambda m: str(int(m.group())*2), text).
Do not parse HTML with regular expressions; html.parser from the standard library or BeautifulSoup copes with broken markup.
html.escape(text) makes user text safe inside HTML and html.unescape reverses it, which protects pages and e-mails built from user input.
urllib.parse.urlparse splits an address into parts, quote and urlencode build safe query text, and parse_qs reads it back.
socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=3) is a quick check that a port is open; always set a timeout so the check cannot hang.
Binding a server to port 0 lets the system pick a free port, and getsockname()[1] tells you which one, useful for tests.
SO_REUSEADDR lets a server restart at once on the same port instead of failing with Address already in use during the TIME_WAIT period.
http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer handles requests in threads, so one slow client does not block the others in small tools.
tempfile.TemporaryDirectory cleans up after the with block and NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False) keeps the file; use them instead of fixed names in /tmp.
shutil.copy2 keeps timestamps, shutil.move works across disks, shutil.rmtree deletes a folder tree and shutil.disk_usage reports free space.
shutil.which('name') finds a program on PATH or returns None, so a script can check for a tool before running it.
os.walk visits a folder tree and you can edit dirs in place to skip folders such as .git or node_modules.
os.stat(path).st_mtime gives the modification time and os.utime sets it; compare it with time.time() to find files older than a number of days.
os.chmod(path, 0o600) limits a file to its owner, important for files that hold tokens or passwords; the 0o prefix marks an octal number.
os.open with flags and mode 0o600 creates a secret file that was never readable by others, avoiding the short window of write then chmod.
fcntl.flock gives a lock between processes on Linux, so only one copy of a script runs at a time; the lock is released when the process ends.
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handler) lets a script clean up when systemd stops it; systemctl stop sends SIGTERM first and SIGKILL after a timeout.
atexit.register(func) runs a function when the program ends normally, but not after SIGKILL, so do not rely on it for important saving.
platform and sys.platform tell the system: sys.platform is 'linux' on a Raspberry Pi, platform.machine() gives aarch64 or armv7l.
os.cpu_count() gives the number of cores and os.getloadavg() the load; compare load to cores before starting heavy work on a small device.
Reading /proc/meminfo or /proc/uptime needs no extra package: float(open('/proc/uptime').read().split()[0]) gives seconds since boot.
gc and memory: a list that only grows, such as a cache without a size limit, is the usual memory leak in long running scripts; use deque(maxlen) or lru_cache(maxsize).
Type hints document code and help editors: def f(x: int, y: str | None = None) -> bool; they are not enforced at run time.
typing.TypedDict and dataclass describe the shape of a JSON object, making typos in key names visible to the editor.
A generator function with yield produces values one at a time, so a script can process a very large file without loading it into memory.
Iterating a file object reads one line at a time and keeps memory low; use for line in f instead of f.readlines() on big logs.
str.splitlines handles all line endings, including Windows ones, while split('\n') leaves carriage returns at the end of each part.
bytes and str are different types: decode bytes with .decode('utf-8', errors='replace') to survive broken input and encode text before sending it over a socket.
int() on a float string fails: int('1.5') raises ValueError, so use int(float('1.5')) and remember that it cuts toward zero.
Integer division // rounds down toward negative infinity and % follows the divisor's sign: -7 // 2 is -4 and -7 % 2 is 1.
Python integers have no size limit, so 2**100 works without overflow, but very large numbers make loops slow.
statistics.mean, median and stdev give quick numbers for sensor readings without installing numpy.
random.seed(n) makes random numbers repeatable for tests, and random.choice, sample and shuffle cover most needs; random is not for security.
math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9) compares floating point numbers safely instead of ==.
textwrap.shorten and textwrap.wrap fit text into a width, handy for messages on small displays and log lines.
difflib.unified_diff shows the difference between two texts and difflib.get_close_matches suggests the nearest word for a typo.
configparser reads INI files with sections and keeps comments out; use getint and getboolean to convert values, with fallback= for missing keys.
tomllib in Python 3.11 and newer reads TOML files from the standard library: tomllib.loads(text) returns a dictionary.
zipfile can create and read archives with the standard library: ZipFile(name, 'w', ZIP_DEFLATED).write(path), and namelist() lists the contents.
Never extract an archive from an untrusted source with extractall without checking names; entries such as ../../x can write outside the target folder.
gzip.open(path, 'rt') reads compressed text files line by line, and gzip.compress(bytes) shrinks data in memory before sending.
pickle can run code when loading, so never unpickle files from other people; use JSON for data you exchange.
input validation: check type, range and length of every value that arrives from a network or file, and reject instead of fixing silently.
Quote variables in bash: "$file" keeps spaces intact, while an unquoted $file splits into several words.
set -euo pipefail stops a script at the first error, at unset variables and at failures inside pipes, which makes scripts safer.
Without pipefail a pipe returns the status of the last command only, so a failing first command goes unnoticed.
${var^^} makes text upper case and ${var,,} lower case in bash 4 and newer; ${#var} is the length.
${var/old/new} replaces the first match and ${var//old/new} every match inside a bash variable.
Arrays in bash: arr=(a "b c"); "${arr[@]}" expands to separate quoted items and ${#arr[@]} is the count.
Use [[ ]] in bash for tests: it needs no quoting of variables, supports patterns [[ $f == *.txt ]] and regular expressions with =~.
The test -n checks for non empty text and -z for empty text; -f is a regular file, -d a folder, -e anything that exists and -x an executable.
$(command) runs a command and inserts its output and is easier to nest than backticks; trailing newlines are removed.
$? holds the exit status of the last command; 0 is success, so test it right away or use if command; then.
Exit codes above 128 mean the program was ended by a signal: 137 is SIGKILL, 143 SIGTERM and 130 Ctrl+C.
The && operator runs the next command only after success and || only after failure; a && b || c runs c also when b fails, so use if for real branching.
Redirects: > overwrites, >> appends, 2>&1 joins error output to normal output, &> file sends both to a file and 2>/dev/null hides errors.
Order matters in redirects: cmd >file 2>&1 sends both to the file, but cmd 2>&1 >file sends errors to the terminal.
A here document feeds several lines to a command: cat <<'EOF' with quotes around EOF prevents variable expansion inside.
A here string passes one value as input: grep -c a <<< "banana" is shorter than echo and a pipe.
Process substitution <(cmd) gives a command output as a file name: diff <(sort a) <(sort b) compares sorted files without temporary files.
trap commands run on signals and on EXIT; trap '' INT ignores Ctrl+C and trap - INT restores the default.
Reading in a loop through a pipe runs in a subshell, so variables set inside are lost; use input redirection or process substitution instead.
Arithmetic in bash uses $(( )): echo $(( 7 / 2 )) is 3 because only integers are supported; use bc or awk for decimals.
awk handles decimals: awk 'BEGIN { printf "%.2f\n", 7/2 }' prints 3.50.
Functions in bash take arguments as $1, $2 and $@, return a status with return and print results with echo to be captured by $( ).
local makes a function variable private; without it every variable in a bash function is global.
shift removes the first argument and "$#" counts them; a while loop with shift parses simple options without getopts.
getopts parses short options: while getopts "vf:" o; do case $o in v) ...;; f) file=$OPTARG;; esac; done.
printf is more predictable than echo: printf '%s\n' "$text" prints text with backslashes and leading dashes unchanged.
Brace expansion creates lists and ranges: echo {a,b}.txt gives a.txt b.txt, {1..3} gives 1 2 3 and mkdir -p proj/{src,docs} makes both folders.
Globs like * do not match hidden files by default; use shopt -s dotglob to include them and nullglob to get an empty list when nothing matches.
Without nullglob an unmatched glob stays as literal text, so a loop over *.log runs once with the text '*.log' when no file exists.
find with -print0 and xargs -0 handle names with spaces and newlines: find . -name '*.tmp' -print0 | xargs -0 ls -l.
find -mtime +7 finds files older than seven days, -mmin -10 files changed in the last ten minutes, -size +10M larger than ten megabytes and -type f only files.
find -maxdepth 1 stays in the current folder and -name uses globs in quotes, so the shell does not expand them first.
grep -r searches folders, -n shows line numbers, -i ignores case, -l lists names only, -v inverts and --include='*.py' limits file types.
grep -E uses extended regular expressions and -F treats the pattern as plain text, which is safer and faster for strings with dots or brackets.
grep -w matches whole words only and -x whole lines; grep -c counts matching lines, not matches.
grep -q is silent and only sets the exit status, perfect inside if statements: if grep -q word file; then ...
grep -A 2 -B 1 shows lines after and before a match, and -C 2 both, handy for reading logs around an error.
sed -i edits a file in place; sed -i.bak keeps a backup copy, and sed -n '5,10p' prints only a line range.
sed 's/old/new/g' replaces every match on a line; use another delimiter such as | when the text contains slashes: sed 's|/a|/b|'.
sed '/pattern/d' deletes matching lines and sed '/^$/d' removes empty lines; sed '1d' removes the first line.
awk '{print $1}' prints the first column, -F, sets the comma as separator and NR gives the line number.
awk can sum a column without a script: awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}' file, and NF is the number of fields in a line.
sort -u removes duplicates, sort -n compares numbers, sort -h understands sizes such as 2K and 1M and sort -k2 sorts by the second column.
uniq only removes neighbouring duplicates, so run sort first; sort | uniq -c | sort -rn counts and ranks lines.
cut -d: -f1 takes the first field and cut -c1-3 the first three characters; for fixed separators it is faster than awk.
tr translates or deletes characters: tr a-z A-Z makes capitals, tr -d '\r' removes Windows line ends and tr -s ' ' squeezes repeated spaces.
wc -l counts lines, wc -w words and wc -c bytes; a file without a final newline has one line less than you might expect.
tee writes to a file and to the screen at once, and tee -a appends: command | tee log.txt shows and saves output.
xargs -n1 runs one command per item and -P4 runs four in parallel, handy for checking many hosts or converting many files.
sudo with a redirect does not elevate the redirect: sudo echo x > /etc/f fails; use echo x | sudo tee /etc/f instead.
timeout 5 cmd stops a command after five seconds with exit code 124, a protection against scripts that hang.
sleep accepts decimals in GNU coreutils, sleep 0.5 waits half a second; use a loop with a check and a limit instead of one long sleep when waiting for a service.
date +%s gives the Unix time, date -d @1700000000 converts it back, date -u uses UTC and date +%F_%H%M%S makes sortable file names.
date -d 'yesterday' and date -d '+1 month' do date calculations in GNU date; use TZ=Europe/Istanbul date to see another zone.
stat -c '%s %a %U' file prints size, permissions and owner in GNU stat, a script friendly alternative to parsing ls.
ls -lt sorts by time and -S by size, -h makes sizes readable and -d lists a folder itself instead of its content.
du -sh folder gives the total size of a folder and du -h --max-depth=1 | sort -h shows which sub folders are big.
chmod +x makes a script runnable, chmod 600 keeps a file private and chmod -R changes a whole tree; numbers are read, write, execute as 4, 2 and 1.
umask sets the default permissions of new files: with umask 077 new files are readable by the owner only.
ln -s target link creates a symbolic link and readlink -f link prints the real path; deleting the link does not delete the target.
cp -a keeps permissions, times and links, and rsync -a does the same with progress and resume; add a trailing slash to the source folder to copy its contents.
mv within one disk is instant and atomic; across disks it copies and deletes, so a failed move can leave both copies.
mkdir -p creates all parent folders and does not fail if the folder exists, which makes it safe to repeat in scripts.
cat -A shows hidden characters: $ marks line ends, ^M a Windows carriage return and ^I a tab, the quick way to find invisible problems in scripts.
file name shows the type of a file, and head -c 4 shows the first bytes; a script starts with #! followed by the interpreter path.
PATH is searched from left to right, so put your own folder first to override a command; command -v name shows what will run.
set -x shows commands as they run and PS4='+ ${LINENO}: ' adds line numbers to the trace.
Quote the pattern in case statements and end each branch with ;; ; use * as the default branch.
A subshell in parentheses keeps changes of folder and variables local: (cd /tmp && command) leaves your current folder unchanged.
Use exec to replace the shell with a program and exec >file to redirect all following output of a script into a file.
A job in the background starts with & and $! holds its process number; wait $! waits for it and returns its exit status.
wait with no argument waits for all background jobs, so a script can start several tasks at once and continue when all finished.
kill -0 PID sends no signal but reports whether a process exists and can be signalled, a simple liveness check.
pgrep -f matches the full command line and may match itself in scripts; pgrep -x matches the exact process name only.
nohup command & keeps a program running after the terminal closes and writes output to nohup.out; for services prefer systemd.
nproc prints the number of processing units and free -m the memory in megabytes; on a Raspberry Pi check both before starting heavy jobs.
uptime -p prints how long the system has run in words and who -b shows the last boot time.
command output with sort -h is useful with du: du -sh * | sort -h puts the biggest folder last.
jq reads JSON on the command line: jq -r '.name' file prints a field without quotes and jq '.[] | select(.a > 1)' filters a list.
jq -e sets the exit status from the result, so if jq -e '.ok' file works in scripts; jq --arg passes a shell value safely.
curl -fsS fails on HTTP errors and still shows the error text, -L follows redirects, -m 10 sets a time limit and -o file saves the output.
curl -w '%{http_code}' -o /dev/null -s url prints only the status code, a one line health check for a service.
curl --retry 3 --retry-delay 2 repeats a request after temporary failures, and --connect-timeout stops waiting for a host that does not answer.
In shell scripts check that a command exists before using it: command -v jq >/dev/null || { echo "jq missing" >&2; exit 1; }.
Send messages for people to stderr with >&2, so that output of a script can still be piped or saved without error text mixed in.
A lock directory is an atomic lock in shell: mkdir /tmp/x.lock succeeds for only one process at a time, and the second gets an error.
flock -n file command runs the command only if no other copy holds the lock, protecting cron jobs that must not overlap.
Check disk space before a big copy: df --output=avail -k . | tail -1 gives the free kilobytes as one number.
cmp -s a b compares files quietly and sets the exit status; cmp reports the first difference and diff shows all of them.
sha256sum file prints a checksum and sha256sum -c list.txt verifies many files at once, to check that a download or copy is complete.
seq 1 5 makes numbers, seq -w pads them with zeros and seq 0 5 20 steps by five; useful for loops in scripts.
yes prints a line forever and head stops it: yes ok | head -3; a pipe closes when the reader ends.
paste -sd, joins lines with a comma and column -t aligns text into columns, simple ways to format output.
comm compares two sorted files in three columns; comm -12 shows lines in both and comm -23 lines only in the first.
basename and dirname split a path; basename file .txt also removes the suffix, and realpath makes an absolute clean path.
printf '%s\n' "${arr[@]}" | sort prints an array one item per line, a clean way to sort items held in a bash array.
IFS=, read -ra parts <<< "a,b,c" splits a text on commas into an array without external tools.
mapfile -t lines < file reads a file into an array with one line per item, with no trailing newlines.
Use [ "$a" -eq "$b" ] for numbers and [ "$a" = "$b" ] for text; comparing numbers as text gives wrong results such as 10 before 9.
Sorting numbers as text puts 10 before 9; sort -n or sort -V fixes it, and sort -V also handles version numbers such as 1.10 and 1.9.
tar --exclude='*.log' leaves matching files out of an archive, and tar -C /path . changes folder first so the archive has no absolute paths.
gzip -k keeps the original file, gunzip -c prints decompressed data without writing it, and zcat reads compressed files like cat.
xz compresses better but slower than gzip, and on a Raspberry Pi the slow compression of big files may take minutes; gzip is a good default for logs.
od -c and xxd show the bytes of a file; hexdump -C is similar, useful for finding invisible characters and checking encodings.
Environment variables set in /etc/environment or a service file are not read by a normal user shell the same way; check with systemctl show -p Environment service.
git status -s gives a short list of changes, git diff --stat a summary of changed lines and git diff --staged shows what the next commit contains.
git restore file throws away uncommitted changes of one file, so check git diff first because there is no undo.
git commit --amend changes the last commit message or adds forgotten files, but only do it before the commit was pushed.
git log --oneline --graph --decorate shows the history as a tree with branch names, and git log -n 5 limits the number of commits.
git log --format=%s prints only commit messages and git log --author=name filters by author, useful for release notes.
git branch name creates a branch and git switch name moves to it; git switch -c name does both in one step.
git branch -d name deletes a merged branch and refuses to delete unmerged work; -D forces it and the lost commits can only be found with git reflog.
git merge --no-ff keeps a merge commit even when a fast forward is possible, so the history shows where a feature began and ended.
git stash saves uncommitted work away, git stash pop brings it back and git stash list shows what is stored.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit and keeps the changes staged, while git reset --hard HEAD~1 discards them completely.
git reflog lists where HEAD was before, so a commit lost by reset --hard can be found and restored with git reset --hard HEAD@{1}.
git tag -a v1.0 -m text makes an annotated tag with a message and git tag -l lists tags; push tags with git push --tags.
git diff branch1..branch2 compares two branches, git diff HEAD~1 compares with the commit before and git diff -- path limits it to a path.
git show commit:path prints a file as it was in an older commit, and git checkout commit -- path restores one file from there.
git blame file shows who last changed each line and git log -L start,end:file shows the history of a line range.
git bisect finds the commit that broke something by binary search; mark commits good and bad and git checks out the middle each time.
git grep pattern searches only tracked files and is faster than grep -r in a repository, because it skips build folders and .git.
.gitignore lists patterns of files git should not track; it does not remove files already tracked, run git rm --cached file for those.
git check-ignore -v file tells which rule ignores a file, the quick way to find out why a new file does not show up.
git rm --cached file stops tracking a file but keeps it on disk, the right fix after you committed a file that should be ignored.
git config --global user.name and user.email set your identity; git config --list --show-origin shows where each value comes from.
git config pull.rebase true makes git pull rebase your commits on top of the remote ones, which keeps a linear history without merge commits.
git pull --rebase before git push avoids a merge commit when somebody else pushed first, the usual fix for a rejected non fast forward push.
git push --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen, which is much safer than --force after a rebase.
git remote -v lists remotes and git remote set-url origin address changes the address after a repository was renamed or moved.
git clone --depth 1 downloads only the latest commit, which is much faster and smaller on a Raspberry Pi, and git fetch --unshallow fetches the rest later.
git clean -n shows which untracked files would be removed and git clean -fd really removes them; always run the dry run first.
git rebase -i is interactive and not for scripts; in automation use git pull --rebase or a merge, which need no editor.
git commit -am adds only tracked files, so a new file needs git add first; git add -A stages new, changed and deleted files.
git diff --check finds trailing spaces and leftover conflict markers before you commit.
git merge --abort returns to the state before a merge that went wrong, and git rebase --abort does the same for a rebase.
git submodule add and git clone --recurse-submodules handle repositories inside repositories; without the flag the submodule folders stay empty.
git worktree add ../folder branch gives a second working folder of the same repository, so you can test another branch without stashing.
git rev-parse --short HEAD prints the short commit id and git describe --tags names a commit by the nearest tag, handy for version strings.
git rev-parse --show-toplevel prints the root folder of the repository from any sub folder, so scripts can find their project.
git shortlog -sn counts commits per author and git rev-list --count HEAD counts all commits, quick project statistics.
core.autocrlf true converts line endings on Windows and input on Linux; a .gitattributes line such as * text=auto makes it part of the repository for everyone.
file mode changes show up as diffs when a file system does not keep executable bits; git config core.fileMode false hides them, git update-index --chmod=+x file records the bit.
git secrets: never commit tokens or passwords; if one was committed, treat it as leaked, change it at the provider and only then clean the history, because clones keep the old copy.
git commit -m with several -m options makes a subject line plus body paragraphs; keep the subject under 50 characters and write what changed and why.
GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 makes git fail instead of asking for a password, which stops scripts and services from waiting for input that nobody gives.
git -C path command runs git in another folder without cd, which keeps scripts simple and the working folder unchanged.
git log --since='2 weeks ago' and --until limit commits by date, and --after with a date works too, for weekly summaries.
git diff --name-only HEAD~1 lists the changed file names only, which a deploy script can use to decide what to restart.
git update-index --assume-unchanged file hides local edits of a tracked file from git status; it is a local trick, not a team solution.
git hooks live in .git/hooks and are not copied by clone; core.hooksPath lets a repository keep them in a tracked folder.
A pre-commit hook that exits with a non zero code stops the commit, a place to run a syntax check or tests before code is saved.
git config --get-regexp alias lists aliases; git config --global alias.st status makes git st work like git status.
git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate refs/heads shows branches with the newest first, a quick way to find stale branches.
git merge-base A B finds the common ancestor of two branches and git log A..B lists the commits in B that A does not have.
DNS names are resolved by the system; getent hosts name shows the answer that programs really get, while dig and nslookup ask a server directly.
The port ranges: below 1024 need root on Linux, 1024 to 49151 are registered and above are temporary; choose 8000 to 9000 for your own web tools.
HTTP status groups: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the request was wrong (401 login needed, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 429 too many) and 5xx the server failed.
http.HTTPStatus(503).phrase is Service Unavailable, the status Render shows while a sleeping free service wakes up, so retry a few seconds later.
A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket; a proxy that does not pass that header breaks the connection.
WebSocket heartbeats: send a ping every few seconds and drop the connection when no pong comes, since a dead connection can look open for minutes.
Reconnect with growing waits: 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds up to a limit and a little random jitter, so many clients do not hit a restarting server at the same moment.
TCP keepalive probes detect dead peers: socket.setsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_KEEPALIVE, 1) turns it on, but the default delay is two hours.
TLS needs the right clock: a device with a wrong date sees valid certificates as expired, so check date first when HTTPS fails on a Raspberry Pi without a clock.
Gzip compression of text responses cuts transfer by 70 percent or more; JSON and HTML compress well, images already compressed do not.
Cache static files with a long max age and a file name that changes with the content, and never cache API answers that carry user data.
CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server: a request from another origin needs Access-Control-Allow-Origin in the answer, and curl is never blocked by it.
Cookies for a login should be HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax or Strict, so scripts cannot read them and other sites cannot send them freely.
Rate limiting by account and by client address slows password guessing; return 429 with a Retry-After header and count failures in a time window.
Webhooks and agents should check a secret or a signature on every request, because anybody who knows the address can send requests to it.

The box-sizing property decides what width means: with content-box padding is added to the width, with border-box it is included, so a 100 pixel box with 10 pixels of padding is 120 or 100 pixels wide.
Flexbox centers a child in both directions with display flex, align-items center and justify-content center on the parent.
The aspect-ratio property keeps a box in proportion: width 160 pixels and aspect-ratio 16 / 9 gives a height of 90 pixels.
An absolutely positioned box is placed relative to the nearest ancestor with a position value; give the parent position relative or the box jumps to the page corner.
position sticky keeps a header visible while scrolling inside its container; it needs a top value and does not work when a parent has overflow hidden.
A flex item with min-width 0 can shrink below its content; without it a long word or a wide table pushes the layout wider than the screen.
The gap property spaces flex and grid items without margins: display flex with gap 10px puts exactly ten pixels between two boxes.
The clamp function sets a size between a minimum and a maximum, for example font-size clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem), so text scales without media queries.
Viewport units follow the window: 100vw includes the scrollbar width, while 100% of the parent does not, a common cause of a small horizontal scroll.
The dvh unit is the visible height on phones when the address bar moves, while vh uses the larger height; use 100dvh for full screen layouts.
The selector :not(.x) and :is(a, b) shorten rules, and :has() selects a parent by its children, which removes a lot of script code.
Specificity decides which rule wins: an id beats a class and a class beats a tag, and !important beats all of them, so avoid it and use a simpler selector.
Margins of vertical neighbours collapse into the larger one, so two boxes with a 20 and a 30 pixel margin are 30 pixels apart, not 50.
z-index only works on positioned elements and inside stacking contexts, so a high number on a static element changes nothing.
overflow auto shows scrollbars only when the content is larger, while overflow scroll always reserves space for them; set a height or max-height or nothing scrolls.
text-overflow ellipsis needs three rules together: white-space nowrap, overflow hidden and a fixed width or a flex item with min-width 0.
A transition animates a change of a property when the value changes, for example transition opacity 0.2s; the property must have a start value that can be calculated.
The media query prefers-reduced-motion lets you switch animations off for people who asked their system for less motion.
The hidden attribute hides an element but a CSS display rule on the same element wins over it; add [hidden]{display:none!important} if your classes set display.
The dialog element with showModal() gives a modal window with focus handling and an Escape key built in, so no custom overlay script is needed.
The details and summary elements make an accordion with no script, and the open attribute shows its state.
FormData(form) collects all fields of a form including files, and Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)) turns simple fields into an object for JSON.
The input event fires on every change while typing and change only when the field loses focus; use input for live validation and search boxes.
A debounce waits until typing stops before it runs a search: clear the timer on each key and start a new setTimeout of 250 to 400 milliseconds.
A throttle runs a function at most once per interval, which fits scroll and resize handlers; a debounce fits search boxes.
fetch does not reject on HTTP errors such as 404 or 500; check response.ok yourself and read the body with response.json() or response.text().
AbortController cancels a fetch: pass its signal to fetch and call abort(), which also makes a simple timeout for requests.
WebSocket in the browser fires open, message, error and close events; wrap reconnecting in a function that waits longer after each failure.
EventSource gives a one way stream from the server over normal HTTP and reconnects by itself, simpler than WebSocket when the page only listens.
navigator.onLine only tells if the device has a network, not if the server answers; call a small health address and measure the answer instead.
The visibilitychange event tells when a tab is hidden, so a page can stop polling in the background and refresh once when it becomes visible again.
IntersectionObserver reports when an element enters the screen, the right tool for lazy loading and endless lists instead of scroll handlers.
ResizeObserver reacts to the size of one element, not only the window, so components can adapt to the space they get.
MutationObserver watches changes in the page structure and is useful to react to content that other scripts add.
requestAnimationFrame runs a function before the next paint, about 60 times a second, and stops in hidden tabs, so use it for animation and not for timers.
A Web Worker runs script in another thread and talks through postMessage, so heavy work does not freeze the page.
A service worker lets a page work offline and caches files; it needs HTTPS or localhost and updates only after all tabs of the old version are closed.
A web app manifest with name, icons, start_url and display standalone lets people install a page to the home screen like an app.
getUserMedia needs HTTPS or localhost; navigator.mediaDevices is undefined on plain HTTP pages, which is why microphone buttons do nothing on insecure addresses.
The Clipboard API navigator.clipboard.writeText needs a secure page and a user click; older code uses a hidden textarea and document.execCommand copy.
The File API reads local files without upload: input type file gives File objects with name, size and text(), so a page can preview before sending.
URL.createObjectURL(blob) makes a temporary address for a download link; call URL.revokeObjectURL afterwards to free the memory.
The download attribute on a link saves a file with a chosen name: a href blob address with download name.txt, and Playwright catches it with expect_download.
Playwright can fill and submit forms: page.fill(selector, text), page.check, page.select_option and page.press('Enter'), always better than blind key presses.
Playwright get_by_role and get_by_label find elements the way users and screen readers see them, which survives layout and class name changes.
page.evaluate runs a function in the page and returns JSON compatible data; page.wait_for_function waits until a condition in the page becomes true.
Playwright can record a trace with context.tracing.start and stop, and the trace viewer shows screenshots, network and console for every step of a failed run.
Playwright can print a page to PDF in Chromium with page.pdf(path='x.pdf'), useful for reports built as HTML.
Playwright can set the time zone and language of a test page: new_context(locale='tr-TR', timezone_id='Europe/Istanbul'), to test date and number formats.
Playwright can fake the position with new_context(geolocation=..., permissions=['geolocation']) and the clock with page.clock, so time based features are testable.
git config init.defaultBranch main sets the name of the first branch in new repositories, avoiding a master and main mismatch with GitHub.
sqlite3 file.db '.backup copy.db' makes a safe copy while the database is in use, unlike copying the file, which can catch a half written state.
CREATE INDEX on the columns used in WHERE and JOIN speeds up queries; EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether an index is used.
LIMIT and OFFSET page results, but a high OFFSET is slow; use WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n for long lists.
Playwright can block requests such as images to make tests faster: page.route('**/*.png', lambda r: r.abort()).
Node reads command line arguments from process.argv.slice(2), and process.exit(code) sets the exit status for shell scripts.
Node 18 and newer has fetch built in, so small scripts need no extra package for HTTP requests.
fs.promises with await reads files without callbacks: const text = await fs.promises.readFile(path, "utf8").
path.join and path.resolve build paths safely for every system, and path.extname and path.basename split names.
process.env holds environment variables as text; Number(process.env.PORT || 3000) gives a port with a default.
A tiny HTTP server needs only the http module: http.createServer((req, res) => res.end("ok")).listen(port).
child_process.execFile runs a program with a list of arguments and no shell, which avoids injection; exec runs a shell string and needs care.
Unhandled promise rejections end the process in current Node versions, so add catch handlers or a process.on("unhandledRejection") logger.
JSON.parse throws on bad input, so wrap it in try and catch when the text comes from users or files.
setInterval keeps the program alive until you call clearInterval, while timer.unref() lets the process end even if the timer is pending.
crypto.createHash("sha256").update(text).digest("hex") makes a checksum and crypto.randomBytes(16).toString("hex") a random token.
crypto.timingSafeEqual compares secrets without leaking timing, both buffers must have the same length.
readline with for await reads a file line by line with low memory: for await (const line of rl) { ... }.
os.cpus().length, os.totalmem() and os.uptime() report the machine state without extra packages.
node --check file.js tests syntax without running, and node --watch file.js restarts a script when it changes in Node 18 and newer.
npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json lists and is faster and safer for servers than npm install; use --omit=dev to skip dev packages.
npm audit lists known problems in packages and npm outdated shows newer versions; update one package at a time and test after each.
Set "type": "module" in package.json to use import and export in .js files; otherwise use require or name files .mjs.
Top level await works in ES modules: await fetch(url) without a wrapper function in a .mjs file.
A stream pipeline copies large files with low memory: stream.pipeline(read, gzip, write, callback) handles errors and closes everything.
Memory limit: node --max-old-space-size=256 script.js limits the heap, useful on a Raspberry Pi where one script should not take all memory.
console.table prints arrays of objects as a table and console.time and console.timeEnd measure a block, both useful while debugging.
structuredClone, Array.prototype.toSorted and Object.groupBy are newer helpers; check your Node version with node -v before using them on an old device.
In SQLite PRAGMA integrity_check returns ok when the database file is healthy, a good first check after a power loss on a Raspberry Pi.
SQLite columns are loosely typed, so text can be stored in an integer column; STRICT tables in version 3.37 and newer enforce the types.
PRAGMA foreign_keys is off by default and must be switched on for every new connection, or foreign keys are never checked.
With foreign keys on, deleting a parent row that still has children fails unless the key says ON DELETE CASCADE.
strftime formats dates inside SQL: strftime('%Y', '2026-11-15') gives 2026 and date('now', '-7 days') calculates a week ago.
VACUUM rewrites the database and gives free space back to the disk, because DELETE alone leaves the file at its old size.
A busy timeout makes a connection wait for a lock instead of failing at once: sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=5) in Python.
Keyset paging is faster than OFFSET for long lists: select where id > last_id order by id limit n reads only the next page.
GROUP BY with HAVING filters whole groups, and COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group.
json_extract reads a field from JSON text inside SQL, so a small document can live in one column and be searched without a second table.
One transaction around many inserts is much faster, because the disk is synced once at the end instead of once per row.
COALESCE returns the first value that is not NULL, so COALESCE(x, 0) gives a default in a query; NULL = NULL is never true, use IS NULL.
In SQLite a column with INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the row id, assigned automatically; AUTOINCREMENT only adds a guarantee that ids are never reused.
cursor.lastrowid gives the id of the row just inserted, and cursor.rowcount the number of rows changed by the last statement.
UNIQUE constraints reject duplicates with an IntegrityError, so catch sqlite3.IntegrityError instead of checking first, which is also safe with two writers.
INSERT OR IGNORE skips a row that would break a unique rule and INSERT OR REPLACE deletes the old row first, which resets columns you did not list.
LIKE in SQLite is case insensitive for plain English letters and uses % and _ as wildcards; escape them with ESCAPE when searching for real percent signs.
Turkish letters in LIKE are not folded: 'İ' like 'i' is false, so search text is best normalised in the program or stored in a second lowercase column.
Full text search with the FTS5 module gives fast word search: create virtual table docs using fts5(title, body) and query with MATCH.
sqlite3.connect(path, check_same_thread=False) allows other threads to use the connection, but you must add your own lock around every use.
Without check_same_thread=False a connection used in another thread raises ProgrammingError, the common error in web servers that use threads.
Parameters with ? stop SQL injection; a value joined into the SQL text with an f-string can change the query, so only table names from a fixed list may be formatted in.
executemany inserts many rows with one call, and iterdump() writes a database as SQL text, a simple portable backup.
sqlite3 Connection.backup(target) copies a live database safely page by page, better than copying the file while a program writes to it.
PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL with WAL mode is faster and still safe against program crashes, and a good setting for small servers on an SD card.
A WAL database has extra files with the endings -wal and -shm; copy them together or use the backup method, or the copy may lose recent changes.
SQLite stores times best as Unix integers or ISO 8601 text; both sort correctly, while formats like 15.11.2026 sort wrong.
A view saves a query under a name: create view v as select ..., and the app can then select from v like a table.
A trigger runs SQL after a change, for example to keep an updated_at column current: create trigger ... after update on t.
Window functions such as row_number() over (partition by k order by t desc) pick the newest row per group, supported since SQLite 3.25.
Common table expressions with WITH make long queries readable, and WITH RECURSIVE builds series and walks trees.
ATTACH DATABASE opens a second file under another name, so one query can copy or compare tables between two databases.
sqlite_master lists the tables, indexes and views of a database: select name from sqlite_master where type='table'.
pragma table_info(table) lists the columns with name and type, handy for a script that adds a column only when it is missing.
ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN works in SQLite, but dropping or changing a column needs a new table in old versions, so plan migrations as numbered steps stored in PRAGMA user_version.
A small migration runner reads user_version, applies the missing steps in a transaction and stores the new number, so every start brings the database up to date.
sqlite3.Row rows behave like tuples and dictionaries; dict(row) turns one into a plain dictionary for JSON output.
Custom SQL functions are easy in Python: conn.create_function('name', 1, func) lets queries call your code, for example to fold Turkish letters.
Never put big files into SQLite rows on a small device; store the file on disk and keep the path and a checksum in the table.
The sqlite3 module opens a transaction before INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE and does not commit by itself, so call commit() or use the with block, or the change is lost.
Two processes writing the same SQLite file take turns; keep write transactions short and read inside a transaction only when you need a consistent view.
csv.DictWriter writes dictionaries to CSV with a header row, and writing with newline='' avoids blank lines on Windows.
A CSV file saved by Excel in Turkey often uses a semicolon and a comma for decimals; csv.reader(f, delimiter=';') reads it and utf-8-sig removes the byte order mark.
XML is parsed with xml.etree.ElementTree: find and findall use paths, and attrib and text give the content; do not parse untrusted XML with big expansions.
YAML is not in the Python standard library; for settings that a person edits, JSON with indent or TOML is readable and needs no extra package.
Write settings to a temporary file and rename it over the old one, so a power cut leaves either the old or the new file, never a half written one.
fsync forces data to disk: flush the file, then os.fsync(f.fileno()), before renaming it, when the data must survive a power loss.
os.scandir is faster than os.listdir when you also need file types or sizes, because the information comes with the directory read.
Path.stat().st_size gives the size in bytes and Path.rename moves a file; Path.unlink(missing_ok=True) deletes without an error when the file is already gone.
Path.resolve() gives the absolute path with links followed, and comparing resolved paths checks whether a user supplied name stays inside a folder.
Path.is_relative_to(base) is the clean check against path traversal: reject any user supplied name where resolve() is not inside the allowed folder.
Log files grow without limit; keep them small with logrotate, with RotatingFileHandler, or by writing to journald, or the SD card fills up.
Temporary data belongs in /tmp, which is cleared at boot or in memory on many Pi images, while data that must stay belongs in the home folder or /var/lib.
Use the same folder for the temporary file and the final file when renaming, because os.replace fails across different disks.
Hard links share one file with two names and need the same disk, symbolic links point to a name and can break; os.link and os.symlink create them.
os.access(path, os.W_OK) tells if the current user may write, but trying to write and catching PermissionError is more reliable than asking first.
shutil.copyfileobj copies between two open files in chunks, and shutil.make_archive creates zip or tar files from a folder in one call.
tail a log file in Python by seeking to the end and reading new lines in a loop with a short sleep; reopen the file if its size becomes smaller, because it was rotated.
A watchdog on file changes can be done with a loop that compares os.stat mtime values every second, which needs no extra package and is enough for config reload.

A Raspberry Pi needs a good power supply: a message about under-voltage or a lightning bolt on screen means random crashes and SD card damage, so use the official power supply and a short thick cable.
vcgencmd get_throttled shows power and heat problems since boot; 0x0 means everything was fine, and any other value means under-voltage or temperature limits were hit.
vcgencmd measure_temp prints the CPU temperature; above 80 degrees the Pi slows itself down, so add a heat sink or a fan when it runs close to that in a case.
SD cards wear out with many small writes; move logs to memory or to an external SSD, and keep a current backup image of a Pi that does important work.
An SSD on USB boots much more reliably than an SD card on models that support USB boot, and it is also much faster for databases and package updates.
Use a card from a known brand with A1 or A2 rating; cheap cards with a fake size are a common reason for corrupt files and failing updates.
Shut the Pi down with sudo shutdown -h now or sudo poweroff before you remove power; pulling the plug while it writes is the most common reason for a broken SD card.
Put a read-only root file system or an overlay on kiosk and display Pis that are switched off by the plug, so a power cut cannot corrupt the system.
raspi-config is the menu tool for settings such as hostname, locale, time zone, Wi-Fi country, SSH and boot to desktop or console.
Set the Wi-Fi country before using Wi-Fi, or the radio stays blocked on newer images; rfkill list shows whether Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is blocked.
Raspberry Pi Imager can set the hostname, user, password, Wi-Fi and SSH key before writing the card, so a headless Pi comes online with no screen at all.
Use SSH keys instead of passwords: ssh-copy-id user@host installs your public key, and PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config closes password logins once the key works.
Before you turn off password login, open a second SSH session and test the key login, so a mistake does not lock you out of a Pi that has no screen.
A fixed address for a Pi is best set as a reservation in the router; setting it on the Pi itself works too but two devices with the same address break each other.
Newer Raspberry Pi OS uses NetworkManager: nmcli device wifi connect NAME password PASS joins a network and nmcli connection show lists saved ones.
nmcli connection modify NAME ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses and ipv4.gateway set a fixed address on a NetworkManager system; restart the connection afterwards.
Older images use dhcpcd and wpa_supplicant.conf; check which one your image uses before you edit network files, because the wrong file is simply ignored.
Wi-Fi power saving can make a Pi drop connections or answer slowly; iw dev wlan0 get power_save shows the state and iw dev wlan0 set power_save off changes it until reboot.
A Pi that is reachable by cable but not by Wi-Fi often has a weak signal behind a metal case; try a short USB extension or a cable connection for servers.
For a server that must always be online prefer Ethernet over Wi-Fi: it has lower delay, no power saving and no roaming problems.
Use sudo raspi-config nonint do_boot_behaviour B4 to boot to the desktop with auto login, and B2 for the console; scripts can use the nonint mode without menus.
The file /boot/firmware/config.txt holds hardware settings on current images and /boot/config.txt on older ones; a mistake there can stop the boot, so keep a copy before editing.
Keep a copy of every system file before editing: sudo cp file file.bak makes it easy to go back when the Pi does not boot or a service does not start.
If the Pi does not boot after a change, put the card in another computer and undo the change in the boot partition; that partition is readable on Windows and Mac.
hdmi_force_hotplug=1 and hdmi_group and hdmi_mode in config.txt force a screen resolution on older images when the display is not detected at boot.
Screen blanking after a few minutes can be turned off in raspi-config under display options, or with xset s off and xset -dpms on X11 for kiosks.
On Wayland desktops the screen saver is set in the compositor; check which session type you run before changing screen settings, because X11 commands have no effect on Wayland.
Autostart a program on the desktop with a .desktop file in ~/.config/autostart or with the compositor's autostart file; a systemd service starts before the desktop exists and cannot open windows.
A service that needs the screen must run as the desktop user with DISPLAY and XAUTHORITY set, or WAYLAND_DISPLAY and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR on Wayland, and should start after graphical.target.
Use WantedBy=graphical.target for services that need the desktop; multi-user.target plus After=graphical.target creates an ordering cycle that systemd silently resolves by dropping the job.
A unit that works when started by hand but not at boot usually depends on something that is not ready yet: the network, the desktop or a mounted disk; check journalctl -b -u name.
systemd-analyze blame lists the slowest parts of the boot and systemd-analyze critical-chain shows what the boot waited for, useful when a Pi takes minutes to start.
Disable services you do not use to speed up boot and save memory: systemctl disable --now bluetooth cups or similar, after checking nothing depends on them.
free -m shows memory; a Pi with 1 GB runs out quickly with a browser, so use zram or a swap file sparingly, and never put heavy swap on an SD card.
zram-tools or the zram generator compress memory instead of swapping to the card, which helps small Pis with a browser and avoids card wear.
Chromium uses a lot of memory on a Pi; use one tab, disable unneeded extensions, and prefer a lightweight page for dashboards and kiosk screens.
A 64-bit image is faster for some software and needed for a few packages, but uses more memory; on a 1 GB model the 32-bit image is often the better choice.
uname -m prints armv7l for 32-bit and aarch64 for 64-bit; check it before you download a program, because the wrong architecture gives exec format error.
dpkg --print-architecture shows armhf or arm64, the names package files use, so you pick the right .deb file.
The Pi has no real time clock by default; without network time the clock restarts from the last saved time, which breaks HTTPS certificates until timesyncd gets the time.
timedatectl shows whether the system clock is synchronised; timedatectl set-timezone Europe/Istanbul sets the time zone, and a battery backed RTC module keeps time offline.
GPIO pins work at 3.3 volts and are not 5 volt tolerant; connecting a 5 volt signal directly can destroy the Pi, so use a level shifter or a resistor divider.
A relay board for 230 volt devices needs careful isolation; use a certified module and a closed housing, and never work on wires while they are connected to mains.
gpiozero is the easy Python library for GPIO: LED(17).on() and Button(2).when_pressed = function cover most simple projects without low level code.
Use pinctrl or gpioget and gpioset from libgpiod on new images; the old sysfs GPIO interface and the RPi.GPIO library may not work on the newest models.
Enable the I2C and SPI interfaces in raspi-config before using sensors, and i2cdetect -y 1 lists the addresses of connected I2C devices.
Pull-up and pull-down resistors keep an input pin at a defined level; a button wired to ground needs a pull-up, which the Pi can switch on in software.
Debounce buttons in software with a short delay, since a mechanical button bounces for a few milliseconds and produces many events per press.
For a USB microphone, arecord -l lists capture devices and arecord -D plughw:1,0 -d 3 test.wav records three seconds; use alsamixer to raise the capture level.
For sound output, aplay -l lists devices and speaker-test -t wav -c 2 plays a test; raspi-config chooses between HDMI, headphone jack and USB.
A camera is tested with rpicam-hello on current images and libcamera-hello on older ones; the old raspistill tool is gone on the newest systems.
Use rpicam-vid or picamera2 for video; hardware encoding keeps the CPU free, while software encoding of large frames can overload a small Pi.
lsusb lists USB devices, dmesg | tail shows what the kernel reported after plugging one in, and a device missing from lsusb has a cable or power problem first.
A USB hub without its own power supply can crash a Pi when drives or cameras draw too much; use a powered hub for disks and many devices.
lsblk lists disks and partitions and blkid shows file system types and UUIDs; use UUIDs in /etc/fstab, since device names such as sda1 can change.
Add nofail to an fstab line for an external disk, so the Pi still boots when the disk is not connected instead of stopping in emergency mode.
Mount options noatime reduces writes on an SD card, and commit or tmpfs for /tmp and /var/log keep frequent writes in memory.
Back up a Pi by making an image of the card with the imager or dd on another computer, and test that the backup boots; a backup you never tested is a hope, not a backup.
Copy only your data and settings with rsync -a to another machine for a daily backup, which is faster than a full image and easy to restore on a fresh system.
Keep the system updated with sudo apt update then sudo apt full-upgrade, and reboot after kernel updates; unattended-upgrades can install security updates by itself.
Do not run rpi-update on a working system; it installs unstable firmware, and the normal apt updates already contain tested kernels.
After changing config.txt, a reboot is needed; changes in /etc services need only systemctl restart name, and daemon-reload after editing a unit file.
Never leave the default password on a Pi that is reachable from the network; bots try common passwords within minutes of an open SSH port.
Do not forward SSH or other admin ports from the router to a Pi; use a VPN or a tunnel, or at least keys only and a tool such as fail2ban.
Use a firewall such as ufw or nftables and allow only the ports you need; sudo ufw allow 22/tcp before sudo ufw enable, or you lock yourself out.
A reverse proxy such as nginx or caddy in front of a small web app gives HTTPS, compression and limits, and keeps the app on a local port.
Run services as a normal user with a systemd unit instead of root; give the unit only the access it needs and it limits the damage of a bug.
Restart=always with RestartSec=5 brings a crashed service back; add StartLimitIntervalSec so a service that crashes at once does not restart forever and fill the logs.
journalctl -u name -f follows a service log live, -b limits it to this boot and --since '10 minutes ago' narrows by time, the first tools to open when a service misbehaves.
Keep the journal small with SystemMaxUse=50M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, or logs fill a small card over months.
A watchdog helps unattended Pis: the hardware watchdog restarts a frozen system, and a systemd unit with WatchdogSec restarts a service that stops responding.
Test power loss behaviour before you deploy: pull the plug ten times and check that the Pi comes back and services start, because the first failure is rarely the last.
Label devices and keep a note of the address, user and purpose of each Pi; a drawer of identical boards without notes costs hours later.
Long jobs on a Pi should write their progress to a file, so after a power cut the job continues where it stopped and does not start from the beginning.
Heat in a closed box raises the temperature quickly in summer; leave air holes, add a small fan or a metal case that works as a heat sink.
The Pi Zero is slow for browsers but fine for agents, sensors and small servers; its single core makes pip installs and compiling take a very long time, so prefer prebuilt packages.
Use apt packages such as python3-numpy instead of building from source with pip on a Pi, because the compile takes hours and may run out of memory.
pip on new Python images refuses system wide installs with an externally managed environment error; use a virtual environment, pipx, or apt packages instead of forcing it.
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages env gives a virtual environment that still sees apt installed packages such as the camera and GPIO libraries.
Services that start with a virtual environment must call env/bin/python in ExecStart, so they use the right packages without activating anything.
Bluetooth tools: bluetoothctl scans and pairs, and a Pi that cannot see devices may have Bluetooth blocked by rfkill or need the right firmware package.
Screen rotation on Wayland is set with wlr-randr or the screen settings, on X11 with xrandr or the display_rotate line in older config files.
A touch screen that is rotated needs its input matrix rotated too, or touches land in the wrong place; the compositor settings or a libinput calibration matrix fix it.
On a headless Pi VNC needs a virtual screen: set a fixed resolution in raspi-config, or the VNC window is tiny or black without a monitor connected.
Remote desktop apps like RealVNC need a graphical session; check systemctl status vncserver-x11-serviced and the session type first when the connection shows a black screen.
Printing and scanning from a Pi works through CUPS and SANE; the CUPS web page on port 631 is local only by default, keep it that way on public networks.
If an update fails with a lock error, another apt process is running; wait for it, and never delete the lock files unless you checked with ps that no apt process exists.
If a download from apt fails with hash sum mismatch, wait and retry or change the mirror; the cause is often a mirror that is updating or a wrong clock.
When storage is full, du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h shows the biggest folders, and apt clean, journalctl --vacuum-size=50M and old logs are the first things to remove.
Store large media on an external disk, not on the card; a full card makes the system read only or break during writes and updates.
An overclock can make a Pi unstable and heat up; keep the default speed for devices that must run for months, and only increase it with proper cooling.
The official documentation and the forum have fixes for most Pi problems; search the exact error text and include the model and OS version when you ask.
A unit file lives in /etc/systemd/system, and systemctl daemon-reload must run after every change, or systemd keeps using the old copy.
systemctl edit name creates an override file that survives package updates, better than editing a unit from a package directly.
systemctl cat name prints the unit with all overrides, and systemctl show name -p ExecStart prints one property, the first checks when a service uses an unexpected setting.
systemctl status name shows state, recent log lines and the main process; Active: failed with a result such as exit-code points to the error in the lines below.
systemctl enable --now name enables at boot and starts at once; enable alone does not start the service until the next boot.
systemctl is-active name and is-enabled name print one word and set the exit code, which makes them easy to use in scripts.
Type=simple is the default for programs that stay in the foreground; Type=forking is for old daemons that detach, and Type=oneshot is for scripts that run and exit.
A service that forks into the background with Type=simple looks finished to systemd and is killed or restarted; keep programs in the foreground under systemd.
After= only sets the order, not a dependency; use Wants= or Requires= to make another unit start, and combine both when your service needs it.

network-online.target means the network is configured, while network.target only means the network software started; services that connect on start need Wants=network-online.target and After=network-online.target.
WorkingDirectory sets the folder a service starts in; relative paths in a script then resolve correctly, and a missing setting is a common cause of file not found errors.
ExecStart needs an absolute path to the program, and pipes, redirects and variables like $HOME are not interpreted; use /bin/sh -c '...' when you need a shell.
Environment=NAME=value and EnvironmentFile=/path set variables for a service; a file with a leading dash in EnvironmentFile=-/path is optional and does not fail when missing.
User= and Group= run a service as a normal user, and a user systemd service in ~/.config/systemd/user needs loginctl enable-linger to run without a login session.
systemctl --user works for services of the logged in user and needs XDG_RUNTIME_DIR; over SSH use loginctl enable-linger user and a login session if it complains about the bus.
Restart=on-failure restarts after crashes only, Restart=always also after a clean exit; RestartSec delays the restart so a crash loop does not use all the CPU.
StartLimitBurst and StartLimitIntervalSec stop a unit that fails too often; after the limit systemctl reset-failed and start are needed before it runs again.
TimeoutStopSec sets how long systemd waits after SIGTERM before it sends SIGKILL; a service that needs time to save should handle SIGTERM and exit quickly.
KillMode=control-group is the default and stops every process of a service, including children; use KillMode=process only for services that must leave children alive.
ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=yes, PrivateTmp=yes and NoNewPrivileges=yes in a unit limit what a service can touch, cheap hardening for network facing programs.
ReadWritePaths= lists the folders a hardened service may still write to, needed after ProtectSystem=strict so the program can save its data.
systemd timers replace cron: a .timer unit with OnCalendar or OnBootSec starts a .service unit, and systemctl list-timers shows the next run and the last run.
systemd-analyze calendar 'Mon *-*-* 09:00' checks a timer expression and prints the next time it fires, so you can test it before enabling.
systemd-analyze verify unit.service reports syntax errors and missing programs in a unit file before you start it.
journalctl -p err -b shows only errors since boot, and journalctl -k shows kernel messages, a quick way to spot hardware and driver problems.
journalctl --disk-usage shows how much space the journal uses and journalctl --vacuum-time=7d deletes entries older than a week.
Logs from a service that prints to standard output appear in the journal automatically, so no log file code is needed; use python3 -u or flush to see lines immediately.
Use SyslogIdentifier=name in a unit to give log lines a clear label, which makes journalctl -t name easy to use.
systemctl mask name prevents a unit from being started at all, even by dependencies, and systemctl unmask reverses it.
systemctl daemon-reexec and reboot are rarely needed; daemon-reload plus restart of the service handles nearly every change of a unit.
systemd path units start a service when a file or folder changes, an alternative to polling in scripts.
A socket unit lets systemd listen on a port and start the service on the first connection, saving memory for rarely used tools.
systemd-run --user --scope command runs a command in its own scope with limits such as MemoryMax, and systemd-run --on-active=30s command runs something once later.
MemoryMax= and CPUQuota= in a unit protect the rest of the system from one runaway service, useful on a small Pi.
Nice= and IOSchedulingClass=idle lower the priority of background jobs, so a backup does not slow down a web server.
The ConditionPathExists= line skips a service quietly when a file is missing, which is cleaner than a script that checks and exits with an error.
ExecStartPre runs commands before the main program, and a minus sign in front of the path ignores its failure; use it for a short check or a cleanup, not for long tasks.
A oneshot service with RemainAfterExit=yes counts as active after the script ran, which lets other units depend on it.
Ordering cycles are logged in the journal as Found ordering cycle; journalctl -b | grep -i cycle shows which units were involved and which job systemd deleted.
Use systemctl list-dependencies name to see what a unit pulls in and systemctl list-dependencies --reverse name to see what depends on it.
hostnamectl set-hostname name changes the hostname, and the same tool shows the machine type, kernel and operating system in one view.
loginctl list-sessions shows who is logged in and whether the session is x11, wayland or tty, which matters for programs that need a screen.
timedatectl set-ntp true turns on time synchronisation and timedatectl timesync-status shows the server in use and the delay.
networkctl and resolvectl show interfaces and DNS settings on systems that use systemd-networkd and systemd-resolved; resolvectl query name tests DNS.
coredumpctl lists crashes of programs with a core dump, and journalctl shows the signal, a good start for a program that disappears without an error message.
apt update downloads package lists and apt upgrade installs newer versions; apt full-upgrade may also remove packages when a dependency changes, which is the right command for kernel updates.
apt search word finds packages, apt show name prints details and apt policy name shows the installed and available versions and where they come from.
apt install --no-install-recommends name installs only what is required, which saves space on small systems and avoids pulling in a desktop for a server tool.
apt remove keeps configuration files, apt purge deletes them too, and apt autoremove removes packages that nothing needs any more.
dpkg -l name shows if a package is installed, dpkg -L name lists its files and dpkg -S /path/file tells which package owns a file.
apt list --installed | grep name finds installed packages, and apt list --upgradable shows what an update would change before you run it.
apt-mark hold name stops a package from being upgraded, useful when a new version breaks your setup; apt-mark unhold lifts it.
apt clean deletes downloaded package files in /var/cache/apt, and apt autoclean removes only old ones, both free space on a small card.
A .deb file is installed with sudo apt install ./file.deb, which also installs its dependencies, unlike dpkg -i, which fails when something is missing.
Third party repositories belong in /etc/apt/sources.list.d with a key file under /etc/apt/keyrings; the old apt-key command is deprecated and gives a warning.
Add only repositories you trust, since a package from them runs scripts as root during installation and can change the whole system.
apt-cache rdepends name lists the packages that depend on a package, a good check before you remove it.
unattended-upgrades installs security updates automatically; check /var/log/unattended-upgrades to see what it did and decide if automatic reboots are acceptable.
needrestart or checkrestart shows services that still run old libraries after an upgrade, and a restart of those services applies the fix without a full reboot.
Package versions have an epoch, upstream version and revision; apt policy shows candidates, and dpkg --compare-versions a lt b checks which one is newer.
The command apt-get is more stable for scripts than apt, and -y answers yes; export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive stops installers from asking questions.
apt-get -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold keeps your configuration files during an unattended upgrade instead of asking whether to replace them.
A held back message means the upgrade needs to add or remove packages; apt full-upgrade resolves it, or look at apt-mark showhold for packages you pinned earlier.
If apt cannot reach a mirror, check the clock, DNS and a proxy setting first; apt -o Debug::Acquire::http=true update prints what it does.
ip addr shows addresses and ip route shows the default gateway; ifconfig and route are old tools and may not be installed.
ip -br addr gives a short table of interfaces and addresses, and ip -br link shows which ones are up.
ping -c 3 host tests basic reachability, but many hosts block ping, so a failed ping alone does not prove the host is down.
traceroute or mtr shows the path to a host and where packets are lost, which tells whether the problem is in your network or far away.
curl -v shows the whole HTTP conversation including TLS and headers, the best single tool to see why a web request fails.
dig +short name shows the DNS answer of the system's resolver and dig @server name asks a specific server, which separates local DNS problems from real ones.
If a name resolves with dig but not in programs, check /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf and the hosts file, because programs use the system resolver.
nc -zv host port tests if a TCP port is open, and nc -l port listens on a port to test connections from another machine.
A firewall can block a port even when the service listens; test locally with curl first, then from another device, to find where the block is.
Two addresses on the same network cannot be the same; if a device keeps losing its connection, look for an address conflict with arp-scan or a router client list.
MTU problems show as pages that start loading and then hang; ping -M do -s 1472 host tests the largest packet that passes without fragmentation.
Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz reaches further and is crowded, 5 GHz is faster and shorter ranged; use a fixed channel away from neighbours for devices that must stay connected.
iwconfig and iw dev wlan0 link show signal strength and bit rate; below minus 70 dBm connections become unreliable.
A captive portal blocks internet access until a web login; devices without a browser cannot pass it, so use a network without a portal for servers and agents.
Dynamic DNS and port forwarding expose home devices to the internet; prefer an outgoing connection to a server, as agents with WebSocket do, which needs no open ports.
Outgoing connections work through NAT without any setup, which is why a device can connect to a cloud server while the cloud cannot connect back to the device.
Mobile data and some office networks close idle connections after a minute; a heartbeat every 15 to 30 seconds keeps a WebSocket open through them.
An HTTP proxy is set through http_proxy and https_proxy variables for curl and many tools, and no_proxy lists addresses that skip it.
Check certificates with openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host, which shows the chain, the expiry date and the protocol that was negotiated.
A certificate error for a correct address is often a wrong clock, a missing intermediate certificate, or an old CA bundle on an old device.
Let's Encrypt certificates last 90 days and renew automatically with certbot or caddy; a renewal that fails silently shows up as a browser warning three months later.
HSTS tells browsers to use HTTPS only; test it carefully, because a long max-age on a site that later loses its certificate locks visitors out.
nginx proxy_pass for WebSockets needs proxy_http_version 1.1 and the Upgrade and Connection headers, and a long proxy_read_timeout so idle connections are not cut.
Compression, caching and keep-alive in the reverse proxy matter more for speed than the app language; measure with curl -w before you change code.
Free hosting tiers may sleep after inactivity and take a minute to wake; a keep-alive request every few minutes or a paid plan avoids the cold start.
A health endpoint that returns plain ok without touching the database is the best target for uptime checks and wake-up polling.
Rate limit login and mail endpoints separately from the rest of the site, and count by account as well as by address, so one attacker behind many addresses is still slowed.
UDP has no connection and no delivery guarantee; use TCP or a protocol on top, such as WebSocket or HTTP, for anything that must arrive in order.
mDNS names ending in .local work inside one network segment only; guest networks and VPNs often block them, so use an address when a name fails.
Speed tests with iperf3 measure the link between two machines: run iperf3 -s on one and iperf3 -c host on the other.
tcpdump -i any port 8000 -nn shows packets of one port on the machine itself, the last resort when logs do not explain a connection problem.
A kiosk setup needs the browser to start after the desktop, with --kiosk, --noerrdialogs, --disable-infobars and --incognito so crash bubbles and warnings never cover the page.
Use --autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required in kiosks and tests, or videos and audio on a page wait for a click that nobody makes.
A page that needs the microphone on a kiosk should run on HTTPS or localhost; browsers refuse getUserMedia on plain HTTP addresses of other machines.
Chromium keeps a separate profile per --user-data-dir, so a kiosk profile never mixes with the normal one and can be deleted to reset the state.
Set the zoom for a kiosk with --force-device-scale-factor=1.25, or with CSS on the page, instead of pressing keys after the start.
Disable translation and password prompts for kiosks with a managed policy or flags, since these bubbles cover pages and block clicks.
Cache problems after an update: a hard reload with Ctrl+Shift+R ignores the cache for one load, and versioned file names (app.js?v=3) solve it for everybody.
The service worker of an old page version may keep serving old files; in developer tools under Application choose Unregister, or change the file name of the worker.
Developer tools stay open on a remote device with --remote-debugging-port, and ssh -L forwards that port, so you can debug a kiosk page from your laptop.
Chromium logs to the terminal when started with --enable-logging=stderr --v=1, which helps when it closes immediately at start.
Hardware acceleration problems show as a black or flickering screen on some Pi setups; --disable-gpu or a different --use-gl setting often fixes it.
If Chromium says that the profile is in use by another process, look for a leftover lock in the profile folder after a crash, and make sure no second copy runs.
A site that needs cookies in an automated browser should use a persistent profile, so the login stays after a restart and no password has to be typed again.
Do not automate a login with the real password typed by a script on shared machines; use a dedicated account with limited rights.
xdotool needs the window to have keyboard focus; xdotool getactivewindow shows which window will receive keys, and windowfocus --sync waits until the switch happened.
Mouse positions from xdotool are in screen pixels, and a scaled display or a different resolution between recording and playback moves every click away from its target.
Wait for the page before you click: a fixed sleep breaks on a slow Pi, so check the screen or the window title with xdotool getwindowname before sending the next step.
If xdotool key does nothing inside a browser, the window may be on Wayland, the focus may be elsewhere, or the page may still be loading; test with a plain text editor window first.
xdotool type with a long text can run into the shell quoting rules; put the text in a file and use xdotool type --file for exact content.
Use xdotool search --name or --class with --onlyvisible to find the right window id, because hidden helper windows with the same class otherwise match first.
Keep the same layout on every screen size by testing at the smallest width first; a design that works on a phone nearly always works on a larger screen.
A button that starts a long task should change at once to a busy state, so users do not press it three times and start three tasks.
Show real names in lists, such as the device name the person chose, not internal ids; ids belong in a details view for support.
Group settings by what the person wants to do, such as account, devices or language, and not by how the program is built.
Give every list a sensible order: most recent first for activity, alphabetical for names and online devices before offline ones.
Update status indicators live and without reloading the page; a green dot that is hours old is worse than no dot.
Give users a way out of every state: a cancel on loading screens that last long, and a retry button on errors instead of an empty page.
A first-run loading screen that says what is happening, such as Waking up the server, feels faster than a blank page, even when the wait is the same length.
Do not mix languages on one screen; if a translation is missing, show the default language for that single text, never a key name like btn_save.
Test with real text lengths, empty lists, 500 items, a failed network and a slow network; most interface bugs appear only in these states.
A password field should have autocomplete="current-password" for logins and "new-password" for sign ups, so password managers fill and propose correctly.
Show a clear message for each validation problem next to its field and move the focus to the first wrong field.
Never block paste in password fields; password managers use paste, and blocking it pushes people toward weaker passwords.
E-mail verification codes should have six digits, expire in about ten minutes and allow a limited number of tries before a new code is needed.
Do not reveal whether an e-mail address has an account in password reset forms; answer with the same message in both cases.
Normalise input on the server: trim spaces, lower-case e-mail addresses for comparison and limit the length, then validate the cleaned value.
Flask debug mode must never be on in production, because the interactive debugger lets anybody who reaches it run code on the server.
