A secret key for sessions belongs in an environment variable, and a new random key at every start logs everybody out, so keep it stable.
Flask's development server is not for production; run the app with gunicorn or waitress behind a reverse proxy, with a few worker processes.
request.get_json(silent=True) returns None for bad JSON instead of raising an error, and jsonify builds JSON answers with the correct content type.
Use abort(404) and errorhandler functions to return consistent error pages or JSON, and never show tracebacks to users.
Set MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH to limit upload size, or one large request can fill memory or disk of a small server.
Use send_from_directory and secure_filename for downloads and uploads, and never build file paths from raw user input.
Store sessions in signed cookies only for small data; set SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE for logins.
For background work on a small server use a thread or a queue, and keep requests short; a request that takes a minute is cut off by proxies.
Check the clock, the disk space and the network first when many things fail at once; these three simple causes explain a large share of strange errors.
Change one thing at a time and write down what you changed, so you can undo it when it did not help.
Read the first error, not the last one; later errors are often only a result of the first.
Search for the exact error text in quotes together with the program name and version; old answers for old versions often do not apply.
Keep a small notes file for every device: address, user, installed services and the commands you used to set it up, which saves hours after a card failure.
Automate a task only after you did it by hand twice, and keep the script simple enough to read in a year.
Make scripts safe to run twice: check if something already exists before you create or add it, so a repeat does not break the setup.
Prefer boring and well known tools on a device that must run for years; every extra service is one more thing to update, secure and debug.

Use a virtual environment per project and keep a requirements.txt with exact versions; pip freeze > requirements.txt records them, and pip install -r requirements.txt rebuilds the setup on another machine.
pip install --upgrade pip inside the virtual environment, not system wide, so old pip versions do not fail on new package formats.
pip list --outdated shows packages with newer versions, and upgrading them one at a time makes it easy to find the update that broke something.
pip check reports installed packages with broken or conflicting requirements, a quick test after installing something new.
Pin versions with == in services that must keep working, and use ranges like >=2,<3 for libraries, so a new major release does not break the app by surprise.
Install with pip install --no-cache-dir on small devices to avoid filling the card with cached wheels, or clean it with pip cache purge.
If pip builds from source and fails with missing headers, install the matching dev package with apt, such as python3-dev or libffi-dev, or choose a version that has a ready wheel.
python3 -m pip is safer than a bare pip command, because it always installs for the Python you called and not for another one on the path.
Use the packages from apt for system tools and the virtual environment for your own apps, so a system update does not replace the libraries your service needs.
A script without a shebang line must be started as python3 script.py; with #!/usr/bin/env python3 and chmod +x it starts directly and finds the right interpreter.
Use if __name__ == '__main__': main() so that the file can be imported by tests without starting the program.
Keep configuration out of code: read settings from environment variables or a file, and give every setting a safe default and a clear error when a required value is missing.
Fail early on bad configuration: check the settings at startup and exit with a message that says which value is wrong, instead of crashing later in the middle of work.
Use logging instead of print in services, with a level for each message, so you can show details when searching a problem and keep logs quiet during normal work.
Log exceptions with logger.exception inside except blocks, which adds the traceback; logging only str(e) hides where the error happened.
Never log passwords, tokens or full personal data; log ids and the kind of event, because logs are copied, shipped and read by more people than the database.
Catch the errors you can handle and let others stop the program loudly; a bare except that continues hides bugs for weeks.
In long running loops catch exceptions around one iteration, log them and continue after a pause, so one bad item does not stop the whole service.
Add a sleep with growing delay in retry loops and a maximum number of tries, or a failing server gets hammered and your logs fill in seconds.
A timeout belongs on every network call: requests.get(url, timeout=10) and socket timeouts, since the default is to wait forever.
requests.Session reuses connections and keeps cookies and headers, so repeated calls to one server are faster and shorter to write.
requests raises for network errors, but not for HTTP errors unless you call response.raise_for_status(); check the status before using the body.
response.json() raises when the body is not JSON, so catch ValueError when an error page may come back, such as a proxy page from a sleeping server.
Send JSON with requests.post(url, json=data), which sets the content type and encodes the body for you; data= sends form fields instead.
Use urllib from the standard library for tiny scripts on devices where installing packages is a problem; urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) covers simple requests.
aiohttp and websockets are good for many connections in one process; an agent that keeps one WebSocket open and reconnects after failures needs only a small asyncio loop.
Asyncio tasks that are never awaited or referenced can be garbage collected; keep references in a set and use add_done_callback to log their errors.
Handle cancellation in async code: catch asyncio.CancelledError only to clean up and raise it again, or the task never ends.
A thread that blocks on input and output is fine for small tools, but share data through a queue instead of global variables, so no two threads change the same list at once.
Use daemon threads for helpers such as keep-alive pings, and stop them with an Event for clean shutdown in services.
The global interpreter lock makes threads good for waiting on input and output but not for heavy calculations; use multiprocessing or a native library for those.
multiprocessing.Pool(processes=2) uses several cores; on a small Pi limit the number of processes to the cores, or memory and CPU run out at once.
Memory use of big lists can be cut with generators, arrays, or reading a file line by line; check with tracemalloc before guessing where the memory goes.
Use __slots__ in classes with millions of small objects to save memory, and use tuples and namedtuple for read only records.
String concatenation in a loop is quadratic for very large text; join a list at the end, or write straight to a file as you go.
Sets and dictionaries test membership in constant time, while lists search slowly; convert a list to a set before looping and checking many items.
Use sorted with key instead of comparing functions, heapq.nsmallest for the top few items, and bisect for sorted lists, which are faster than full sorting every time.
Profile before optimising: python3 -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py shows where the time goes, and most programs spend it in two or three functions.
Cache expensive results with functools.lru_cache or a dictionary with a time stamp, and make sure the cache cannot grow without limit on a small device.
Use pathlib instead of string paths, and open files with a with statement so they close even when an error happens.
Open text files with an explicit encoding, newline handling and errors setting; a file with a Turkish letter written on Windows may differ from one written on the Pi without it.
Treat all external data as untrusted: check types and ranges of JSON fields before using them, because a missing key or a wrong type is the common cause of crashes in services.
Use dict.get and default values for optional JSON fields, and raise a clear error for required ones, so a client bug does not produce a KeyError traceback in the log.
Use dataclasses or TypedDict for the messages between agent and server, so field names are defined in one place and typos show up in the editor.
A protocol between programs should have a version field and ignore unknown fields, so old agents and new servers keep working during updates.
Use time.monotonic for timeouts and time.time for timestamps; a clock change by network time can make time.time jump backwards or forwards.
Use datetime with time zones: store UTC, show local time in the interface, and never compare naive and aware datetimes, which raises an error.
Use zoneinfo for time zones in Python 3.9 and newer; on a minimal system the tzdata package may be missing and ZoneInfo raises an error, so install it.
The locale of the system changes sorting and number formats; use explicit formats in logs and files, and locale only for text shown to the user.
str.format and f-strings do not escape user text; for HTML use html.escape, for shell use shlex.quote and for SQL use parameters, a different tool for each target.
Use secrets for tokens and passwords, never random; secrets.token_urlsafe(32) is long enough for session and device tokens.
Store passwords only as slow salted hashes with hashlib.scrypt, argon2 or bcrypt, never as plain text, md5 or an unsalted sha256.
Compare tokens with hmac.compare_digest, so the time taken does not reveal how many characters were correct.
Keep secrets out of the repository: use environment variables or a file with mode 600 outside the project, and add that file name to .gitignore from the first day.
Rotate a token that was ever printed in a log, chat or commit, because logs and history spread widely and cannot be recalled.
Validate file names from users with pathlib: resolve the path and check is_relative_to the allowed folder, so names like ../../etc cannot escape.
Use signal handlers for SIGTERM and SIGINT in services to finish the current work and exit with code 0, so systemd sees a clean stop.
Check at start that another copy is not running, with a lock file and fcntl.flock or a lock directory, to avoid two agents fighting over one port or one device.
Write a PID file only if you really need it; under systemd the service manager already knows the main process and stops it correctly.
Use argparse for options with help text, types and defaults, so python3 script.py --help documents the tool without a separate file.
Use exit codes consistently: 0 for success, 1 for general errors and 2 for wrong usage; shell scripts and systemd read them to decide what to do.
Write tests for the parts that break most: parsing, calculations and protocol handling; a few small pytest functions catch regressions after every change.
pytest finds files named test_*.py, shows the failing line and value, and tmp_path gives each test a clean temporary folder.
Use monkeypatch and small fakes to test code that talks to hardware, the network or the clock, so tests run on a laptop without the device.
Test failure paths too: a server that returns 500, a file that is missing, a timeout; the happy path rarely contains the bugs that users meet.
python3 -m compileall folder compiles all files and reports syntax errors in one run, a cheap check before you restart a service on a remote device.
python3 -m pyflakes or flake8 finds unused imports and undefined names without running the code, and ruff does the same much faster.
Format code with black or ruff format, so reviews talk about logic and not about spaces and line breaks.
Use type hints on function signatures; mypy or pyright finds calls with the wrong type before the program runs on the device.
Docstrings should say what a function does and what it returns in one or two lines; comments should explain why, since the code already shows how.
Keep functions short and give them one job; a function you can describe in one sentence is easy to test and to reuse.
Name things after what they mean in the program: device_id, retry_count and last_seen are better than d, n and t after three months.
Avoid global state; pass settings and connections as arguments or keep them in a small class, so tests can replace them.
Use enumerate, zip, any, all, sum and sorted instead of index loops; the code is shorter, and there are fewer off by one errors.
Prefer early returns to deep nesting: handle bad cases at the top of a function and leave the main path unindented.
Use constants for numbers and strings that appear more than once, and put them at the top of the file, so a change needs only one edit.
Python version differences matter on old devices: match statements need 3.10, tomllib 3.11 and the | type syntax 3.10; check python3 --version before you use new features.
Use importlib.metadata.version('package') to read the installed version of a package, helpful in bug reports and when a service prints its versions at start.
Build a command line tool with a pyproject.toml entry point, or keep it as one file with a shebang; one file is the easiest to copy to many devices.
Package an application for Windows with PyInstaller or a Go wrapper; test the result on a clean machine, since antivirus tools often flag unsigned executables.
Python on Windows may call the interpreter python or py; py -3 -m pip selects Python 3 and avoids the store stub that opens the Microsoft Store.
Windows paths use backslashes; use raw strings, forward slashes or pathlib to avoid escape problems such as \t becoming a tab.
Console output on Windows may use a different encoding; set PYTHONUTF8=1 or reconfigure stdout to utf-8 when Turkish letters appear as question marks.
A script started by double click on Windows closes its window at the end; run it from a terminal, or write the log to a file, to see errors.
Keep configuration files in a known place such as /etc/name for system services and ~/.config/name for user programs, so people and tools can find them.
Use mode 600 for files that hold tokens and 644 for normal files, and make folders 755 unless they must be private; look at ls -l before and after copying.
A file copied with scp or rsync may change owner; use rsync -a with the right user, or chown afterwards, so a service can read what you deployed.
rsync -av --delete src/ dest/ makes dest an exact copy and removes files that no longer exist in src; run it with --dry-run first, because a swapped path deletes the wrong side.
rsync -avz compresses data in transit, which helps on slow links, and --partial keeps interrupted files so the next run resumes.
scp copies one file over SSH, and scp -r a folder; rsync is better for big folders because it sends only changes.
Use ssh -L to forward a port: ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 user@host makes the remote web page available at localhost:8080 on your computer, with no open ports on the Pi.
A tarball keeps permissions and links; extract it as the same user that will run the program, and use tar --numeric-owner when restoring system files.
Check an archive before you extract it: tar -tf file.tar | head lists the first names, and a path starting with / or .. is a warning sign.
Disk full errors can also mean no free inodes; df -i shows inodes, and a folder with millions of small files, such as a mail queue or cache, is the usual cause.
find / -xdev -type f -size +100M lists big files on the root disk only, without walking into other disks and virtual folders.
ls -lh and du -h show sizes in readable units, and ncdu gives an interactive size browser that finds space eaters in seconds.
Use mktemp -d for scratch folders in scripts and remove them with a trap on EXIT, so crashed scripts do not fill the disk with leftovers.
Store application data in a dedicated folder and back up that folder only; mixing data into the program folder makes updates and backups harder.
trash-cli or a _to_delete folder gives an undo for manual cleanups; real deletion is final on Linux, and file recovery on an SD card rarely works.
Keep a copy of an important file before you edit it automatically; write the new version to a temporary file, compare with diff and then move it into place.
Compare folders with diff -rq a b, which lists files that differ or exist only on one side, a quick check after a copy or restore.
Use checksums to verify copies: sha256sum on both sides and compare, since size and name alone do not prove that a file arrived complete.
A partially downloaded file looks normal until it is used; download to a .part name and rename after the size or checksum matches.
File watchers like inotifywait react to changes without polling; inotifywait -m folder prints events, though some network and special file systems do not send them.
Mount points and permissions: a USB disk with FAT or exFAT has no Linux permissions, and ext4 is the right format for disks that hold program data.
Do not store a database or many small writes on exFAT or FAT; these file systems lose data easily after power loss and cannot keep links or modes.
NTFS disks can be read on Linux with ntfs-3g, but unclean Windows shutdowns leave them marked dirty and the mount may be read only until checked on Windows.
File names are case sensitive on Linux and often not on Windows and Mac, so Readme.md and README.md are different files that may collide after a copy.
Avoid spaces and special letters in file names of scripts and services, and use lowercase with dashes or underscores; it avoids quoting mistakes everywhere.
Line endings differ: Windows uses CRLF and Linux LF; a shell script with CRLF fails with a strange bad interpreter message, fix it with sed or dos2unix.
Text encodings: save files as UTF-8 without a byte order mark for scripts and configs; a BOM at the start of a shell script or JSON file causes odd errors.
Use the file command to see what a file really is, and head -c 100 to look at its first bytes; an HTML error page saved as a download is a classic surprise.
When a download is much smaller than expected, open it as text; it is often an error message or a login page instead of the real file.
Compressed log files can be searched without extracting: zgrep pattern file.gz and zcat file.gz | less work like grep and cat.
logrotate rotates, compresses and deletes old logs by size or time; a file in /etc/logrotate.d with rotate 7, daily, compress and missingok is enough for most services.
Large directories are slow to list on SD cards; keep folders under a few thousand files, and spread files over sub folders named by date or the first letters of the name.
Symbolic links are good for switching versions: point current to releases/20261115 and switch the link with ln -sfn, which makes a deploy atomic and a rollback instant.
A deployment script should copy to a new folder, test it, then switch a link, and keep the last two versions so you can go back in seconds.
Keep generated files out of git; commit the source and the build recipe, and list build folders in .gitignore, so the repository stays small and clean.
Large binary files make git history heavy; keep installers and images in releases or storage, and only a small reference to them in the repository.
JSON is readable and universal for settings; keep keys in a stable order and use indent=2, so diffs in git show real changes only.
CSV is the simplest exchange format for tables; always include a header row, use UTF-8, quote text fields and state the separator and decimal mark in your documentation.
Excel opens UTF-8 CSV correctly when the file starts with a BOM, and in Turkish regional settings it expects a semicolon as separator instead of a comma.
Use ISO 8601 dates, 2026-11-15, in files and logs; they sort correctly as text, are unambiguous in every country and parse in every language.
Keep timestamps in UTC in files and show the local time only when displaying, so logs from devices in several time zones can be merged and compared.
Rotate and compress old data instead of deleting at once; keep recent days at full detail and older ones as summaries to fit small disks.
Backups should follow the 3-2-1 idea: three copies, two kinds of media, one off site; and a restore test once a quarter proves they work.
Encrypt backups that leave your home, with age, gpg or an encrypted archive, and keep the key somewhere other than the backup itself.
Name backups with a date and keep a small manifest with checksums, so you can see at a glance what is complete and what is old.
Commit small and often with a message that says why, not only what; a history of tiny clear commits is easy to review, bisect and revert.
Write commit subjects in the imperative, under about 50 characters, such as Fix wake page polling; add a blank line and a body when the reason is not obvious.
Use branches for experiments and keep main working; a failed experiment is then deleted instead of cleaned up with many reverting commits.
Pull before you push and push often; long lived local work makes merges hard and risks losing everything with the machine.
Do not commit secrets, build output or large files; add them to .gitignore first, because removing them later needs history rewriting and the secret is still leaked.
A leaked token must be revoked at once at its provider; deleting the commit does not help because clones, caches and forks still have it.
git log -p -S'text' finds commits that added or removed a string, the fastest way to find out when and why something changed.
git diff --stat before every commit shows what you are about to save; surprises such as a generated file or a whole file changing line endings show up immediately.
Tag releases with git tag -a v1.2.0 -m message and push the tag; a version that is tagged can be rebuilt and compared later.
A shallow clone with --depth 1 is perfect for deployment on small devices; use git pull to update and git fetch --depth 1 when history is not needed.
Use git pull --ff-only in deploy scripts, so they stop with an error instead of creating a merge commit or overwriting local changes on the device.
git reset --hard origin/main makes a deployed working copy exactly equal to the remote; it deletes local changes, so use it only on machines where nobody edits.
Keep deployment keys read only and per machine; a deploy key with write access on a Pi that gets stolen can change your repository.
GitHub Actions run on a schedule with cron syntax in UTC, and a scheduled workflow in a repository with no activity for 60 days is disabled automatically.
A workflow that commits back to the repository can trigger itself; use [skip ci] in the message or limit triggers to paths that the commit does not change.
Use concurrency groups in workflows so two runs that push to the same branch do not collide, and git pull --rebase before pushing from a workflow.
Branch protection and required checks stop broken code from reaching main, even for one person projects they prevent a push at the wrong moment.
GitHub issues are a simple task list; labels such as bug, idea and verified group them, and a template makes reports contain the details you need.
Read the diff of a pull request yourself before merging, even for your own work; reading the change as a reviewer finds mistakes that writing never shows.
Keep a CHANGELOG with short entries per version, and the README's first lines should say what the project is, how to install it and how to run it.
A good README has a quick start that works when copied line by line, a list of requirements and a section for common problems and their fixes.
Start scripts with a shebang and set -u so that a mistyped variable name stops the script instead of expanding to an empty string.
Use readonly for constants and local for function variables; accidental overwriting of globals causes some of the most confusing script bugs.
Always quote $@ as "$@" to pass arguments through unchanged, including arguments with spaces and empty ones.
Use printf rather than echo for output you will parse, because echo behaves differently across shells with backslashes and options such as -n.
Use [[ ]] over [ ] in bash, and = or == for strings, -eq for integers; mixing them is a frequent cause of syntax errors with empty values.
Check that a command succeeded: command || { echo failed >&2; exit 1; }, because a script that ignores errors continues with half done work.
Use trap to clean up temporary files and to report the line number of a failure: trap 'echo failed at $LINENO' ERR with set -E shows where it stopped.
Use here documents to write config files from scripts, with a quoted delimiter when the text contains dollar signs that must stay as they are.
To append a line to a file only if it is not already there, use grep -qxF 'line' file || echo 'line' >> file, which makes a script safe to run twice.
sed -i changes files in place and works differently on Mac and Linux; on Linux sed -i is enough, and a backup suffix like -i.bak keeps the old version.
Use awk for column work and sed for line edits; for anything with structure like JSON use jq and not grep, because text tools break on formatting changes.
Use find ... -print0 | xargs -0 for file names with spaces, and while IFS= read -r for lines, instead of unquoted for loops over command output.
Use command substitution with quotes: result="$(command)", and check the exit status with a separate line, because local x=$(cmd) hides the status.
Use ss, ip and journalctl in scripts that run on modern systems; old tools such as netstat and ifconfig may be missing on minimal images.
Test a cron command by running it with env -i HOME=$HOME /bin/sh -c 'command', which imitates the bare cron environment and shows missing paths.
Cron has no stdout to show; mail is often not installed, so append >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1 to every cron line to keep the output.
Use flock with cron jobs so a slow run does not overlap the next one: flock -n /tmp/job.lock command.
Use sleep with random jitter in jobs that many devices run at the same time, so they do not all hit the server in the same second.
Use timeout command for steps that can hang, such as network calls in scripts, so one stuck step does not block the whole job forever.
Show progress for long scripts with echo lines that have time stamps, and write them also to a file with tee, so a failure in the middle is easy to locate.
Keep one script per job and pass settings as arguments or environment variables, so the same script works on every device without edits.
When copying commands from a web page, paste them into a text editor first; hidden characters and different quote marks can change what a command does.
Use history | grep word or Ctrl+R to find an old command, and prefix a command with a space to keep it out of the history when it contains a secret, if HISTCONTROL=ignorespace is set.
Use screen or tmux for long jobs over SSH, so a lost connection does not stop them; tmux attach returns to the same session later.
watch -n 2 command repeats a command every two seconds and shows changes, handy for temperatures, logs sizes and service states.
less +F file follows a growing file like tail -f but lets you scroll back with Ctrl+C and return with F, the better way to read a live log.
Use column -t to align output, and sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to count and rank, two quick tools to make sense of long logs.
Use xargs -I{} with care: it runs one command per line, and names with quotes break it unless you use -0 with null separated input.
Learn three keys in bash: Ctrl+A and Ctrl+E to jump to line start and end, Ctrl+W to delete a word and Ctrl+L to clear the screen; they save time every day.
A service that works locally but not remotely is often bound to localhost or blocked by a firewall; check ss -ltn for the listening address and the firewall rules next.
Name resolution problems look like timeouts; test the address and the name separately with curl to tell DNS errors from connection errors.
A web socket behind a proxy needs the upgrade headers and a read timeout longer than your heartbeat interval, or the proxy closes quiet connections.
For a device that connects out to a server, no router settings are needed; the server only needs a public address and TLS, which makes this the safest design for home devices.
Treat every port you open as a door: close what you do not use, require authentication on the rest, and keep the software behind it updated.
A VPN such as WireGuard gives secure access to your home network with one open UDP port and small configuration, much safer than exposing a web interface.
Tailscale or a similar mesh VPN reaches devices behind any router without port forwarding, and gives each device a stable name inside the private network.
Use HTTPS everywhere, including inside a home network when it carries passwords; browsers also block microphone and camera on plain HTTP pages from other hosts.
Check the date and time on a device when HTTPS fails; a clock that is years off is the most common reason for certificate errors on a Pi without a battery.
HTTP caching headers matter for speed; static files with long max-age and hashed names load instantly, and API answers should say no-store when they hold user data.
Large responses should be compressed and paged; sending a whole database as one JSON file wastes mobile data and memory on small devices.
Retries must be safe: make requests idempotent or give them an id, so a repeated request after a timeout does not create a second record.
Time out and give up gracefully on slow networks, show the user what is happening, and retry in the background with growing waits.
Measure latency from the user's point of view, with the browser developer tools network panel, because server logs do not show DNS, TLS and download time.
A load balancer or proxy hides the real client address; read X-Forwarded-For only from your own proxy, or users can fake their address in logs and rate limits.
Keep WebSocket messages small and typed, with an id and a type field, and send a version in the first message, so protocol changes can be handled on both sides.
Backpressure matters on slow clients: do not send faster than the receiver reads, or memory on the server grows with every slow connection.
Authenticate a WebSocket in the first message or with a short lived token, not with a long lived secret in the address, which appears in logs and browser history.
Cloud free tiers share resources; expect cold starts, limited memory and restarts at any time, and design the app to recover its state from the database after a restart.
Keep state in a database or file on a persistent disk, not in memory only; a restart or deploy on a hosting service wipes everything held in process memory.
Use semantic HTML elements such as button, nav, main, header and label; they bring keyboard support and screen reader meaning that a div with a click handler does not have.
A button element is focusable and works with Enter and Space by default; a clickable div needs tabindex, a role and key handlers to reach the same level.
Set the lang attribute on the html element, such as lang="tr", so screen readers pronounce text correctly and browsers offer the right translation and hyphenation.
Add the viewport meta tag width=device-width, initial-scale=1 to every page, or phones show a zoomed out desktop layout.
Use rem for font sizes and padding so the page follows the user's browser font setting, and px only for thin borders and shadows.
Use CSS custom properties for colors and spacing; one :root block makes a dark theme a few lines long and keeps every component consistent.
Support dark mode with @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) and a manual switch that sets a data-theme attribute, and apply the stored theme in the head to avoid a white flash.
Use color-scheme: light dark in CSS so form controls and scrollbars follow the theme without extra styling.
Do not rely on color alone; add an icon or text to status dots, such as Online and Offline, for color blind users and for screens with poor color.
Keep focus outlines visible; use :focus-visible to show them for keyboard users only, and never write outline: none without a replacement.
Provide alt text for images that carry meaning and an empty alt for decoration, so screen readers skip pure decoration.
Give icon-only buttons an aria-label or visually hidden text, such as Close, because a screen reader otherwise says only button.
Use aria-live="polite" on a status area, so changes such as Connected or Saved are announced without moving the focus.
Set loading="lazy" on images below the fold and width and height attributes on all images, so the page does not jump while pictures load.
Use the picture element or srcset with sizes to serve smaller images to phones; one huge image for every device wastes mobile data.
Prefer SVG for icons and simple graphics: they stay sharp at every size, are small, and can use currentColor to follow the text color.
Inline SVG with fill="currentColor" lets a button color its icon in hover, disabled and dark states with no extra files.
Preload only the one or two files needed for the first screen with link rel="preload"; preloading many files slows the page down.
Put scripts at the end of body or use defer, so the page shows before the scripts run; async scripts run in unknown order.
Use type="module" for modern scripts: they are deferred by default, have their own scope and can import other files.
Avoid inline event handlers like onclick in markup when you use a strict Content-Security-Policy; add listeners in a script file instead.
A Content-Security-Policy such as default-src 'self' blocks scripts from other origins and inline code, a strong shield against injected scripts.
Escape user text before putting it into HTML: textContent is safe, innerHTML is not; building lists with createElement and textContent avoids injection.
Do not store tokens in localStorage when an httpOnly cookie is possible; any script on the page can read localStorage, but not an httpOnly cookie.
Use SameSite cookies and a CSRF token for state changing requests; a form on another site can otherwise send a request with your cookies.
Use the rel="noopener noreferrer" attribute on links with target="_blank", so the opened page cannot control your page and does not receive the address.
Check that every form field has a label and a name, and the right type and autocomplete values, so mobile keyboards and password managers behave.
Use input type="search" for search fields and enterkeyhint="search" or "go" so mobile keyboards show the matching button.
Handle the submit event of the form, not the click of the button, so pressing Enter in a field works as well and event.preventDefault stops the page reload.
Disable the submit button and show a busy state during a request, and enable it again in a finally block so errors do not leave it stuck.
Validation with the browser's constraint API: form.reportValidity() shows the built-in messages and input.setCustomValidity('text') sets your own.
Remember form values with the autocomplete attribute and avoid autocomplete off for logins; browsers and password managers ignore it anyway.
Make tap targets at least 44 pixels and add spacing; a phone user hits a small close button next to a large one by mistake.
Use touch-action: manipulation to remove the double tap zoom delay on buttons, and avoid hover only interactions on touch devices.
Test on a real phone: the on screen keyboard covers the lower half of the screen, and position: fixed footers jump when it opens.
Use 100dvh instead of 100vh for full screen layouts on phones, since the address bar changes the visible height while scrolling.
Keep the layout in a single column on phones, switch to two columns with a min-width media query, and test at 320 pixels wide.
Avoid horizontal scrolling: tables that may be wide go inside a container with overflow-x: auto, and long words get overflow-wrap: anywhere.
A sticky header needs top: 0 and a background color, or content shows through; also add padding at the top of anchored sections with scroll-margin-top.
Use scroll-behavior: smooth only for in page links, and respect prefers-reduced-motion, since smooth scrolling can make some users feel unwell.
Animate transform and opacity, not width, height or top; they run on the graphics chip and stay smooth even on a small device.
Add will-change only on elements that are about to animate, and remove it afterwards; using it everywhere uses more memory instead of speeding things up.
A loading skeleton or spinner after 300 milliseconds feels faster than none; for very short waits show nothing, to avoid a flicker.
Handle the offline state: catch failed fetches, show a clear message with a retry button and keep the last known data visible instead of a blank page.
Reconnect WebSocket connections after the tab was in the background; the visibilitychange event is the right moment to check the connection and refresh data.
setInterval polling should pause when the tab is hidden and use the server's answer to adjust the interval; it saves battery and requests.
Use fetch with AbortController and a timeout, so a request to a sleeping server does not hang for minutes and you can show a waking up message instead.
Use Promise.allSettled for independent requests so one failure does not hide the other results, and Promise.all only when all results are needed.
Format dates and numbers with Intl.DateTimeFormat and Intl.NumberFormat using the user's language, instead of building strings by hand.
Use Intl.RelativeTimeFormat for text such as 5 minutes ago, and recalculate it on a timer for pages that stay open.
Keep translations in one object per language and fall back to English for missing keys; switching language should not need a page reload.
Turkish needs care with case: toLocaleUpperCase('tr') maps i to İ, and sorting with localeCompare('tr') puts ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü after their base letters.
Avoid concatenating translated fragments; use whole sentences with placeholders, because word order differs between languages.
Test right to left languages if you plan them: use logical properties such as margin-inline-start instead of margin-left, so layouts flip without rewriting.
A progressive web app needs a manifest and HTTPS; icons of 192 and 512 pixels, a name, start_url and display standalone let people install it from the browser menu.
Use localStorage only for small per-user preferences like theme and language, and always wrap access in try and catch, since private windows and policies can block it.
IndexedDB stores larger structured data in the browser; use a small wrapper library or the promise form, because the callback API is hard to use correctly.
Store timestamps with the data in the browser storage, so you can ignore stale entries and clear old caches after an app update.
The History API pushState changes the address without reload; handle popstate for the back button and keep every view reachable by its own address.
Use hash routes like /#win=1 for small apps with no server routing; the part after the hash is never sent to the server and survives redirects.
A page opened in a desktop app's webview may differ from the browser; test the permissions for microphone, clipboard and notifications there, since they are controlled by the host app.
WebView2 on Windows needs the runtime installed; Windows 11 has it, and Windows 10 may need the evergreen runtime installer, so the app should show a clear message if it is missing.
A WebView in Android apps needs JavaScript enabled, DOM storage turned on and a WebChromeClient to handle permission requests such as the microphone.
Microphone access in an Android WebView needs the RECORD_AUDIO runtime permission in the app and onPermissionRequest to grant it to the page; both are required.
Speech recognition in the browser, webkitSpeechRecognition, depends on Google servers in Chrome and does not exist in every WebView; test it on the target device early.
MediaRecorder records audio from getUserMedia into chunks; send them as a Blob to the server for transcription, and pick a mime type that the browser supports using isTypeSupported.
Start audio recording only after a user gesture, and stop all tracks with stream.getTracks().forEach(t => t.stop()) when done, or the microphone indicator stays on.
AudioContext starts suspended until a user gesture on most browsers; call resume() in a click handler before playing generated sound.
Show a visible recording indicator and a level meter while the microphone is on; people trust a voice feature more when it shows that it hears them.
Handle permission denied errors from getUserMedia with a clear message that says how to allow the microphone in the browser or app settings.
Text to speech with speechSynthesis works offline in most browsers, but the available voices depend on the system; check getVoices after the voiceschanged event.
For file downloads from a page, create a Blob, make an object URL and click a temporary link with the download attribute, and revoke the URL afterwards.
For file uploads use FormData and fetch without setting the Content-Type header yourself; the browser adds the multipart boundary correctly.
Show upload progress with XMLHttpRequest upload events or a streaming approach; fetch does not report upload progress in all browsers.
The Fullscreen API needs a user gesture: element.requestFullscreen() from a click, and document.exitFullscreen() to leave; kiosk pages often rely on browser flags instead.
Prevent the screen from sleeping during a task with the Screen Wake Lock API, navigator.wakeLock.request('screen'), and request it again after the page becomes visible.
Use the Notification API only after a user gesture and explain why before asking; a permission prompt on page load is almost always denied.
Vibration, battery and device orientation APIs vary widely between browsers; feature detect with typeof or in checks and keep the page working without them.
Feature detect instead of browser sniffing: if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) is reliable, while user agent strings lie and change.
Handle errors globally with window.onerror and unhandledrejection listeners, and send a short report to the server in production, so you hear about crashes users never report.
console.log objects with console.table or JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2) while debugging; the console shows live objects that may change after logging.
Use the Network panel's throttling and the Offline checkbox to test slow and missing connections, and disable cache while developer tools are open to see real loads.
Use the Lighthouse panel to check performance, accessibility and best practice; fix the biggest items first, since a few images and scripts usually cause most of the slowness.
Compress and resize images before upload, preferably to WebP or AVIF, and set a maximum dimension; a phone photo of five megabytes is rarely needed on a web page.
Minify and bundle only when the page needs it; a small app with a few files over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 loads fast without a build step.
Keep dependencies few; every library adds download size, security updates and breaking changes, and small utilities are often shorter to write than to import.
Check a library's last release, open issues and license before using it, and pin the version so updates happen when you decide.
Load third party scripts such as analytics last and with defer, and ask whether they are needed at all; they slow pages and send visitor data elsewhere.
Use a strict, clear error page for 404 and 500 with a link back home; a plain server error with a stack trace tells attackers how your server works.
Cache bust with a version in the file name, such as app.3f2a.js, so browsers keep old files for a long time but fetch the new file as soon as you deploy.
In single page apps, update the document title and heading when the view changes, and move the focus to the main heading, so keyboard and screen reader users notice the change.
Use the browser's built-in validation for password and e-mail types, and show hints before errors, such as At least 8 characters, instead of after the first failed attempt.
Keep one source of truth for state in the page and render from it; copying the same value into several places is the origin of the screens that disagree with each other.
Re-render only what changed: update the text of an element or the class of a dot, rather than rebuilding the whole list every two seconds, so scroll position and focus stay.
When polling a list every few seconds, compare with the last data and skip the update if nothing changed, which avoids flicker and saves CPU on a small tablet.
Show offline devices in a calm gray and online ones in green with the word, and sort online first; changes in status should update in place without moving the other rows.
Stick to short, specific button labels like Start recording and Delete device, and use sentence case; clear verbs reduce the need for help text.
Show confirmation after actions: a short toast saying Saved or Device removed for two seconds, and an undo link when the action can be reversed.
Do not trap users in modal dialogs: Escape and a visible close button must work, focus must move into the dialog when it opens and return to the opener when it closes.
Avoid auto playing sound and moving content on load; start media only when the user asks, and give a way to pause anything that moves for more than five seconds.
Chromium's remote debugging port gives full control of the browser to any local process that can connect; bind it to localhost only and never expose it to the network.
Use a separate user data directory for automation, so test cookies and extensions never touch the daily profile, and delete the directory to start clean.
Headless Chromium has no window, so features that need a display, such as some extensions and permission prompts, behave differently from the visible browser.
A page that detects automation may block you; use your own pages and services, or ask for an API, instead of working around bot protection.
Set a fixed window size and device scale factor for visual checks, so screenshots from different runs can be compared pixel by pixel.
Wait for elements instead of sleeping: Playwright locators wait automatically, and a fixed sleep either wastes time or fails on a slow device.
Collect console messages and failed requests during a test run; they often show the real cause when a page looks broken but no test step failed.
Take a screenshot when a test fails, together with the page's HTML or accessibility snapshot, so you can see what the browser saw without repeating the run.
Use the accessibility tree, roles and labels as selectors; they match what people see and survive style changes better than long CSS paths.
Chromium on a Pi uses a lot of memory when many tabs are open; for a kiosk keep one tab, and restart the browser nightly with a timer to clear leaks.
Keep Chromium updated through apt on a Pi, as security fixes arrive often; an old browser also stops working with new web features and sites.
Chromium's password manager and sync prompts can cover a kiosk page; disable them in policies, and use a fresh profile for the display user.
Use --disk-cache-dir=/tmp/cache on SD card systems so the browser cache lives in memory and does not wear the card with constant writes.
If a page shows ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID, check the device clock first; if it shows ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED, check DNS and Wi-Fi before the page itself.
ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED means nothing listens on that port, ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT means packets are dropped, and ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE means the server closed without data.
Chrome's ctrl+shift+i opens developer tools, ctrl+r reloads, ctrl+shift+r reloads ignoring cache, and F12 does the same as the first on most systems.
Take a screenshot before and after each automated action and compare; automation without feedback only works until the first unexpected dialog appears.
Use window titles and classes to check that the right application has focus before typing; typing a password into the wrong window is the worst automation mistake.
xdotool key Return presses Enter, Tab moves to the next field, and ctrl+a selects all, ctrl+c and ctrl+v copy and paste, the base of most form filling scripts.
xdotool mousemove_relative moves the pointer from its current position, and xdotool getmouselocation prints x, y, screen and window, for calibration of click positions.
xdotool click --window ID sends a click to a window without moving the pointer on some applications, but many ignore synthetic events, so test it per application.
Delays between steps should be based on conditions, such as the window title changing or a screenshot matching, rather than guessed sleeps.
xdotool is for X11; on Wayland use ydotool with its daemon, or the compositor's own tools, and note that Wayland deliberately limits input injection for security.
A settings screen should apply changes immediately or have one clear Save button; mixing both makes people unsure whether their change was kept.
Show the current value of every setting and a short explanation of what it does, such as Language: Türkçe; no one should have to open a menu to find out the state.
Keep destructive actions away from frequent ones and style them as secondary until confirmation; a red Delete button next to Save invites mistakes.
Error messages should say what failed, why if known and what to do next, in plain language; Server did not answer, trying again in 5 seconds is better than Error 502.
A progress screen should show real progress or an honest indeterminate animation with a message; fake progress bars lose trust the first time they stall.
Make the app usable in the first five seconds: show content or a clear loading message at once, and fill in details as they arrive.
Do not require sign in before showing what the app does; a short description and a sign in button on one screen explain more than a blank form.
Remember the person's last choices, such as the selected device and language, and restore them on the next start without asking again.
Use platform conventions: Ctrl+W closes, F11 toggles full screen, Esc leaves dialogs on Windows; people expect these without reading help.
Test the interface with someone who has never seen it; the first place they hesitate shows what to rename or move.
Write the requirement as a test before you change code: when the test passes you know the change works, and it keeps working after later changes.
Ship a small working version first and improve it with real feedback; a perfect plan that is never used teaches less than a rough version in use.
Document the commands you used to set up a machine in a file in the repository; the next setup becomes copy and paste and the knowledge survives your memory.
Make failures visible: a status page, a log line and a notification on errors; a silent failure is found only by the person who needed the result.
Avoid single points of failure for important data: keep the source in git, the data backed up elsewhere and the secrets in a password manager.
Give each automated job an owner, a log and a way to turn it off; jobs nobody remembers are the ones that fill disks and send mail at three in the morning.
Prefer reversible changes: make a copy, change the copy, test, then switch; this turns a risky edit on a live device into a safe one.
When estimating time, add what testing, deployment and unexpected problems will take; the code is often the smaller part of the work.
Check assumptions with a tiny experiment rather than a long discussion; a two minute test often ends a debate about how a tool behaves.
Version your data formats and your protocols from the start; the first incompatible change is far easier with a version number already in place.
Slicing a list with a step, items[::2], takes every second item, and items[-3:] takes the last three, both without an index loop.
Unpack with a star to split a list: first, *rest = items puts the first item in first and the others in rest, which is a clean way to handle a command and its arguments.
Swap two variables without a helper: a, b = b, a, because the right side is evaluated completely before the assignment.
Chained comparisons work as in mathematics: 0 < x < 10 is true only when both parts are true, and it reads better than two comparisons joined with and.
A conditional expression picks a value in one line: value = a if condition else b; use it for short choices, and a normal if block for anything longer.
The or operator returns the first truthy value, so name = given or 'default' fills in a default for empty strings and None, but also for 0, which may be wrong.
Truthiness: empty strings, empty lists, zero and None are false, so if items: tests for a non empty list, but if x: is wrong when 0 is a valid value.
Compare with None using is, never ==: if x is None, because == can be changed by a class and give surprising answers.
is checks identity and == checks equality; small integers and short strings may look identical with is, but this is an implementation detail, so never use it for values.
Copy lists correctly: b = a only gives a second name for the same list, a.copy() or a[:] makes a shallow copy and copy.deepcopy copies nested lists as well.
Multiplying a list of lists, [[0]] * 3, repeats the same inner list three times; build independent rows with a list comprehension, [[0] for _ in range(3)].
Do not change a list while looping over it; loop over a copy, or build a new list with a comprehension, or items are skipped.
Dictionaries keep insertion order since Python 3.7, and changing the size of a dictionary during iteration raises RuntimeError; iterate over list(d) when you must delete.
dict.items() gives key and value pairs, and sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True) ranks by value.
A dictionary comprehension builds a mapping in one line: {k: v for k, v in pairs if v}, and swapping keys and values is {v: k for k, v in d.items()}.
Sets support math: a | b is union, a & b intersection, a - b difference and a ^ b the items in only one; comparing two device lists takes one line.
Tuples are fixed and hashable, so they can be dictionary keys: positions[(3, 4)] = 'x' works while a list as key raises TypeError.
String methods you will use daily: strip, split, join, replace, startswith, endswith, lower, find and format; learn them before reaching for regular expressions.
str.isdigit accepts some non ASCII digits and str.isnumeric more, so for safe input validation use a regular expression or try int() and catch ValueError.
The in operator tests membership in strings, lists, sets and dictionary keys: 'ab' in 'cabd' is a substring test, and key in d checks keys, not values.
Use zip(*rows) to transpose a table: list(zip(*[[1,2],[3,4]])) gives the columns as tuples, handy for column sums of data read from CSV.
sum(x for x in data) and max(data, key=len) work on any iterable, and max and min accept default=value for empty inputs, which avoids a ValueError.
int(x) cuts toward zero, math.floor rounds down, math.ceil rounds up and round goes to the nearest even number at .5, four different results for negative and half numbers.
Numbers can have underscores for readability: 1_000_000 is the same as 1000000, and format(n, ',') prints the number with thousands separators.
divmod(total_seconds, 60) gives minutes and seconds in one call, and a second divmod gives hours, a short way to format durations.
bool is a subclass of int, so True + True is 2 and sum of booleans counts the true items, a short way to count matches.
A function without return gives None; a common bug is using the result of list.sort() or list.append(), which return None, instead of the changed list.
Use *args and **kwargs to pass arguments through to another function, and keyword only arguments after a star force callers to name them, which prevents mixed up values.
Functions are objects: you can store them in dictionaries as a dispatch table, handlers['start'](), which is clearer than a long if and elif chain.
Decorators wrap functions to add behaviour such as logging, timing or retrying; use functools.wraps so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring.
A retry decorator with a loop, a limited number of tries and time.sleep between them keeps the retry logic out of every function that calls the network.
Classes group data and behaviour; use a plain function when there is no state, and a dataclass when you only need to hold values together.
Use @property for computed attributes with a simple name, and keep expensive work out of it, since callers expect attribute access to be cheap.
Class attributes are shared by all instances while instance attributes belong to one; a list defined at class level is a shared list, a classic bug.
__repr__ should show enough to recreate or identify an object and appears in logs and the console, while __str__ is for readable output; define __repr__ first.
Context managers are classes with __enter__ and __exit__ or generator functions with @contextmanager; use them for locks, files, temporary changes and timers.
Iterators implement __iter__ and __next__, but a generator function is almost always shorter; use yield from to pass values through from another generator.
next(iterator, default) returns a default instead of raising StopIteration, and next(x for x in items if cond) finds the first match in one line.
Use sorted(set(items)) for unique sorted values, and dict.fromkeys(items) for unique values that keep their first order of appearance.
A chunking helper with range and slicing, [items[i:i+n] for i in range(0, len(items), n)], splits a list into batches for APIs with limits.
Flatten one level of nesting with a comprehension, [x for row in rows for x in row], and use itertools.chain.from_iterable for large inputs.
Counting with Counter and merging with +: Counter('aab') + Counter('b') adds counts, and subtract and update work in place, simple for statistics from logs.
Use heapq for a priority queue: heappush and heappop work on a plain list, and nlargest(3, items) returns the three largest without sorting everything.
bisect.insort keeps a list sorted while inserting, and bisect_left finds the position in logarithmic time, good for sorted time series.
Use itertools.product for all combinations of several lists, permutations for orders and combinations for choices without order, instead of nested loops.
itertools.cycle repeats a sequence forever and itertools.count counts up, useful with zip to label items or rotate through servers.
Use operator.itemgetter and attrgetter as fast sort keys: sorted(rows, key=itemgetter('age')) is shorter and faster than a lambda.
Regular expression flags: re.I ignores case, re.M makes ^ and $ match at every line and re.S lets the dot match newlines; write them in the pattern with (?i).
re.split with a pattern splits on several separators at once, re.split(r'[,;]\s*', text), which str.split cannot do.
Use re.escape(text) to match user text literally inside a pattern, so dots and brackets in the text are not treated as pattern syntax.
Catastrophic backtracking: nested quantifiers like (a+)+ can take exponential time on bad input; keep patterns simple and limit the input length for text from outside.
Parse numbers from text with a pattern such as r'-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?' and convert with float; the dot and the minus sign are the parts people forget.
Use str.translate with str.maketrans to replace many characters at once, for example to remove Turkish letters from a file name.
unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', text) splits letters from accents, and filtering combining characters gives a simple ASCII slug for file names and addresses.
Slug a title for file names by lowercasing, replacing non letters with a dash and stripping dashes: re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9]+', '-', text.lower()).strip('-').
Use textwrap.dedent for multi-line strings inside indented code, so the text does not carry the code's leading spaces.
String comparison is by code point; sorted(['b','B','a']) gives uppercase first, and sorted(..., key=str.casefold) gives a case independent order.
Use int.from_bytes and to_bytes for binary data, and bytes.hex() with bytes.fromhex() for readable dumps of a packet or a key.
bytearray is a mutable bytes object for building packets; append and extend work on it, and bytes(buf) makes an immutable copy to send.
Use memoryview to slice large byte buffers without copying, useful when parsing a stream of audio chunks on a small device.
wave module reads and writes WAV files from the standard library: wave.open(path).getparams() gives channels, sample width and frame rate.
Speech recognition models usually want 16 kHz, 16 bit, mono audio; convert recordings with ffmpeg -ar 16000 -ac 1 before sending them to a transcription service.
audioop-free level meter: compute the RMS of 16 bit samples with struct.unpack and math.sqrt to show a microphone level bar without extra packages.
json.dumps(obj, separators=(',', ':')) makes the smallest JSON without spaces, useful for messages over slow links; indent only for human readable files.
json.dumps fails on datetime, bytes and sets; pass default=str, or convert the values yourself, and use ISO strings for dates.
Read large JSON files with json.load only when they fit in memory; for big logs use JSON Lines and read one line at a time.
The uuid module makes unique ids: uuid.uuid4() is random, and str(uuid.uuid4()).replace('-', '') gives 32 hex characters for device and message ids.
secrets.choice and a character set make random codes; for sign-in codes use secrets.randbelow(10**6) with zero padding, never random.randint.
Store a code's hash and expiry time rather than the code itself, and delete it after the first successful use.
Rate limit attempts with a dictionary of deques keyed by address or account, dropping timestamps older than the window; a few lines protect login and code checks.
Compare versions with tuples of integers, tuple(map(int, '1.10.2'.split('.'))), because comparing version strings as text puts 1.10 before 1.9.
Use sys.version_info >= (3, 9) to branch on the Python version, and platform.system() returns Linux, Windows or Darwin for platform specific code.
Read standard input in a script with sys.stdin.read() or a loop over sys.stdin, which lets your program sit in a shell pipeline like any other tool.
Write errors to sys.stderr with print(..., file=sys.stderr) so a pipeline's output stays clean and error text still appears on the terminal.
getpass.getpass() reads a password without showing it, and falls back with a warning when no terminal exists; do not use input() for secrets.
Use readline-like input() prompts only for interactive tools; services must read settings from files or the environment, because no one is there to type.
time.sleep in a loop blocks the thread; for periodic work with drift correction compute the next run time from time.monotonic and sleep only the remaining time.
Use Event.wait(timeout) instead of time.sleep in worker threads, so setting the stop event wakes the thread at once and shutdown is fast.
threading.Timer runs a function once after a delay and can be cancelled with cancel(); for repeating jobs start a new timer at the end of each run.
Exceptions in threads do not stop the main program; wrap the thread body in try and except with logging, or the thread ends silently and the feature stops working.
Use concurrent.futures.as_completed to handle results in the order they finish, and future.result(timeout=5) to wait with a limit.
A global dictionary shared between threads needs a lock for read modify write steps such as d[k] += 1; single operations are atomic, but sequences of them are not.
weakref and gc are rarely needed; if memory grows in a long running service, first look for unbounded lists, dictionaries and caches, and for connections that are never closed.
sys.getsizeof shows the size of one object without its contents; tracemalloc.take_snapshot compares allocations between two points to find leaks.
Use resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss for the peak memory of the current process on Linux, reported in kilobytes.
A remote control agent should connect outward to the server and keep the connection open, so it works behind home routers and firewalls without any port forwarding.
Give every agent a stable device id and a human name; the id is for the system and never changes, the name is what the person sees and can edit.
An agent should report its own state regularly: version, uptime, load and last error; a status that comes only from the agent itself is more trustworthy than one guessed by the server.
Server side probing complements agent heartbeats: the server pings every connected agent every few seconds and drops those that do not answer, so offline devices show as offline fast.
Mark a device as online only while its connection is alive; a last seen time stamp alone leaves devices looking online for minutes after power loss.
Agent updates should be atomic: download the new file next to the old one, check its checksum, rename it into place and restart, with the old copy kept for a quick rollback.
Check the checksum or signature of an update before running it; an update channel without verification lets anyone who controls the download run code on every device.
Run the agent as an unprivileged user wherever possible, and give it a small allow list of actions; a remote agent that can run any command is the most valuable target in the system.
Log every command an agent executes with time, requester and result; when something goes wrong the log is the only way to know what happened and who asked for it.
Commands sent to agents should have an id and a timeout, and the agent should answer with the same id, so the server can match replies and show clear failures.
Do not run commands that need confirmation on unattended devices; commands that wait for input hang forever, so use non-interactive flags and a timeout on every command.
Ask before any destructive action such as deleting files, formatting disks or changing network settings; remote devices are hard to repair when a change cuts the connection.
Before changing network settings remotely, schedule an automatic undo, for example a command that restores the old settings in five minutes unless cancelled, so a mistake does not lock you out.
A remote shell is powerful and risky; limit who may use it, require a strong login, and keep a record of sessions, preferably with short lived access.
Screen sharing from an agent should show a clear indicator on the device and ask for consent where the owner is present; hidden remote viewing is a privacy and legal problem.
Voice commands need confirmation for risky actions: repeat what was understood and ask Should I do it, because speech recognition mistakes are common.
A voice assistant should work with short, natural commands, handle fillers such as um, and show the recognised text on screen, so the person can see and correct what was heard.
Wake word detection should run on the device and send audio only after the wake word, so the microphone is not streaming all the time to a server.
Show a visible and audible sign when a device starts listening, and a clear way to switch the microphone off; trust in a voice feature depends on obvious control.
Speech recognition errors cluster around names, numbers and rare words; allow spelling out, offer corrections and keep a list of the person's own words such as device names.
Turkish speech recognition works better with complete sentences than single words, and case endings change words, so match commands by meaning and not only by exact text.
Normalise recognised text before matching: lowercase with Turkish rules, remove punctuation, trim spaces and map number words to digits, so Üç and 3 mean the same.
Offer both voice and text input, since noisy rooms, quiet places and privacy needs make one of them unusable at times.
Voice input latency matters: start sending audio while the person is still speaking, show partial text and stop when silence lasts about one second.
Protect transcripts like any personal data: keep them only as long as needed, store them with the account, and let the person delete them.
An assistant that controls a computer should work in small verified steps: do one action, look at the result, then decide the next action, instead of running a long script blindly.
Take a screenshot after each step of computer control and compare it with what you expect; if the screen is not as expected, stop and ask or retry instead of clicking on.
Prefer structured access over clicking pixels: a command line tool, an API or a browser with accessible selectors is faster and more reliable than screen coordinates.
When a window may move or resize, find it by title each time and compute click positions from its current geometry, never from stored absolute coordinates.
Keep a human in the loop for anything that spends money, sends messages or deletes data; automation should prepare and confirm, not act silently.
Test automations on a copy or a test account first; a script that works in a test with real data once is not tested.
Idempotent steps make automation safe to repeat: ensure that a setting has a value instead of toggling it, and check before creating something that may already exist.
Rate limit your own automations; a loop that retries without delay can lock an account, trigger anti abuse systems or fill a disk with logs in minutes.
Prefer official APIs over scraping; pages change without notice, and scraping may violate the terms of the site, while an API has documented limits and stable fields.
Respect robots files, terms and rate limits when you fetch data from websites, and identify your tool with a clear user agent string.
Cache data you fetch repeatedly and refresh it by time or by change markers such as ETag, so you reduce traffic, speed up responses and avoid being blocked.
Keep user data separated by account in every query: filter by user id in the database layer, so one missing check cannot show another person's devices.
Authorisation checks belong on the server for every request; hiding a button in the interface does not stop someone from sending the request directly.
Use short lived tokens for sessions and a refresh mechanism, and let users sign out everywhere; a stolen long lived token is valid until someone notices.
Hash and salt passwords with a slow algorithm, limit login attempts, and offer sign in codes or passkeys; passwords alone remain the weakest link of most services.
Send security relevant mail for new sign ins, password changes and new devices; the account owner notices misuse faster than any monitoring.
Close sign ups when not needed; an open registration form on a small server attracts bots, mail abuse and database growth within days.
Validate and limit everything that comes from outside: sizes, counts, types and formats; unbounded input is the common start of crashes and denial of service.
Keep dependencies updated; subscribe to security advisories for the libraries you use, because known holes in old versions are what attackers try first.
Separate secrets from code and rotate them on a schedule; with environment variables on the host and an example file in the repository, new setups need no guesses.
Use the principle of least privilege for tokens: a deploy token that only writes to one repository does much less harm than a personal token with access to everything.
Back up the database before every migration, and run migrations in a transaction where the database supports it; a failed migration without a backup is a long day.
Make deployments boring: one command, the same every time, with a quick health check at the end and an easy rollback; the fear of deploying is a sign to automate it.
Watch the first minutes after a deployment: check the health endpoint, logs and one real action, since many failures show up only after the first real request.
Use a staging environment or at least a local copy with the same versions of the database and the runtime, so you find version differences before users do.
Write errors for the person using the system, and put technical detail in the log; a message with a short reference id lets support find the log line.
Add a public status or health page for services you run; it saves time when users ask whether it is down, and your own checks can use it too.
Plan for the free tier's limits: sleeping services, limited memory, no persistent disk and monthly hours; know what happens when the limit is reached and how to move up.
Keep a runbook for each service: how to start, stop, deploy, check health, restore from backup and where the logs are; the person who needs it at night is often you in a hurry.
Time zones: store UTC, show local time by the viewer's setting, and test around daylight saving changes; for Turkey the time offset is a fixed three hours, but other countries change.
Treat names and text as Unicode everywhere; test with Turkish letters, emoji and long names, and never assume that one character is one byte.
Do not trust the clock of a device for security decisions; a device with a wrong time can break certificates, sessions and signed messages.
Count and log, but avoid collecting personal data you do not need; every stored field is something to protect, explain and delete on request.
Write simple privacy text in plain language: what you store, why, for how long and how to delete it; people trust a service that explains this without legal fog.
Accessibility and clear language are part of quality: large enough text, strong contrast, labels for everything and plain words help every user, not only those with disabilities.
Localise from the beginning: keep texts in one table, use language codes, and test the longest language, because adding a second language later touches every screen.
Ask for feedback inside the app with one short question and a free text box; users rarely write long emails, but many will answer one question.
Release notes in plain language, saying what changed for the user, build trust; a list of internal ticket numbers does not.
Version numbers should mean something: increase the last number for fixes, the middle for features and the first for changes that break compatibility.
Keep the minimum supported versions of operating systems and browsers written down; supporting everything slows development and testing without helping many users.
Test on the slowest device you support; something that runs well on a developer laptop can be unusable on an old phone or a Pi Zero.
Measure before you optimise: find the slow part with a profiler or timing, change one thing and measure again, otherwise you spend days on a part that was not the problem.
A small, well chosen set of automated checks that run on every push, such as syntax check, tests and a build, finds most mistakes at the cheapest moment.
Review your own changes after a break: reading a diff the next morning finds mistakes that were invisible while you wrote the code.
Prefer clear code to clever code; the next reader, often you, will spend ten times longer reading than the author spent writing.
Delete code you do not use; dead code still has to be read, secured and updated, and git keeps the history if you need it back.
Split big changes into steps that each work; a series of small working changes is easy to review and easy to revert one by one.
Do not fix several unrelated problems in one change; separate commits let you undo the one that caused trouble without losing the good ones.
When you cannot find a bug, explain the problem aloud to someone or something, even a rubber duck; putting it into words reveals the wrong assumption.
Take breaks when stuck for more than an hour; a walk often solves what another hour of staring does not, and tired people introduce new bugs.
Keep a log of decisions with the reason, such as why a library was chosen; six months later the reason is worth more than the choice itself.
When a tool surprises you, read its documentation for that one feature rather than guessing; five minutes of reading often saves an afternoon of experiments.
Learn one editor and one shell very well; the time you save every day with shortcuts, search and macros adds up to weeks over a year.
Keep your personal tools and notes in a repository, including dotfiles and scripts, so a new machine becomes productive in minutes.
Passwords belong in a password manager with unique long passwords for every account; reuse across sites is how one leak becomes ten.
Turn on two step verification for e-mail, code hosting and hosting providers first; these accounts can reset every other account.
Keep recovery codes of important accounts printed or in a separate safe place, because a lost phone with the only authenticator can lock you out for good.
Never paste secrets into chats, tickets or public issues; if it happens, rotate the secret immediately, and do not rely on deleting the message.
Phishing messages create urgency; check the sender address and the real link target, and go to the site by typing its name yourself instead of using the link.
Update the operating system and applications regularly; most successful attacks use holes that have had a fix available for months.
Use full disk encryption on laptops and phones, so a lost device does not mean lost data, and keep the recovery key somewhere safe and separate.
Lock the screen when you leave, and set a short automatic lock time; a few seconds of open access is enough for harm in shared spaces.
Network hygiene at home: change the router's default admin password, keep its firmware updated, turn off WPS and use WPA2 or WPA3 for Wi-Fi.
Put guests and smart home devices on a separate network from your computers when your router supports it, so a weak gadget cannot reach your files.
Test your backups by restoring a file at least once; many people discover that the backup was empty or encrypted with a lost key on the day they need it.
Document how to recover each device: how to reflash, which settings are needed and where the configuration is stored; recovery steps written in advance are quick, and improvised ones are not.
A quick health check for a Pi service host: vcgencmd get_throttled, vcgencmd measure_temp, free -m, df -h and systemctl --failed together show power, heat, memory, disk and failures in seconds.
Use a script that prints the Pi's temperature, load and free space and send it to the server with the agent heartbeat, so problems show up before the device stops responding.
If a Pi hangs without any message, suspect power first, then the SD card, then heat; replace the power supply and the card before spending hours on software.
Corrupted file systems show as read only mounts and I/O errors in dmesg; fsck from another computer with the card removed can repair them, but a card with many errors should be replaced.
Use the overlay file system option in raspi-config for devices that are shut down by cutting power; changes are lost at reboot, so keep settings and data on a separate writable partition.
Keep a spare, already configured SD card for important Pis; swapping cards is the fastest repair, and updating the spare from time to time keeps it useful.
Write the card image with a verified write option in the imager; a failed write that was never verified produces boot problems that look like software bugs.
