On first boot the Pi expands its file system and may restart once; wait a few minutes before concluding that it hangs, and do not cut power during that first start.
A monitor that stays black on a Pi that is running often needs a different HDMI cable or port, or an hdmi_force_hotplug setting; connect the monitor before power on.
Micro HDMI ports on the Pi 4 and 5 are labelled, use the port closest to the power connector first for the primary display when only one monitor is connected.
For touch displays that connect by DSI or USB, check the driver lines in config.txt for your exact display model, and test touch with evtest to see if events arrive at all.
A USB speaker or microphone is usually plug and play on Linux; check with aplay -l and arecord -l, and set the default card in the desktop settings or in an asound configuration.
When sound plays too quietly or too loudly, adjust alsamixer, not just the application volume; the capture gain of a microphone matters for speech recognition.
Use a cheap USB sound card for microphone input if the Pi has no analogue input; the quality is far better than most on-board solutions and the setup needs no drivers.
A pi that runs a voice assistant benefits from a good microphone close to the speaker; echo and room noise reduce recognition more than the choice of software does.
Use the vcgencmd and sensors tools in a loop with a timestamp and write a CSV, to see temperature and throttling trends during long tasks.
A fan controlled by a GPIO pin or by the case's own controller keeps the Pi below throttling limits during long jobs; check that it runs by measuring temperature under load.
stress or a simple busy loop with python3 shows how hot the Pi gets under full load; run it for ten minutes before deciding the cooling is enough.
The official Raspberry Pi documentation lists current commands for each OS version; options change between releases, so check it when an old tutorial command fails.
Use raspi-config nonint commands in setup scripts to switch interfaces, hostnames and locales without menus, and run the script twice to be sure it is safe to repeat.
Write the setup of a Pi as a script in git: packages, files, services and settings; reinstalling after a card failure then takes minutes instead of an evening.
Use a common ground between the Pi and external circuits; signals without a shared ground are unreliable and can damage parts.
For motors use a motor driver board and a separate supply; never connect a motor directly to the Pi, since the reverse voltage when it stops can damage pins.
I2C sensors need pull-up resistors, which most breakout boards already have; long cables lower the reliable speed, so keep them short or reduce the bus speed.
1-wire temperature sensors such as DS18B20 appear under /sys/bus/w1/devices after enabling the one wire overlay; read the w1_slave file and parse the t= value.
For reliable timing in measurements use hardware features or a microcontroller; Linux is not a real time system, and a loop with sleep can jitter by many milliseconds.
Serial communication needs the console on the serial port disabled in raspi-config and matching baud rates; use /dev/serial0 and check permissions with the dialout group.
Add your user to the groups gpio, i2c, spi, dialout and video to use hardware without sudo; log out and in again after changing groups.
A udev rule gives stable names to USB devices by their serial number, so /dev/ttyUSB0 and /dev/ttyUSB1 do not swap places after a reboot.
If a service cannot open a device, check permissions with ls -l /dev/name and the service user's groups with id; adding SupplementaryGroups in the unit is the systemd way.
A Pi can run as a Wi-Fi access point with NetworkManager hotspot support, useful for first time setup of a device that has no screen.
Bluetooth audio and gamepads work through bluez; pair with bluetoothctl scan on, pair, trust and connect, and mark the device as trusted to reconnect after reboot.
Use Ethernet gadget mode on a Pi Zero to connect it to a computer over USB, and ssh to its address with no router; enable the dwc2 overlay and the g_ether module.
A Pi can boot from the network or from USB mass storage; for important systems an SSD on USB 3 is a major upgrade in speed and reliability over an SD card.
Use the rpi-eeprom-update tool to check the bootloader version; newer versions fix USB boot and power issues, so update through apt and the official tool, not by random files.
A Pi 5 needs a 5 volt 5 ampere supply for full USB power; with a weaker supply it limits USB current, and some drives or hubs then fail.
Camera ribbon cables must be fully seated with the contacts facing the right way; a camera not detected is usually the cable, not the software.
Time lapse or motion capture on a Pi writes many files; save them to a USB disk or send them away, and delete old ones by age with find -mtime.
If Chromium on a Pi is slow, close other programs, lower the page's animation, and use a lighter page for kiosks; a Pi 4 or 5 handles normal pages, a Pi Zero does not.
Use the official Raspberry Pi Connect or an SSH tunnel for remote desktop to a Pi without opening router ports, instead of exposing VNC to the internet.
Add a cron or timer that restarts the browser each night in kiosk setups, to clear memory leaks, and log the time to check later that it ran.
When copying a card to a larger card the partition does not grow by itself; run raspi-config to expand the file system or use the imager to start fresh.
Document the model, OS version and the date of setup in a text file on the device; two Pis that look the same often differ in firmware, and support questions start with that.
openssl dgst -sha256 file prints a checksum, and openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac key signs a message, both without extra tools.
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 encrypts a file with a password; use -pbkdf2 so the key derivation is strong, and decrypt with -d and the same password.
openssl x509 -noout -enddate -in cert.pem shows when a certificate expires, and -checkend 86400 exits non-zero if it ends within a day, good for monitoring.
A self signed certificate for local tests: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 365 -subj /CN=name; browsers warn about it, so use it only inside your own network.
openssl s_client -connect host:443 shows the certificate chain a server sends and openssl verify checks a certificate against trusted roots.
zip -r archive.zip folder creates a zip that Windows opens, unzip -l lists contents and unzip -d dir extracts to a folder.
Use unzip -t to test an archive without extracting, and zip -T after creating; a damaged archive reports errors before you rely on it.
file --mime-type -b name prints the MIME type, which is more reliable than the extension when you check uploads or odd downloads.
xmllint --noout file.xml checks that an XML file is well formed, and xmllint --xpath selects values, both useful in scripts.
jq . file pretty prints JSON and also validates it, with an exit code of 2 or more for bad input; a quick check before a service reads the file.
jq -r '.items[].name' prints one value per line without quotes, ready for a shell loop, and jq -s collects many JSON lines into one array.
jq '. + {x: 1}' adds a key and jq 'del(.a)' removes one, so JSON settings can be edited in scripts without regular expressions.
jq 'map(select(.age > 18))' filters a list and jq 'sort_by(.name)' sorts it, and group_by and length make counts without a script.
jq -n --arg name "value" '{name: $name}' builds JSON with safe quoting, better than echo with string concatenation, and --argjson passes numbers and booleans.
jq 'to_entries[] | "\(.key)=\(.value)"' turns an object into key=value lines, a quick way to build an environment file from JSON.
jq 'paths' and 'getpath' navigate unknown structures, and jq 'keys' lists the top level names, helpful when exploring a new API response.
yq edits YAML like jq edits JSON: yq '.a.b = 1' file.yaml; check which yq you have, because there are two different programs with that name.
pandoc converts between document formats, for example pandoc file.md -o file.html or file.docx, handy for turning notes into documents.
convert from ImageMagick resizes images: convert in.jpg -resize 800x out.jpg keeps proportions and -quality 80 reduces the file size.
identify -format '%wx%h' image prints the size of an image, and identify -verbose shows details; check sizes before uploading large photos.
convert -strip removes metadata such as GPS positions from photos before you share them, and -auto-orient applies the rotation stored by the camera.
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -ar 16000 -ac 1 out.wav extracts speech ready audio at 16 kilohertz mono, the format most recognition systems prefer.
ffmpeg -ss 5 -t 10 -i in -c copy out cuts a piece without re-encoding, which is instant and loses no quality, but cuts only at keyframes for video.
ffmpeg -af loudnorm or volume=2.0 adjusts audio level, and silenceremove cuts silence at the start and the end, useful before sending recordings to speech recognition.
ffmpeg -i in.wav -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 64k out.mp3 makes a small mp3; for speech 32 to 64 kilobits per second is enough and saves mobile data.
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i testsrc=duration=1:size=320x240:rate=5 makes a test video without any camera, and the same works for audio with sine, a good way to test pipelines.
ffmpeg -vf scale=640:-2 resizes video and keeps the aspect ratio with an even height, which many encoders require.
ffmpeg -vframes 1 -i video out.jpg takes a single frame as an image, and fps=1 saves one frame per second for a contact sheet.
perl -pi -e 's/old/new/g' file edits in place like sed but with more powerful regular expressions, and perl -ne 'print if /text/' filters lines.
perl -lane 'print $F[0]' prints the first column, like awk, and is useful when awk is not installed; -F: sets the separator.
bc does decimal math in scripts: echo 'scale=2; 10/3' | bc prints 3.33, and bc -l loads a math library with sine, cosine and logarithm.
Convert number bases with bc: echo 'obase=16; 255' | bc prints FF, and echo 'ibase=2; 1010' | bc prints 10, useful for masks and flags.
Use printf '%d' 0xff to convert hex to decimal and printf '%x' 255 for the other way, with no extra program.
Go builds a single static binary: GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build gives an exe from Linux, and CGO_ENABLED=0 avoids a C compiler and library dependencies.
go build -ldflags "-s -w" strips symbol tables and makes smaller binaries, and -X main.version=1.2 sets a string variable at build time.
Go's standard library has an HTTP server, JSON, crypto and WebSocket helpers in x packages, so a small tool needs no frameworks and compiles to one file.
gcc -Wall -O2 file.c -o prog compiles C with common warnings; read every warning, since most of them point to real bugs.
make runs the first target of a Makefile by default; use .PHONY for targets that are not files and tabs, not spaces, for the command lines.
ruby -e or ruby file.rb runs scripts and gem install adds libraries; on a Pi prefer apt packages for system tools written in Ruby to avoid long builds.
tmux new -d -s name 'command' starts a command in a detached session, tmux ls lists sessions and tmux kill-session -t name ends one, handy for long jobs.
tmux send-keys -t name 'text' Enter types into a session and tmux capture-pane -p -t name prints what it shows, a simple way to script interactive programs.
strace -f -e trace=openat command shows which files a program opens, the fastest way to find a missing config file or a permission problem.
strace -c command prints a summary of system calls and their time, and strace -p PID attaches to a running process to see why it hangs.
lsof -p PID lists files and sockets a process has open, and lsof -i :8000 shows who listens on a port; both need the same user or root to see everything.
wget -q -O file url downloads quietly and wget -c continues an interrupted download, simple on devices without curl.
diff -u old new makes a unified diff and patch -p1 < file.diff applies it, so a small change can be sent as text and applied on another machine.
diff -r --brief dir1 dir2 lists which files differ between two folders, and cmp -l shows the differing bytes of binary files.
Use tree -L 2 to show a folder structure two levels deep, and tree -I node_modules to skip noisy folders; paste the output into a README.
file -b and head -c show what is inside an unknown file; with cat -v control characters become visible, so a binary file in a text pipeline is easy to spot.
sort -t, -k2,2n file.csv sorts a CSV by the second column numerically, and sort -u removes repeated lines; the -t option sets the separator.
join file1 file2 merges two sorted files on a common first column like a database join, and comm shows the lines that differ.
expand and unexpand convert tabs and spaces, and fold -w 40 wraps long lines; small tools that fix formatting problems in one command.
rev reverses each line, tac prints a file backwards, shuf shuffles lines and shuf -n 1 picks a random line; handy for tests and samples.
nl numbers lines, cat -n does the same, and sed -n '3,5p' prints a range; use them to refer to line numbers in logs and scripts.
split and csplit cut big files, and the cat command joins them again in order; the pieces must keep their order because names sort alphabetically.
truncate -s 10M file makes a file of a given size filled with zeros, and fallocate does it faster; useful for swap files and test data.
head -c 16 /dev/urandom | xxd -p or od -An -tx1 makes random bytes in hex, and /dev/urandom never blocks, unlike old /dev/random behaviour.
stat -c %y file prints the modification time in readable form and touch -d '2026-01-01' file sets it, useful for testing cleanup scripts.
find -newer file lists files modified after another file, a simple way to find what changed since a marker, such as the time of the last backup.
find -empty finds empty files and folders, and find -type l lists symbolic links; find -xtype l shows broken links.
find -perm -u+x lists files the owner can execute, and find -user name filters by owner; permissions problems after a copy show up fast.
find -printf '%p %s\n' prints names and sizes without ls, and sort -k2 -n -r ranks them, the standard way to list the biggest files.
du -b prints exact bytes and du -s sums a folder; du --exclude='*.log' leaves out patterns, so you can compare sizes of what matters.
ls -1 prints one name per line, ls -a includes hidden files, and ls -R lists folders recursively; for scripts use find or globs instead of parsing ls.
wc -m counts characters while wc -c counts bytes; for Turkish text they differ because letters such as ş use two bytes in UTF-8.
printf 'ş' | wc -m shows 1 in a UTF-8 locale and 2 in the C locale, because the locale decides what a character is; set LANG to a UTF-8 locale in services.
sort order depends on the locale: LC_ALL=C sort gives byte order, which is stable across machines and what scripts and diffs need.
export LC_ALL=C in scripts that parse tool output, because messages in other languages break grep patterns such as 'No such file'.
Use date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ for ISO 8601 time in UTC, which sorts correctly, is unambiguous and is accepted by most tools and programming languages.
date -d 'last monday' and date -d '2026-11-15 + 3 days' make calendar calculations in scripts, but they are GNU specific and do not exist on Mac.
Convert between zones with TZ: TZ=Europe/Istanbul date -d '2026-11-15 12:00 UTC' shows Turkish time, which is UTC plus three hours all year.
cal and ncal show calendars in the terminal, and date +%V gives the ISO week number and date +%u the day of the week, with Monday as 1.
seq with dates: for i in $(seq 0 6); do date -d "2026-11-15 + $i days" +%a; done lists the next days, useful in schedules and reports.
sleep until a time: compute seconds with date +%s and sleep that long, or use a systemd timer, which survives reboots and is easier to monitor.
Unix time in seconds is 10 digits and in milliseconds 13 digits; JavaScript uses milliseconds and most Unix tools use seconds, a common mistake when exchanging time stamps.
Year 2038: 32-bit time stamps overflow in January 2038; on old 32-bit systems check that your tools use 64-bit time, which current Raspberry Pi OS does.
expr, let and $(( )) do integer math in shells; $(( )) is the portable choice, and variables inside it need no dollar sign.
awk 'BEGIN{print 10/4}' does floating point math, and awk handles columns of numbers well; printf in awk formats like in C.
awk -F, 'NR>1 {s+=$2} END {print s/(NR-1)}' averages a column of a CSV and skips the header, a one line statistic.
awk '!seen[$0]++' removes duplicate lines and keeps the first occurrence in order, which sort -u cannot do because it sorts.
awk 'length($0) > 80' lists long lines, and awk 'NR==5' prints one line; awk reads the file once, so it is fast for large logs.
awk -v name=value '{print name}' passes a shell variable safely into awk, instead of splicing it into the program text.
awk '$3 > 100 {print $1}' filters rows by a numeric column and prints another one, a short report tool for logs and tables.
sed -E 's/([a-z]+)@([a-z.]+)/\2/' uses extended expressions with groups, and sed -n '/start/,/end/p' prints the block between two markers.
sed '$d' deletes the last line, sed '1i text' inserts a line at the top and sed '$a text' appends one at the end.
sed 's/^/  /' indents every line and sed 's/[ \t]*$//' removes trailing spaces, tiny formatting jobs without an editor.
sed -n 'l' shows hidden characters like tabs and line ends, a simple way to find why a pattern does not match.
grep -o prints only the matching part, so grep -oE '[0-9]+' extracts all numbers from a text, and grep -c counts matching lines.
grep -P enables Perl regular expressions with lookahead and \d, available in GNU grep; use it for patterns that basic and extended syntax cannot express.
grep --color=never and grep -h are useful in scripts; -h hides file names when searching many files, and -s hides errors about unreadable files.
grep -f patterns.txt file searches for many patterns at once, and -F -f is the fast way to look up a list of fixed words in a big log.
grep -r --exclude-dir=.git --exclude='*.min.js' pattern . skips noise when searching a project, and rg is a faster tool if installed.
xargs -P4 -n1 runs jobs in parallel, such as converting many files at once; use the number of CPU cores as a starting point, and fewer on a Pi to avoid heat.
parallel processing with background jobs and wait works in plain bash: start jobs with & in a loop and call wait at the end for all of them.
mkfifo makes a named pipe that two programs can use to talk, and timeout protects the reader from waiting forever when the writer never starts.
A coprocess in bash with coproc lets a script talk to a long running helper through two pipes, useful for tools that must keep state between requests.
exec 3< file opens a file on descriptor 3 and read -u 3 reads from it, while other commands use standard input freely; close it with exec 3<&-.
Use printf '%q' to quote a string so it can be reused as shell input, which helps when scripts generate commands for another shell.
A bash function can return a string by printing it and the caller captures it with $( ); returning numbers through $? only works for 0 to 255.
Use getopts for options, and a case statement for subcommands; a script with start, stop and status arguments is simple to write and easy to put into a unit file.
set -- a b c sets the positional parameters, and for x in "$@" loops over them; this helps to test argument handling inside a function.
A script can find its own folder with dir=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd), so it works no matter where it is started from.
source a config file with simple KEY=value lines to load settings, but only from files you control, since sourcing runs every command in the file.
set -a before sourcing exports every variable in the file, and set +a stops it; this makes an env file usable by programs started from the script.
Environment files for systemd must not use export or quotes the way a shell does; keep them as plain NAME=value lines, one per line, without command substitution.
Flask test client lets you test routes without starting a server: app.test_client().get('/path') returns a response with status_code and data.
jsonify returns a JSON response with the right content type, and returning a dictionary from a view does the same in current Flask versions.
abort(404) stops a view with that status and an errorhandler function can return a JSON body for it, so the API answers consistently.
before_request runs before every request and can return a response to stop it, a good place for an authentication check on all routes.
after_request can add headers to every response, such as X-Content-Type-Options nosniff and Cache-Control no-store for API answers.
MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH makes Flask answer 413 for request bodies that are too large, which protects small servers from big uploads.
session data is stored in a signed cookie, so the secret key must be set and kept stable, or sessions are invalid after each restart.
Cookie flags are set with config keys: SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax', which harden login sessions.
url_for builds addresses from function names, so renaming a route does not break links, and it escapes values correctly.
Blueprints split a large app into modules: define routes on a Blueprint and register it with a url_prefix, which keeps files short.
render_template_string and Jinja2 escape variables by default, so user text in templates cannot inject HTML unless you mark it safe.
Never build templates from user supplied strings with render_template_string; the template language can run code, so pass user data only as variables.
send_file and send_from_directory serve downloads safely; send_from_directory refuses paths that leave the folder, unlike open() with a user supplied name.
werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash and check_password_hash store and verify passwords with salt, so no plain text passwords are saved.
secure_filename from werkzeug.utils removes path parts and odd characters from uploaded file names, and you should still store files under generated names.
In Flask the request.remote_addr is the proxy's address behind nginx; ProxyFix from werkzeug reads X-Forwarded-For only when you trust that proxy.
A health route that returns plain ok without touching the database keeps uptime checks fast and independent of other failures.
Use app.config.from_prefixed_env() or os.environ for settings, and check required values at start, so a missing secret stops the app with a clear message.
app.logger writes through the logging module; configure the level once at start, and log with %s style arguments so formatting happens only when the line is used.
aiohttp test utilities start a server on a free port for tests; aiohttp.test_utils.TestClient and TestServer need no fixed port.
A WebSocket handler in aiohttp is ws = web.WebSocketResponse(heartbeat=20), await ws.prepare(request) and async for msg in ws; the heartbeat drops dead peers.
aiohttp ClientSession should be created once and reused, and used with async with; creating one per request wastes connections and prints warnings.
Set a total timeout in aiohttp with ClientTimeout(total=10), or a request to a sleeping server can wait for minutes before failing.
websockets.serve and websockets.connect give a small WebSocket server and client; await ws.send(text) and async for message in ws are all you need for simple protocols.
websockets.connect(url, ping_interval=20, ping_timeout=20) sends pings and closes the connection when no answer arrives, which detects half dead connections.
A reconnect loop for a WebSocket client wraps connect in while True with try and except, waits with growing delay, and resets the delay after a successful connection.
requests.get(url, timeout=(3, 10)) sets a connect timeout of three and a read timeout of ten seconds; one number sets both.
requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter with urllib3 Retry retries on 502, 503 and 504 with backoff, useful for services that wake up slowly.
raise_for_status() turns 4xx and 5xx answers into exceptions, and response.status_code lets you handle codes yourself, for example waiting on 503.
Pass parameters with params={...} so requests encodes them, and json={...} for the body; building the query by hand breaks on spaces and special characters.
Headers carry the login: headers={'Authorization': 'Bearer token'}; never put tokens in the URL, since URLs appear in logs and browser history.
psutil gives system information without parsing commands: psutil.cpu_percent(), virtual_memory().percent, disk_usage('/').percent and sensors_temperatures() on Linux.
psutil.net_if_addrs lists interfaces and addresses, and psutil.net_io_counters gives bytes sent and received, enough for a simple network status report.
psutil.process_iter(['pid','name']) lists processes safely and psutil.Process(pid).terminate() ends one; this is more portable than parsing ps output.
psutil.boot_time() and time.time() give uptime in seconds, and psutil.getloadavg() works on Windows too, so one agent code path serves several systems.
yaml.safe_load parses YAML without running code, while yaml.load with the full loader can build arbitrary objects; always use safe_load for files you did not write.
YAML turns the words yes, no, on and off into booleans in older versions, and 1.10 into a number; quote such values to keep them as text.
Jinja2 templates generate config files and e-mails: Template('{{ name }}').render(name='x'), with loops {% for %} and conditions {% if %} in the text.
BeautifulSoup parses messy HTML: soup.select('a[href]') takes CSS selectors, get_text() strips tags, and the lxml or html.parser backend decides speed.
Pillow resizes and converts images: Image.open(path).resize((w, h)).save(out), and thumbnail((w, h)) keeps the aspect ratio in place.
Pillow can save JPEG with quality=80 and optimize=True for smaller files, and convert('RGB') is needed before saving an image with alpha as JPEG.
Pillow ImageOps.exif_transpose applies the camera's rotation flag, so photos from phones are not shown sideways after processing.
Compare two screenshots with ImageChops.difference and getbbox(); a result of None means the images are identical, a simple check for visual regression.
pandas.read_csv(path, encoding='utf-8-sig', sep=';') reads Excel exports from Turkey, and decimal=',' handles decimal commas.
pandas groupby('k')['v'].sum() totals by group and sort_values(ascending=False) ranks them; for small data this is shorter than loops and dictionaries.
pandas to_json(orient='records') and to_csv(index=False) export tables in the formats other programs expect, and read_json reads them back.
numpy arrays do math on whole columns at once: a * 2 + 1 is much faster than a loop; np.mean, np.std and np.percentile summarise sensor values.
A pydantic model validates incoming data and gives clear errors: class M(BaseModel) with typed fields, and M.model_validate(data) raises ValidationError for bad input.
click builds command line tools with decorators: @click.command and @click.option('--name'), and click.testing.CliRunner tests them without a shell.
markdown.markdown(text) turns Markdown into HTML for notes and README pages, and the result must be sanitised before showing text from other users.
cryptography's Fernet gives simple authenticated encryption: Fernet.generate_key(), f.encrypt(data) and f.decrypt(token); keep the key separate from the data.
Fernet tokens expire if you pass ttl to decrypt, and a wrong key or a changed byte raises InvalidToken, so catch that error for bad input.
pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test with many inputs, and pytest -x stops at the first failure, pytest -k name selects tests by name.
pytest fixtures with tmp_path give each test its own folder, and monkeypatch.setenv changes environment variables only for that test.
pytest.raises checks that code raises the expected error, and match= compares the message with a pattern, so error handling is tested like normal behaviour.
Test time dependent code by passing the time or a clock function as an argument; code that calls time.time() directly is hard to test without patching.
unittest.mock.patch replaces a function for one test and records calls; assert_called_once_with checks the arguments, so you can test code that sends e-mail without sending any.
Property based thinking helps tests: for any input the result of parse(format(x)) should equal x, so a loop over many random values finds odd cases.
Use coverage run -m pytest and coverage report to see untested lines, but a high number is not the goal; untested error paths are the useful finding.
Run tests in CI on every push with a matrix of Python versions, so a feature from a newer version does not silently break the old one on your Pi.
http.client and urllib.request send requests without installing requests; urllib.request.Request(url, headers={...}) sets headers, and timeouts apply to urlopen.
smtplib sends mail through a server with SMTP over TLS: smtplib.SMTP_SSL(host, 465) or SMTP(host, 587) with starttls(); keep the password in the environment, not in code.
email.message.EmailMessage builds a mail with headers and a text body, set_content for the text and add_alternative for HTML, and handles UTF-8 for Turkish letters.
Mail headers must not contain line breaks from user input; EmailMessage rejects them, which prevents header injection when you build mail from form fields.
A sign in code mail should say what it is for and how long it works; the plain text part must contain the code, since some clients do not show HTML.
git log --oneline -n 3 shows recent commits in one line each, and git log --stat adds the changed files, a fast way to see what a teammate or a bot pushed.
git diff HEAD --name-status shows A, M and D for added, modified and deleted files, a compact summary for scripts.
git show --stat HEAD prints the last commit with its changed files, and git show HEAD~2:file prints a file from three commits ago.
git log --follow file shows the history of a file across renames, and git log --diff-filter=D lists commits that deleted files.
git stash push -m name saves changes with a label, git stash list shows labels and git stash apply keeps the stash after applying it.
git stash drop removes one stash and git stash clear removes all, so check git stash list first; there is no recycle bin for dropped stashes except the reflog of dangling commits.
git switch - returns to the previous branch, like cd -, and git checkout - does the same in older versions.
git branch -m new-name renames the current branch, and git push origin -u new-name sets the upstream; rename the remote default branch in the hosting settings.
git log main..feature shows commits that the feature branch has and main does not, and three dots show the changes on both sides, a quick check before a merge.
git config user.email in a repository overrides the global address for that project only, so work and private projects can use different identities.
git status --porcelain gives stable machine readable output, so a script can test whether the working tree is clean with test -z "$(git status --porcelain)".
git diff --exit-code returns 1 when there are changes and 0 when there are none, so a script can branch on it without parsing output.
git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main counts commits you are behind and the reverse counts commits you are ahead, used to show update status in a prompt.
git ls-remote url refs/heads/main shows the commit id of a remote branch without cloning, so a script can check for updates cheaply.
git fetch --prune removes local references to branches that were deleted on the remote, which keeps git branch -r tidy.
git diff -w ignores whitespace changes and git diff --ignore-blank-lines skips empty lines, so reformatting does not hide the real change.
git add -N path marks a new file as intent to add, so it appears in git diff before you stage it, handy for reviewing new files together with edits.
git commit --allow-empty -m text makes a commit with no changes, a trick to trigger a CI run or a deploy hook without editing a file.
git commit --date and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE set the time of a commit, which is rarely a good idea except for importing old history; the real time is more honest.
git tag -d name deletes a local tag and git push origin :refs/tags/name deletes it on the remote; moving a published tag confuses everybody who already fetched it.
git describe --tags --always prints the nearest tag and the distance, such as v1.2-3-gabc1234, or just the short id when no tag exists, ideal for version strings in builds.
git archive --prefix=name/ -o file.tar.gz HEAD packs a clean copy of the project without .git, the standard way to make a source release.
git gc cleans and packs the repository, git count-objects -vH shows its size; on a small device run git gc --prune=now occasionally to free space.
git fsck checks the repository for corruption; a repository damaged by a power loss often shows missing objects there, and recloning is usually the quickest repair.
git update-ref and git symbolic-ref are low level tools; git symbolic-ref --short HEAD prints the current branch name, safe in scripts and empty on a detached HEAD.
git hash-object file prints the id git would give a file, and git cat-file -p id prints an object, useful to understand how content is stored.
git cat-file -t id prints the type of an object: blob for files, tree for folders, commit and tag; git ls-tree HEAD lists a folder's content.
git notes add -m text attaches a note to a commit without changing it, handy for build results or review comments that must not alter history.
A .git-blame-ignore-revs file with formatting commit ids, set with blame.ignoreRevsFile, keeps mass reformat commits out of blame output.
git rerere remembers how you resolved a conflict and applies the same fix the next time the same conflict appears, useful for long running rebases.
git diff --stat --summary shows mode changes and renames, git diff -M detects renames, so moved files appear as moves and not as delete plus add.
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard lists untracked files that are not ignored, the files that git add . would add.
git check-attr and .gitattributes control line endings, diff drivers and export rules per file pattern; * text=auto eol=lf forces LF in the working tree.
git credential helpers store passwords; credential.helper cache keeps them in memory for a time, and store writes them in plain text, so prefer a token with minimal rights.
HTTPS remotes use a personal access token as the password, and SSH remotes use keys; fine grained tokens limited to one repository and with an expiry date reduce the damage of a leak.
git push -u origin branch sets the upstream once, and after that git push and git pull need no arguments; git branch -vv shows which remote branch is tracked.
git push --tags pushes all tags and git push origin v1.0 one tag; git push --follow-tags pushes commits with the annotated tags that point to them.
git pull --ff-only fails instead of merging when histories diverged, which is the safe choice for deployment scripts on devices.
git reset --hard origin/main throws away local commits and changes and makes the folder identical to the remote; run git status and git stash first if anything there matters.
git clean -fdx removes untracked and ignored files too, including build output and local settings; use -n first, and never run it on a folder that holds data files.
git checkout -b new commit starts a branch at an older commit, and git branch name commit does it without switching, a safe way to keep a lost commit alive.
git restore --source=HEAD~1 file restores a file from an older commit into the working tree without moving the branch.
git rm file removes and stages the deletion at once, and git mv old new renames with staging; both keep history working with --follow.
git add -u stages changes of tracked files only, git add . stages everything in the current folder and below, and git add -A stages the whole repository.
git config core.editor 'nano' chooses the editor for messages; in scripts pass -m or use GIT_EDITOR=true to skip the editor.
GIT_EDITOR=true git rebase --continue accepts the existing message without opening an editor, useful in automation.
A fresh machine fails to commit with Please tell me who you are; set user.name and user.email globally once and the message disappears for every repository.
gh is the GitHub command line tool: gh repo clone, gh pr create and gh run list cover most daily tasks, and gh auth login stores a token safely.
Cron uses the system time zone and runs missed jobs never; for jobs that must run after downtime use a systemd timer with Persistent=true or anacron.
watch -d highlights what changed between runs, and watch -n 1 'cmd' repeats every second, a quick way to observe a counter, a log size or a temperature.
Use ssh -o ConnectTimeout=5 -o BatchMode=yes in scripts, so a missing host or a password prompt fails fast instead of hanging a loop over many devices.
ssh -o ServerAliveInterval=30 keeps a session alive through routers that drop idle connections, and ServerAliveCountMax ends it after a number of failed probes.
Permissions matter for SSH: the ~/.ssh folder needs mode 700 and private keys mode 600, or ssh refuses to use them with a warning about unprotected keys.
scp -P port uses a capital P for the port while ssh -p uses lower case, a small difference that causes many failed copies.
rsync -e 'ssh -p 2222' uses another port, and rsync -avz --progress shows the transfer; trailing slashes on the source decide whether the folder or its content is copied.
autossh or a systemd unit with Restart=always keeps a tunnel alive; add ServerAliveInterval so a dead tunnel is noticed and restarted.
